0.title: In the Beginning: The Book of Origins
0.overview:
Genesis is the book of beginnings — and every beginning in the Bible finds its root here. The creation of the cosmos, the dignity of humanity as image-bearers of God, the catastrophe of the fall, the first promise of redemption, the flood and new creation, the scattering of nations, and then the extraordinary narrowing of God's redemptive focus onto one man, one family, one people through whom all the families of the earth will be blessed (12:3). To read Genesis is to stand at the headwaters of everything that follows in Scripture.

The book divides naturally into two great movements. The primeval history (chapters 1–11) moves from creation to catastrophe to new beginning — from the garden of Eden to the tower of Babel — tracing the spread of sin and the persistence of grace. The patriarchal history (chapters 12–50) follows Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, tracing the covenant God makes and keeps across four generations in spite of every human failure. Throughout both movements, one thread holds everything together: the seed of the woman (3:15), the promise that will not be extinguished, the line that leads through flood and famine and fratricide and exile to the One who crushes the serpent's head.

Genesis is also the fountainhead of the Bible's great typological stream. Adam is the type of the One to come (Romans 5:14) — and where Adam fails, Christ succeeds. The sacrifice of Isaac on Moriah (chapter 22) is the most luminous prefiguration of Calvary in the Old Testament: a father, a son, a mountain, a substitute, and the word of the LORD: "The LORD will provide." Joseph — rejected by his brothers, sold for silver, condemned unjustly, exalted to the right hand of power, and the savior of the very brothers who betrayed him — is the most sustained type of Christ in Genesis, and one of the most beautiful in all of Scripture.

Who wrote it. Genesis is the first of the five books of Moses. Many modern scholars hold that these books were stitched together centuries later from several written sources (the so-called documentary hypothesis). The traditional view, held by Jews and Christians alike and followed here, is the more likely: Moses wrote them, as the books themselves repeatedly say he wrote (Exod. 17:14; 24:4; Num. 33:2; Deut. 31:9), and as Jesus himself said: For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me (John 5:46). He calls them the Law of Moses (Luke 24:44). A few small touches were added later under the same inspiration, most obviously the account of Moses’ own death and burial (Deut. 34), but the books are his.

Is Genesis 1–11 history? Some read these chapters as myth, stories that carry truth without claiming events; others as a literary frame for theology, with the events left open. But the chapters are written as ordered narrative, not poetry, tied to what follows by the same “these are the generations” formula that introduces Abraham and Jacob, and the New Testament treats Adam, Abel and Noah as real men (Luke 3:38; Rom 5:12–19; Matt 24:37–39; Heb 11:4–7). They are history, told in elevated, carefully shaped prose. On the age of the earth, Genesis gives no number. But six ordinary days (cf. 1:5) and genealogies that tie Adam to Abraham point to a young creation, not one of billions of years. That is the natural reading, though careful believers who hold an old earth (day-age, framework) are brothers, not enemies of the text.

The governing conviction is that Genesis is not a problem to be defended but a gift to be received — and that every page, rightly read, leads to Jesus Christ, in whom all the promises of God find their Yes and Amen (2 Corinthians 1:20).

1.title: In the Beginning, God
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.<sup>2</sup>The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters.<sup>3</sup>And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light.<sup>4</sup>And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness.<sup>5</sup>God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, the first day.<sup>6</sup>And God said, "Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate the waters from the waters."<sup>7</sup>And God made the expanse and separated the waters that were under the expanse from the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.<sup>8</sup>And God called the expanse Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, the second day.<sup>9</sup>And God said, "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear." And it was so.<sup>10</sup>God called the dry land Earth, and the waters that were gathered together he called Seas. And God saw that it was good.<sup>11</sup>And God said, "Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind, on the earth." And it was so.<sup>12</sup>The earth brought forth vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their own kinds, and trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.<sup>13</sup>And there was evening and there was morning, the third day.<sup>14</sup>And God said, "Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate the day from the night. And let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years,<sup>15</sup>and let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to give light upon the earth." And it was so.<sup>16</sup>And God made the two great lights—the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night—and the stars.<sup>17</sup>And God set them in the expanse of the heavens to give light on the earth,<sup>18</sup>to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good.<sup>19</sup>And there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day.<sup>20</sup>And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the heavens."<sup>21</sup>So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.<sup>22</sup>And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth."<sup>23</sup>And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day.<sup>24</sup>And God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—livestock and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kinds." And it was so.<sup>25</sup>And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds and the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that creeps on the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.<sup>26</sup>Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth."<sup>27</sup>So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.<sup>28</sup>And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth."<sup>29</sup>And God said, "Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food.<sup>30</sup>And to every beast of the earth and to every bird of the heavens and to everything that creeps on the earth, everything that has the breath of life, I have given every green plant for food." And it was so.<sup>31</sup>And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
1.overview:
The first verse of Genesis is the most momentous sentence ever written: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth." Before the cosmos, before time, before anything — there was God. Creation is not God (pantheism), and matter is not evil (dualism) — it is the good gift of a God who exists in glorious self-sufficiency and chooses to bring another into existence out of pure generosity.

The sovereign creative word — "and God said" — echoes ten times through the chapter, each time calling something new into existence. The same Word that spoke at creation became flesh in Jesus Christ (John 1:1–3; Col. 1:16). Creation is a trinitarian act: the Father creates, the Spirit hovers, the Son is the Word through whom all things are made.

The climax is the creation of humanity in the image of God (imago Dei, vv.26–27). Unlike every other element of creation, humanity is made not by divine command but by divine deliberation — "Let us make" — and is stamped with the divine likeness. This image is not a faculty but a relational and vocational reality: humanity is made to represent God in the world and rule the creation as vice-regents under his lordship. The chapter closes with the Creator's own verdict: "it was very good."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Creation Days One through Three
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis opens not with argument but with proclamation: God created. The majestic, measured cadence of the creation account — God speaks, it is so, God sees that it is good, evening and morning — establishes the sovereignty, goodness, and rationality of the Creator before any human being appears. Days one through three bring order out of formlessness: light separated from darkness, waters above from waters below, dry land distinguished from sea, and the earth clothed with vegetation.
verseByVerse.theology: Days one to three give the formless world its form: light from darkness, waters above from waters below, sea from dry land, and the land clothed with plants. God creates by speaking, and each thing he makes he calls good.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel's neighbours told of gods battling chaos to make a world; Genesis has one God speak and the chaos obey. Now: the same Spirit who hovered over the dark deep is the one who makes a new creation in Christ (2 Cor. 5:17).

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God alone brought everything into being; before him there was nothing, and nothing exists apart from his will.

In the beginning. Time itself starts here. God is before it.

Created. Bara: in the Old Testament only God is its subject. It needs no material.

The heavens and the earth. A Hebrew way of saying “everything”.

What it does not mean. The universe is not eternal, not divine, and not an accident. The sun and sea are things made, not gods to be feared, unlike in the myths of Israel’s neighbours.

The New Testament. John 1:1–3 opens the same way and names the Word through whom all things were made. Hebrews 11:3: what is seen was not made from things visible.

Translation note. Some modern versions read “When God began to create”, making v. 1 a time clause. The traditional reading, kept by the ESV, makes it a complete statement, and best supports creation from nothing, which Scripture teaches elsewhere (Romans 4:17).

On a Tuesday. Everything you touch today was made by God, and belongs to him.

For worship. Praise God the Creator, before whom there was nothing.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis means “origin.” Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses with the five books of the Law. “Created” translates bara, a verb used in the Old Testament only with God as its subject.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The newly created earth was formless and empty, in darkness under the deep, and God’s Spirit hovered over the waters, ready to shape it.

Without form and void. Tohu wabohu: unformed and unfilled. Days 1–3 form; days 4–6 fill.

The Spirit of God. Hovering like a bird over its young (Deuteronomy 32:11). The Trinity is present at creation.

Where Christians differ: the gap theory. Some taught a ruined first creation between vv. 1 and 2, to make room for long ages. Verdict: the grammar does not support a gap; v. 2 describes the state of the earth God had just made, not a ruin.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit who brought order from chaos can bring order to yours.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks, light comes into being, he sees it is good, and he separates it from the darkness.

God said. Creation by word (Psalm 33:6, 9). No struggle, only command.

Light before the sun. Light comes from God before the lights are made on day 4. God, not the sun, is the source of light (Revelation 22:5).

Good. The world is good, not evil, as some later thought.

2 Corinthians 4:6. The God who said “Let light shine” shines in our hearts in Christ.

For worship. Thank God for light, and for the light of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, the first day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names the light Day and the darkness Night, and evening and morning make the first day.

Naming. To name is to rule. Day and night are God’s.

Evening and morning. The Hebrew day began at evening.

Where Christians differ: the days of creation. Some hold six literal 24-hour days; others see long ages (day-age); others a literary framework (days 1–3 matching 4–6); others God’s workdays described by analogy to ours. Verdict: Reformed believers hold different views here in good conscience. All must affirm that God created all things from nothing, by his word, that Adam was a real man specially created, and that creation was very good before the fall. The text’s chief aim is to show who made the world and why.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate the waters from the waters." And God made the expanse and separated the waters that were under the expanse from the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes an expanse to separate the waters above from the waters below.

The expanse. The sky, pictured as a stretched-out canopy (Psalm 104:2).

Waters above. Probably the clouds and rain.

What it does not mean. Genesis describes the world as it appears to an observer. It is not a science textbook, nor does it endorse an ancient cosmology as a scientific claim.

verseByVerse.quote: And God called the expanse Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, the second day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names the expanse Heaven, and the second day ends.

No “it was good”. The separation of the waters is completed on day 3, where the phrase comes twice.

For worship. Look at the sky today and praise its Maker (Psalm 19:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear." And it was so. God called the dry land Earth, and the waters that were gathered together he called Seas. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gathers the waters into seas and lets dry land appear, naming them Earth and Seas, and sees that it is good.

Boundaries. God sets the sea its limits (Job 38:8–11).

Land for life. Preparing a home for people.

On a Tuesday. The ground under your feet is God’s gift.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind, on the earth." And it was so. The earth brought forth vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their own kinds, and trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands the earth to produce plants and fruit trees, each bearing seed according to its kind, and it is so.

According to their kinds. Ordered variety. Life reproduces after its kind.

Seed. Creation is built to continue and multiply.

What it does not mean. “Kinds” is not a technical term for modern species. The point is order and fruitfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was evening and there was morning, the third day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third day ends.

Form complete. Light, sky and sea, land and plants: the spaces of creation are ready to be filled.

For worship. Thank God for the orderly world he made.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–31 — Creation Days Four through Six: Lights, Living Creatures, and the Image of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second triad of creation fills the domains established in days one through three. The lights fill the sky and govern time; sea creatures and birds fill the waters and expanse; land animals and finally humanity fill the earth. The account builds to its climax in the creation of the human being in the image of God — male and female — entrusted with dominion over the whole creation. God's final verdict on the completed creation is not merely 'good' but 'very good.'
verseByVerse.theology: Days four to six fill the domains made on days one to three, and the account climbs to the making of man, male and female, in the image of God and under a blessing to fill and rule the earth. The verdict on the whole is "very good."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the sun, moon and sea monsters that the nations worshipped or feared are simply God's creatures. Now: every human being, of whatever age, ability or usefulness, bears the image of God, and ordinary work is the fulfilment of the sixth-day commission.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate the day from the night. And let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years, and let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to give light upon the earth." And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes lights in the sky to separate day from night and mark signs, seasons, days and years.

Day 4 fills day 1. Lights for the light.

Seasons. The same word as Israel’s appointed feasts. Time is ordered for worship.

What it does not mean. Not astrology. The stars mark time; they do not rule destiny (Jeremiah 10:2).
verseByVerse.note: “Seasons” can also be rendered “appointed times” (ESV note) — the festival calendar.

verseByVerse.quote: And God made the two great lights—the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night—and the stars. And God set them in the expanse of the heavens to give light on the earth,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the greater light to rule the day, the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars.

Not named. The sun and moon are not named, perhaps because neighbouring nations worshipped them as gods. Here they are lamps.

And the stars. Billions of galaxies, mentioned in three words.

For worship. If God made the stars so easily, nothing is too hard for him (Isaiah 40:26).

verseByVerse.quote: to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lights rule day and night and separate light from darkness; God sees it is good, and the fourth day ends.

Rule. Delegated authority, under God.

On a Tuesday. The rhythm of day and night is God’s gift. Rest when he gives the night.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the heavens." So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God fills the waters with creatures and the sky with birds, including the great sea creatures, and sees that it is good.

Day 5 fills day 2. Sea and sky are populated.

Great sea creatures. Tanninim, monsters feared in pagan myth. Here they are simply God’s creatures.

Created. Bara again, for the first animal life.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth." And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses the sea creatures and birds, telling them to be fruitful and multiply, and the fifth day ends.

Blessing. God’s first blessing is on animals. He delights in his creatures.

Be fruitful. Life is God’s gift and purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—livestock and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kinds." And it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds and the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that creeps on the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes land animals of every kind, livestock, creeping things and wild beasts, and sees that it is good.

Day 6 fills day 3. The land is populated.

Livestock and wild. Domestic and wild animals, both made by God.

On a Tuesday. Care for animals as God’s creatures (Proverbs 12:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth." So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness,” to rule over the creatures, and creates mankind in his image, male and female.

Let us. Where Christians differ. A plural of majesty, God speaking to angels, or a hint of the Trinity. Verdict: angels are never said to create or to share God’s image. In the light of the New Testament, this is a first hint of the plurality within the one God (John 1:3).

The image of God. Humans represent God and reflect him: in rule, relationship, reason and moral nature. The image is damaged by the fall, but not lost (Genesis 9:6; James 3:9).

Male and female. Both fully in God’s image, equal in dignity, and different by design.

Created three times. Bara is used three times in v. 27: the climax of creation.

On a Tuesday. Every person you meet today bears God’s image. Treat them so.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes explain that the Hebrew for man (adam) is the general word for mankind and becomes the proper name Adam.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses humanity and commands them to be fruitful, fill the earth, subdue it and rule over every living creature.

The creation mandate. Family, work and culture are God’s calling.

Subdue and rule. As stewards, not tyrants (Genesis 2:15: “work it and keep it”).

What it does not mean. Not licence to exploit or destroy creation. We rule as God rules: for good.

On a Tuesday. Your daily work is part of this calling.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food. And to every beast of the earth and to every bird of the heavens and to everything that creeps on the earth, everything that has the breath of life, I have given every green plant for food." And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives seed-bearing plants and fruit to people for food, and green plants to the animals.

A plant diet. Before the fall; permission to eat meat comes after the flood (9:3).

Provision. God provides for all his creatures (Psalm 104:27–28).

For worship. Thank God for your food.

verseByVerse.quote: And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sees everything he has made, and it is very good; and the sixth day ends.

Very good. The only time. Creation complete, with humanity at its head.

No evil yet. Sin, death and suffering are intruders, not part of God’s original design (Romans 5:12).

The body is good. Matter, sex and food are not evil (1 Timothy 4:4).

For worship. Praise God for his very good creation, which he will one day renew (Revelation 21:5).

1.theology:
The Trinity in Creation. Genesis 1 contains seeds the New Testament flowers. The Spirit hovers (v.2); God speaks his Word (v.3); the Father creates (v.1). John 1:1–3 identifies the creative Word with the eternal Son: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made." Colossians 1:16 and Hebrews 1:2 confirm: the universe was made through and for Christ. Creation is a trinitarian act.

The Image of God and Human Dignity. The imago Dei (vv.26–27) is the theological foundation of every claim about human dignity — not achievement, intelligence, beauty, or utility, but the image of God stamped on every human being from conception. This is why the taking of human life is an assault on God himself (Gen. 9:6). In an age of competing accounts of human value, Genesis 1:27 remains the most radical claim ever made: every person bears the image of the Creator of the cosmos.
1.examples:
Then: Israel's neighbors had elaborate creation myths — the Babylonian Enuma Elish featured warring gods and humanity created as divine slave labor. Genesis 1 is a quiet, majestic polemic: one God, sovereign speech, ordered goodness, humanity as image-bearers rather than slaves. The chapter was simultaneously theological and political — a declaration that Israel's God alone is Creator and Lord.

Now: Contemporary cosmology traces the universe to a beginning (the Big Bang), confirming what Genesis asserted millennia ago. But science cannot tell us whether the beginning had a Beholder. Genesis answers with the confidence of revelation. And the imago Dei cuts against every modern reductionism — the person reduced to their productivity, genome, or social utility has had their image-bearing dignity denied. The church holds the most radical account of human worth available in the contemporary marketplace of ideas.

2.title: The LORD God Formed the Man
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.<sup>2</sup>And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.<sup>3</sup>So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.<sup>4</sup>These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens.<sup>5</sup>When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant of the field had yet sprung up—for the LORD God had not caused it to rain on the land, and there was no man to work the ground,<sup>6</sup>and a mist was going up from the land and was watering the whole face of the ground—<sup>7</sup>then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed.<sup>9</sup>And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.<sup>10</sup>A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and there it divided and became four rivers.<sup>11</sup>The name of the first is the Pishon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.<sup>12</sup>And the gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx stone are there.<sup>13</sup>The name of the second river is the Gihon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Cush.<sup>14</sup>And the name of the third river is the Tigris, which flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.<sup>15</sup>The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.<sup>16</sup>And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden,<sup>17</sup>but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die."<sup>18</sup>Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him."<sup>19</sup>Now out of the ground the LORD God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. And whatever the man called every living creature, that was its name.<sup>20</sup>The man gave names to all livestock and to the birds of the heavens and to every beast of the field. But for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him.<sup>21</sup>So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept took one of his ribs and closed up its place with flesh.<sup>22</sup>And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man.<sup>23</sup>Then the man said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man."<sup>24</sup>Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.<sup>25</sup>And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
2.overview:
Where Genesis 1 surveys creation from the cosmic perspective, Genesis 2 zooms in — camera descending from the heavens to settle on a garden, a man formed from dust, the breath of God filling his lungs. The change of divine name is significant: chapter 1 uses Elohim (God, the transcendent Creator); chapter 2 introduces YHWH Elohim (the LORD God), the covenant name that will define all of Israel's subsequent relationship with this God. The Creator is not merely a force but a Person who walks in gardens and calls for conversation.

The garden of Eden is not merely a pleasant park but a sacred space — a temple-garden where God dwells with humanity. The man's vocation to "work it and keep it" (v.15) uses the same Hebrew verbs (abad and shamar) used later for priestly service in the tabernacle (Num. 3:7–8). Adam is simultaneously a gardener and a priest — his work is worship and his worship is work.

The creation of woman is the chapter's climax. "It is not good that the man should be alone" (v.18) — the first "not good" in Genesis — reveals that even paradise without community is incomplete. Marriage is the first human institution, established before the fall. Paul calls it a "profound mystery" that images Christ's union with the church (Eph. 5:31–32) — and Jesus upholds its creational authority when asked about divorce (Matt. 19:4–6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Seventh Day and the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The creation account concludes with the Sabbath rest of God — the first holy time in Scripture — and then zooms in to tell the story of human origins with vivid particularity. Chapter 2 is not a contradiction of chapter 1 but a complementary close-up: where chapter 1 gives the cosmic panorama, chapter 2 gives the intimate portrait of the man formed from dust and the woman formed from his side, placed in a garden designed for abundance and communion with God.
verseByVerse.theology: God rests on the seventh day and blesses it, the first thing in Scripture he makes holy. Then the camera comes down to a garden, where the LORD God forms the man from dust, breathes life into him, and sets him to work and keep it under one prohibition.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Eden was described in the language of the sanctuary, and Israel would recognise its gold, onyx and guarding cherubim in the tabernacle. Now: work is a gift given before the fall, and rest is a gift given before any work was done.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation is complete, and on the seventh day God finishes his work and rests.

Finished. Nothing is missing.

Rested. Ceased, not because he was tired (Isaiah 40:28), but because the work was done.

No evening and morning. The seventh day has no closing formula. Hebrews 4 sees God’s rest as still open for his people to enter.

verseByVerse.quote: So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses the seventh day and makes it holy, because on it he rested from all his work.

Blessed and holy. Set apart. Time itself is given a rhythm of work and rest.

Where Christians differ: a creation ordinance. Sabbatarians (the Westminster tradition) see here a weekly Sabbath binding on all people for all time, now kept on the Lord’s Day. Others note that no command is given until Exodus 16 and 20. Verdict: the pattern of work and rest is built into creation and is good for all people. For Christians, the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ’s rest (Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a privilege for worship and rest, not a set of rules binding the conscience. Hold the view charitably.

On a Tuesday. Do you work as though everything depends on you, with no rest?

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens. When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant of the field had yet sprung up—for the LORD God had not caused it to rain on the land, and there was no man to work the ground, and a mist was going up from the land and was watering the whole face of the ground—
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the account of the heavens and the earth, when the LORD God made them, before shrubs or plants had sprung up and before there was rain or anyone to work the ground.

These are the generations. Toledot: a heading that divides Genesis into ten sections.

The LORD God. God’s covenant name, Yahweh, joined to God, Elohim. The Creator of chapter 1 is Israel’s covenant God.

Where Christians differ: two creation accounts? Critical scholars have seen two contradictory sources (the documentary hypothesis). Verdict: chapter 1 gives the wide view of all creation; chapter 2 zooms in on the making of man and woman and the garden. They complement each other, as Jesus treated them together (Matthew 19:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD God forms the man from the dust of the ground, breathes into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man becomes a living being.

Formed. Like a potter (Jeremiah 18:6). Personal, hands-on care.

Dust. Humble origin (3:19; Psalm 103:14).

Breath of life. Life directly from God. Humans are both earthly and spiritual.

Where Christians differ: a historical Adam? Some today accept that humans evolved, with Adam as a symbol or a representative chosen from among early humans. Verdict: Scripture treats Adam as a real, specially created first man, from whom all humanity descends (Luke 3:38; Acts 17:26; Romans 5:12–19). The gospel’s logic of the first and last Adam depends on it.

For worship. Thank God for the breath in your lungs.
verseByVerse.note: “Man” (adam) and “ground” (adamah) sound alike in Hebrew: man is made from the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed. And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God plants a garden in Eden, puts the man there, and makes every beautiful and good tree grow, with the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in the middle.

Eden. “Delight”. A sanctuary where God dwells with man, the first temple.

Pleasant and good. Beauty and usefulness both from God.

The tree of life. Restored in the new creation (Revelation 22:2).

The knowledge of good and evil. Deciding good and evil for oneself, apart from God.
verseByVerse.note: “Eden” sounds like a Hebrew word for delight.

verseByVerse.quote: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and there it divided and became four rivers. The name of the first is the Pishon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold. And the gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx stone are there. The name of the second river is the Gihon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Cush. And the name of the third river is the Tigris, which flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A river flows out of Eden and divides into four rivers, including the Tigris and the Euphrates, through lands rich in gold and precious stones.

Real geography. Eden is placed in the real world, in the region of Mesopotamia.

A river of life. Echoed in Ezekiel 47 and Revelation 22:1.

Gold and onyx. Materials later used in the tabernacle. Eden is a sanctuary.
verseByVerse.note: The Tigris and Euphrates are known rivers of Mesopotamia; the Pishon and Gihon cannot now be identified.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD God puts the man in the garden to work it and keep it.

Work and keep. The same verbs describe the priests’ service in the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7–8). Adam is a priest-gardener.

Work before the fall. Work is not a curse; the curse makes it toilsome (3:17–19).

On a Tuesday. Your work is a calling from God, not merely a way to pay bills.
verseByVerse.note: The two verbs, work and keep, are later used of the priests’ service in the tabernacle.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands the man that he may eat from every tree, but not from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for on the day he eats of it he will surely die.

Every tree. Generous freedom first.

One prohibition. A test of trust and obedience.

Surely die. Spiritual death at once, physical death in time.

Where Christians differ: a covenant of works? Reformed theology has seen here a covenant of works: life promised for obedience, death threatened for disobedience, with Adam as the head of humanity. Some object that “covenant” is not used. Verdict: the elements of a covenant are present (Hosea 6:7), and Romans 5:12–21 treats Adam as a representative head, as Christ is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Creation of Woman and the First Marriage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The creation of Eve completes the image of God in humanity and establishes marriage as the foundational human institution. God's declaration that "it is not good" for man to be alone is the first 'not good' in Scripture — interrupting the rhythm of 'it was good' from chapter 1 to underscore that human beings are inherently relational. The woman is not an afterthought but the completion of what the man could not be alone.
verseByVerse.theology: The first "not good" in Scripture is a man alone. God builds the woman from the man's side and brings her to him, and the first marriage becomes the pattern for every marriage and a picture of Christ and the church (Eph. 5:31–32).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jesus settled the divorce question by going back to this chapter (Matt. 19:4–6). Now: loneliness is a need God named before sin entered, and the answer he gives is marriage for many and his people for all.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says it is not good for the man to be alone, and he will make a helper fit for him.

Not good. The first “not good” in a very good world.

A helper. Ezer, used often of God himself (Psalm 121:1–2). Not an inferior.

Fit for him. Corresponding to him: like him, yet different.

Where Christians differ: roles in marriage. Egalitarians read equality without distinct roles. Complementarians see equality of worth with a loving headship given to the husband, as Paul argues from this order (1 Corinthians 11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13). Verdict: complementarian, held with care: men and women equal in dignity, different by design, with servant headship in marriage and the church.

On a Tuesday. If you are lonely, God sees it as “not good” too. Seek friendship and the family of the church.
verseByVerse.note: “Helper” is often used of God himself helping his people; it implies no inferiority. “Fit for him” can be rendered “corresponding to him” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now out of the ground the LORD God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. And whatever the man called every living creature, that was its name. The man gave names to all livestock and to the birds of the heavens and to every beast of the field. But for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings the animals to the man to see what he will name them, but among them no fitting helper is found.

Naming. Adam exercises dominion and wisdom.

No helper. Animals are good, but no substitute for a human partner.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept took one of his ribs and closed up its place with flesh. And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God puts the man into a deep sleep, takes one of his ribs, and makes it into a woman, and brings her to the man.

A rib. Or “side”. From beside his heart.

Made. Literally “built”.

Brought her. God himself gives the bride away.

For worship. Thank God for the gift of marriage, which he designed.
verseByVerse.note: “Made into a woman” is literally “built” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the man said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man exclaims, “This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.”

The first poem. Delight and wonder.

Woman. Ishshah from ish: a wordplay showing their unity.

At last. What the animals could not supply.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the Hebrew words for woman (ishshah) and man (ish) sound alike.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore a man leaves his father and mother and holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh.

Leave and cleave. A new primary loyalty.

One flesh. A lifelong, exclusive, sexual union.

The basis of marriage. Jesus quotes this against easy divorce (Matthew 19:4–6). Paul sees in it Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32).

One man and one woman. God’s design for marriage. The church holds the historic view of sexuality, speaking it with compassion to all who struggle.

On a Tuesday. If married, what would “holding fast” look like today?

verseByVerse.quote: And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man and his wife are both naked and not ashamed.

No shame. Nothing to hide from God or each other.

A setup. After the fall they hide (3:7–10).

Restored. In Christ our shame is covered (Hebrews 12:2).

For worship. Thank God that he covers our shame in Christ.

2.theology:
The Garden as Temple. Eden is the original sacred space — the place where heaven and earth overlap, where God walks with humanity. The imagery recurs in the tabernacle (gold, cherubim, guarded entrance) and temple. Revelation 21–22 closes the canon with the new Jerusalem as a garden-city in which the temple is the Lord God himself: God and humanity dwelling together without barrier, the original vision of Eden fully restored and surpassed.

The Second Adam. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 turns on the contrast between Adam and Christ. Adam, formed from dust, given every permission, faced one prohibition, failed, and brought death to all. Christ, the eternal Son who took on flesh, faced every temptation the first Adam faced, obeyed perfectly, and brought life to all in him. The garden of Gethsemane is the counter-garden of Eden: where Adam chose his will over God's, Christ prayed "not my will, but yours be done."
2.examples:
Then: The garden-temple imagery was immediately legible to an Israelite audience familiar with the tabernacle. The cherubim guarding Eden's entrance (3:24) matched the cherubim woven into the tabernacle veil. The gold and onyx of Eden (2:11–12) matched the temple's materials. The man's priestly vocation prepared Israel to understand the priesthood as a restoration project — attempting to restore, through ritual, the access to God's presence lost at the fall.

Now: The theology of work in Genesis 2 is urgently needed in a culture that either deifies career (finding identity in productivity) or denigrates it (work as mere necessity). Genesis 2 says: work is a gift before it is a burden, a vocation before it is a job. And the chapter's account of gender and marriage — the complementarity of male and female, the one-flesh covenant, the goodness of embodiment — flows from creation design, not cultural construction. To recover a theology of Genesis 2 is to recover a theology of the human person.

3.title: The Fall
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?"<sup>2</sup>And the woman said to the serpent, "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden,<sup>3</sup>but God said, 'You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.'"<sup>4</sup>But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die.<sup>5</sup>For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."<sup>6</sup>So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate.<sup>7</sup>Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.<sup>8</sup>And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.<sup>9</sup>But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?"<sup>10</sup>And he said, "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself."<sup>11</sup>He said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?"<sup>12</sup>The man said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate."<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."<sup>14</sup>The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.<sup>15</sup>I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."<sup>16</sup>To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you."<sup>17</sup>And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life;<sup>18</sup>thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field.<sup>19</sup>By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return."<sup>20</sup>The man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.<sup>22</sup>Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—"<sup>23</sup>therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken.<sup>24</sup>He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the hinge of all human history — the chapter that makes every other chapter in the Bible necessary. Without the fall, there is no need for a flood, a covenant, a law, a temple, a sacrifice, a prophet, a Messiah, a cross, or a resurrection. Every subsequent movement of Scripture is a movement of redemption, and redemption only makes sense in light of what is lost here.

The serpent's strategy is a masterpiece of misdirection. He begins not with a command but with a question: "Did God actually say?" — casting doubt on the divine word, then on the divine motive. The lie is plausible. "You will be like God" — and they already were, made in his image. The serpent offers a counterfeit of what they already possess. This is the anatomy of every temptation: the distortion of a good thing into a god-thing.

But before any judgment is announced, God speaks the first gospel — the protevangelium of verse 15: the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head. And before expelling them from the garden, God clothes them with skins — the first sacrifice, the first covering of shame by divine grace. The gospel is embedded in the fall itself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Temptation and the Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 3 is the hinge of all Scripture — the pivot between creation's goodness and the fallen world we inhabit. The serpent's strategy is subtle: not a frontal assault on God's existence but a quiet questioning of his goodness. Eve is drawn into dialogue, then doubt, then desire, then action. Adam stands passively by and eats. In a moment, the entire fabric of human life with God is torn. The nakedness and hiding that follow are the symptoms of a rupture that touches every dimension of existence.
verseByVerse.theology: The serpent questions God's word, denies his warning and slanders his motive. The woman sees, desires, takes and eats; the man beside her eats too. Their eyes are opened to their own nakedness, they hide, and under God's questions each passes the blame while still admitting, "and I ate."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the three appeals of verse 6 are the ones John names in 1 John 2:16, and the ones Jesus refused in the wilderness. Now: the lie at the root of every sin is still that God is withholding something good.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crafty serpent asks the woman whether God really said she must not eat from any tree in the garden.

Crafty. Arum, a play on arummim, “naked” (2:25).

The serpent. A creature, but the voice behind it is Satan, “that ancient serpent” (Revelation 12:9; John 8:44).

Did God actually say? The first attack is on God’s word, by doubt and distortion. God gave every tree but one.

On a Tuesday. Temptation often starts by making God seem stingy.
verseByVerse.note: The serpent is later identified as Satan. In Hebrew, “you” in vv. 1–5 is plural: the serpent speaks to both (ESV note). “Crafty” (‘arum) echoes “naked” (‘arummim) in 2:25 — a deliberate sound-link.

verseByVerse.quote: And the woman said to the serpent, "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden, but God said, 'You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman answers that they may eat of the trees, but God said not to eat or touch the tree in the middle, or they will die.

Adding. “Neither shall you touch it” was not in God’s command (2:17).

Softening. She omits “surely” and “every”.

On a Tuesday. Know exactly what God has said, neither adding nor subtracting.

verseByVerse.quote: But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The serpent says, “You will not surely die,” for God knows that eating will open their eyes and make them like God, knowing good and evil.

A direct denial. The first lie.

God is hiding something. The slander that God is holding them back.

Like God. The root of sin: to be one’s own god.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the tree is good for food, a delight to the eyes and desirable to make one wise, she takes and eats, and gives to her husband with her, and he eats.

Three appeals. Appetite, beauty, wisdom: “the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life” (1 John 2:16).

With her. Adam was there and said nothing.

Where Christians differ: history or myth? Some read the fall as a symbol of every person’s story. Verdict: Scripture treats it as a real event that brought sin and death into the world (Romans 5:12; 1 Timothy 2:14). It is also every person’s story.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their eyes are opened, they know they are naked, and they sew fig leaves to cover themselves.

Eyes opened. But to shame, not glory.

Fig leaves. The first attempt at self-covering.

On a Tuesday. What are your fig leaves? Only God can truly cover sin.

verseByVerse.quote: And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, they hide among the trees, and God calls, “Where are you?”

Walking in the garden. God’s presence, once a delight.

They hid. Sin breaks fellowship.

Where are you? Not for information, but an invitation to come out. God seeks the sinner first.

For worship. Thank God who comes looking for sinners (Luke 19:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." He said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man says he hid because he was afraid and naked, and God asks who told him he was naked and whether he has eaten of the tree.

Afraid. Guilt produces fear of God.

Questions. God gives Adam room to confess.

verseByVerse.quote: The man said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man blames the woman God gave him.

Blame-shifting. On the woman, and on God.

Broken relationships. Sin turns husband against wife.

On a Tuesday. Watch how quickly you blame others.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God asks the woman what she has done, and she says, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

Deceived. True (2 Corinthians 11:3), but not an excuse.

Adam responsible. Paul says sin came through Adam, as head (Romans 5:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — The Curse and the Expulsion from the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The consequences of the fall are pronounced in three stages: curse upon the serpent, consequences for the woman, consequences for the man and the ground. But embedded in the curse on the serpent is the first gospel proclamation — the protoevangelium — the promise that the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head. Judgment falls, but within the judgment is the seed of redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: The serpent is cursed, and in the curse the first gospel is spoken: the offspring of the woman will bruise its head. The woman's pain and the man's toil are multiplied, death is pronounced, and God himself clothes them in skins before barring the way to the tree of life.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the promise of verse 15 is traced through the whole Old Testament until God sends his Son, "born of woman" (Gal. 4:4). Now: the sword that closed the garden fell on Christ, and through him the way to the tree of life is open again (Rev. 22:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God curses the serpent to crawl and eat dust, and puts enmity between it and the woman, and between their offspring; he will bruise its head, and it will bruise his heel.

Cursed. No questions to the serpent. No mercy.

Enmity. God puts hostility between his people and Satan.

The first gospel. The protoevangelium. One offspring of the woman will crush the serpent, at the cost of a wound. Fulfilled in Christ’s death and victory (Galatians 4:4; Hebrews 2:14; Romans 16:20).

Offspring. Both collective (the godly line) and individual (“he”).

Where Christians differ: “she shall bruise”? The Latin Vulgate read “she shall crush”, applied to Mary. Verdict: the Hebrew reads “he” (or “it”), the offspring. It points to Christ, not Mary.

For worship. Praise God that the gospel promise came at the moment of the fall.
verseByVerse.note: Often called the “first gospel” — the first promise of a Saviour, the woman’s offspring, who will crush the serpent. The ESV notes that “offspring” is literally “seed.”

verseByVerse.quote: To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the woman God says he will multiply her pain in childbearing; her desire will be for her husband, and he will rule over her.

Pain. Not childbirth itself, but pain in it.

Where Christians differ: her desire. Some read sexual or emotional longing; others a desire to master him, as in 4:7, where the same words describe sin’s desire. Verdict: the parallel with 4:7 suggests a sinful struggle for control between the sexes, answered by harsh rule. Both distort the good order of chapter 2. In Christ, marriage is restored to loving headship and glad help (Ephesians 5:22–33).

What it does not mean. Not a command for men to dominate women. It describes the curse, which Christ came to undo.
verseByVerse.note: “For your husband” can also be rendered “to,” “toward” or “against” (ESV note); the same phrase returns in 4:7 of sin’s desire to master Cain.

verseByVerse.quote: And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To Adam God says that because he listened to his wife and ate, the ground is cursed; in pain he will eat from it, and it will bring thorns and thistles.

Listened to your wife. Over God’s voice.

The ground cursed. Creation suffers with humanity (Romans 8:20–22).

Thorns. Christ wore a crown of them.

On a Tuesday. When work is frustrating, remember why, and the hope of renewal.

verseByVerse.quote: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the sweat of his face he will eat bread until he returns to the ground, for he is dust and to dust he will return.

Toil. Work becomes hard.

To dust. Death. Spoken at funerals since.

The penalty fulfilled. “You shall surely die” (2:17).

For worship. Thank Christ who tasted death so that dust will rise (1 Corinthians 15:22).

verseByVerse.quote: The man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adam names his wife Eve, because she is the mother of all the living.

Eve. Chawwah, sounding like the word for “life”.

Faith. Under the sentence of death, Adam names her for life. He believes the promise of v. 15.

All living. All humanity descends from one couple (Acts 17:26).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Eve” sounds like the Hebrew for “life-giver” and resembles the word for “living.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD God makes garments of skins for Adam and his wife and clothes them.

God clothes them. Replacing their fig leaves.

Skins. Perhaps the first death of animals, a hint of sacrifice covering sin.

Grace. Mercy in the midst of judgment.

For worship. Thank God who clothes us in Christ’s righteousness (Isaiah 61:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—" therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil, and must not take from the tree of life and live for ever, so he sends him out to work the ground.

Like one of us. Plural again (1:26). Man now decides good and evil for himself.

Lest he live for ever. A mercy: not to live for ever in a fallen state.

Sent out. Exile from God’s presence.

verseByVerse.quote: He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God drives the man out and places cherubim and a flaming, turning sword east of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life.

East of Eden. Later the tabernacle and temple faced east, and cherubim were embroidered on the veil (Exodus 26:31).

The way closed. Until Christ opens it (Hebrews 10:19–20).

The tree regained. Revelation 22:14.

On a Tuesday. You were made for Eden. Only Christ brings you home.

For worship. Thank Christ who opened the way back to God.
verseByVerse.note: Cherubim are angelic guardians of God’s holy presence; they were later woven into the tabernacle curtain.

3.theology:
The Anatomy of Sin. Genesis 3 gives the Bible's most complete account of how sin operates. It begins with doubt about the word of God (v.1), moves to distrust of the character of God (vv.4–5), leads to autonomous action against the will of God (v.6), and produces shame, fear, and broken relationship (vv.7–13). The root is the displacement of God from the center of life — the claim, in practice if not theory, that I am a better judge of my good than my Creator is.

The Protevangelium and Redemptive History. Verse 15 is the seed from which all of redemptive history grows. Every subsequent act of God in Scripture — the call of Abraham, the exodus, the Davidic covenant, the prophets, the incarnation — is an unfolding of this one promise. The enmity between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent is the great conflict structuring all of history, and its resolution is the cross and resurrection. To read Genesis 3 without verse 15 is to miss the point of the chapter entirely.
3.examples:
Then: Ancient Near Eastern creation-and-fall narratives — the Gilgamesh epic, the Adapa myth — portrayed sin as a cosmic accident or work of rival gods. Genesis 3 subverts them all: sin is the free act of human creatures endowed with the image of God. The curse on the ground (v.17) and painful childbirth (v.16) were daily realities for ancient Israel; Genesis 3 explained not just that these things are hard but why, and with the implication that the curse can be reversed.

Now: The fall answers what every philosophy and therapy system eventually confronts: what is wrong with us? Not ignorance, not environment, not psychology — but moral rebellion against the Creator, a structural disorder of the will requiring not improvement but redemption. The gospel begins with Genesis 3's diagnosis: we are not basically good people who occasionally do bad things, but fallen image-bearers who need a new creation. And it ends with Genesis 3's promise: the seed of the woman has come, and the serpent's head is crushed.

4.title: Am I My Brother's Keeper?
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD."<sup>2</sup>And again, she bore his brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground.<sup>3</sup>In the course of time Cain brought to the LORD an offering of the fruit of the ground,<sup>4</sup>and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering,<sup>5</sup>but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his face fell.<sup>6</sup>The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?<sup>7</sup>If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it."<sup>8</sup>Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.<sup>9</sup>Then the LORD said to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He said, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?"<sup>10</sup>And the LORD said, "What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground.<sup>11</sup>And now you are cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand.<sup>12</sup>When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength. You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."<sup>13</sup>Cain said to the LORD, "My punishment is greater than I can bear.<sup>14</sup>Behold, you have driven me today away from the ground, and from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me."<sup>15</sup>Then the LORD said to him, "Not so! If anyone kills Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold." And the LORD put a mark on Cain, lest any who found him should attack him.<sup>16</sup>Then Cain went away from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.<sup>17</sup>Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. When he built a city, he called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch.<sup>18</sup>To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech.<sup>19</sup>And Lamech took two wives. The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah.<sup>20</sup>Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock.<sup>21</sup>His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who play the lyre and pipe.<sup>22</sup>Zillah also bore Tubal-cain; he was the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.<sup>23</sup>Lamech said to his wives: "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; you wives of Lamech, listen to what I say: I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me.<sup>24</sup>If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold."<sup>25</sup>And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, for she said, "God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him."<sup>26</sup>To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD.
4.overview:
The fall of Genesis 3 moves immediately into fratricide in Genesis 4. The speed is deliberate: sin does not stay contained. Once the relationship with God is broken, the relationship between human beings fractures next, then the relationship with the ground (v.12). The spread of sin is not a trickle but a flood — and that flood is coming.

The contrast between Cain and Abel cuts deeper than jealousy. The LORD had "regard" for Abel and his offering, not for Cain's. Hebrews 11:4 says Abel offered his sacrifice "by faith," suggesting the issue was not the material offered but the orientation of the heart. Worship is always first a matter of the heart. God's gracious warning to Cain (v.7) is extraordinary: before the murder, God gives him the opportunity to see what is happening and choose differently. Cain refuses.

The chapter closes with hope in the darkness: "At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD" (v.26). Even after murder, the human impulse toward the Creator is not extinguished. The line of Seth — those who call on the name of the LORD — will carry the seed of the woman through every catastrophe until the Promised One arrives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Cain and Abel: The First Murder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fall of Genesis 3 bears its first fruit in Genesis 4: fratricide. Cain and Abel are the first human brothers, and the first human murder is a brother's murder. The story moves from worship (offerings) to warning (God's counsel to Cain) to violence (the killing of Abel) to judgment (Cain cursed and exiled). The trajectory of sin — from one tree to one murder — accelerates rapidly, and the question of how fallen humanity will live east of Eden is posed in its starkest form.
verseByVerse.theology: The first brothers bring offerings, and God regards Abel and his offering, not Cain and his. God warns Cain that sin is crouching at the door, but Cain kills his brother, denies he is his keeper, and is sent out a wanderer — yet marked by God for protection.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews says Abel offered "by faith" (Heb. 11:4), and John warns the church not to be like Cain (1 John 3:12). Now: God still hears the blood of the wronged, and the blood of Jesus speaks a better word than Abel's (Heb. 12:24).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adam and Eve have a son, Cain, and Eve says she has gotten a man with the LORD’s help.

Knew. Sexual union, personal knowledge.

With the help of the LORD. Eve sees God’s hand. Perhaps she hoped Cain was the promised offspring (3:15).

Cain. Sounds like the word “gotten”.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Cain” sounds like the Hebrew for “gotten.”

verseByVerse.quote: And again, she bore his brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eve also bears Abel; Abel keeps sheep and Cain works the ground.

Abel. Breath or vapour, the word the ESV renders “vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). His life will be short.

Two callings. Both honourable. The difference is not in their work.

verseByVerse.quote: In the course of time Cain brought to the LORD an offering of the fruit of the ground, and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering, but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his face fell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cain brings an offering of the ground’s fruit, and Abel the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions; the LORD regards Abel’s offering, but not Cain’s, and Cain is very angry.

Where Christians differ: why was Abel accepted? Some say because his offering was a blood sacrifice. Verdict: Hebrews 11:4 says Abel offered by faith. He gave the firstborn and the best; Cain simply gave “some”. God looked at the offerer first, then the offering. Grain offerings were acceptable later (Leviticus 2).

His face fell. Anger and resentment.

On a Tuesday. Do you give God your best, or your leftovers?

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Cain, "Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD asks Cain why he is angry; if he does well, he will be accepted, but if not, sin is crouching at the door, desiring him, and he must rule over it.

Grace. God reasons with Cain before he sins.

Sin crouching. Like a predator at the door.

Desire and rule. The same words as 3:16. Sin wants to master you.

On a Tuesday. Anger left unchecked opens the door to worse sin (Ephesians 4:26–27).

verseByVerse.quote: Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cain speaks to Abel, and in the field he rises up and kills him.

The first murder. Within one generation of the fall.

His brother. Said seven times in this chapter.

Why? Because his own deeds were evil and his brother’s righteous (1 John 3:12).

Textual note. The Hebrew does not say what Cain said. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the Greek and other ancient versions add, “Let us go out to the field.” The ESV follows the Hebrew.
verseByVerse.note: Ancient versions add “Let us go out to the field” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He said, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?" And the LORD said, "What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD asks where Abel is; Cain says, “I do not know; am I my brother’s keeper?” and God says Abel’s blood cries out from the ground.

Where is your brother? As “Where are you?” (3:9).

A lie and a sneer. Sin hardens.

My brother’s keeper. Yes. God expects us to care for one another.

Blood crying. Injustice is heard by God. Jesus’ blood speaks a better word (Hebrews 12:24).

For worship. Thank God for Christ’s blood, which cries for mercy, not vengeance.

verseByVerse.quote: And now you are cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. When you work the ground, it shall no longer yield to you its strength. You shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cain is cursed from the ground that received his brother’s blood: it will not yield its strength, and he will be a wanderer.

Cursed. Not the ground this time, but Cain.

A wanderer. Restless, homeless.

verseByVerse.quote: Cain said to the LORD, "My punishment is greater than I can bear. Behold, you have driven me today away from the ground, and from your face I shall be hidden. I shall be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth, and whoever finds me will kill me." Then the LORD said to him, "Not so! If anyone kills Cain, vengeance shall be taken on him sevenfold." And the LORD put a mark on Cain, lest any who found him should attack him. Then Cain went away from the presence of the LORD and settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cain complains that his punishment is too great and that whoever finds him will kill him; God puts a mark on him so no one will kill him, and Cain goes away to the land of Nod.

Self-pity, not repentance. He grieves the penalty, not the sin.

The mark. Protection: mercy even for a murderer.

What it does not mean. The “mark of Cain” has been grievously misused to justify racism and slavery. The text says nothing of skin or race.

Nod. “Wandering”.

Away from the presence of the LORD. The deepest punishment.
verseByVerse.note: “Nod” means wandering (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–26 — The Lines of Cain and Seth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 4 closes with two contrasting genealogical trajectories. The line of Cain produces the builders of cities and the inventors of culture — metalworking, music, husbandry — but also the escalating violence of Lamech, who boasts of killing for a mere wound and claims seventy-seven-fold vengeance. Over against this, Seth is born as the replacement for Abel, and with his son Enosh comes the first mention of calling upon the name of the LORD — the beginning of public worship of the LORD by name.
verseByVerse.theology: Cain's line builds the first city and brings music and metalwork into the world, and ends in Lamech's song of seventy-sevenfold revenge. Seth is born in Abel's place, and people begin to call on the name of the LORD.
