verseByVerse.examples: Then: culture flourished in the line under judgment, a gift of God's common kindness to the undeserving. Now: Jesus turned Lamech's seventy-seven into the measure of forgiveness (Matt. 18:22), and everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Rom. 10:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Cain knew his wife, and she conceived and bore Enoch. When he built a city, he called the name of the city after the name of his son, Enoch. To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methushael, and Methushael fathered Lamech. And Lamech took two wives. The name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah. Adah bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock. His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who play the lyre and pipe. Zillah also bore Tubal-cain; he was the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cain builds a city and has descendants who become the founders of herding, music and metalwork.

Cain’s wife. A sister or other relative (5:4). Close marriage was not yet forbidden (Leviticus 18).

Culture. Cities, music and technology are developed by Cain’s line. Culture is good, but can be used without God.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for skills and arts, and use them for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Lamech said to his wives: "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice; you wives of Lamech, listen to what I say: I have killed a man for wounding me, a young man for striking me. If Cain's revenge is sevenfold, then Lamech's is seventy-sevenfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lamech boasts to his two wives that he has killed a man for wounding him, and if Cain is avenged sevenfold, Lamech will be seventy-sevenfold.

Two wives. The first polygamy, a departure from God’s design (2:24).

A song of revenge. Violence celebrated.

Seventy-sevenfold. Jesus reverses it: forgive seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:22).

On a Tuesday. Are you keeping score of wrongs?

verseByVerse.quote: And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son and called his name Seth, for she said, "God has appointed for me another offspring instead of Abel, for Cain killed him." To Seth also a son was born, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adam and Eve have another son, Seth, appointed in place of Abel; Seth has a son, Enosh, and then people begin to call on the name of the LORD.

Seth. “Appointed”. The godly line continues.

Calling on the name. Public worship begins.

Two lines. Cain’s line ends in violence; Seth’s in prayer.

For worship. Call on the name of the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Seth” sounds like the Hebrew for “he appointed.”

4.theology:
Worship and the Heart. Genesis 4 establishes that acceptable worship is never merely formal. The issue with Cain was not his occupation or his offering's material but his heart. The entire sacrificial system of the Mosaic law, the prophets' critique of hollow ritual (Amos 5:21–24; Isa. 1:11–17), and Jesus's own teaching ("God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth," John 4:24) all flow from this foundational principle: you cannot separate the offering from the offerer.

The Spread of Sin. Genesis 4 traces what theologians call the total depravity of sin — not that fallen humanity is as bad as it could be, but that sin corrupts every dimension of human existence. The broken relationship with God (ch.3) produces broken relationships between humans (ch.4), and those broken relationships produce increasingly violent culture (Lamech's boast, vv.23–24). The flood of chapters 6–9 is not an overreaction; it is the logical consequence of a trajectory Genesis 4 has already mapped.
4.examples:
Then: The story of Cain and Abel addressed real questions for ancient Israel: why does faithful worship sometimes seem unrewarded? Why does the unjust prosper? The answers are theological, not pragmatic: God sees the heart, God protects even the guilty, and the line of faith persists through every catastrophe. For a people who had watched the righteous suffer in Egypt, these were not abstract questions.

Now: "Am I my brother's keeper?" remains the defining question of every era's social ethics. Individualism answers no; the gospel answers yes, at infinite cost. The mark of Cain speaks to criminal justice and mercy: even the guilty bear the image of God and cannot simply be discarded. And verse 26 — people calling on the name of the LORD in the midst of a violent world — is the posture of the church in every generation: not a triumphant majority but a remnant that calls on the name of the One who alone can heal what Cain began.

5.title: The Book of the Generations of Adam
5.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God.<sup>2</sup>Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and named them Man when they were created.<sup>3</sup>When Adam had lived 130 years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth.<sup>4</sup>The days of Adam after he fathered Seth were 800 years; and he had other sons and daughters.<sup>5</sup>Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died.<sup>6</sup>When Seth had lived 105 years, he fathered Enosh.<sup>7</sup>Seth lived after he fathered Enosh 807 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>8</sup>Thus all the days of Seth were 912 years, and he died.<sup>9</sup>When Enosh had lived 90 years, he fathered Kenan.<sup>10</sup>Enosh lived after he fathered Kenan 815 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>11</sup>Thus all the days of Enosh were 905 years, and he died.<sup>12</sup>When Kenan had lived 70 years, he fathered Mahalalel.<sup>13</sup>Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel 840 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>14</sup>Thus all the days of Kenan were 910 years, and he died.<sup>15</sup>When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared.<sup>16</sup>Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared 830 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>17</sup>Thus all the days of Mahalalel were 895 years, and he died.<sup>18</sup>When Jared had lived 162 years, he fathered Enoch.<sup>19</sup>Jared lived after he fathered Enoch 800 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>20</sup>Thus all the days of Jared were 962 years, and he died.<sup>21</sup>When Enoch had lived 65 years, he fathered Methuselah.<sup>22</sup>Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah 300 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>23</sup>Thus all the days of Enoch were 365 years.<sup>24</sup>Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.<sup>25</sup>When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he fathered Lamech.<sup>26</sup>Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech 782 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>27</sup>Thus all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died.<sup>28</sup>When Lamech had lived 182 years, he fathered a son<sup>29</sup>and called his name Noah, saying, "Out of the ground that the LORD has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands."<sup>30</sup>Lamech lived after he fathered Noah 595 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>31</sup>Thus all the days of Lamech were 777 years, and he died.<sup>32</sup>After Noah was 500 years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the first great genealogy of Genesis — ten generations from Adam to Noah, each entry following the same rhythm: he lived, he fathered, he had other sons and daughters, and he died. The drumbeat of death is relentless. Chapter 2 warned that disobedience would bring death; chapter 5 confirms it. The wages of sin is death (Rom. 6:23), and the genealogy is the receipt.

Yet the chapter is not merely a list of fatalities. Three interruptions crack the monotony. First, it opens by re-anchoring the genealogy in the imago Dei (v.1) — these are not merely mortal creatures but image-bearers whose death is therefore a tragedy, not a natural event. Second, Enoch “walked with God” (vv.22, 24) — the only character in the genealogy described by relationship rather than longevity — and was taken without dying: a luminous exception that proves the rule and anticipates resurrection. Third, Noah arrives with a father’s hope that he will bring relief from the curse.

The genealogy traces the line of the seed of the woman (3:15) through Seth, the replacement for Abel. Luke 3:38 traces Jesus’s genealogy to Adam, showing that the line of chapter 5 runs all the way to Bethlehem — the death-rhythm broken at last by the One who is the resurrection and the life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–32 — The Generations from Adam to Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The genealogy of Genesis 5 serves as a bridge between the primeval narratives of chapters 1–4 and the flood narrative of chapters 6–9. Its repetitive structure — birth, years of life, death — is deliberate: the refrain 'and he died' tolls like a funeral bell, confirming the judgment of Genesis 2:17 with grim regularity. Death is now the universal human experience. But within the repetition are two interruptions: Enoch, who walked with God and was taken; and Noah, named with a prophecy of rest and relief.
verseByVerse.theology: From Adam to Noah the refrain tolls: he lived, he fathered, and he died. Only Enoch breaks it — he walked with God and was taken — and the list ends on Noah, whose father hoped he would bring relief from the cursed ground.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the long lives of the first generations did not outrun the sentence of 2:17. Now: Enoch's exception, commended in Hebrews 11:5, points to a God who is stronger than the drumbeat of death.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the book of the generations of Adam. When God created man, he made him in the likeness of God. Male and female he created them, and he blessed them and named them Man when they were created.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book of Adam’s generations begins by recalling that God made man in his likeness, male and female, blessed them and named them Man.

The book. A written record, linking Adam to Noah.

Likeness. The image of God remains after the fall (9:6).

Named them Man. Adam, humanity, both male and female.

verseByVerse.quote: When Adam had lived 130 years, he fathered a son in his own likeness, after his image, and named him Seth. The days of Adam after he fathered Seth were 800 years; and he had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days that Adam lived were 930 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Adam fathers Seth in his own likeness and image, lives 930 years, and dies.

In his own likeness. Seth bears Adam’s image, including his fallen nature (Romans 5:12).

And he died. The refrain of the chapter. God’s word in 2:17 came true.

Where Christians differ: the long lifespans. Some take them as symbolic or as reigns of clans. Verdict: the text presents them as real lives, gradually shortening after the flood, as the effects of sin take hold. We need not explain how.

verseByVerse.quote: When Seth had lived 105 years, he fathered Enosh. Seth lived after he fathered Enosh 807 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Seth were 912 years, and he died. When Enosh had lived 90 years, he fathered Kenan. Enosh lived after he fathered Kenan 815 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Enosh were 905 years, and he died. When Kenan had lived 70 years, he fathered Mahalalel. Kenan lived after he fathered Mahalalel 840 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Kenan were 910 years, and he died. When Mahalalel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared. Mahalalel lived after he fathered Jared 830 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Mahalalel were 895 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel and Jared each live long, father sons and daughters, and die.

A pattern. Lived, fathered, died. Each life matters to God, and each ends.

Where Christians differ: gaps and dates. Archbishop Ussher used these numbers to date creation to 4004 BC. Others note that Hebrew genealogies often skip generations (compare Matthew 1:8 with 1 Chronicles 3:11–12). Verdict: the genealogies are true history, but may not be complete chronologies. Christians differ on the earth’s age in good conscience.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament and Samaritan Pentateuch give different ages from the Hebrew in this chapter. The ESV follows the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jared had lived 162 years, he fathered Enoch. Jared lived after he fathered Enoch 800 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Jared were 962 years, and he died. When Enoch had lived 65 years, he fathered Methuselah. Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah 300 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Enoch were 365 years. Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enoch walks with God three hundred years after fathering Methuselah, and then he is not, for God takes him.

Walked with God. Close, daily fellowship, while raising a family.

He was not. No “and he died”. A break in the pattern.

God took him. Without dying (Hebrews 11:5), like Elijah. A sign that death will not have the last word.

Jude 14–15. Enoch prophesied judgment.

On a Tuesday. Walking with God is possible in ordinary family life.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek Old Testament reads “pleased God” and “was not found” (ESV notes) — the wording Hebrews uses.

verseByVerse.quote: When Methuselah had lived 187 years, he fathered Lamech. Methuselah lived after he fathered Lamech 782 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Methuselah were 969 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Methuselah lives 969 years, the longest life recorded, and dies.

Longest. Yet still “and he died”.

The year of the flood. By the Hebrew numbers, Methuselah died in the year of the flood. God’s patience was long.
verseByVerse.note: By the ages given, Methuselah died in the year of the flood.

verseByVerse.quote: When Lamech had lived 182 years, he fathered a son and called his name Noah, saying, "Out of the ground that the LORD has cursed, this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands." Lamech lived after he fathered Noah 595 years and had other sons and daughters. Thus all the days of Lamech were 777 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lamech fathers Noah, saying he will bring relief from the painful toil of the cursed ground, and dies at 777.

Noah. Sounds like “relief” or “rest”.

Hope. Lamech longs for the curse to be lifted (3:17).

A different Lamech. Not the violent Lamech of 4:23.

On a Tuesday. Our longing for rest from toil is answered in Christ (Matthew 11:28).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Noah” sounds like the Hebrew for “rest.”

verseByVerse.quote: After Noah was 500 years old, Noah fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Noah is five hundred, he fathers Shem, Ham and Japheth.

Three sons. The ancestors of all nations after the flood (chapter 10).

For worship. Thank God for his faithfulness through every generation.

5.theology:
Death as Theological Fact. The genealogy of chapter 5 is a historical record that also makes a theological argument: death is real, universal, and unnatural. It is not the way things were supposed to be. This is the foundation of the Christian hope of resurrection — not merely that death is hard but that it is wrong, a catastrophe demanding reversal. The New Testament proclaims that reversal in the resurrection of Jesus: “the last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. 15:26).

Walking with God. Enoch’s “walking with God” (vv.22, 24) is the most compressed definition of the life of faith in the Old Testament. It is not spectacular achievement but sustained orientation — a whole life turned toward God. The New Testament develops this as walking “by the Spirit” (Gal. 5:16), walking “in the light” (1 John 1:7), walking “worthy of the Lord” (Col. 1:10). Enoch’s translation is the sign that this kind of life has a destination beyond death — not because it earns immortality but because the God with whom one walks is the God of resurrection.
5.examples:
Then: Ancient Near Eastern king lists also recorded extraordinary lifespans for pre-flood monarchs (sometimes hundreds of thousands of years), presenting long life as divine favor. Genesis 5’s genealogy engages this cultural form while subverting it: the long-lived patriarchs all die, making the point that longevity does not conquer death. Enoch’s exception is therefore all the more striking in this context.

Now: The genealogy speaks to every culture obsessed with longevity and anti-aging — the biotech investment in immortality, the desperate attempt to outrun the death-rhythm. Genesis 5 says: you cannot. The only path past death runs through the One who walked into it and out the other side. And Enoch’s “walking with God” is the counter-cultural definition of a life well-lived: not accumulated experiences, achievements, or years, but a whole life in the direction of God.

6.title: Noah Found Favor in the Eyes of the LORD
6.text: <sup>1</sup>When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them,<sup>2</sup>the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose.<sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said, "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years."<sup>4</sup>The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown.<sup>5</sup>The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.<sup>7</sup>So the LORD said, "I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them."<sup>8</sup>But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God.<sup>10</sup>And Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.<sup>11</sup>Now the earth was corrupt in God's sight, and the earth was filled with violence.<sup>12</sup>And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.<sup>13</sup>And God said to Noah, "I have determined to make an end of all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them with the earth.<sup>14</sup>Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch.<sup>15</sup>This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits.<sup>16</sup>Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to a cubit above, and set the door of the ark in its side. Make it with lower, second, and third decks.<sup>17</sup>For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall die.<sup>18</sup>But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives with you.<sup>19</sup>And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ark to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female.<sup>20</sup>Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground, according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive.<sup>21</sup>Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up. It shall serve as food for you and for them."<sup>22</sup>Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is one of the most theologically dense chapters in Genesis, containing the divine assessment of human corruption (“every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually,” v.5), the grief of God (v.6), the announcement of the flood (vv.7, 13), and the extraordinary counter-declaration: “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (v.8). That “but” is one of the most important conjunctions in Scripture — a pivot from universal condemnation to particular grace.

The grief of God (v.6) is one of the most striking anthropomorphic statements in the Old Testament. The God who cannot be surprised or defeated is described as grieved, as regretting. This is not a divine mistake but a genuine expression of the pain that human rebellion causes to the God who made humanity for fellowship with himself. The cross was not a plan B — the suffering of God over human sin is woven into the divine-human relationship from the beginning.

Noah’s ark is one of the Bible’s most developed types of Christ. Just as Noah and his family were saved through the ark while judgment fell on the world outside, so those who are “in Christ” are safe from the judgment that falls on sin. 1 Peter 3:20–21 makes this explicit, calling the ark a type of baptism — the waters of judgment becoming the waters of salvation for those inside the vessel God provided.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Corruption of the Earth and the Call of Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 6 opens with one of the most debated passages in Scripture — the sons of God and the daughters of man — and moves to the shattering announcement of divine judgment: God will blot out the human race he has made. The corruption of the earth is so pervasive that God regrets making man. Yet within this overwhelming judgment stands one man: Noah, who found favor in the eyes of the LORD. The chapter ends with God's call to Noah and the commission to build the ark.
verseByVerse.theology: The sons of God take wives as they choose, and the earth fills with corruption and violence until the LORD is grieved to his heart and resolves to blot out man. But Noah finds favour, and God covenants with him and commands the ark.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Noah built for years for a judgment nobody else believed in, and Hebrews calls it faith (Heb. 11:7). Now: grace comes first and righteousness follows, as verse 8 comes before verse 9.

verseByVerse.quote: When man began to multiply on the face of the land and daughters were born to them, the sons of God saw that the daughters of man were attractive. And they took as their wives any they chose. Then the LORD said, "My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years." The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of man and they bore children to them. These were the mighty men who were of old, the men of renown.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As people multiply, the sons of God take human wives as they choose; God limits man’s days to 120 years, and the Nephilim were on the earth then.

Where Christians differ: the sons of God. Some see fallen angels (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4); some the godly line of Seth marrying Cain’s ungodly line; some tyrant kings. Verdict: the question is genuinely hard. The angel view is ancient and has New Testament support; the Sethite view fits the chapters’ focus on two lines and avoids angels marrying (Matthew 22:30). Either way, the boundaries God set were broken, and evil grew.

120 years. Either a shortened lifespan or a countdown to the flood.

Nephilim. “Fallen ones” or giants. Mighty, famous men.

Textual note. The Hebrew verb in v. 3 is uncertain: “abide in”, “strive with”, or “contend with” man.
verseByVerse.note: “Sons of God” is read either as angels, or as the line of Seth, or as ruling men. The Nephilim (“giants,” ESV note) are otherwise unknown, apart from the spies’ report.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. And the LORD regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD sees that human wickedness is great and every intention of their hearts is only evil continually, and he regrets making man and is grieved to his heart.

Every intention. Total depravity: sin reaches every part (Jeremiah 17:9; Romans 3:10–18).

Regretted. Where Christians differ. Open theists take this to mean God did not know what would happen. Verdict: God does not change his mind as humans do (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). Scripture speaks of God in human terms to show his real grief at sin, without denying his knowledge or purpose.

Grieved. God is not indifferent to sin.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD said, "I will blot out man whom I have created from the face of the land, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens, for I am sorry that I have made them." But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD resolves to blot out man and beast, for he regrets making them; but Noah finds favour in the LORD’s eyes.

Blot out. Judgment on the whole world.

But Noah. The turning point.

Found favour. Literally “found grace”. The first time grace is named. Grace comes before Noah’s righteousness is described.

For worship. Thank God that his grace finds sinners in a judged world.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first time the Bible uses the word “favor” (grace).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God. And Noah had three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Now the earth was corrupt in God's sight, and the earth was filled with violence. And God saw the earth, and behold, it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah is righteous, blameless in his generation, and walks with God, while the earth is corrupt and full of violence.

Righteous. By faith (Hebrews 11:7).

Walked with God. Like Enoch.

Corrupt and violent. The two marks of the world before the flood.

On a Tuesday. You can walk with God in a corrupt world.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Noah, "I have determined to make an end of all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them with the earth. Make yourself an ark of gopher wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it inside and out with pitch. This is how you are to make it: the length of the ark 300 cubits, its breadth 50 cubits, and its height 30 cubits. Make a roof for the ark, and finish it to a cubit above, and set the door of the ark in its side. Make it with lower, second, and third decks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Noah he will end all flesh, and commands him to build an ark of gopher wood, coated with pitch, with rooms, three decks, a window and a door.

The ark. A huge box, about 450 feet long: built to float, not sail.

Pitch. The word is related to “atonement”, meaning to cover.

Gopher wood. Unknown; perhaps cypress.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a cubit was about 18 inches, so the ark was about 450 by 75 by 45 feet. “Gopher wood” is a transliteration; the tree is unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, I will bring a flood of waters upon the earth to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life under heaven. Everything that is on the earth shall die. But I will establish my covenant with you, and you shall come into the ark, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons' wives with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will bring a flood to destroy all flesh, but he will establish his covenant with Noah, and Noah’s family will enter the ark.

My covenant. The first time “covenant” appears in the Bible.

Where Christians differ: global or local? Some hold a worldwide flood; others a regional one covering the world known to Noah. Verdict: the language of the text is universal, and the New Testament treats the flood as a real judgment on the world (2 Peter 3:6). Christians differ in good conscience on its extent, but all must affirm it as a real event.

His family. Saved with him.
verseByVerse.note: The first mention of “covenant” in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ark to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female. Of the birds according to their kinds, and of the animals according to their kinds, of every creeping thing of the ground, according to its kind, two of every sort shall come in to you to keep them alive. Also take with you every sort of food that is eaten, and store it up. It shall serve as food for you and for them." Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah is to bring two of every kind of animal into the ark, with food for all; and Noah does everything God commands.

Two of every sort. And seven pairs of clean animals (7:2).

He did all. Obedience without seeing the flood. Faith works (Hebrews 11:7).

A picture of salvation. One ark, one door; safety in God’s provision (1 Peter 3:20–21).

On a Tuesday. Obey God’s word even when the world thinks you are foolish.

For worship. Thank God for Christ, the ark of our salvation.

6.theology:
The Grief of God. Verse 6 reveals that God is not a detached First Cause but a personal God whose relationship with humanity involves genuine pain when that relationship is violated. The theological tradition has rightly distinguished between divine impassibility (God is not controlled by passions as we are) and divine feeling (God genuinely responds to his creation). The cross is the definitive statement: God’s response to human sin was not detached judgment but the grief of the Father and the suffering of the Son.

The Ark as Type of Christ. Peter explicitly calls the ark a type (1 Pet. 3:20–21): as Noah and his family were saved through water while the world outside perished, so baptism — the sign of union with Christ — saves through the death and resurrection of the One who bore judgment for us. The ark is not an escape from judgment but a vessel that goes through judgment while bearing its passengers safely. Christ does not remove his people from the presence of death; he goes through death with them and out the other side.
6.examples:
Then: The flood narrative has parallels in ancient Near Eastern literature (especially the Gilgamesh epic), confirming that memory of a great flood was widespread in the ancient world. Genesis engages these traditions while transforming them: the flood is not the whim of competing gods disturbed by human noise but the just response of the one holy God to universal corruption, tempered by grace for one man and his family. The theological difference is total.

Now: Verse 5’s diagnosis of the human heart (“only evil continually”) sounds extreme to ears formed by Enlightenment optimism about human nature. But the twentieth century — with its genocides, gulags, and weapons of mass destruction — has provided empirical support for the biblical diagnosis. The culture that denies total depravity has no adequate account of Auschwitz. And verse 8 — “But Noah found favor” — is the grace that every generation needs: not a better moral strategy but a God who intervenes.

7.title: The Flood
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Noah, "Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation.<sup>2</sup>Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals, the male and his mate, and a pair of the animals that are not clean, the male and his mate,<sup>3</sup>and seven pairs of the birds of the heavens also, male and female, to keep their offspring alive on the face of all the earth.<sup>4</sup>For in seven days I will send rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and every living thing that I have made I will blot out from the face of the ground."<sup>5</sup>And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.<sup>6</sup>Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came upon the earth.<sup>7</sup>And Noah and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him went into the ark to escape the waters of the flood.<sup>8</sup>Of clean animals, and of animals that are not clean, and of birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground,<sup>9</sup>two and two, male and female, went into the ark with Noah, as God had commanded Noah.<sup>10</sup>And after seven days the waters of the flood came upon the earth.<sup>11</sup>In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened.<sup>12</sup>And rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights.<sup>13</sup>On the very same day Noah and his sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them entered the ark,<sup>14</sup>they and every beast, according to its kind, and all the livestock according to their kinds, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, according to its kind, and every bird, according to its kind, every winged creature.<sup>15</sup>They went into the ark with Noah, two and two of all flesh in which there was the breath of life.<sup>16</sup>And those that entered, male and female of all flesh, went in as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in.<sup>17</sup>The flood continued forty days on the earth. The waters increased and bore up the ark, and it rose high above the earth.<sup>18</sup>The waters prevailed and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters.<sup>19</sup>And the waters prevailed so mightily on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered.<sup>20</sup>The waters prevailed above the mountains, covering them fifteen cubits deep.<sup>21</sup>And all flesh died that moved on the earth, birds, livestock, beasts, all swarming creatures that swarm on the earth, and all mankind.<sup>22</sup>Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died.<sup>23</sup>He blotted out every living thing that was on the face of the ground, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens. They were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark.<sup>24</sup>And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 is the flood itself — de-creation and judgment on the grandest scale the Old Testament records. The waters of chaos that God separated on day two of creation (1:6–8) now return: the “fountains of the great deep” burst open and the “windows of the heavens” open, and creation is undone. The carefully ordered world of Genesis 1 is overwhelmed. This is not merely weather; it is cosmic judgment, a reversal of creation by the Creator himself.

In the midst of the catastrophe, one of the most tender verses in Genesis: “And the LORD shut him in” (v.16). God himself closes the door of the ark. Noah does not secure his own salvation; the God who commanded him to build the ark is the same God who seals him inside it. This small detail carries enormous theological weight: salvation from first to last is the work of God, not the achievement of the saved.

Jesus uses the flood as a picture of the suddenness of eschatological judgment: “As were the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24:37). The world goes about its business, eating and drinking, until the judgment arrives. The flood is not merely a past event but a type of the final judgment — and the ark is not merely a boat but a picture of the only safety that judgment day will leave standing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–24 — The Flood: Judgment and Preservation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 7 narrates the flood itself: the entry into the ark, the coming of the waters, and the comprehensive destruction of all life outside the ark. The precision of the dates and the systematic enumeration of those who entered and those who died serve the text's theological purposes: this is real history, not mythology, and its reality is the basis for its typological significance throughout Scripture.
verseByVerse.theology: Noah goes in with his family and the animals, the LORD shuts him in, and the fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven are opened. Everything outside the ark dies; the waters prevail for 150 days.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the same waters that destroyed the world bore up the ark, and Peter saw baptism in it (1 Pet. 3:20–21). Now: Jesus warned that his coming will be like the days of Noah (Matt. 24:37–39), and safety lies in being in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Noah, "Go into the ark, you and all your household, for I have seen that you are righteous before me in this generation. Take with you seven pairs of all clean animals, the male and his mate, and a pair of the animals that are not clean, the male and his mate, and seven pairs of the birds of the heavens also, male and female, to keep their offspring alive on the face of all the earth. For in seven days I will send rain on the earth forty days and forty nights, and every living thing that I have made I will blot out from the face of the ground." And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD tells Noah to go into the ark with his household and to take seven pairs of every clean animal and one pair of the unclean, for in seven days the rain will begin.

Righteous before me. Noah is counted righteous by God (Hebrews 11:7).

Clean and unclean. Known before Sinai. The extra clean animals are for sacrifice (8:20).

Seven days. A last week of grace.

Noah did all. Obedience again.
verseByVerse.note: “Seven pairs” may mean seven of each kind (ESV note). Clean animals were needed for sacrifice (8:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Noah was six hundred years old when the flood of waters came upon the earth. And Noah and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him went into the ark to escape the waters of the flood. Of clean animals, and of animals that are not clean, and of birds, and of everything that creeps on the ground, two and two, male and female, went into the ark with Noah, as God had commanded Noah. And after seven days the waters of the flood came upon the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At six hundred, Noah enters the ark with his family and the animals, two by two, as God commanded, and after seven days the flood comes.

Two by two. God brings the animals; Noah does not have to round them up (6:20).

The waiting. Seven days in a closed ark before a drop fell. Faith waits.

verseByVerse.quote: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened. And rain fell upon the earth forty days and forty nights. On the very same day Noah and his sons, Shem and Ham and Japheth, and Noah's wife and the three wives of his sons with them entered the ark, they and every beast, according to its kind, and all the livestock according to their kinds, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, according to its kind, and every bird, according to its kind, every winged creature. They went into the ark with Noah, two and two of all flesh in which there was the breath of life. And those that entered, male and female of all flesh, went in as God had commanded him. And the LORD shut him in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On a dated day the fountains of the deep burst open and the windows of heaven open; rain falls forty days and nights, and the LORD shuts Noah in.

A precise date. Presented as history.

The deep and the heavens. Creation’s separations (1:6–9) undone. The flood is un-creation.

The LORD shut him in. Salvation is God’s work; his people are kept safe by him (John 10:28).

For worship. Thank God who shuts his people in safely.

verseByVerse.quote: The flood continued forty days on the earth. The waters increased and bore up the ark, and it rose high above the earth. The waters prevailed and increased greatly on the earth, and the ark floated on the face of the waters. And the waters prevailed so mightily on the earth that all the high mountains under the whole heaven were covered. The waters prevailed above the mountains, covering them fifteen cubits deep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The waters rise and lift the ark until the highest mountains are covered.

The ark rose. The same waters that judged the world lifted the ark.

Fifteen cubits. About twenty-two feet above the peaks.

A picture. Peter sees baptism here: saved through water by God’s appointed means (1 Peter 3:20–21).

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some read 1 Peter 3:21 as baptismal regeneration. Verdict: Peter adds, “not as a removal of dirt… but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.” Baptism signifies salvation through Christ; it does not save by itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And all flesh died that moved on the earth, birds, livestock, beasts, all swarming creatures that swarm on the earth, and all mankind. Everything on the dry land in whose nostrils was the breath of life died. He blotted out every living thing that was on the face of the ground, man and animals and creeping things and birds of the heavens. They were blotted out from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark. And the waters prevailed on the earth 150 days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All flesh on the land dies, and only Noah and those with him in the ark are left, while the waters prevail 150 days.

All died. God’s judgment on sin is real (2 Peter 2:5).

Only Noah. A remnant saved by grace.

Jesus’ warning. As in the days of Noah, so will it be at his coming (Luke 17:26–27).

On a Tuesday. Be in the ark: be in Christ.

For worship. Thank God for Christ, in whom you are safe from judgment.

7.theology:
Judgment and Grace. The flood holds together two truths that the contemporary mind tends to separate: God’s holiness demands judgment on sin, and God’s love provides a way of salvation within judgment. These are not in tension; the cross is their resolution. At Calvary, the judgment that the flood pre-figured falls on the Son of God, and those who are in him are shut into the safety he provides. The flood without the ark is law without gospel; the ark without the flood is cheap grace. Genesis 7 holds both.

De-creation and New Creation. The flood’s reversal of creation (the return of the deep, the dissolution of the dry land) establishes a pattern: judgment is de-creation, and salvation is new creation. This pattern recurs in the exodus (the Red Sea as de-creation for Egypt, new creation for Israel), in the exile (the return to formlessness), and supremely in the death and resurrection of Christ. The resurrection is the new creation that the flood dimly foreshadowed: the old creation undone, the new creation breaking through.
7.examples:
Then: The forty days and forty nights of rain (v.4) became a symbolic number in Israel’s imagination: Moses was on the mountain forty days (Exod. 24:18), the spies searched Canaan forty days (Num. 13:25), Israel wandered forty years, and Jesus fasted forty days (Matt. 4:2). The number carries the weight of trial, purification, and preparation for what comes next. Ancient Israel knew the flood story as the paradigm for all subsequent tests of faithfulness.

Now: Jesus’s use of the flood in Matthew 24:37–39 is a standing warning against spiritual complacency: the world before the flood did not see it coming because it was too busy with ordinary life to read the signs. The application is not that Christians should be anxious about the end but that they should be alert — “watching” in the posture of faith that characterized Noah. And the remnant theology of verse 23 speaks to every minority church in a hostile culture: you are not a failed majority but a preserved remnant, held by the same God who shut Noah in.

8.title: God Remembered Noah
8.text: <sup>1</sup>But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided.<sup>2</sup>The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, the rain from the heavens was restrained,<sup>3</sup>and the waters receded from the earth continually. At the end of 150 days the waters had abated,<sup>4</sup>and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat.<sup>5</sup>And the waters continued to abate until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen.<sup>6</sup>At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made<sup>7</sup>and sent forth a raven. It went to and fro until the waters were dried up from the earth.<sup>8</sup>Then he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the ground.<sup>9</sup>But the dove found no place to set her foot, and she returned to him to the ark, for the waters were still on the face of the whole earth. So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him.<sup>10</sup>He waited another seven days, and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark.<sup>11</sup>And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had subsided from the earth.<sup>12</sup>Then he waited another seven days and sent forth the dove, and she did not return to him anymore.<sup>13</sup>In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried from off the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry.<sup>14</sup>In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth had dried out.<sup>15</sup>Then God said to Noah,<sup>16</sup>"Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons' wives with you.<sup>17</sup>Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh—birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth."<sup>18</sup>So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him.<sup>19</sup>Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out by families from the ark.<sup>20</sup>Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar.<sup>21</sup>And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, "I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth. Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done.<sup>22</sup>While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease."
8.overview:
The flood ends the way it began — with a divine act and a divine word. “But God remembered Noah” (v.1) does not mean God had forgotten; in biblical idiom, to “remember” someone is to act on their behalf in covenant faithfulness. God’s memory is always active. The wind that drives back the waters deliberately echoes the Spirit hovering over the deep at creation (1:2) — the flood’s judgment giving way to new creation.

Noah’s first act upon leaving the ark is worship: he builds an altar and offers burnt offerings (v.20). Before planting, before settling — he worships. This is the proper ordering of a restored life: the first response to salvation is doxology. The LORD’s response — “I will never again curse the ground because of man” (v.21) — is not a declaration that humanity has improved but a unilateral commitment of grace. God acknowledges that “the intention of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (v.21) and commits to patience anyway.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Recession of the Flood and Noah's Worship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 8 narrates the recession of the flood and Noah's emergence from the ark with the same careful precision that marked its onset. The pivot of the chapter — and of the entire flood narrative — is verse 1: 'But God remembered Noah.' This divine remembrance is not the recovery of forgotten information but the decisive, saving action of a God who acts on his covenant commitments. The flood recedes; the earth dries; Noah exits; and his first act on dry ground is to build an altar and offer burnt offerings.
verseByVerse.theology: God remembers Noah, sends a wind over the waters, and the flood recedes. Noah waits for the raven, the dove and the olive leaf, and then for God's word to go out. His first act on dry ground is an altar, and God promises never again to curse the ground or to cut off every living creature.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God's remembering is always God acting, as it was for Israel in Egypt and for Hannah. Now: seedtime and harvest, day and night, still keep the promise of 8:22, made to a race still evil from its youth.

verseByVerse.quote: But God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock that were with him in the ark. And God made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters subsided. The fountains of the deep and the windows of the heavens were closed, the rain from the heavens was restrained, and the waters receded from the earth continually. At the end of 150 days the waters had abated, and in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. And the waters continued to abate until the tenth month; in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were seen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God remembers Noah and the animals, sends a wind over the earth, closes the fountains and windows, and the waters recede until the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat.

God remembered. Not that he had forgotten. He acts on his covenant (Exodus 2:24).

A wind. The same word as “Spirit” in 1:2. A new creation begins.

Ararat. A mountainous region in modern eastern Turkey and Armenia.

For worship. Thank God that he remembers you.
verseByVerse.note: Ararat is the region of eastern Turkey and Armenia; the text speaks of its mountains, not a single peak.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of forty days Noah opened the window of the ark that he had made and sent forth a raven. It went to and fro until the waters were dried up from the earth. Then he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the ground. But the dove found no place to set her foot, and she returned to him to the ark, for the waters were still on the face of the whole earth. So he put out his hand and took her and brought her into the ark with him. He waited another seven days, and again he sent forth the dove out of the ark. And the dove came back to him in the evening, and behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters had subsided from the earth. Then he waited another seven days and sent forth the dove, and she did not return to him anymore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah sends out a raven, which flies to and fro, and then a dove, which returns; after seven days he sends it again, and it returns with an olive leaf; after another seven it does not return.

Waiting. Noah tests before he moves.

The olive leaf. New life. A symbol of peace ever since.

On a Tuesday. Wait patiently for God’s timing.

verseByVerse.quote: In the six hundred and first year, in the first month, the first day of the month, the waters were dried from off the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark and looked, and behold, the face of the ground was dry. In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth had dried out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On New Year’s Day of Noah’s 601st year the ground is dry, and by the second month the earth is fully dry.

The first day of the first month. A new beginning.

Over a year in the ark. A long trial of faith.
verseByVerse.note: Noah was in the ark a little over a year.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to Noah, "Go out from the ark, you and your wife, and your sons and your sons' wives with you. Bring out with you every living thing that is with you of all flesh—birds and animals and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth—that they may swarm on the earth, and be fruitful and multiply on the earth." So Noah went out, and his sons and his wife and his sons' wives with him. Every beast, every creeping thing, and every bird, everything that moves on the earth, went out by families from the ark.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Noah to leave the ark with his family and the animals, to be fruitful and multiply, and they go out by families.

Go out. Noah waits for God’s word to leave, as to enter.

Be fruitful. The creation blessing renewed (1:22, 28).

A new Adam. Noah starts humanity again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Noah built an altar to the LORD and took some of every clean animal and some of every clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. And when the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, the LORD said in his heart, "I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth. Neither will I ever again strike down every living creature as I have done. While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings, the LORD smells the pleasing aroma, and promises never again to curse the ground or strike every living thing, though man’s heart is evil from youth; while the earth remains, seasons will not cease.

First, worship. Before building a house, Noah builds an altar.

A pleasing aroma. Pointing to Christ’s sacrifice (Ephesians 5:2).

Evil from youth. The flood did not change the human heart. Original sin remains. Only grace can.

Seedtime and harvest. God’s common grace to all people (Acts 14:17).

For worship. Thank God for every harvest and season.
verseByVerse.note: The first altar in the Bible.

8.theology:
New Creation. Genesis 8 deliberately echoes Genesis 1: the wind (Spirit) moves over the waters, the dry land appears, the living creatures come out. The flood was de-creation; the recession of the waters is new creation. This typological pattern runs through Scripture — exodus, return from exile, and the resurrection of Christ (the new creation breaking into the old). Every act of divine redemption is a new creation, and the final new creation is the new heavens and earth of Revelation 21.

The Patience of God. Verse 21 is one of the Bible’s most profound statements about grace: God commits to patience with a race whose “heart is evil from youth.” Peter calls it “the patience of our Lord” (2 Pet. 3:15) and connects it to salvation: God waits so that more might be saved. The cross is what made it possible for God to commit to this patience without compromising his justice.
8.examples:
Then: Noah’s immediate act of worship (v.20) would have been instructive to Israelite readers familiar with burnt offerings: the great patriarch of the renewed creation was, above all, a worshiper. The olive leaf (v.11) became a universal symbol of peace precisely because of this story’s cultural reach across ancient civilization.

Now: “God remembered Noah” (v.1) is the pastoral anchor of the chapter. In the long silences — the unanswered prayer, the protracted suffering, the season in which God seems absent — the covenant promise is: he has not forgotten. His remembering is always the turn of the tide. And verse 21’s honest anthropology — evil from youth, yet God commits to patience — is the realistic foundation of Christian mission: we do not expect the gospel to improve human nature but to create new creatures within fallen nature.

9.title: The Covenant with Noah
9.text: <sup>1</sup>And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.<sup>2</sup>The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are delivered.<sup>3</sup>Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. And as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything.<sup>4</sup>But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood.<sup>5</sup>And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man.<sup>6</sup>"Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image.<sup>7</sup>And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it."<sup>8</sup>Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him,<sup>9</sup>"Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you,<sup>10</sup>and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth.<sup>11</sup>I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth."<sup>12</sup>And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations:<sup>13</sup>I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.<sup>14</sup>When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds,<sup>15</sup>I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh.<sup>16</sup>When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth."<sup>17</sup>God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth."<sup>18</sup>The sons of Noah who went forth from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.)<sup>19</sup>These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed.<sup>20</sup>Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard.<sup>21</sup>He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent.<sup>22</sup>And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside.<sup>23</sup>Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness.<sup>24</sup>When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him,<sup>25</sup>he said, "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers."<sup>26</sup>He also said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant.<sup>27</sup>May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant."<sup>28</sup>After the flood Noah lived 350 years.<sup>29</sup>All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died.
9.overview:
Chapter 9 establishes the Noahic covenant — the first of the great biblical covenants to be formally ratified with a sign. God re-issues the cultural mandate (v.1, echoing 1:28), establishes the sanctity of human life rooted in the imago Dei (v.6), and seals his promise with a rainbow. The covenant is explicitly universal: not just with Noah and his family but with “every living creature” (v.10) and “all future generations” (v.12). It is the framework within which all subsequent history, and all subsequent covenants, operate.

The rainbow is one of Scripture’s most theologically rich signs. God hangs his weapon of war in the sky — a bow pointed upward, toward heaven — as a pledge that he will not destroy the earth by flood again. The sign is primarily for God, not humanity: “when I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant” (vv.14–15). The chapter closes honestly: Noah’s drunkenness and shame (vv.20–21) remind us that the flood did not change human nature. The new creation still needs a new Adam.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 9 establishes the first formally named covenant in Scripture. God blesses Noah with the creation mandate renewed, grants permission to eat meat, institutes capital punishment as the sanction for murder (grounding it in the image of God), and seals the covenant with the sign of the rainbow. The covenant is unconditional, universal, and everlasting — encompassing all humanity and all living creatures, not just Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: God blesses Noah as he blessed Adam, gives the animals for food but forbids blood, and requires the life of any who sheds man's blood, for man is made in God's image. He covenants with every living creature never again to flood the earth, and sets his bow in the cloud as the sign.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the first covenant in Scripture has no conditions and includes the animals. Now: the sign is put where God will see it and remember, as the Passover blood was (Exod. 12:13); assurance rests on what God has undertaken, not on how well we remember.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth. The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth and upon every bird of the heavens, upon everything that creeps on the ground and all the fish of the sea. Into your hand they are delivered. Every moving thing that lives shall be food for you. And as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blesses Noah and his sons, tells them to fill the earth, puts the fear of man on the animals, and gives them every moving thing for food, as he gave the green plants.

Blessing renewed. The creation mandate again.

Meat permitted. A new permission after the flood.

Fear of you. The relationship with animals changes.

On a Tuesday. Receive food with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: But you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood. And for your lifeblood I will require a reckoning: from every beast I will require it and from man. From his fellow man I will require a reckoning for the life of man. "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image. And you, be fruitful and multiply, increase greatly on the earth and multiply in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must not eat flesh with its blood, and God will require a reckoning for human blood: whoever sheds man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his image.

Blood. Life belongs to God (Leviticus 17:11).

In his image. Murder is an attack on God’s image.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some see this as a permanent command; others as permission superseded by grace. Verdict: given to all humanity before Israel, it grounds the state’s right to use the sword for murder (Romans 13:4), to be exercised with great care for justice.

Where Christians differ: blood transfusions. Jehovah’s Witnesses forbid them from this verse. Verdict: the command concerns eating blood, honouring life. Giving blood to save life honours the same principle.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to Noah and to his sons with him, "Behold, I establish my covenant with you and your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, the birds, the livestock, and every beast of the earth with you, as many as came out of the ark; it is for every beast of the earth. I establish my covenant with you, that never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of the flood, and never again shall there be a flood to destroy the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God establishes his covenant with Noah, his descendants and every living creature: never again will a flood destroy the earth.

A covenant with all creation. Not only with believers. Common grace.

Never again. A promise God has kept.

What it does not mean. Not that there will be no final judgment. The next will be by fire (2 Peter 3:7).

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "This is the sign of the covenant that I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for all future generations: I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth. When I bring clouds over the earth and the bow is seen in the clouds, I will remember my covenant that is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh. And the waters shall never again become a flood to destroy all flesh. When the bow is in the clouds, I will see it and remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth." God said to Noah, "This is the sign of the covenant that I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets his bow in the clouds as the sign of the covenant, and when he sees it, he will remember his covenant with every living creature.

The bow. A warrior’s bow, hung up, pointing away from earth.

I will remember. The sign reminds God, and assures us.

Around the throne. A rainbow encircles God’s throne (Revelation 4:3).

For worship. When you see a rainbow, thank God for his faithfulness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–29 — The Sin of Ham and the Prophecy over the Sons of Noah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Genesis 9 introduces the first post-flood failure: Noah's drunkenness and the sin of Ham. The episode is brief and difficult — its precise nature debated — but its consequences are long-lasting: the curse of Canaan and the blessing of Shem, anticipating the entire subsequent history of Israel's relationship to the Canaanites. The chapter ends with Noah's death at 950 years.
verseByVerse.theology: Noah plants a vineyard, gets drunk and lies uncovered. Ham sees and tells; Shem and Japheth cover their father without looking. Noah curses Canaan, blesses the God of Shem, and prays that Japheth may dwell in Shem's tents.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the curse concerns the Canaanite nations Israel was about to meet, not any race alive today. Now: the flood cleaned the earth but not the heart, and love still covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8).

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Noah who went forth from the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. (Ham was the father of Canaan.) These three were the sons of Noah, and from these the people of the whole earth were dispersed. Noah began to be a man of the soil, and he planted a vineyard. He drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father and told his two brothers outside. Then Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on both their shoulders, and walked backward and covered the nakedness of their father. Their faces were turned backward, and they did not see their father's nakedness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah’s sons are Shem, Ham (father of Canaan) and Japheth; Noah plants a vineyard, gets drunk and lies uncovered; Ham sees and tells his brothers, who cover their father without looking.

A man of the soil. The new Adam falls in a garden of his own.

Drunk. The Bible records the sins of its heroes honestly.

What Ham did. Some see a sexual act; most likely he shamed his father by looking and telling, while his brothers honoured him.

On a Tuesday. Cover others’ shame rather than expose it (1 Peter 4:8).

verseByVerse.quote: When Noah awoke from his wine and knew what his youngest son had done to him, he said, "Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers." He also said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem; and let Canaan be his servant. May God enlarge Japheth, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem, and let Canaan be his servant." After the flood Noah lived 350 years. All the days of Noah were 950 years, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Noah curses Canaan to be a servant to his brothers, blesses the God of Shem, and prays that Japheth be enlarged and dwell in Shem’s tents; Noah dies at 950.

Canaan, not Ham. The curse falls on Canaan, ancestor of the Canaanites whose immorality Israel would later encounter (Leviticus 18:3).

What it does not mean. The so-called curse of Ham was used to justify the enslavement of Africans. This is a grievous misuse: the curse names Canaan, not Ham’s other descendants, and was fulfilled in Israel’s history. It says nothing about race.

The God of Shem. The line of promise runs through Shem to Abraham.

Japheth in Shem’s tents. Perhaps the Gentiles sharing in Israel’s blessings (Ephesians 2:13).

For worship. Thank God that his blessing reaches every nation.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Japheth” sounds like the Hebrew for “enlarge.” The curse falls on Canaan, ancestor of the peoples Israel would later displace.

9.theology:
Common Grace. The Noahic covenant introduces what Reformed theology calls “common grace” — God’s non-saving grace extended to all people, preserving the created order and enabling human civilization. The regularity of seasons (8:22), the restraint of evil, the capacity for beauty and justice even among the unredeemed — all flow from this covenant. Common grace does not save, but it makes human life possible and valuable, and it is the framework within which saving grace operates.

The Rainbow and the Cross. The rainbow as God’s sign — a weapon pointed upward — prefigures the cross. At Calvary, the judgment that the flood represented fell on the Son of God, satisfying divine justice and making it possible for God to commit to patience with a fallen world. The rainbow promises the flood will not return; the cross explains how God can keep that promise without ignoring sin.
9.examples:
Then: The Noahic covenant established the framework for all human civilization and law. Verse 6 (blood for blood) is the basis for proportional justice underlying all legal systems. The rainbow was a visible covenant sign in an era before written documents — God’s public promise inscribed in the sky for every generation.

Now: The misuse of verses 24–27 to justify slavery demands explicit correction: the “curse of Ham” has no biblical basis and is one of the most destructive exegetical errors in history. The chapter’s actual message is the Noahic covenant’s universal scope: every morning that dawns, every harvest that succeeds, every civilization that sustains human life — these are gifts of covenant faithfulness to a world that does not deserve them. Creation care is therefore not merely a secular concern but a theological one.

10.title: The Table of Nations
10.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood.<sup>2</sup>The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.<sup>3</sup>The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim.<sup>5</sup>From these the coastland peoples spread in their lands, each with his own language, by their clans, in their nations.<sup>6</sup>The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.<sup>8</sup>Cush fathered Nimrod; he was the first on earth to be a mighty man.<sup>9</sup>He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. Therefore it is said, "Like Nimrod a mighty hunter before the LORD."<sup>10</sup>The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar.<sup>11</sup>From that land he went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and<sup>12</sup>Resen between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city.<sup>13</sup>Egypt fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,<sup>14</sup>Pathrusim, Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorim.<sup>15</sup>Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth,<sup>16</sup>and the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites,<sup>17</sup>the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites,<sup>18</sup>the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites dispersed.<sup>19</sup>And the territory of the Canaanites extended from Sidon in the direction of Gerar as far as Gaza, and in the direction of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha.<sup>20</sup>These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.<sup>21</sup>To Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber, the elder brother of Japheth, children were born.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash.<sup>24</sup>Arpachshad fathered Shelah; and Shelah fathered Eber.<sup>25</sup>To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and his brother's name was Joktan.<sup>26</sup>Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah,<sup>27</sup>Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah,<sup>28</sup>Obal, Abimael, Sheba,<sup>29</sup>Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan.<sup>30</sup>The territory in which they lived extended from Mesha in the direction of Sephar to the hill country of the east.<sup>31</sup>These are the sons of Shem, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.<sup>32</sup>These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, in their nations, and from these the nations spread abroad on the earth after the flood.
10.overview:
The Table of Nations in Genesis 10 is one of the most remarkable documents in the ancient world — a comprehensive map of human ethnicity covering seventy nations descended from Noah’s three sons. It is theology presented as geography: every people group on earth is connected to the one family preserved in the ark, and therefore to the one God who preserved them.

The chapter sits between the Noahic covenant (ch.9) and the Tower of Babel (ch.11), showing that God’s covenant has produced a fruitful humanity while laying the groundwork for the Babel narrative. The seventy nations will become a recurring number in Israel’s theology — the seventy elders of Exodus 24, the seventy-two sent by Jesus in Luke 10 — signaling the scope of God’s concern for all peoples. The genealogy traces through Shem to Eber (the ancestor of the Hebrews), narrowing toward Abraham: from seventy nations, God will call one man, through whom he intends to bless all the others.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 10, the table of nations, is one of the most remarkable chapters in the ancient world's literature — a comprehensive genealogical map of the known world's peoples derived from Noah's three sons. Seventy nations are listed, organized by geography and kinship, establishing the unity of the human race in its diversity: all humanity descends from Noah, and through him from Adam. The table answers the question raised by the flood: what happened to the nations that came from Noah's sons?
verseByVerse.theology: The descendants of Japheth, Ham and Shem spread into the nations of the known world. Nimrod founds Babel and Nineveh, the Canaanite clans are mapped, and Shem's line is traced through Eber and Peleg towards Abram.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel heard in this list every nation it would meet, all of them cousins. Now: God "made from one man every nation of mankind" (Acts 17:26), and the multitude before the throne comes from every one of them (Rev. 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of the sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood. The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. From these the coastland peoples spread in their lands, each with his own language, by their clans, in their nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The descendants of Noah’s sons spread out after the flood, beginning with Japheth’s line, from whom the coastland peoples spread, each with its own language, clans and nations.

The table of nations. Seventy nations in the Hebrew text: a symbol of the whole world.

Japheth. Peoples to the north and west, around the Mediterranean and Asia Minor.

One family. All nations descend from one family (Acts 17:26). There is no basis for racial superiority.

On a Tuesday. Every person you meet, of whatever nation, is your relative.
verseByVerse.note: The “table of nations” — seventy names, the whole known world descended from Noah’s three sons.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan. The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. Cush fathered Nimrod; he was the first on earth to be a mighty man. He was a mighty hunter before the LORD. Therefore it is said, "Like Nimrod a mighty hunter before the LORD." The beginning of his kingdom was Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, in the land of Shinar. From that land he went into Assyria and built Nineveh, Rehoboth-Ir, Calah, and Resen between Nineveh and Calah; that is the great city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ham’s sons include Cush, Egypt, Put and Canaan; Cush fathers Nimrod, a mighty hunter, whose kingdom begins with Babel and spreads to Assyria, where he builds Nineveh.

Nimrod. The first empire-builder. His name may suggest “we will rebel”.

Babel and Nineveh. Two great cities later opposed to God’s people.

Before the LORD. Even mighty men live under God’s eye.
verseByVerse.note: Nimrod founded cities in Babylonia (Shinar) and Assyria, including Babel and Nineveh.

verseByVerse.quote: Egypt fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorim. Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth, and the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. Afterward the clans of the Canaanites dispersed. And the territory of the Canaanites extended from Sidon in the direction of Gerar as far as Gaza, and in the direction of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, as far as Lasha. These are the sons of Ham, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt’s descendants include the ancestors of the Philistines, and Canaan’s include the Sidonians, Hittites, Jebusites, Amorites and others, whose territory reached from Sidon to Gaza and to Sodom.

The Canaanites. The peoples of the land God would give Abraham (15:18–21).

Sodom and Gomorrah. Mentioned ahead of their story (chapter 19).
