verseByVerse.quote: To Shem also, the father of all the children of Eber, the elder brother of Japheth, children were born. The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. The sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Arpachshad fathered Shelah; and Shelah fathered Eber. To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and his brother's name was Joktan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shem, ancestor of all the children of Eber, also has descendants; in Peleg’s days the earth was divided.

Eber. Perhaps the source of the word “Hebrew”.

The earth divided. Probably at Babel (chapter 11). Peleg means “division”.

Shem last. The chosen line is told last, leading on to Abraham.
verseByVerse.note: “Peleg” means division (ESV note), perhaps pointing to the scattering at Babel.

verseByVerse.quote: Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan. The territory in which they lived extended from Mesha in the direction of Sephar to the hill country of the east. These are the sons of Shem, by their clans, their languages, their lands, and their nations. These are the clans of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, in their nations, and from these the nations spread abroad on the earth after the flood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joktan’s many sons live in the east; these are the clans of Noah’s sons, from whom the nations spread after the flood.

The nations spread. Fulfilling “fill the earth” (9:1), though Babel will try to resist it.

God’s plan for the nations. Abraham’s call is for “all the families of the earth” (12:3).

For worship. Praise God for the gospel’s reach to every nation listed here, and beyond (Revelation 7:9).

10.theology:
The Unity of Humanity. Genesis 10 establishes that all human diversity — ethnic, linguistic, cultural — flows from a single source. Racism is therefore not merely a social problem but a theological one, a denial of the common humanity Genesis 10 affirms. Paul makes this explicit in Acts 17:26 and in his theology of the one new humanity in Christ (Eph. 2:14–16), where the dividing wall between peoples is abolished at the cross.

Election and Mission. The Table of Nations sets the stage for Genesis 12’s call of Abraham. The widening of chapter 10 — seventy nations spreading across the earth — makes the narrowing of chapter 12 intelligible as a missional strategy, not ethnic favoritism. God narrows his focus to Abraham not to exclude the nations but to bless them through him. The “all the families of the earth” of 12:3 points back to the families of chapter 10.
10.examples:
Then: The Table of Nations has no parallel in ancient literature for its scope. No ancient text attempts a map of all known humanity. Genesis 10 is a theological declaration that one God made all peoples — a claim with no parallel in the ancient world’s polytheistic frameworks where different nations had different gods.

Now: The Table of Nations is a standing rebuke to every form of ethnic nationalism claiming divine sanction for one people’s superiority. All nations equally descend from the same family, preserved by the same grace, destined in God’s purpose to be blessed through the same seed (12:3; Rev. 5:9). The diversity of nations is a gift, not a problem — the beautiful filling of the earth that God commanded and Genesis 10 maps.

11.title: The Tower of Babel
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the whole earth had one language and the same words.<sup>2</sup>And as people migrated from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there.<sup>3</sup>And they said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks, and burn them thoroughly." And they had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar.<sup>4</sup>Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be dispersed over the face of the whole earth."<sup>5</sup>And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of man had built.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said, "Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them.<sup>7</sup>Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another's speech."<sup>8</sup>So the LORD dispersed them from there over the face of all the earth, and they left off building the city.<sup>9</sup>Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. And from there the LORD dispersed them over the face of all the earth.<sup>10</sup>These are the generations of Shem. When Shem was 100 years old, he fathered Arpachshad two years after the flood.<sup>11</sup>And Shem lived after he fathered Arpachshad 500 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>12</sup>When Arpachshad had lived 35 years, he fathered Shelah.<sup>13</sup>And Arpachshad lived after he fathered Shelah 403 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>14</sup>When Shelah had lived 30 years, he fathered Eber.<sup>15</sup>And Shelah lived after he fathered Eber 403 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>16</sup>When Eber had lived 34 years, he fathered Peleg.<sup>17</sup>And Eber lived after he fathered Peleg 430 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>18</sup>When Peleg had lived 30 years, he fathered Reu.<sup>19</sup>And Peleg lived after he fathered Reu 209 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>20</sup>When Reu had lived 32 years, he fathered Serug.<sup>21</sup>And Reu lived after he fathered Serug 207 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>22</sup>When Serug had lived 30 years, he fathered Nahor.<sup>23</sup>And Serug lived after he fathered Nahor 200 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>24</sup>When Nahor had lived 29 years, he fathered Terah.<sup>25</sup>And Nahor lived after he fathered Terah 119 years and had other sons and daughters.<sup>26</sup>When Terah had lived 70 years, he fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.<sup>27</sup>Now these are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot.<sup>28</sup>Haran died in the presence of his father Terah in the land of his kindred, in Ur of the Chaldeans.<sup>29</sup>And Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran the father of Milcah and Iscah.<sup>30</sup>Now Sarai was barren; she had no child.<sup>31</sup>Terah took Abram his son and Lot the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram's wife, and they went forth together from Ur of the Chaldeans to go into the land of Canaan, but when they came to Haran, they settled there.<sup>32</sup>The days of Terah were 205 years, and Terah died in Haran.
11.overview:
The Tower of Babel is the climax of the primeval history (chapters 1–11) and the low-water mark of the human project. After the flood, after the Noahic covenant, after the Table of Nations — humanity unites in collective rebellion: “Let us make a name for ourselves” (v.4). Two “let us” speeches stand at either end of the primeval history: the Creator’s (“let us make man,” 1:26) and the fallen creature’s (“let us make a name,” 11:4). After Babel comes God’s call to one man (“Go from your country,” 12:1). The arc is creation, rebellion, call.

Babel is the anti-Pentecost. At Pentecost (Acts 2), the Holy Spirit reverses the confusion of languages — people from “every nation under heaven” hear the gospel each in their own tongue, and the divided humanity of Babel begins its reunion in the body of Christ. What sin scattered, grace re-gathers. The city of Babel reappears in Revelation as Babylon — the great empire that makes its name at the expense of the nations — and it falls (Rev. 18). The New Jerusalem replaces it: built by God, not human ambition, with the Lamb as its light.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Babel narrative is one of the most compressed and theologically rich passages in Genesis. In nine verses, the text explains the origin of the world's linguistic and cultural diversity, diagnoses the fundamental sin of human civilization, and describes God's decisive intervention. The unity of language that existed before Babel was not merely a linguistic fact but a theological state — a world organized around a common human project of self-glorification rather than the worship of God. The scattering and confusion of languages is not divine cruelty but covenant faithfulness: God will not allow humanity to build its way to autonomy.
verseByVerse.theology: With one language, the people settle in Shinar and build a city and a tower to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. The LORD comes down, confuses their language, and scatters them; the city is called Babel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the ziggurat that reached for heaven was so small that God had to come down to see it. Now: at Pentecost the Spirit reversed the confusion of tongues (Acts 2:5–11), gathering the scattered into one people in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the whole earth had one language and the same words. And as people migrated from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and settled there. And they said to one another, "Come, let us make bricks, and burn them thoroughly." And they had brick for stone, and bitumen for mortar. Then they said, "Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, and let us make a name for ourselves, lest we be dispersed over the face of the whole earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With one language, people settle in Shinar and resolve to build a city and a tower with its top in the heavens, to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered.

Shinar. Babylonia.

Bricks for stone. Human technology, used in pride.

A tower to heaven. Probably a ziggurat, a temple-tower to reach the gods.

A name for ourselves. Self-glory. God will give Abram a great name as a gift (12:2).

Lest we be scattered. Defying God’s command to fill the earth.

On a Tuesday. Where are you building a name for yourself?
verseByVerse.note: The tower was probably a ziggurat, a stepped temple-tower of Mesopotamia. Shinar is Babylonia.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of man had built. And the LORD said, "Behold, they are one people, and they have all one language, and this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them. Come, let us go down and there confuse their language, so that they may not understand one another's speech." So the LORD dispersed them from there over the face of all the earth, and they left off building the city. Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. And from there the LORD dispersed them over the face of all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD comes down to see the tower, confuses their language so they cannot understand one another, and scatters them over the earth; so the city is called Babel.

Came down. Irony: their tower to heaven was so small that God had to come down to see it.

Let us. As at creation (1:26).

Confusion. Babel sounds like the Hebrew for “confuse”. Babylon claimed it meant “gate of god”.

Mercy in judgment. Scattering limits united rebellion.

Pentecost. Babel reversed: one gospel heard in many languages (Acts 2:5–11).

For worship. Thank God who unites the nations in Christ, not in pride.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Babel” sounds like the Hebrew for “confused.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–26 — The Genealogy from Shem to Abram
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The genealogy from Shem to Abram connects the flood narrative to the patriarchal narratives with the same careful structure as the genealogy of chapter 5 — but with one crucial difference: the lifespans are dramatically shorter. The long lives of the pre-flood patriarchs (averaging 900+ years) give way to steadily shorter lives in Shem's line (600 for Shem, 239 for Peleg, 148 for Nahor, 205 for Terah), still far longer than ours. The genealogy narrows the camera: from all the nations of the earth (ch.10) to Shem's line specifically, and within that line to the family through whom God's redemptive purpose will run.
verseByVerse.theology: Ten generations lead from Shem to Abram, with lifespans shortening towards the span we know. The line of promise is kept in order through ordinary fathers and sons.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God was keeping a family tree while Babel was building. Now: Luke traces Jesus back through these names (Luke 3:34–36); they are the beams of a line that ends in a manger.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Shem. When Shem was 100 years old, he fathered Arpachshad two years after the flood. And Shem lived after he fathered Arpachshad 500 years and had other sons and daughters. When Arpachshad had lived 35 years, he fathered Shelah. And Arpachshad lived after he fathered Shelah 403 years and had other sons and daughters. When Shelah had lived 30 years, he fathered Eber. And Shelah lived after he fathered Eber 403 years and had other sons and daughters. When Eber had lived 34 years, he fathered Peleg. And Eber lived after he fathered Peleg 430 years and had other sons and daughters. When Peleg had lived 30 years, he fathered Reu. And Peleg lived after he fathered Reu 209 years and had other sons and daughters. When Reu had lived 32 years, he fathered Serug. And Reu lived after he fathered Serug 207 years and had other sons and daughters. When Serug had lived 30 years, he fathered Nahor. And Serug lived after he fathered Nahor 200 years and had other sons and daughters. When Nahor had lived 29 years, he fathered Terah. And Nahor lived after he fathered Terah 119 years and had other sons and daughters. When Terah had lived 70 years, he fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shem’s line runs through ten generations to Terah, with lifespans getting shorter.

Ten generations. As from Adam to Noah (chapter 5).

Shorter lives. From about 600 to around 200 years.

No “and he died”. Unlike chapter 5. The focus moves forward to Abram.

Textual note. The Greek Old Testament adds a Cainan between Arpachshad and Shelah, which Luke follows (Luke 3:36), and gives different ages. The Hebrew omits him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The genealogy transitions from the formula-chain of Shem's descendants to a fuller narrative introduction of Terah's family. These six verses are transitional tissue between the primeval history and the patriarchal narrative proper. They introduce the cast — Abram, Nahor, Haran, Lot, Sarai, Milcah — and they plant the first great obstacle: Sarai is barren. They also begin a journey that does not reach its destination: Terah sets out for Canaan but stops at Haran and dies there. The final step — Canaan — will require the call of God in chapter 12.
verseByVerse.theology: Terah's family is introduced: Abram, Nahor, Haran (who dies in Ur), Lot, Milcah, and Sarai, who is barren. Terah sets out for Canaan but settles in Haran and dies there.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the promise of offspring is about to be given to a man whose wife cannot conceive. Now: many lives set out for the right place and settle halfway; God's purpose goes on to the one he calls.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the generations of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot. Haran died in the presence of his father Terah in the land of his kindred, in Ur of the Chaldeans. And Abram and Nahor took wives. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran the father of Milcah and Iscah. Now Sarai was barren; she had no child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terah fathers Abram, Nahor and Haran; Haran dies in Ur, Abram marries Sarai, and Sarai is barren.

Ur of the Chaldeans. A great city in southern Mesopotamia, centred on worship of the moon god (Joshua 24:2).

Sarai was barren. The promised line seems to end here. God’s promise will come through impossibility.

On a Tuesday. Where things seem impossible, God often begins.
verseByVerse.note: Ur was a great city of southern Mesopotamia. Sarai’s barrenness sets up the whole Abraham story: the promise depends on God alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Terah took Abram his son and Lot the son of Haran, his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram's wife, and they went forth together from Ur of the Chaldeans to go into the land of Canaan, but when they came to Haran, they settled there. The days of Terah were 205 years, and Terah died in Haran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terah takes Abram, Lot and Sarai from Ur towards Canaan, but they settle in Haran, where Terah dies.

Towards Canaan. God had already called Abram in Ur (Acts 7:2–4).

Settled in Haran. Stopping halfway.

For worship. Thank God who calls people out of idolatry to himself.
verseByVerse.note: Haran lay in northern Mesopotamia, on the route from Ur to Canaan.

11.theology:
Babel and Pentecost. The confusion of languages at Babel is explicitly reversed at Pentecost (Acts 2): the Spirit falls, and “each one was hearing them speak in his own language” (Acts 2:6). What sin scattered, the Spirit re-gathers. The church — the community of every tribe and tongue and people — is the new humanity that Babel failed to produce: united not by self-aggrandizement but by a common Spirit, a common Lord, a common calling. Babel sought unity through uniformity; the gospel creates unity through reconciliation.

The City of God. Augustine’s great work draws the line this text draws: the City of Man (Babel/Babylon) built on self-love, and the City of God built on love of God. Every human empire is a version of Babel — unified by a common name, organized around collective self-interest, finite and fallen. The City of God is the New Jerusalem of Revelation 21: built by God, inhabited by the redeemed from every nation, with the Lamb as its temple and light.
11.examples:
Then: The tower of Babel was almost certainly a ziggurat — the stepped temple-towers of Mesopotamia seeking a place where heaven and earth met. Genesis subverts the ziggurat theology: the LORD “comes down” not because the tower brought him closer but because the tower was so small he had to descend to see it. The meeting place between heaven and earth cannot be built from below; it must be given from above.

Now: Every age builds its Babel: the utopian project, the techno-optimist vision of unlimited human capability, the nation that makes its name at the expense of others. The twentieth century’s most ambitious Babels — Soviet communism, National Socialism — demonstrated most vividly what Genesis 11 warned: unlimited collective human capacity directed by a godless vision produces world-historical catastrophe. The antidote is not better planning but the fear of the LORD — recognition that human civilization is always derivative, always dependent, always accountable to the God who “came down to see” what we were building.

12.title: Go from Your Country
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the LORD said to Abram, "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.<sup>2</sup>And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing.<sup>3</sup>I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed."<sup>4</sup>So Abram went, as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran.<sup>5</sup>And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people that they had acquired in Haran, and they set out to go to the land of Canaan. When they came to the land of Canaan,<sup>6</sup>Abram passed through the land to the place at Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time the Canaanites were in the land.<sup>7</sup>Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, "To your offspring I will give this land." So he built there an altar to the LORD, who had appeared to him.<sup>8</sup>From there he moved to the hill country on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. And there he built an altar to the LORD and called upon the name of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And Abram journeyed on, still going toward the Negeb.<sup>10</sup>Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was severe in the land.<sup>11</sup>When he was about to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, "I know that you are a woman beautiful in appearance,<sup>12</sup>and when the Egyptians see you, they will say, 'This is his wife.' Then they will kill me, but they will let you live.<sup>13</sup>Say you are my sister, that it may go well with me because of you, and that my life may be spared for your sake."<sup>14</sup>When Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful.<sup>15</sup>And when the princes of Pharaoh saw her, they praised her to Pharaoh. And the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house.<sup>16</sup>And for her sake he dealt well with Abram; and he had sheep, oxen, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels.<sup>17</sup>But the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram's wife.<sup>18</sup>So Pharaoh called Abram and said, "What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife?<sup>19</sup>Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her for my wife? Now then, here is your wife; take her, and go."<sup>20</sup>And Pharaoh gave men orders concerning him, and they sent him away with his wife and all that he had.
12.overview:
Genesis 12:1–3 is the pivot of the entire Old Testament — and, in a real sense, the pivot of all of human history. The primeval narrative (chapters 1–11) has traced the spread of sin from the garden to Babel, the progressive corruption of humanity, the futility of every human attempt to secure its own future. Now, into that darkness, God speaks to one man: “Go.” The call is not explained or justified; it is sovereign, gracious, and unconditional. From the thousands of post-Babel families scattered across the earth, God chooses Abram — not because of his merit but because of his mercy.

The threefold promise is the theological spine of the entire Abrahamic narrative and, ultimately, of the whole Bible: land (a place to be, a home, an inheritance), seed (a family, a nation, a people), and blessing (a purpose — “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed”). Paul identifies this blessing as the gospel itself: “the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘In you shall all the nations be blessed’” (Gal. 3:8). Genesis 12 is the gospel in seed form.

The chapter also contains Abram’s first recorded failure: in Egypt, afraid for his life, he passes off his wife Sarai as his sister, allowing Pharaoh to take her into his household (vv.10–20). The man God has just called to be the father of the blessed nation immediately fails to protect his wife. The patriarchal narrative is relentlessly honest: the vessels through whom God works are cracked. Grace runs through broken people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Call of Abram and the Covenant Promise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 12:1–3 is the hinge of the entire Bible. After eleven chapters of de-creation — the fall, Cain's murder, the flood, Babel — God calls one man and makes him the bearer of a promise that encompasses all humanity: 'in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.' The call is unconditional and sovereign: God commands, and Abram obeys. The promise is comprehensive: land, seed, and blessing — three dimensions that structure the entire subsequent biblical narrative. Abram's departure is the great pattern of biblical faith.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD calls Abram to leave country, kindred and father's house for a land he will be shown, and promises a great nation, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth. Abram goes, and builds altars in a land the Canaanites still hold.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abram went out "not knowing where he was going" (Heb. 11:8). Now: Paul calls this promise the gospel preached beforehand (Gal. 3:8), and every believing Gentile is its fulfilment.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD said to Abram, "Go from your country and your kindred and your father's house to the land that I will show you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD calls Abram to leave his country, kindred and father’s house and go to a land God will show him.

The turning point of Genesis. After Babel, God starts again with one man.

Three leavings. Each harder than the last.

A land I will show you. He goes without knowing where (Hebrews 11:8).

On a Tuesday. What is God asking you to leave to follow him?

verseByVerse.quote: And I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you and make your name great, so that you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and him who dishonors you I will curse, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to make Abram a great nation, bless him, make his name great, bless those who bless him and curse those who dishonour him, and in him bless all the families of the earth.

Seven promises. Nation, blessing, name, a blessing to others, protection, judgment, worldwide blessing.

A name. What Babel grasped for (11:4), God gives.

All the families. The gospel announced in advance (Galatians 3:8). Fulfilled in Christ, Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:16).

Where Christians differ: bless Israel today? Some Christian Zionists apply “I will bless those who bless you” to support for the modern state of Israel. Verdict: the promise is fulfilled in Christ and in all who belong to him by faith (Galatians 3:7–9, 29). Christians should love the Jewish people and pray for their salvation, and judge any nation’s actions by God’s justice.
verseByVerse.note: The promise to bless “all the families of the earth” through Abram is fulfilled in Christ and the gospel going to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abram went, as the LORD had told him, and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the people that they had acquired in Haran, and they set out to go to the land of Canaan. When they came to the land of Canaan, Abram passed through the land to the place at Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. At that time the Canaanites were in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abram goes as the LORD told him, at seventy-five, taking Sarai, Lot and their possessions to the land of Canaan, where the Canaanites are living.

Abram went. Faith obeys.

Seventy-five. Never too late for God’s call.

The Canaanite was in the land. The promise faces real obstacles.
verseByVerse.note: Shechem lay in the hill country at the heart of Canaan. The “oak” may be a terebinth (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said, "To your offspring I will give this land." So he built there an altar to the LORD, who had appeared to him. From there he moved to the hill country on the east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. And there he built an altar to the LORD and called upon the name of the LORD. And Abram journeyed on, still going toward the Negeb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD appears and promises the land to Abram’s offspring, and Abram builds altars and calls on the LORD’s name.

To your offspring. Not to Abram himself, who will own only a grave (23:19; Acts 7:5).

Where Christians differ: the land promise. Dispensationalists expect its future fulfilment to ethnic Israel. Verdict: it was fulfilled in Joshua’s day (Joshua 21:43–45), and points beyond Canaan to the whole world (Romans 4:13) and the new earth that Abraham himself looked for (Hebrews 11:10, 16).

Altars. Worship marks the land as God’s.

For worship. Build an altar wherever you live: make it a place of worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — Abram in Egypt: Faith and Failure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sojourn in Egypt is the first test of the covenant and the first recorded failure of the covenant patriarch. Famine drives Abram south, and fear drives him to a half-truth that endangers Sarai and the covenant promise. Yet God protects Sarai, protects the promise, and restores Abram without destroying him. The episode establishes a pattern that will recur throughout Genesis: the patriarch's faith fails, the covenant is endangered by human faithlessness, God preserves what the human cannot, and the story continues. Grace is more tenacious than human failure.
verseByVerse.theology: Famine drives Abram to Egypt, where fear makes him pass Sarai off as his sister. Pharaoh takes her, and the LORD strikes Pharaoh's house with plagues until she is returned and Abram is sent away.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the episode rehearses the exodus — famine, Egypt, plagues, and a departure with wealth. Now: the promise rests not on the faithfulness of the man carrying it but on the God who made it (2 Tim. 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a famine in the land. So Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was severe in the land. When he was about to enter Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife, "I know that you are a woman beautiful in appearance, and when the Egyptians see you, they will say, 'This is his wife.' Then they will kill me, but they will let you live. Say you are my sister, that it may go well with me because of you, and that my life may be spared for your sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When famine comes, Abram goes to Egypt and asks Sarai to say she is his sister, so that the Egyptians will not kill him.

Famine. A test right after the promise.

Fear. The man of faith acts in fear.

A half-truth. She was his half-sister (20:12), but the aim was to deceive.

On a Tuesday. Faith in one area does not guarantee it in another. Watch your weak points.
verseByVerse.note: Sarai was in fact Abram’s half-sister (20:12).

verseByVerse.quote: When Abram entered Egypt, the Egyptians saw that the woman was very beautiful. And when the princes of Pharaoh saw her, they praised her to Pharaoh. And the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house. And for her sake he dealt well with Abram; and he had sheep, oxen, male donkeys, male servants, female servants, female donkeys, and camels. But the LORD afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s officials praise Sarai’s beauty, she is taken into his house, Abram is enriched, and the LORD strikes Pharaoh’s house with plagues.

Sarai endangered. The mother of the promised line, in a foreign king’s harem.

Abram profits. From his deception.

God intervenes. He protects his promise when his servant fails.

Plagues on Egypt. A foreshadowing of the exodus.

verseByVerse.quote: So Pharaoh called Abram and said, "What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she was your wife? Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her for my wife? Now then, here is your wife; take her, and go." And Pharaoh gave men orders concerning him, and they sent him away with his wife and all that he had.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh rebukes Abram for not telling him she was his wife, returns her, and sends them away.

Rebuked by a pagan. A humiliating moment for the man of God.

What it does not mean. Scripture does not approve Abram’s lie; it records it honestly.

For worship. Thank God who keeps his promises despite our failures.

12.theology:
Election and Mission. Genesis 12:1–3 is the Bible’s foundational text on election: God chooses Abram not because of his merit but because of his sovereign purpose. But the election is always missional: Abram is chosen so that “all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” Election in the Bible is never an end in itself; it is always a means to a universal end. The chosen people exist for the unchosen peoples. Israel is elect so that the nations might be saved. The church is chosen in Christ (Eph. 1:4) to be the instrument through which the blessing of Abraham reaches every people.

The Gospel in Seed. Paul’s identification of Genesis 12:3 as “the gospel preached beforehand” (Gal. 3:8) is one of the New Testament’s most striking exegetical moves. The blessing to all nations was always, at its root, the justification of the ungodly by faith in the one through whom the blessing comes. The seed of Abraham through whom all nations are blessed is Christ (Gal. 3:16). Genesis 12 is not prologue to the gospel; it is the gospel’s first public announcement.
12.examples:
Then: Abram’s departure from Ur and Haran was geographically and culturally momentous — leaving the most advanced civilization of the ancient world (Mesopotamia) for a nomadic existence in an unknown land. Ur was a major city with a sophisticated culture; Abram left security for promise. The Egyptian episode (vv.10–20) reflects the political realities of the ancient Near East: a powerful Pharaoh could take whatever he wanted, and a foreign visitor had no recourse. Only divine intervention (v.17) could protect the powerless.

Now: The call of Abram is the paradigm for every Christian vocation: “go... to the land I will show you.” Not a detailed plan but a direction and a Caller. The three promises — land, seed, blessing — find their fulfillment in Christ and the new creation: the land is the new earth (Rom. 4:13: Abraham is “heir of the world”), the seed is Christ and all in him (Gal. 3:29), and the blessing is the gospel offered to all nations. Every Sunday, the church gathers around the heir of Abraham, receiving the blessing promised before any one of us existed.

13.title: Lot and Abram Part Ways
13.text: <sup>1</sup>So Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the Negeb.<sup>2</sup>Now Abram was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold.<sup>3</sup>And he journeyed on from the Negeb as far as Bethel to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai,<sup>4</sup>to the place where he had made an altar at the first. And there Abram called upon the name of the LORD.<sup>5</sup>And Lot, who went with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents,<sup>6</sup>so that the land could not support both of them dwelling together; for their possessions were so great that they could not dwell together,<sup>7</sup>and there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot's livestock. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were dwelling in the land.<sup>8</sup>Then Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen, for we are kinsmen.<sup>9</sup>Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself from me. If you take the left hand, then I will go to the right, or if you take the right hand, then I will go to the left."<sup>10</sup>And Lot lifted up his eyes and saw that the Jordan Valley was well watered everywhere like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, in the direction of Zoar. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.)<sup>11</sup>So Lot chose for himself all the Jordan Valley, and Lot journeyed east. Thus they separated from each other.<sup>12</sup>Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled among the cities of the valley and moved his tent as far as Sodom.<sup>13</sup>Now the men of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD.<sup>14</sup>The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward,<sup>15</sup>for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.<sup>16</sup>I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if one can count the dust of the earth, your offspring also can be counted.<sup>17</sup>Arise, walk through the length and the breadth of the land, for I will give it to you."<sup>18</sup>So Abram moved his tent and came and settled by the oaks of Mamre, which are at Hebron, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
13.overview:
The separation of Abram and Lot is one of Scripture’s most revealing character studies — a double portrait of two ways of living before God. Abram, the man of promise, defers to his nephew and gives him the choice of land. Lot, the man of sight, “lifted up his eyes” and chose what looked best — a valley well-watered “like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt” (v.10). The comparison is ominous: the garden of the LORD is where humanity fell; Egypt is where Abram’s faith failed. Lot is choosing by appearance, by the visible and the attractive, and his choice will lead him to Sodom.

Abram’s generosity is extraordinary. As the senior kinsman with the right of first choice, he gives the choice to Lot — and does so without condition or complaint. It is the act of a man whose security is not in the land but in the God who promised the land. Because Abram holds the promise lightly, he can afford to be generous with what the promise includes. The person whose identity is in God can give away what the person whose identity is in possessions must protect at all costs.

After Lot departs, God renews the covenant promise (vv.14–17) — this time more expansively, extending the gift to Abram’s offspring “forever.” Generosity does not impoverish the person of faith; it creates space for God to reaffirm and expand what he has already given.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Abram and Lot Separate; the Promise Renewed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 13 narrates the peaceful separation of Abram and Lot and the magnificent renewal of the covenant promise. The episode is a study in contrasts: Lot lifts his eyes and chooses by sight — the well-watered Jordan plain, like Egypt, like Eden — and goes toward Sodom. Abram does not choose; God gives. After Lot has departed in the direction that looks most promising, God speaks to Abram and renews the promise in its fullest form yet: the land as far as the eye can see in every direction, the seed as numerous as the dust of the earth. The one who does not grasp receives everything; the one who grasps by sight ends up in Sodom.
verseByVerse.theology: Abram returns from Egypt to his first altar. When the land cannot hold both households, he lets Lot choose; Lot chooses the well-watered valley and moves his tent towards Sodom. Then God tells Abram to lift up his eyes, and gives him all the land he can see and offspring like the dust of the earth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lot chose by sight what looked like Eden and like Egypt, six chapters before the fire. Now: the believer who is sure of his inheritance can afford to give way, because the supply is not finite.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the Negeb. Now Abram was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold. And he journeyed on from the Negeb as far as Bethel to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai, to the place where he had made an altar at the first. And there Abram called upon the name of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abram returns from Egypt very rich, and goes back to the place of his first altar near Bethel, where he calls on the LORD.

Very rich. Wealth will bring its own trouble.

Back to the altar. Returning to where he had worshipped before Egypt: a picture of repentance.

On a Tuesday. After failure, return to the place of worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And Lot, who went with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents, so that the land could not support both of them dwelling together; for their possessions were so great that they could not dwell together, and there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's livestock and the herdsmen of Lot's livestock. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were dwelling in the land. Then Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen, for we are kinsmen. Is not the whole land before you? Separate yourself from me. If you take the left hand, then I will go to the right, or if you take the right hand, then I will go to the left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abram and Lot have so many flocks that the land cannot support both, and their herdsmen quarrel; Abram says there must be no strife between them, and offers Lot the choice of land.

Prosperity and strife. Wealth can divide families.

We are kinsmen. Peace matters more than possessions.

Abram gives way. The elder, who holds the promise, lets the younger choose. Faith can afford to be generous.

On a Tuesday. Where could you give up your rights for the sake of peace?

verseByVerse.quote: And Lot lifted up his eyes and saw that the Jordan Valley was well watered everywhere like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, in the direction of Zoar. (This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.) So Lot chose for himself all the Jordan Valley, and Lot journeyed east. Thus they separated from each other. Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled among the cities of the valley and moved his tent as far as Sodom. Now the men of Sodom were wicked, great sinners against the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lot sees the well-watered Jordan Valley, like the garden of the LORD, chooses it, and settles near Sodom, whose men are very wicked.

Lifted up his eyes. He chooses by sight.

Like Eden and Egypt. Beautiful and prosperous.

Towards Sodom. Step by step: towards, near, then inside (19:1).

On a Tuesday. Choose by God’s values, not only by what looks good.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him, "Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for all the land that you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever. I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth, so that if one can count the dust of the earth, your offspring also can be counted. Arise, walk through the length and the breadth of the land, for I will give it to you." So Abram moved his tent and came and settled by the oaks of Mamre, which are at Hebron, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Lot leaves, the LORD tells Abram to look in every direction, for he will give him and his offspring all the land for ever, and make his offspring like the dust; Abram settles at Hebron and builds an altar.

Lift up your eyes. Abram too looks, but at God’s promise.

Like the dust. Countless.

Walk the land. Claiming it by faith.

For worship. Thank God that he gives more than we give up.
verseByVerse.note: Hebron, about 20 miles south of Jerusalem, became Abraham’s main home.

13.theology:
Walking by Faith vs. Walking by Sight. The contrast between Abram and Lot is the Old Testament’s sharpest illustration of 2 Corinthians 5:7: “we walk by faith, not by sight.” Lot chose by what he could see — the attractive, the productive, the comfortable. Abram gave away the visible and received the covenant promise — invisible, future, vast. The theology of faith in the entire biblical tradition is grounded in this kind of choice: to trust the word of God over the evidence of the eyes, to hold the present loosely for the sake of the promised future.

Generosity and the Covenant. Abram’s generosity is not merely a moral virtue but a theological posture: he holds the land loosely because he knows his security is in the God who promised the land, not in the land itself. This is the freedom of the person whose identity is in God rather than in possessions. This is the distinctive freedom the gospel creates: because we are already “blessed with every spiritual blessing in Christ” (Eph. 1:3), we can be radically generous with earthly blessings, holding them as stewards rather than owners.
13.examples:
Then: The conflict between Abram’s and Lot’s herdsmen reflects the genuine pastoral economics of the ancient Near East: grazing land was a scarce and fiercely contested resource. Abram’s offer to let Lot choose first was a remarkable act of social deference in a culture where seniority and clan rights were taken extremely seriously. The Sodom reference (v.13) would have immediately signaled danger to the original reader: Sodom was already a byword for wickedness before chapters 18–19 make it explicit.

Now: Lot’s incremental drift toward Sodom is a timeless spiritual warning: the most dangerous moral movements are rarely sudden. The gradual normalization of what once seemed clearly wrong, the slow adjustment of proximity to what we know to be destructive, the reasonable-sounding series of small choices that ends in a place we never intended to be — this is Lot’s journey. And Abram’s generosity challenges every Christian instinct toward self-protection: the one who gives the first choice away, trusting in the covenant promise, receives a promise that makes the sacrificed land look small.

14.title: Melchizedek King of Salem
14.text: <sup>1</sup>In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim,<sup>2</sup>these kings made war with Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar).<sup>3</sup>And all these joined forces in the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea).<sup>4</sup>Twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled.<sup>5</sup>In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and defeated the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim,<sup>6</sup>and the Horites in their hill country of Seir as far as El-paran on the border of the wilderness.<sup>7</sup>Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh) and defeated all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who were dwelling in Hazazon-tamar.<sup>8</sup>Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) went out, and they joined battle in the Valley of Siddim<sup>9</sup>with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five.<sup>10</sup>Now the Valley of Siddim was full of bitumen pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some fell into them, and the rest fled to the hill country.<sup>11</sup>So the enemy took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their provisions, and went their way.<sup>12</sup>They also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, who was dwelling in Sodom, and his possessions, and went their way.<sup>13</sup>Then one who had escaped came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and of Aner. These were allies of Abram.<sup>14</sup>When Abram heard that his kinsman had been taken captive, he led forth his trained men, born in his house, 318 of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan.<sup>15</sup>And he divided his forces against them by night, he and his servants, and defeated them and pursued them to Hobah, north of Damascus.<sup>16</sup>Then he brought back all the possessions, and also brought back his kinsman Lot with his possessions, and the women and the people.<sup>17</sup>After his return from the defeat of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him at the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King's Valley).<sup>18</sup>And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.)<sup>19</sup>And he blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth;<sup>20</sup>and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!" And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.<sup>21</sup>And the king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the persons, but take the goods for yourself."<sup>22</sup>But Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth,<sup>23</sup>that I would not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours, lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.'<sup>24</sup>I will take nothing but what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me. Let Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre take their share."
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is one of the most theologically compressed chapters in Genesis. A regional war, Lot’s capture, Abram’s rescue mission, and then — at the chapter’s center — an encounter that the letter to the Hebrews calls one of the most significant in the entire Old Testament: the meeting with Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High (vv.18–20). This mysterious figure appears without genealogy, blesses Abram, receives a tithe from him, and disappears from the Genesis narrative. In the Old Testament he will appear again only in Psalm 110:4, where the coming king is declared “a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.”

Hebrews 5–7 develops the Melchizedek typology with extraordinary richness: Melchizedek is greater than Abraham (Abraham paid him a tithe, not the reverse), greater than the Levitical priesthood (which descended from Abraham and therefore, in a sense, paid Melchizedek a tithe while still in Abraham’s loins), and he is a type of Christ — king and priest simultaneously, without beginning or end of days as recorded in Scripture, offering blessing rather than requiring sacrifice. Jesus is the true Melchizedek: the eternal king-priest whose priesthood supersedes the Levitical order and accomplishes what it could only anticipate.

The bread and wine Melchizedek brings (v.18) have drawn eucharistic reflection from the earliest church fathers: the one who is type of Christ brings the elements that Christ himself will use at the Last Supper to seal the new covenant. The encounter is brief but reverberates across the entire canon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Battle of the Kings and the Rescue of Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 14 introduces a different literary register: the world of international politics, military alliance, and urban civilization. Four kings defeat five; the cities of the plain are sacked; Lot is taken captive. Abram responds with extraordinary military skill — 318 trained men defeating a coalition that has already defeated the five cities of the plain — and recovers both Lot and the plunder. The chapter establishes Abram as a significant figure in the world of nations, a man of military capability who uses his power in the service of covenant loyalty.
verseByVerse.theology: Four eastern kings crush a rebellion of the five cities of the plain and carry off Lot, who is now living in Sodom. Abram the Hebrew pursues with 318 trained men and his Amorite allies, attacks by night, and brings back Lot, the people and the goods.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man who pitches his life in Sodom shares its weather. Now: Abram rescued a nephew who owed him nothing, the fruit of grace doing its slow work in him.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam, and Tidal king of Goiim, these kings made war with Bera king of Sodom, Birsha king of Gomorrah, Shinab king of Admah, Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar). And all these joined forces in the Valley of Siddim (that is, the Salt Sea). Twelve years they had served Chedorlaomer, but in the thirteenth year they rebelled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four eastern kings make war against five kings of the cities of the plain, including Sodom and Gomorrah.

A world at war. Abram lives among competing powers.

Real history. Kings named, with places and alliances.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourteenth year Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him came and defeated the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim in Shaveh-kiriathaim, and the Horites in their hill country of Seir as far as El-paran on the border of the wilderness. Then they turned back and came to En-mishpat (that is, Kadesh) and defeated all the country of the Amalekites, and also the Amorites who were dwelling in Hazazon-tamar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After twelve years’ subjection, the five kings rebel, and Chedorlaomer and his allies sweep through the region defeating many peoples.

Rebellion. Politics of tribute and revolt.

Rephaim and others. Peoples later met in the conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Sodom, the king of Gomorrah, the king of Admah, the king of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela (that is, Zoar) went out, and they joined battle in the Valley of Siddim with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Tidal king of Goiim, Amraphel king of Shinar, and Arioch king of Ellasar, four kings against five. Now the Valley of Siddim was full of bitumen pits, and as the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah fled, some fell into them, and the rest fled to the hill country. So the enemy took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, and all their provisions, and went their way. They also took Lot, the son of Abram's brother, who was dwelling in Sodom, and his possessions, and went their way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kings of the plain are defeated, some fall into bitumen pits, Sodom and Gomorrah are plundered, and Lot, now living in Sodom, is taken captive.

Lot in Sodom. His choice has caught up with him.

On a Tuesday. Compromising choices carry consequences.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one who had escaped came and told Abram the Hebrew, who was living by the oaks of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and of Aner. These were allies of Abram. When Abram heard that his kinsman had been taken captive, he led forth his trained men, born in his house, 318 of them, and went in pursuit as far as Dan. And he divided his forces against them by night, he and his servants, and defeated them and pursued them to Hobah, north of Damascus. Then he brought back all the possessions, and also brought back his kinsman Lot with his possessions, and the women and the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing of Lot’s capture, Abram the Hebrew leads 318 trained men in pursuit, attacks at night, defeats the kings and brings back Lot, the women, the people and the goods.

Abram the Hebrew. The first use of the word.

His kinsman. Abram rescues Lot despite Lot’s selfish choice.

A just war. To rescue the captured, not for gain.

On a Tuesday. Help the people who have treated you poorly.
verseByVerse.note: The first time the word “Hebrew” appears in the Bible. Dan lay in the far north of Canaan.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Melchizedek and the King of Sodom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The return from battle brings Abram into encounters with two kings that function as a theological test: Melchizedek of Salem blesses Abram in the name of God Most High and receives tithes; the king of Sodom offers Abram the plunder. Abram's response to each encounter reveals his theological convictions: he honors Melchizedek as a priest of the true God and refuses the king of Sodom's gift so that his prosperity will be attributed to God alone and not to any earthly king.
verseByVerse.theology: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine, blesses Abram and receives a tenth of everything. The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods; Abram refuses, having sworn to God Most High that no one should say, "I have made Abram rich."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Psalm 110:4 promises a king who will be "a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek," and Hebrews 7 finds him in Jesus. Now: the refusal of a windfall is decided before the offer comes.

verseByVerse.quote: After his return from the defeat of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, the king of Sodom went out to meet him at the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King's Valley). And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Sodom comes out to meet Abram, and Melchizedek king of Salem, priest of God Most High, brings out bread and wine.

Two kings. Sodom’s king and Salem’s, a contrast.

Melchizedek. “King of righteousness”. Salem: “peace”, probably Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2).

Priest of God Most High. A priest of the true God outside Abraham’s family.

Where Christians differ: bread and wine. Roman Catholic tradition sees a sacrifice prefiguring the Mass. Verdict: Melchizedek gives a meal of refreshment and blessing; Scripture does not call it a sacrifice. Hebrews sees him as a type of Christ’s priesthood, not of the Mass.
verseByVerse.note: Melchizedek means “king of righteousness”; Salem is usually identified with Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And he blessed him and said, "Blessed be Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand!" And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Melchizedek blesses Abram by God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth, and blesses God for the victory, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything.

The greater blesses the lesser. Hebrews 7:7.

A tenth. Abram recognises Melchizedek’s priesthood.

Where Christians differ: who was Melchizedek? Some think he was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, since he is described as “having neither beginning of days nor end of life” (Hebrews 7:3). Verdict: he was a real king-priest whose lack of recorded genealogy makes him a type of Christ, the priest for ever (Psalm 110:4).

Where Christians differ: tithing. Some argue the tithe predates the law and so still binds. Verdict: this was a voluntary gift; the New Testament calls for generous, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7), for which a tenth is a helpful guide.

For worship. Praise Christ, our king-priest.
verseByVerse.note: The first tithe in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king of Sodom said to Abram, "Give me the persons, but take the goods for yourself." But Abram said to the king of Sodom, "I have lifted my hand to the LORD, God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth, that I would not take a thread or a sandal strap or anything that is yours, lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.' I will take nothing but what the young men have eaten, and the share of the men who went with me. Let Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre take their share."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods if he returns the people, but Abram refuses even a thread, lest it be said the king made him rich, taking only his men’s share.

A test. After Melchizedek’s blessing, Sodom’s offer.

Not a thread. Abram will owe his wealth to God alone.

Fairness to others. His allies may take their share.

On a Tuesday. Refuse gains that would compromise your witness.

For worship. Thank God, Possessor of heaven and earth, the source of all you have.

14.theology:
The Order of Melchizedek. Melchizedek is the Bible’s most developed Christological type before the New Testament. The four elements of his description — king and priest simultaneously, king of peace (Salem), priest of God Most High, bringer of bread and wine — each find their fulfillment in Jesus: the king who is also high priest (Heb. 4:14), whose kingdom is peace (Eph. 2:14–15), who is the Son of God Most High (Mark 5:7), and who at the Last Supper institutes the bread and wine of the new covenant. To read Genesis 14 in canonical context is to see Christ present in the shadows of Abram’s world.

The Superiority of Christ’s Priesthood. Hebrews’ use of Melchizedek establishes the theological argument for the new covenant: the Levitical priesthood, however divinely ordained, was never the final word. It was itself subordinate to an older, greater order — a priesthood without genealogical succession and without repeated sacrifice. Jesus fulfils this order perfectly: he is priest by divine oath (“the LORD has sworn and will not change his mind,” Ps. 110:4), his priesthood is permanent (“forever”), and his sacrifice is once for all (Heb. 7:27).
14.examples:
Then: The coalition of kings in chapter 14 reflects the political realities of the ancient Near East, where city-states formed and broke alliances constantly and where regional hegemony shifted with military campaigns. That Abram — a single clan patriarch with 318 trained men — defeated a coalition of kings is presented as a miracle of divine enabling (v.20: “God Most High... has delivered your enemies into your hand”), not military strategy. Salem (Jerusalem) appears here for the first time — the city that will eventually house the temple and the throne of David, where the Son of David will be crucified and rise.

Now: The Melchizedek encounter speaks directly to the contemporary temptation to allow worldly sources — employers, governments, markets, benefactors — to become the perceived source of our prosperity, such that their claims on us feel as strong as God’s. Abram’s refusal of Sodom’s king’s goods (“lest you should say I have made Abram rich”) is the posture of the person who knows where their life comes from and cannot afford to let that clarity be muddied. And the bread and wine of Melchizedek are the standing invitation: the eternal priest-king still brings the table, and every eucharist is a meeting with the one who is greater than Abraham.

15.title: The LORD Your Shield and Reward
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: "Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great."<sup>2</sup>But Abram said, "O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?"<sup>3</sup>And Abram said, "Behold, you have given me no offspring, and a member of my household will be my heir."<sup>4</sup>And behold, the word of the LORD came to him: "This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir."<sup>5</sup>And he brought him outside and said, "Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them." Then he said to him, "So shall your offspring be."<sup>6</sup>And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.<sup>7</sup>And he said to him, "I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess."<sup>8</sup>But he said, "O Lord GOD, how am I to know that I shall possess it?"<sup>9</sup>He said to him, "Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon."<sup>10</sup>And he brought him all these, cut them in half, and laid each half over against the other. But he did not cut the birds in half.<sup>11</sup>And when birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away.<sup>12</sup>As the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. And behold, dreadful and great darkness fell upon him.<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted for four hundred years.<sup>14</sup>But I will bring judgment on the nation that they serve, and afterward they shall come out with great possessions.<sup>15</sup>As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age.<sup>16</sup>And they shall come back here in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."<sup>17</sup>When the sun had gone down and it was dark, behold, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces.<sup>18</sup>On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates,<sup>19</sup>the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites,<sup>20</sup>the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim,<sup>21</sup>the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites and the Jebusites."
15.overview:
Genesis 15 contains two of the most theologically significant moments in the entire Bible. The first is verse 6: “And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.” Paul quotes this verse in Romans 4:3 and Galatians 3:6 as the definitive Old Testament statement of justification by faith — the declaration that right standing before God comes not through works but through trust in God’s promise. This verse is the theological center of gravity of the entire patriarchal narrative and, ultimately, of the doctrine of salvation.

The second is the covenant-cutting ceremony of verses 9–17. Abram prepares the animals, splits them in two, and lays the halves opposite each other — the standard form of an ancient Near Eastern covenant ceremony, in which both parties would walk between the pieces, invoking the self-curse: “may what happened to these animals happen to me if I break this covenant.” Then Abram falls into a deep sleep, and God alone — represented by the smoking fire pot and flaming torch — passes between the pieces. Abram does not walk. The covenant is unilateral: God swears by himself (Heb. 6:13), taking the full obligation of the covenant on himself. If the covenant breaks, it will cost God, not Abram.

This is the theological shape of grace: God takes the curse of covenant-breaking upon himself. The cross is where that self-curse was fulfilled: God the Son bore the judgment that the broken covenant demanded, walking through the pieces so that his people would not have to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Covenant Confirmed: Abram's Faith and God's Oath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 15 is one of the most theologically significant chapters in the Old Testament. It contains the first direct divine statement that faith is credited as righteousness (v.6), the formal ratification of the covenant by divine oath (vv.9–21), and the first explicit prophecy of Israel's Egyptian bondage and the Exodus (vv.13–16). The chapter is in two movements: a dialogue about the promise of offspring (vv.1–6), and a covenant ratification ceremony about the promise of land (vv.7–21).
verseByVerse.theology: God tells Abram not to fear, and answers his complaint of childlessness with the stars: "So shall your offspring be." Abram believes, and it is counted to him as righteousness. Then God cuts a covenant for the land, foretells four hundred years of affliction, and passes alone between the pieces as a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul builds justification by faith on verse 6, reckoned before circumcision (Rom. 4:9–12). Now: God took both sides of the covenant on himself, and in Christ he bore its curse (Gal. 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: After these things the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision: "Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great." But Abram said, "O Lord GOD, what will you give me, for I continue childless, and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus?" And Abram said, "Behold, you have given me no offspring, and a member of my household will be my heir."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a vision God tells Abram not to fear, for he is his shield and great reward; but Abram asks what God can give him while he is childless, with a servant as his heir.

Fear not. After the battle, fear of reprisal.

Your shield. God himself is his protection and his reward, not the spoils he refused (14:23).

An honest complaint. Faith can voice its questions to God.

On a Tuesday. Bring God your real disappointment.
verseByVerse.note: Damascus was a city of Syria, north of Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the word of the LORD came to him: "This man shall not be your heir; your very own son shall be your heir." And he brought him outside and said, "Look toward heaven, and number the stars, if you are able to number them." Then he said to him, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says his heir will be his own son, takes him outside, and tells him his offspring will be as many as the stars.

Your very own son. Specific and impossible.

Count the stars. From dust (13:16) to stars.

For worship. Look up at the stars and remember God’s promises.

verseByVerse.quote: And he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abram believes the LORD, and the LORD counts it to him as righteousness.

Believed. Trusted God’s word, though nothing had changed.

Counted. Credited, reckoned. Righteousness was put to his account.

The key text. Paul builds justification by faith on this verse (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6).

Where Christians differ: what is counted? Some read Abram’s faith itself as the righteous act God rewards. Verdict: faith is the instrument, not the ground. God counts righteous the one who trusts him, apart from works (Romans 4:4–5), on the ground of Christ’s righteousness credited to him (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Before circumcision. Paul notes it (Romans 4:10).

For worship. Thank God that he counts believers righteous.
verseByVerse.note: One of the most quoted verses of the Old Testament in the New: righteousness counted to the one who believes.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I am the LORD who brought you out from Ur of the Chaldeans to give you this land to possess." But he said, "O Lord GOD, how am I to know that I shall possess it?" He said to him, "Bring me a heifer three years old, a female goat three years old, a ram three years old, a turtledove, and a young pigeon." And he brought him all these, cut them in half, and laid each half over against the other. But he did not cut the birds in half. And when birds of prey came down on the carcasses, Abram drove them away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God reminds Abram he brought him from Ur to give him the land; when Abram asks how he will know, God tells him to bring animals, which he cuts in half and arranges, driving away birds of prey.

How shall I know? A request for assurance, not unbelief.

Cut in two. A covenant ritual (Jeremiah 34:18–20): the parties walked between the halves, calling death on themselves if they broke it.

verseByVerse.quote: As the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell on Abram. And behold, dreadful and great darkness fell upon him. Then the LORD said to Abram, "Know for certain that your offspring will be sojourners in a land that is not theirs and will be servants there, and they will be afflicted for four hundred years. But I will bring judgment on the nation that they serve, and afterward they shall come out with great possessions. As for you, you shall go to your fathers in peace; you shall be buried in a good old age. And they shall come back here in the fourth generation, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the sun sets, a deep sleep and a dreadful darkness fall on Abram, and God tells him his offspring will be sojourners and slaves for four hundred years, then come out with great possessions, returning in the fourth generation, for the Amorites’ iniquity is not yet complete.

Egypt foretold. Slavery and exodus.

Not yet complete. God waits until judgment is fully deserved.

Where Christians differ: the conquest. How can God give one people’s land to another? Verdict: the conquest was God’s judgment on centuries of wickedness, delayed in patience (Leviticus 18:24–25). It was a unique act of God, not a pattern for nations today.

On a Tuesday. God’s delay in judgment is patience, not indifference.
verseByVerse.note: “Four hundred years” is a round figure; Exodus gives 430 years.

verseByVerse.quote: When the sun had gone down and it was dark, behold, a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch passed between these pieces. On that day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, "To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates, the land of the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites and the Jebusites."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the dark a smoking fire pot and flaming torch pass between the pieces, and God makes a covenant giving Abram’s offspring the land from Egypt’s river to the Euphrates.

Smoke and fire. God’s presence, as at Sinai.

God alone passes through. Abram is asleep. God takes the whole obligation on himself: a covenant of grace.

The cross. God would bear the curse of the broken covenant himself, in Christ (Galatians 3:13).

For worship. Praise God who binds himself to his promises.
verseByVerse.note: In ancient covenants the parties passed between cut animals, calling the same fate on themselves if they broke their word. Here God alone passes through.

15.theology:
Justification by Faith. Genesis 15:6 is the Old Testament’s clearest statement of what the Reformation recovered: righteousness before God comes through faith, not works. Paul’s argument in Romans 4 is that this has always been the case — Abraham was justified before circumcision, before the law, before any ritual or moral achievement. The God who credited faith as righteousness to Abram “also will be counted to us who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Rom. 4:24–25). The path to God has never changed: not by works but by trust in the promise.

The Unilateral Covenant. The covenant-cutting ceremony of Genesis 15 establishes the unconditional character of God’s commitment to Abraham. God swears by himself (there is no greater oath, Heb. 6:13–14) and takes the full burden of covenant obligation on himself. This does not mean Abram’s obedience is irrelevant — it means that the security of the promise does not rest on Abram’s faithfulness but on God’s. The cross is the climactic fulfillment of this self-imposed obligation: God the Son bore the curse his own covenant required, guaranteeing the blessing by absorbing the judgment.
15.examples:
Then: The covenant ceremony of Genesis 15 would have been immediately recognizable to ancient Near Eastern readers: the splitting of animals and walking between the pieces was a documented treaty form (Jer. 34:18–20 uses the same imagery as a warning). What was radical was that only one party walked. The stars as the symbol of the promise (v.5) would have carried enormous weight in the ancient world, where stars were associated with divine power and destiny. God is saying: what you associate with divine power and destiny — I am using to promise you a family.

Now: The honesty of Abram’s complaint (vv.2–3) is a standing permission for lament in Christian prayer. The prosperity-gospel version of faith — perpetual positivity, suppressed doubt, cheerful acceptance of unanswered prayer — has no biblical precedent. Abram brought his pain directly to God, and God met him there. The church that creates space for honest lament is more biblically faithful than the church that expects its members to perform contentment. And verse 6 remains the theological foundation of every sinner’s only hope: not what I have done, but what I have trusted.

16.title: Hagar and Ishmael
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. She had a female Egyptian servant whose name was Hagar.<sup>2</sup>And Sarai said to Abram, "Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her." And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.<sup>3</sup>So, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife.<sup>4</sup>And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived. And when she saw that she had conceived, she looked with contempt on her mistress.<sup>5</sup>And Sarai said to Abram, "May the wrong done to me be on you! I gave my servant to your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she looked on me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me!"<sup>6</sup>But Abram said to Sarai, "Behold, your servant is in your power; do to her as you please." Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her.<sup>7</sup>The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur.<sup>8</sup>And he said, "Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?" She said, "I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai."<sup>9</sup>The angel of the LORD said to her, "Return to your mistress and submit to her."<sup>10</sup>The angel of the LORD also said to her, "I will surely multiply your offspring so that they cannot be numbered for multitude."<sup>11</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to her, "Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction.<sup>12</sup>He shall be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he shall dwell over against all his kinsmen."<sup>13</sup>So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are a God of seeing," for she said, "Truly here I have seen him who looks after me."<sup>14</sup>Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered.<sup>15</sup>And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.<sup>16</sup>Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
16.overview:
Genesis 16 is a story of faith’s impatience — of what happens when the people of God try to help God keep his promises. Ten years have passed since Abram entered Canaan, and Sarai is still childless. Her solution is practical and culturally sanctioned: give her servant Hagar to Abram as a surrogate, and build a family through her. It was standard practice in the ancient Near East. It was also a failure of faith — an attempt to achieve through human strategy what God had promised to accomplish by his own means.

Paul reads the Hagar-Ishmael / Sarah-Isaac narrative as an allegory of law and gospel (Gal. 4:21–31): Hagar represents the Sinai covenant (works-based approach to God, producing slaves), and Sarah represents the covenant of promise (grace-based, producing free children). The child born of the flesh (Ishmael) and the child born of the Spirit (Isaac) represent the two fundamentally different ways of relating to God — by human effort or by divine promise. Ishmael is not evil, but he is not the promised son.

The chapter contains one of the most beautiful divine encounters in Genesis: the angel of the LORD meets Hagar in the wilderness, sees her affliction, and speaks to her personally. Hagar — a slave woman, an Egyptian, a social nobody — gives God a name: “El Roi,” the God who sees (v.13). She is the only person in Scripture who does. The God who chose Abraham is also the God who sees the overlooked and forgotten.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Hagar and Ishmael: Faith's Impatience
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 16 narrates the first recorded human attempt to help God fulfill his promise — and its tragic consequences.
