Ten years have passed since the covenant promise of offspring (ch.12), and Sarai is still barren. The solution proposed — Abram taking Hagar as a surrogate wife — was legally common in the ancient Near East, but it represents faith's capitulation to worldly wisdom over divine patience. The result is relational catastrophe: contempt, affliction, flight, and the birth of a son who will be 'a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone.' The first child of the promise period is not the covenant child but the child of impatience.
verseByVerse.theology: After ten years in Canaan, Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, and the household falls apart in contempt, cruelty and flight. The angel of the LORD finds Hagar in the wilderness, sends her back with a promise, and names her son Ishmael, "God hears"; she names the LORD "a God of seeing."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul reads the two mothers as two covenants, slavery and freedom (Gal. 4:21–31). Now: impatience with God's timetable produces arrangements that outlive us, and the God who sees still finds the overlooked.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children. She had a female Egyptian servant whose name was Hagar. And Sarai said to Abram, "Behold now, the LORD has prevented me from bearing children. Go in to my servant; it may be that I shall obtain children by her." And Abram listened to the voice of Sarai. So, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, and gave her to Abram her husband as a wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Childless Sarai gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram as a wife, hoping to obtain children through her, and Abram agrees.

Surrogacy. A common custom in that world.

The LORD has prevented me. Sarai sees God’s hand, but takes matters into her own.

Listened to Sarai. As Adam listened to Eve (3:17).

On a Tuesday. Where are you trying to force God’s promise by your own methods?
verseByVerse.note: A wife giving her servant to bear children for her was an accepted custom of the time. The ESV notes a wordplay: “obtain children” is literally “be built up.”

verseByVerse.quote: And he went in to Hagar, and she conceived. And when she saw that she had conceived, she looked with contempt on her mistress. And Sarai said to Abram, "May the wrong done to me be on you! I gave my servant to your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she looked on me with contempt. May the LORD judge between you and me!" But Abram said to Sarai, "Behold, your servant is in your power; do to her as you please." Then Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hagar conceives and looks on Sarai with contempt; Sarai blames Abram, he gives Hagar into her power, and Sarai treats her harshly so that she flees.

Contempt, blame, harshness. The fruit of a shortcut.

Abram passive. He abdicates.

Mistreated. The same verb used of Egypt’s oppression of Israel (15:13).

verseByVerse.quote: The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, the spring on the way to Shur. And he said, "Hagar, servant of Sarai, where have you come from and where are you going?" She said, "I am fleeing from my mistress Sarai." The angel of the LORD said to her, "Return to your mistress and submit to her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel of the LORD finds Hagar by a spring in the wilderness and asks where she has come from and where she is going, and tells her to return and submit to Sarai.

The angel of the LORD. Where Christians differ. A created angel speaking for God, or a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son. Verdict: he speaks as God and is called God (v. 13), so many Reformed interpreters see the Son of God appearing before his incarnation.

Found her. God seeks the runaway slave.

Return. Hard, but for her and her son’s good.
verseByVerse.note: Shur lay on the way to Egypt. “The angel of the LORD” speaks as God himself (v. 13).

verseByVerse.quote: The angel of the LORD also said to her, "I will surely multiply your offspring so that they cannot be numbered for multitude." And the angel of the LORD said to her, "Behold, you are pregnant and shall bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your affliction. He shall be a wild donkey of a man, his hand against everyone and everyone's hand against him, and he shall dwell over against all his kinsmen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel promises Hagar countless offspring and tells her to name her son Ishmael, for the LORD has heard her affliction; he will be a wild donkey of a man.

Ishmael. “God hears”.

A wild donkey. Free, untamed, independent.

A promise to an outsider. God cares for Hagar too.
verseByVerse.note: “Ishmael” means God hears (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So she called the name of the LORD who spoke to her, "You are a God of seeing," for she said, "Truly here I have seen him who looks after me." Therefore the well was called Beer-lahai-roi; it lies between Kadesh and Bered. And Hagar bore Abram a son, and Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael. Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hagar names the LORD “You are a God of seeing,” for she has seen the one who sees her; she bears Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six.

The God who sees. El Roi. The only person in Scripture to give God a name, and she is a slave woman.

Ishmael and Islam. Muslim tradition traces descent to Ishmael. God’s promise of blessing to him was real (17:20), but the covenant line is through Isaac.

For worship. Thank the God who sees you, when no one else does.
verseByVerse.note: “Beer-lahai-roi” means the well of the Living One who sees me (ESV note).

16.theology:
The Two Sons as Allegory. Paul’s allegory in Galatians 4:21–31 is the New Testament’s definitive reading of the Hagar-Sarah narrative. Hagar/Ishmael represents the Sinai covenant, the attempt to achieve righteousness through law-keeping, the slavery of works-based religion. Sarah/Isaac represents the covenant of promise, the freedom of those who are children of grace. The application is pointed: those who seek to be justified by law are, in the deepest sense, children of Hagar — slaves, not sons. Those who trust the promise of the gospel are children of Sarah — free, heirs, sons of God.

The God Who Sees the Overlooked. The divine encounter with Hagar establishes a principle that the entire Bible will develop: the God of Israel is also the God of the outsider, the slave, the forgotten. The Psalms celebrate him as the one who “lifts the needy from the ash heap” (Ps. 113:7). The prophets condemn Israel for forgetting the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner — those whom God specially sees. Jesus embodies this perfectly: his ministry is persistently oriented toward those who have no social claim on grace.
16.examples:
Then: Surrogacy through a female slave was legally recognized in the ancient Near East (documented in the Code of Hammurabi and the Nuzi tablets). Sarai’s proposal was therefore not scandalous to her contemporaries but entirely normal. What Genesis presents as a failure of faith, the ancient world would have seen as reasonable problem-solving. The narrative is an implicit critique of the “reasonable” human solution that bypasses trust in divine promise.

Now: The Hagar episode speaks to every Christian who has grown impatient with God’s timing and implemented their own solution — the marriage that seemed close enough to God’s will, the career decision that got ahead of his leading, the ministry strategy that substituted human cleverness for divine direction. The “Ishmael solutions” of our lives produce their own conflicts and do not become the promised child simply because we name them after God’s promise. And the El Roi encounter speaks to everyone who feels invisible: the God who found Hagar in the wilderness is still the God who sees what no one else notices.

17.title: Walk Before Me and Be Blameless
17.text: <sup>1</sup>When Abram was ninety-nine years old the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, "I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless,<sup>2</sup>that I may make my covenant between me and you, and may multiply you greatly."<sup>3</sup>Then Abram fell on his face. And God said to him,<sup>4</sup>"Behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations.<sup>5</sup>No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.<sup>6</sup>I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come from you.<sup>7</sup>And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you.<sup>8</sup>And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God."<sup>9</sup>And God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations.<sup>10</sup>This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised.<sup>11</sup>You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you.<sup>12</sup>He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your house or bought with your money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring,<sup>13</sup>both he who is born in your house and he who is bought with your money, shall surely be circumcised. So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant.<sup>14</sup>Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant."<sup>15</sup>And God said to Abraham, "As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name.<sup>16</sup>I will bless her, and moreover, I will give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she shall become nations; kings of peoples shall come from her."<sup>17</sup>Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said to himself, "Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?"<sup>18</sup>And Abraham said to God, "Oh that Ishmael might live before you!"<sup>19</sup>God said, "No, but Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him.<sup>20</sup>As for Ishmael, I have heard you; behold, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He shall father twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation.<sup>21</sup>But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year."<sup>22</sup>When he had finished talking with him, God went up from Abraham.<sup>23</sup>Then Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his house or bought with his money, every male among the men of Abraham's house, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day, as God had said to him.<sup>24</sup>Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.<sup>25</sup>And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.<sup>26</sup>That very day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised.<sup>27</sup>And all the men of his house, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.
17.overview:
Chapter 17 marks a new stage in the Abrahamic covenant: after thirteen years of silence (Ishmael is now thirteen, v.25), God appears again with a new divine name, a new human name for Abram, a new covenant sign, and the most specific promise yet — Sarah herself will bear the son of promise (v.16). The silence of those thirteen years was not divine absence but divine patience, and its end is a renewal and deepening of everything promised in chapters 12 and 15.

God introduces himself as “God Almighty” (El Shaddai) — a name that appears at key moments of covenant-making and is associated with the power to do what is humanly impossible. He is not merely the God of Abraham’s tribe but the God of impossible things. The command that follows — “walk before me, and be blameless” — is not a condition of the covenant but its ethical shape. The covenant creates a people; “walk before me and be blameless” describes what that people looks like in motion.

Circumcision is established as the sign of the covenant — a permanent, embodied mark that distinguishes the covenant community and, importantly, is applied to every male, including slaves and foreigners (vv.12–13). The sign is inclusive beyond bloodline, yet specific in its requirement. Paul’s interpretation in Romans 4:11 is key: circumcision was a sign of the righteousness that Abram already had by faith (15:6) before circumcision was instituted. The sign follows the faith; it does not create it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 17 records a fresh divine appearance to Abram when he is 99 years old — thirteen years after Ishmael's birth. God comes with a new name (El Shaddai, God Almighty), a new command (walk before me and be blameless), a new covenant sign (circumcision), and new names for both Abram and Sarai. The covenant is formally established with every male in Abram's household. The chapter is the most covenant-dense passage in the Abraham narrative: the word 'covenant' appears thirteen times, forming the backbone of the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: After thirteen years of silence God appears as God Almighty, commands Abram to walk before him and be blameless, renames him Abraham, father of a multitude, and promises to be God to him and his offspring. Circumcision is given as the sign of the covenant, for every male of the household at eight days old.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul calls circumcision "a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith" (Rom. 4:11). Now: the sign was always pointing to a circumcised heart (Deut. 10:16; Rom. 2:28–29), which no outward rite can supply.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abram was ninety-nine years old the LORD appeared to Abram and said to him, "I am God Almighty; walk before me, and be blameless, that I may make my covenant between me and you, and may multiply you greatly." Then Abram fell on his face. And God said to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Abram is ninety-nine, the LORD appears as God Almighty, tells him to walk before him and be blameless, and promises to multiply him greatly; Abram falls on his face.

Thirteen years. Silence since Ishmael’s birth.

God Almighty. El Shaddai. The God who can do the impossible.

Walk before me. Grace calls for a holy life.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” translates El Shaddai (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, my covenant is with you, and you shall be the father of a multitude of nations. No longer shall your name be called Abram, but your name shall be Abraham, for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations. I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make you into nations, and kings shall come from you. And I will establish my covenant between me and you and your offspring after you throughout their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be God to you and to your offspring after you. And I will give to you and to your offspring after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession, and I will be their God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God renames Abram as Abraham, father of a multitude of nations, and promises kings, an everlasting covenant, and the land of Canaan as an everlasting possession.

Abraham. “Father of a multitude”. A name to grow into.

Many nations. Fulfilled as Gentiles become his children by faith (Romans 4:16–17).

To be God to you. The heart of every covenant.

For worship. Thank God who is your God and your children’s God.
verseByVerse.note: Abram means “exalted father”; Abraham means “father of a multitude” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Abraham, "As for you, you shall keep my covenant, you and your offspring after you throughout their generations. This is my covenant, which you shall keep, between me and you and your offspring after you: Every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall be circumcised in the flesh of your foreskins, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. He who is eight days old among you shall be circumcised. Every male throughout your generations, whether born in your house or bought with your money from any foreigner who is not of your offspring, both he who is born in your house and he who is bought with your money, shall surely be circumcised. So shall my covenant be in your flesh an everlasting covenant. Any uncircumcised male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin shall be cut off from his people; he has broken my covenant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands that every male among Abraham’s household be circumcised on the eighth day as the sign of the covenant; any uncircumcised male is cut off.

A sign in the flesh. Marking Abraham’s family as God’s.

The heart. The deeper meaning is a circumcised heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; Romans 2:29).

Where Christians differ: circumcision and baptism. Paedobaptists argue that as circumcision was given to infants in the covenant, so baptism, its New Testament counterpart (Colossians 2:11–12), should be. Credobaptists reply that the new covenant community is made of those born of the Spirit, so its sign is for those who profess faith. Verdict: credobaptist, held charitably. Brothers in the Reformed tradition differ here in good conscience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–27 — Sarah's New Name and the Promise of Isaac
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Genesis 17 brings the covenant promise to its sharpest and most personal focus: Sarah will bear a son, and his name will be Isaac. The promise has been moving from the general (offspring like the stars, ch.15) to the specific (a son from your own body, 15:4) and now to the most specific of all: a named son, born within one year, from a wife who is 90 years old and long past menopause. Abraham's laughter at this announcement is the most humanly understandable response in the chapter — and God's patient response to it is among the most grace-filled moments in the patriarchal narrative.
verseByVerse.theology: Sarai becomes Sarah, and God promises a son by her within the year. Abraham falls on his face and laughs, and pleads for Ishmael; God blesses Ishmael but establishes his covenant with Isaac. That same day Abraham circumcises himself and his whole household.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul says Abraham did not weaken in faith though he considered his body as good as dead (Rom. 4:19). Now: God's no to the shape of a prayer is often a yes to the person prayed for.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to Abraham, "As for Sarai your wife, you shall not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name. I will bless her, and moreover, I will give you a son by her. I will bless her, and she shall become nations; kings of peoples shall come from her." Then Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said to himself, "Shall a child be born to a man who is a hundred years old? Shall Sarah, who is ninety years old, bear a child?" And Abraham said to God, "Oh that Ishmael might live before you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God renames Sarai as Sarah and promises she will bear Abraham a son and become mother of nations; Abraham laughs and asks that Ishmael might live before God.

Sarah. “Princess”.

Abraham laughed. Mixed wonder and disbelief.

Oh that Ishmael. A father’s love, and settling for less.
verseByVerse.note: Sarai and Sarah both mean “princess” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: God said, "No, but Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant for his offspring after him. As for Ishmael, I have heard you; behold, I have blessed him and will make him fruitful and multiply him greatly. He shall father twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year." When he had finished talking with him, God went up from Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says Sarah will bear a son named Isaac, with whom he will establish his everlasting covenant; Ishmael too will be blessed and become a great nation, but the covenant is with Isaac.

Isaac. “He laughs”.

Ishmael blessed. Twelve princes. God answers Abraham’s prayer.

The covenant with Isaac. God’s free choice (Romans 9:7–9).
verseByVerse.note: “Isaac” means “he laughs” (ESV note) — echoing Abraham’s laughter in v. 17.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his house or bought with his money, every male among the men of Abraham's house, and he circumcised the flesh of their foreskins that very day, as God had said to him. Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. And Ishmael his son was thirteen years old when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin. That very day Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised. And all the men of his house, those born in the house and those bought with money from a foreigner, were circumcised with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That very day Abraham circumcises Ishmael and all the males of his household, as God commanded.

That very day. Prompt obedience at ninety-nine.

Ishmael too. Under the covenant sign, though not the line of promise.

On a Tuesday. Obey God’s word promptly.

For worship. Thank God for the covenant he keeps with his people.

17.theology:
Covenant Sign and Seal. Circumcision is the Old Testament’s primary covenant sign — an embodied, permanent, given-before-performance mark of belonging to the covenant community. Paul’s point in Romans 4 is that it is a sign (pointing to something, namely the righteousness of faith) and a seal (confirming what faith has received), not the thing itself. The Reformers used this distinction to explain baptism: as circumcision was the sign and seal of the old covenant, baptism is the sign and seal of the new. Baptists agree that baptism is the new covenant sign but give it only to those who profess faith, the view these notes take (see on vv. 9–14). The sign does not create faith; it marks the community of those who receive the promise by faith.

The God Who Renames. The renaming of Abram and Sarai is a pattern of divine sovereignty over identity. God renames Jacob (Israel), Simon (Peter), and Saul (Paul). In each case, the new name is not a description of present character but a declaration of covenantal destiny — a new identity spoken into existence before it is lived out. The resurrection is the ultimate renaming: “I will give him a white stone, with a new name written on the stone that no one knows except the one who receives it” (Rev. 2:17). Our truest identity is always the one God speaks, not the one we construct.
17.examples:
Then: Thirteen years of silence between chapters 16 and 17 are compressed into a single verse (16:16 to 17:1). For the original audience, familiar with the frustration of waiting on covenant promises in the wilderness, this long silence would have resonated painfully. The reappearance of God after silence — with more specific and more expansive promises — was the narrative pattern of Israel’s own experience: silence in Egypt, then the burning bush; silence during the exile, then the return. God’s silence is not absence.

Now: The command “walk before me, and be blameless” (v.1) is the Old Testament’s summary of the Christian life: not occasional acts of obedience but a life lived in the continuous awareness of divine presence. It is the life lived coram Deo — before the face of God. The person who lives this way does not need an audience for their virtue, does not perform goodness when watched and relax it when unobserved, because they are always in the presence of the one who sees everything. And Abraham’s laughter (v.17) gives permission for the honest emotional response to grace: the promise is so good it seems laughable, and God is not offended by the laughter.

18.title: Is Anything Too Hard for the LORD?
18.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent in the heat of the day.<sup>2</sup>He lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing in front of him. When he saw them, he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed himself to the earth<sup>3</sup>and said, "O Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant.<sup>4</sup>Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree,<sup>5</sup>while I bring a morsel of bread, that you may refresh yourselves, and after that you may pass on— since you have come to your servant." So they said, "Do as you have said."<sup>6</sup>And Abraham went quickly into the tent to Sarah and said, "Quick! Three seahs of fine flour! Knead it, and make cakes."<sup>7</sup>And Abraham ran to the herd and took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to a young man, who prepared it quickly.<sup>8</sup>Then he took curds and milk and the calf that he had prepared, and set it before them. And he stood by them under the tree while they ate.<sup>9</sup>They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" And he said, "She is in the tent."<sup>10</sup>The LORD said, "I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son." And Sarah was listening at the tent door behind him.<sup>11</sup>Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years. The way of women had ceased to be with Sarah.<sup>12</sup>So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, "After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?"<sup>13</sup>The LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh and say, 'Shall I indeed bear a child, now that I am old?'<sup>14</sup>Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah shall have a son."<sup>15</sup>But Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."<sup>16</sup>Then the men set out from there, and they looked down toward Sodom. And Abraham went with them to set them on their way.<sup>17</sup>The LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,<sup>18</sup>seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?<sup>19</sup>For I have chosen him, that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised him."<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said, "Because the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is very grave,<sup>21</sup>I will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me. And if not, I will know."<sup>22</sup>So the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the LORD.<sup>23</sup>Then Abraham drew near and said, "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?<sup>24</sup>Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city. Will you then sweep away the place and not spare it for the fifty righteous who are in it?<sup>25</sup>Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be that from you! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?"<sup>26</sup>And the LORD said, "If I find at Sodom fifty righteous in the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."<sup>27</sup>Abraham answered and said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes.<sup>28</sup>Suppose five of the fifty righteous are lacking. Will you destroy the whole city for lack of five?" And he said, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there."<sup>29</sup>Again he spoke to him and said, "Suppose forty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of forty I will not do it."<sup>30</sup>Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there." He answered, "I will not do it, if I find thirty there."<sup>31</sup>He said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord. Suppose twenty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of twenty I will not destroy it."<sup>32</sup>Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten are found there." He answered, "For the sake of ten I will not destroy it."<sup>33</sup>And the LORD went his way, when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
18.overview:
Genesis 18 is one of the most intimate chapters in all of Scripture. Three visitors appear at the heat of the day, and Abraham runs to meet them, providing lavish hospitality. Only gradually does the narrative reveal who these visitors are: the LORD himself, accompanied by two angels (cf. 19:1). The New Testament reflects on this encounter with the observation: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb. 13:2). The divine condescension to appear in human form, to receive food and rest in a human tent, anticipates the incarnation — God choosing to enter the creaturely world in the most particular and embodied way.

The chapter centers on two dramatic moments: the promise of a son within the year (vv.9–15), met with Sarah’s incredulous laughter and the divine challenge “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (v.14); and Abraham’s intercessory prayer for Sodom (vv.22–33), in which he boldly negotiates with God on behalf of the righteous. The two moments are linked: the same God who can give a child to a ninety-year-old woman can hear the prayer of one man on behalf of a city. Nothing is too hard for the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Three Visitors and the Promise to Sarah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 18 opens with one of the most intimate theophanies in Scripture: three men appear to Abraham at the oaks of Mamre, and in the course of a meal, the covenant promise of Isaac is renewed directly to Sarah — who hears it for the first time and laughs. The scene is domestic, warm, and theologically profound. Abraham's hospitality is exemplary; the meal is prepared with care; and the divine visitors eat, recline, and speak in the most ordinary human setting. The God who made heaven and earth sits under a terebinth tree at midday and eats with a nomadic patriarch.
verseByVerse.theology: Three men come to Abraham's tent at Mamre in the heat of the day, and he serves them a feast standing. The LORD promises that Sarah will have a son by this time next year; Sarah laughs to herself and denies it, and the LORD asks, "Is anything too hard for the LORD?"
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews recalls those who "entertained angels unawares" (Heb. 13:2). Now: God hears the laugh of the buried hope, and the question of verse 14 still stands over every impossible prayer (Luke 1:37).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. He lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing in front of him. When he saw them, he ran from the tent door to meet them and bowed himself to the earth and said, "O Lord, if I have found favor in your sight, do not pass by your servant. Let a little water be brought, and wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree, while I bring a morsel of bread, that you may refresh yourselves, and after that you may pass on— since you have come to your servant." So they said, "Do as you have said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD appears to Abraham at Mamre as three men, and Abraham runs to meet them, bows, and urges them to rest and eat.

Three men. The LORD and two angels (19:1).

Where Christians differ: a picture of the Trinity? Many church fathers, and Rublev’s famous icon, saw the Trinity. Verdict: the text distinguishes the LORD from the two who go to Sodom as angels. It is more likely an appearance of the LORD, perhaps the Son, with two angels.

Hospitality. Abraham runs, at the hottest part of the day.

Hebrews 13:2. Some have entertained angels unawares.

On a Tuesday. Welcome strangers generously.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham went quickly into the tent to Sarah and said, "Quick! Three seahs of fine flour! Knead it, and make cakes." And Abraham ran to the herd and took a calf, tender and good, and gave it to a young man, who prepared it quickly. Then he took curds and milk and the calf that he had prepared, and set it before them. And he stood by them under the tree while they ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham hurries to prepare a lavish meal of bread, a tender calf, curds and milk, and stands by while they eat.

Quick! Eager service.

Generous. Far more than the “morsel” he offered.

The LORD ate. A real appearance in human form.
verseByVerse.note: Three seahs was about 23 quarts (22 liters) of flour (ESV note) — a lavish meal.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Where is Sarah your wife?" And he said, "She is in the tent." The LORD said, "I will surely return to you about this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son." And Sarah was listening at the tent door behind him. Now Abraham and Sarah were old, advanced in years. The way of women had ceased to be with Sarah. So Sarah laughed to herself, saying, "After I am worn out, and my lord is old, shall I have pleasure?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask for Sarah, and the LORD promises that she will have a son by this time next year; Sarah, listening at the tent door, laughs to herself, for she is old.

Where is Sarah? The message is for her too.

She laughed. To herself, in disbelief.

Old and worn out. Humanly impossible.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh and say, 'Shall I indeed bear a child, now that I am old?' Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, about this time next year, and Sarah shall have a son." But Sarah denied it, saying, "I did not laugh," for she was afraid. He said, "No, but you did laugh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD asks why Sarah laughed, and says, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” She denies laughing out of fear, and he says, “No, but you did laugh.”

Is anything too hard? The question echoed through Scripture (Jeremiah 32:17; Luke 1:37).

He knew. He heard her silent laughter.

Gentle correction. No rejection, only truth.

On a Tuesday. What are you laughing off as impossible that God has promised?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second movement of Genesis 18 is the most remarkable intercession in the Old Testament before Moses. God discloses to Abraham that he is going to investigate Sodom's wickedness and determine whether it merits destruction. Abraham then engages God in a negotiation that begins at fifty righteous people and descends to ten — and God agrees to spare the city for the sake of ten. The passage establishes the principle of intercession as a covenant privilege and reveals the character of God as a judge who desires justice but is willing to be moved by prayer.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD tells Abraham, his friend, that he is going down to see Sodom's sin. Abraham draws near and pleads on the ground of God's justice — "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" — and God agrees to spare the city for fifty, and at last for ten.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the prayer did not save the city but it brought Lot out, because "God remembered Abraham" (19:29). Now: a few righteous people are salt in a place (Matt. 5:13), and one righteous man at Calvary was enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men set out from there, and they looked down toward Sodom. And Abraham went with them to set them on their way. The LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do, seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him? For I have chosen him, that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, so that the LORD may bring to Abraham what he has promised him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the men look towards Sodom, the LORD asks whether he should hide from Abraham what he is about to do, since Abraham will be a great nation and must teach his children righteousness and justice.

Shall I hide? God takes Abraham into his confidence as a friend (James 2:23).

Chosen to teach. Election has a purpose: a family that keeps the way of the LORD.

On a Tuesday. Teach your household God’s ways.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "Because the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is very grave, I will go down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me. And if not, I will know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD says the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin very grave, and he will go down to see.

The outcry. The cry of victims (Ezekiel 16:49–50: pride, excess, neglect of the poor) and of sexual violence (19:5; Jude 7).

I will go down to see. Not ignorance, but just and careful judgment, as at Babel.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the LORD. Then Abraham drew near and said, "Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked? Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city. Will you then sweep away the place and not spare it for the fifty righteous who are in it? Far be it from you to do such a thing, to put the righteous to death with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be that from you! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?" And the LORD said, "If I find at Sodom fifty righteous in the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham stands before the LORD and asks whether he will sweep away the righteous with the wicked: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” and the LORD agrees to spare the city for fifty righteous.

Drew near. Intercession.

The Judge of all the earth. Abraham appeals to God’s own character.

For the sake of the righteous. A few godly people can be a blessing to a whole city.

For worship. Praise the Judge of all the earth, who always does what is right.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham answered and said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord, I who am but dust and ashes. Suppose five of the fifty righteous are lacking. Will you destroy the whole city for lack of five?" And he said, "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there." Again he spoke to him and said, "Suppose forty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of forty I will not do it." Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak. Suppose thirty are found there." He answered, "I will not do it, if I find thirty there." He said, "Behold, I have undertaken to speak to the Lord. Suppose twenty are found there." He answered, "For the sake of twenty I will not destroy it." Then he said, "Oh let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak again but this once. Suppose ten are found there." He answered, "For the sake of ten I will not destroy it." And the LORD went his way, when he had finished speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humbly calling himself dust and ashes, Abraham asks again and again, down to ten righteous, and each time the LORD agrees; then the LORD goes his way.

Dust and ashes. Boldness and humility together.

Down to ten. Persistent prayer.

Not even ten. Sodom will fall, but Lot will be rescued (19:29).

On a Tuesday. Pray persistently for your city.

For worship. Thank God that he hears the prayers of his friends.

18.theology:
Divine Condescension. The appearance of the LORD in human form at Mamre — eating food, receiving hospitality, sitting in a tent in the heat of the day — is one of the Old Testament’s most striking anticipations of the incarnation. The God who fills the heavens condescends to the particular, the creaturely, the embodied. John’s Prologue is the full statement: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The incarnation is not alien to the character of the God revealed in Genesis; it is its fullest expression.

Intercessory Prayer. Abraham’s intercession for Sodom establishes the pattern and the permission for bold intercessory prayer. He argues from divine justice, not human sentimentality. He persists without presuming — “let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak” (v.30). He does not give up prematurely. The New Testament develops this into the image of the persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8) and Jesus’s own perpetual intercession (Heb. 7:25: “he always lives to make intercession for them”). We pray within the intercession of the one who is both the Abraham who pleads and the LORD who hears.
18.examples:
Then: Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty in the ancient Near East — refusal was a serious social transgression. Sodom’s violation of Lot’s guests in chapter 19 is therefore not only a sexual sin but a profound violation of the hospitality code that structured ancient society. Abraham’s extravagant welcome to the three visitors is the counter-portrait: the covenant community defined by generous welcome, not hostile rejection.

Now: “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (v.14) is the question every prayer should begin with — not as a formula but as a genuine theological orientation. When we are tempted to edit our prayers to fit what seems possible, this verse calls us back: the God to whom we pray is the God of the impossible. And Abraham’s bold intercession gives permission for passionate, specific, persistent prayer for those who are perishing. To stand before the LORD and plead for the lost city is not presumption; it is the highest form of friendship with God available to the creature.

19.title: The Destruction of Sodom
19.text: <sup>1</sup>The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed himself with his face to the earth<sup>2</sup>and said, "My lords, please turn aside to your servant's house and spend the night and wash your feet. Then you may rise up early and go on your way." They said, "No; we will spend the night in the town square."<sup>3</sup>But he pressed them strongly; so they turned aside to him and entered his house. And he made them a feast and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.<sup>4</sup>But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, both young and old, all the people to the last man, surrounded the house.<sup>5</sup>And they called to Lot, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them."<sup>6</sup>Lot went out to the men at the entrance, shut the door after him,<sup>7</sup>and said, "I beg you, my brothers, do not act so wickedly.<sup>8</sup>Behold, I have two daughters who have not known any man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them as you please. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof."<sup>9</sup>But they said, "Stand back!" And they said, "This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge! Now we will deal worse with you than with them." Then they pressed hard against the man Lot, and drew near to break the door down.<sup>10</sup>But the men reached out their hands and brought Lot into the house with them and shut the door.<sup>11</sup>And they struck with blindness the men who were at the entrance of the house, both small and great, so that they wore themselves out groping for the door.<sup>12</sup>Then the men said to Lot, "Have you anyone else here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or anyone you have in the city, bring them out of the place.<sup>13</sup>For we are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has become great before the LORD, and the LORD has sent us to destroy it."<sup>14</sup>So Lot went out and said to his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, "Up! Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city." But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting.<sup>15</sup>As morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying, "Up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the punishment of the city."<sup>16</sup>But he lingered. So the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city.<sup>17</sup>And as they brought them out, one said, "Escape for your life. Do not look back or stop anywhere in the valley. Escape to the hills, lest you be swept away."<sup>18</sup>And Lot said to them, "Oh, no, my lords.<sup>19</sup>Behold, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness in saving my life. But I cannot escape to the hills, lest the disaster overtake me and I die.<sup>20</sup>Behold, this city is near enough to flee to, and it is a little one. Let me escape there—is it not a little one?—and my life will be saved!"<sup>21</sup>He said to him, "Behold, I grant you this favor also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken.<sup>22</sup>Escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there." Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.<sup>23</sup>The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar.<sup>24</sup>Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven.<sup>25</sup>And he overthrew those cities, and all the valley, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground.<sup>26</sup>But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.<sup>27</sup>And Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD.<sup>28</sup>And he looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and toward all the land of the valley, and he looked and, behold, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace.<sup>29</sup>So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the valley, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow when he overthrew the cities in which Lot had lived.<sup>30</sup>Now Lot went up out of Zoar and lived in the hills with his two daughters, for he was afraid to live in Zoar. So he lived in a cave with his two daughters.<sup>31</sup>And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is not a man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth.<sup>32</sup>Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father."<sup>33</sup>So they made their father drink wine that night. And the firstborn went in and lay with her father. He did not know when she lay down or when she arose.<sup>34</sup>The next day, the firstborn said to the younger, "Behold, I lay last night with my father. Let us make him drink wine tonight also. Then you go in and lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father."<sup>35</sup>So they made their father drink wine that night also. And the younger arose and lay with him, and he did not know when she lay down or when she arose.<sup>36</sup>Thus both the daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father.<sup>37</sup>The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day.<sup>38</sup>The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.
19.overview:
Genesis 19 is one of the most difficult chapters in the Bible — difficult morally (Lot’s offer of his daughters, vv.8; his daughters’ later actions, vv.30–38), difficult theologically (the total destruction of the cities), and difficult pastorally (it has been used and misused in every generation). The chapter must be read carefully and canonically.

The wickedness of Sodom, often reduced in popular discussion to a single sin, is described in the Old Testament more broadly: “Behold, this was the guilt of your sister Sodom: she and her daughters had pride, excess of food, and prosperous ease, but did not aid the poor and needy” (Ezek. 16:49). The violation of Lot’s guests in chapter 19 is the culminating expression of a comprehensive moral collapse, of which the sexual dimension is one symptom among many. The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah becomes the Old Testament’s paradigmatic image of divine judgment — cited throughout the prophets (Isa. 1:9; Amos 4:11) and by Jesus himself (Matt. 10:15; Luke 17:29).

The theological center of the chapter is verse 29: “God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out.” Lot is saved not because of his own righteousness but because of Abraham’s intercession. He lingered (v.16) — hesitating to leave even as the city was about to be destroyed — and the angels had to physically drag him and his family to safety (“the LORD being merciful to him”). Salvation always comes from outside; it is always the merciful hand of God dragging us from the city we are unwilling to leave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Destruction of Sodom and the Rescue of Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 19 is one of the most sobering chapters in the Old Testament. The wickedness of Sodom — described with harrowing specificity in the attempted assault on the two angels — demonstrates beyond any doubt that the city's destruction is just. Lot's compromised position (sitting in the gate, married into the city, with sons-in-law who mock the warning) shows the full cost of his earlier choice. The deliverance of Lot, his wife, and his daughters is accomplished by divine mercy against Lot's own hesitation; but the salvation is incomplete — Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt, and the chapter ends with Lot hiding in a cave, his daughters engineering the continuation of his line through incest.
verseByVerse.theology: The two angels come to Sodom, where Lot sits in the gate. The whole city surrounds his house demanding the guests, and Lot offers his daughters. The angels strike the mob blind, warn Lot's family, and drag the lingering Lot out by the hand. Fire falls; Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt; and God remembers Abraham.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ezekiel names Sodom's pride and neglect of the poor (Ezek. 16:49), Jude its sexual immorality (Jude 7). Now: Jesus said, "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32) — it is possible to be out of the city and still facing it.

verseByVerse.quote: The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them, he rose to meet them and bowed himself with his face to the earth and said, "My lords, please turn aside to your servant's house and spend the night and wash your feet. Then you may rise up early and go on your way." They said, "No; we will spend the night in the town square." But he pressed them strongly; so they turned aside to him and entered his house. And he made them a feast and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two angels arrive in Sodom at evening; Lot, sitting in the gate, insists they stay in his house rather than the square, and makes them a feast.

In the gate. Lot has become a leading citizen of Sodom.

He pressed them. He knows the danger of the streets.

Hospitality. Like Abraham’s, though in a darker place.
verseByVerse.note: The city gate was where elders sat and business was done.

verseByVerse.quote: But before they lay down, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, both young and old, all the people to the last man, surrounded the house. And they called to Lot, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before they lie down, all the men of Sodom surround the house and demand that Lot bring the visitors out so that they may know them.

All the men. Young and old: a whole city corrupted.

Know them. Sexual violence (v. 8).

Where Christians differ: the sin of Sodom. Some argue the sin was only inhospitality or rape, not same-sex relations as such. Verdict: Scripture names Sodom’s pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50), and how it “indulged in sexual immorality and pursued unnatural desire” (Jude 7). The historic Christian view sees same-sex acts among its sins, spoken with care and compassion, remembering that all sinners need the same grace.

verseByVerse.quote: Lot went out to the men at the entrance, shut the door after him, and said, "I beg you, my brothers, do not act so wickedly. Behold, I have two daughters who have not known any man. Let me bring them out to you, and do to them as you please. Only do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lot goes out, shuts the door, begs them not to act wickedly, and offers his two virgin daughters instead.

My brothers. Lot is too at home in Sodom.

His daughters. A shocking offer.

What it does not mean. Scripture records it, but does not approve it. Protecting guests did not justify sacrificing daughters.

verseByVerse.quote: But they said, "Stand back!" And they said, "This fellow came to sojourn, and he has become the judge! Now we will deal worse with you than with them." Then they pressed hard against the man Lot, and drew near to break the door down. But the men reached out their hands and brought Lot into the house with them and shut the door. And they struck with blindness the men who were at the entrance of the house, both small and great, so that they wore themselves out groping for the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men try to break down the door, but the angels pull Lot in and strike the men with blindness, so they cannot find the door.

He judges us. They resent Lot’s rebuke.

Blindness. Physical blindness matches spiritual blindness.

They wore themselves out. Even blind, they keep trying. Sin is relentless.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men said to Lot, "Have you anyone else here? Sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or anyone you have in the city, bring them out of the place. For we are about to destroy this place, because the outcry against its people has become great before the LORD, and the LORD has sent us to destroy it." So Lot went out and said to his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, "Up! Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city." But he seemed to his sons-in-law to be jesting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angels tell Lot to bring out his family, for the LORD has sent them to destroy the city; Lot warns his sons-in-law, but they think he is joking.

The outcry is great. As God said (18:20).

As if jesting. Lot’s life had given his words no weight.

On a Tuesday. Does your life give weight to your words about God?

verseByVerse.quote: As morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying, "Up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be swept away in the punishment of the city." But he lingered. So the men seized him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, the LORD being merciful to him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city. And as they brought them out, one said, "Escape for your life. Do not look back or stop anywhere in the valley. Escape to the hills, lest you be swept away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At dawn the angels urge Lot to flee; when he lingers, they seize him and his family by the hand and bring them out, for the LORD was merciful, and tell them to escape to the hills without looking back.

He lingered. Reluctant to leave.

Seized by the hand. Rescue by grace, almost against his will.

The LORD being merciful. The reason he was saved.

Righteous Lot. Peter calls him righteous and tormented by Sodom’s lawlessness (2 Peter 2:7–8). A believer, but a compromised one.

For worship. Thank God that he drags us out of danger by the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And Lot said to them, "Oh, no, my lords. Behold, your servant has found favor in your sight, and you have shown me great kindness in saving my life. But I cannot escape to the hills, lest the disaster overtake me and I die. Behold, this city is near enough to flee to, and it is a little one. Let me escape there—is it not a little one?—and my life will be saved!" He said to him, "Behold, I grant you this favor also, that I will not overthrow the city of which you have spoken. Escape there quickly, for I can do nothing till you arrive there." Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lot pleads not to flee to the hills but to a small city nearby, and the angel grants it, so the town is called Zoar.

A little one. Lot still bargains for comfort.

Granted. God is patient with weak faith.

Zoar. “Little”.
verseByVerse.note: “Zoar” means little (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The sun had risen on the earth when Lot came to Zoar. Then the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire from the LORD out of heaven. And he overthrew those cities, and all the valley, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Lot reaches Zoar, the LORD rains sulphur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah and overthrows the cities, the valley and everything that grew there.

From the LORD out of heaven. A direct judgment.

An example. Of the judgment to come (2 Peter 2:6; Jude 7; Luke 17:28–30).

On a Tuesday. God’s patience with sin has an end.

verseByVerse.quote: But Lot's wife, behind him, looked back, and she became a pillar of salt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.

Looked back. Longing for what she left.

Remember Lot’s wife. Jesus’ warning (Luke 17:32).

On a Tuesday. What are you looking back to?

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham went early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD. And he looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and toward all the land of the valley, and he looked and, behold, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace. So it was that, when God destroyed the cities of the valley, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow when he overthrew the cities in which Lot had lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Early next morning Abraham looks down towards Sodom and sees smoke rising like a furnace; and God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the overthrow.

Where he had stood. The place of his intercession.

God remembered Abraham. Lot was saved because of Abraham’s prayer.

For worship. Thank God that he answers prayer for others.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final episode of Genesis 19 is the darkest in the Lot narrative: hiding in a cave after leaving Zoar, Lot's daughters conclude that there are no men left to continue their family line and engineer pregnancies through their father. The resulting children — Moab and Ammon — are the ancestors of Israel's eastern neighbors and persistent adversaries. The episode is presented without editorial comment, but its horror is obvious and its consequences long-lasting.
verseByVerse.theology: Afraid to stay in Zoar, Lot lives in a cave with his two daughters, who make him drunk and conceive by him. Their sons are Moab and Ben-ammi, the fathers of the Moabites and Ammonites.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the choice by sight that began in 13:10 ends in a cave. Now: Ruth the Moabitess stands in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt. 1:5); no one is disqualified by where they came from.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Lot went up out of Zoar and lived in the hills with his two daughters, for he was afraid to live in Zoar. So he lived in a cave with his two daughters. And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is not a man on earth to come in to us after the manner of all the earth. Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father." So they made their father drink wine that night. And the firstborn went in and lay with her father. He did not know when she lay down or when she arose. The next day, the firstborn said to the younger, "Behold, I lay last night with my father. Let us make him drink wine tonight also. Then you go in and lie with him, that we may preserve offspring from our father." So they made their father drink wine that night also. And the younger arose and lay with him, and he did not know when she lay down or when she arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afraid to stay in Zoar, Lot lives in a cave with his daughters, who get him drunk and lie with him, to preserve offspring.

From city to cave. Lot ends with nothing.

Sodom’s influence. His daughters had absorbed its values.

Drunkenness. As with Noah (9:21), wine leads to shame.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus both the daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father. The firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab. He is the father of the Moabites to this day. The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-ammi. He is the father of the Ammonites to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both daughters bear sons: Moab and Ben-ammi, ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.

Moab and Ammon. Later enemies of Israel.

Grace beyond shame. Ruth the Moabitess would become an ancestor of David and of Christ (Ruth 4:17; Matthew 1:5).

For worship. Praise God whose grace reaches even the families of shame.
verseByVerse.note: Moab sounds like the Hebrew for “from father”; Ben-ammi means “son of my people” (ESV notes). Ruth would come from Moab.

19.theology:
Divine Judgment. The destruction of Sodom establishes that God’s patience with corporate wickedness is real but not infinite. The outcry against Sodom was “great” (18:20) — the accumulated weight of injustice toward the vulnerable, pride and contempt for the weak, and violence against the stranger. When that weight reaches the tipping point, judgment falls. The New Testament does not soften this: “it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). The gospel does not abolish judgment; it provides the only refuge from it — the one who bore the fire of judgment so that those in him would not be consumed by it.

Saved Through Another’s Intercession. Lot’s salvation by virtue of Abraham’s intercession (v.29) is one of Genesis’s clearest prefigurations of the gospel: we are not saved by our own righteousness but by the righteousness and advocacy of another. Romans 5:10 — “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” — is Lot’s story told at universal scale. We were lingering in the city of destruction, and the Son came not to condemn but to drag us out.
19.examples:
Then: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah left a lasting mark on the ancient Near East’s cultural memory — some archaeologists argue for a dramatic destruction event in the region of the Dead Sea in the Middle Bronze Age. For Israel, Sodom was the paradigmatic destroyed city: the prophets regularly invoked it as the standard of total divine judgment (Isa. 1:9; Jer. 49:18; Amos 4:11). The warning was not abstract; it was a geographic reality their ancestors had witnessed.

Now: The chapter speaks to the danger of cultural accommodation — the Lot who moved toward Sodom gradually, integrated fully, and then found himself unable to leave freely. The church in every generation faces the temptation to integrate so thoroughly with the surrounding culture that its distinctiveness is lost and, when the moment of choice comes, it finds itself lingering. And “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17:32) is the perpetual warning against half-hearted discipleship: grace that drags you out of destruction also requires that you face the direction of your salvation, not the city you were rescued from.

20.title: Abraham and Abimelech
20.text: <sup>1</sup>From there Abraham journeyed toward the territory of the Negeb and lived between Kadesh and Shur; and he sojourned in Gerar.<sup>2</sup>And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, "She is my sister." And Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.<sup>3</sup>But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him, "Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man's wife."<sup>4</sup>Now Abimelech had not approached her. So he said, "Lord, will you kill an innocent people?<sup>5</sup>Did he not himself say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she herself said, 'He is my brother.' In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands I have done this."<sup>6</sup>Then God said to him in the dream, "Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her.<sup>7</sup>Now then, return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, so that he will pray for you, and you shall live. But if you do not return her, know that you shall surely die, you and all who are yours."<sup>8</sup>So Abimelech rose early in the morning and called all his servants and told them all these things. And the men were very much afraid.<sup>9</sup>Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and my kingdom a great sin? You have done to me things that ought not to be done."<sup>10</sup>And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What did you see, that you did this thing?"<sup>11</sup>Abraham said, "I did it because I thought, 'There is no fear of God at all in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.'<sup>12</sup>Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife.<sup>13</sup>And when God caused me to wander from my father's house, I said to her, 'This is the kindness you must do me: at every place to which we come, say of me, "He is my brother."'"<sup>14</sup>Then Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and male servants and female servants, and gave them to Abraham, and returned Sarah his wife to him.<sup>15</sup>And Abimelech said, "Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you."<sup>16</sup>To Sarah he said, "Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated."<sup>17</sup>Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and also healed his wife and female slaves so that they bore children.<sup>18</sup>For the LORD had closed all the wombs of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.
20.overview:
Genesis 20 is the second occurrence of Abraham’s “she is my sister” deception (the first was in Egypt, ch.12) — a repeat failure that reveals both the persistent weakness of the patriarch and the relentless protection of the covenant promise. The child of promise has not yet been born; if Sarah is taken into another man’s household, the covenant line is in jeopardy. God intervenes, this time not with plagues (as in Egypt) but with a direct divine warning to Abimelech in a dream.

The episode contains a theological surprise: Abimelech the Philistine king acts with more integrity than Abraham the covenant patriarch. God himself acknowledges this (v.6: “I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart”) and attributes Abimelech’s not-sinning to divine restraint rather than human virtue (“it was I who kept you from sinning against me”). The general revelation of conscience, operating in a pagan king, produces behavior that the special-revelation recipient fails to match. This is not comfortable for any theology that too easily equates covenant membership with moral superiority.

The chapter ends with Abraham praying for Abimelech — the prophet who failed to protect his wife now interceding for the king he deceived. Grace is full of these inversions: the one who sinned becomes the instrument of healing for the one who was sinned against. This is the gospel logic: the sinner restored becomes the intercessor.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Abraham and Abimelech: The Sister-Wife Repeated
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 20 records Abraham's second deception about Sarah's identity — this time with Abimelech king of Gerar. Coming immediately after the destruction of Sodom and the rescue of Lot, the episode is sobering: the covenant patriarch, the man through whom all nations will be blessed, repeats his Egypt lie in a new setting. The repetition is not a duplicate tradition but a deliberately repeated test of the same weakness. Abraham learned from Egypt that God protects Sarah; he has not learned to trust that protection.
verseByVerse.theology: In Gerar Abraham again says of Sarah, "She is my sister," and Abimelech takes her. God warns the king in a dream, having kept him from sinning, and calls Abraham a prophet. Abimelech rebukes Abraham, returns Sarah with gifts and a public vindication, and Abraham prays for his household to be healed.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God shut every womb in Gerar so that no question could hang over Isaac's birth. Now: besetting sins return under the same conditions, and much of our integrity is God's restraint rather than our strength.

verseByVerse.quote: From there Abraham journeyed toward the territory of the Negeb and lived between Kadesh and Shur; and he sojourned in Gerar. And Abraham said of Sarah his wife, "She is my sister." And Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took Sarah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Gerar Abraham again says Sarah is his sister, and King Abimelech takes her.

Again. The same sin as in Egypt (12:10–20), years later.

Just before Isaac. The promise is again at risk.

On a Tuesday. Old sins return. Watch for your repeated weaknesses.
verseByVerse.note: Gerar lay in the western Negeb, near Gaza.

verseByVerse.quote: But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him, "Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man's wife." Now Abimelech had not approached her. So he said, "Lord, will you kill an innocent people? Did he not himself say to me, 'She is my sister'? And she herself said, 'He is my brother.' In the integrity of my heart and the innocence of my hands I have done this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God comes to Abimelech in a dream and says he is a dead man because of the woman, for she is married; Abimelech protests that he acted in innocence.

God speaks to a pagan king. He protects his promise.

Integrity. Abimelech acted in ignorance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said to him in the dream, "Yes, I know that you have done this in the integrity of your heart, and it was I who kept you from sinning against me. Therefore I did not let you touch her. Now then, return the man's wife, for he is a prophet, so that he will pray for you, and you shall live. But if you do not return her, know that you shall surely die, you and all who are yours."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says he knows Abimelech’s integrity and kept him from sinning, and tells him to return Sarah, for Abraham is a prophet who will pray for him.

I kept you. God restrains sin, even in unbelievers.

A prophet. The first time the word appears. Abraham is God’s spokesman despite his lie.

For worship. Thank God for the sins he has kept you from.
verseByVerse.note: The first time the Bible calls anyone a prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abimelech rose early in the morning and called all his servants and told them all these things. And the men were very much afraid. Then Abimelech called Abraham and said to him, "What have you done to us? And how have I sinned against you, that you have brought on me and my kingdom a great sin? You have done to me things that ought not to be done." And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What did you see, that you did this thing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech tells his servants, who are afraid, and rebukes Abraham for bringing such guilt on him and his kingdom.

Rebuked by a pagan. Again.

Things that ought not be done. Abimelech shows more moral sense than Abraham.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham said, "I did it because I thought, 'There is no fear of God at all in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.' Besides, she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father though not the daughter of my mother, and she became my wife. And when God caused me to wander from my father's house, I said to her, 'This is the kindness you must do me: at every place to which we come, say of me, "He is my brother."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham explains he thought there was no fear of God there, and that Sarah is truly his half-sister, and that they had agreed on this plan long before.

No fear of God here. He misjudged them.

Half-truth. A technical truth used to deceive.

A long-standing plan. Fear had become a habit.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abimelech took sheep and oxen, and male servants and female servants, and gave them to Abraham, and returned Sarah his wife to him. And Abimelech said, "Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you." To Sarah he said, "Behold, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver. It is a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech gives Abraham livestock and servants, returns Sarah, offers him land, and gives a thousand pieces of silver to vindicate Sarah.

Generous. The pagan king outdoes the believer.

Vindication. Sarah’s honour restored.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech, and also healed his wife and female slaves so that they bore children. For the LORD had closed all the wombs of the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham prays, and God heals Abimelech’s household, for God had closed their wombs because of Sarah.

Abraham prayed. The flawed prophet intercedes.

Wombs opened. Just before Sarah’s womb is opened (21:1).

For worship. Praise God who works through imperfect servants.

20.theology:
Common Grace and Moral Conscience. Abimelech’s integrity in chapter 20 demonstrates what Reformed theology calls “common grace” at work in the moral realm: the image of God, though distorted by sin, still functions as a moral compass in unregenerate humanity. Abimelech acted with integrity not because he had the Torah but because God had written the basic moral law on the human heart (Rom. 2:14–15) and personally restrained him from sin (v.6). The church has no monopoly on moral conscience; it has the unique gift of the Spirit who enables what conscience alone cannot sustain.

The Irrevocability of Calling. God calls Abraham “a prophet” (v.7) immediately after Abraham has failed as a husband and as an honest man. The calling is not contingent on the immediate moral performance. Paul makes this explicit for the new covenant: “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom. 11:29). This is both comfort (our failures do not revoke our calling) and warning (our calling does not excuse our failures). The cracked vessel is still in the Potter’s hands.
20.examples:
Then: The episode with Abimelech reflects the political vulnerability of a patriarch traveling through Philistine territory with a beautiful wife. In the power dynamics of the ancient Near East, a foreign woman was effectively unprotected — a king could take her with impunity. Abraham’s deception was pragmatic cowardice, not irrational fear. But God’s protection of Sarah through a Philistine king’s conscience demonstrates that divine providence operates through unexpected moral actors.

Now: The repeat failure of Abraham (same sin as chapter 12) speaks to every Christian who has been mortified to discover that they are still vulnerable to sins they thought they had put behind them. The specific, persistent sin does not disqualify from covenant relationship or from prophetic calling — but it does need to be addressed, confessed, and brought repeatedly to the God who holds his people not by their grip on him but by his grip on them. And Abimelech’s integrity should keep the church humble: God works through moral conscientiousness in unexpected places, and the covenant community has no exclusive claim on ethical seriousness.

21.title: God Has Made Laughter for Me
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised.<sup>2</sup>And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him.<sup>3</sup>Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac.<sup>4</sup>And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.<sup>5</sup>Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.<sup>6</sup>And Sarah said, "God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me."<sup>7</sup>And she said, "Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age."<sup>8</sup>And the child grew and was weaned. And Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned.<sup>9</sup>But Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, laughing.<sup>10</sup>So she said to Abraham, "Cast out this slave woman with her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac."<sup>11</sup>And the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son.<sup>12</sup>But God said to Abraham, "Be not displeased because of the boy and because of your slave woman. Whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you, for through Isaac shall your offspring be named.<sup>13</sup>And I will make a nation of the son of the slave woman also, because he is your offspring."<sup>14</sup>So Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, along with the child, and sent her away. And she departed and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.<sup>15</sup>When the water in the skin was gone, she put the child under one of the bushes.<sup>16</sup>Then she went and sat down opposite him a good way off, about the distance of a bowshot, for she said, "Let me not look on the death of the child." And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept.<sup>17</sup>And God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, "What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.<sup>18</sup>Up! Lift up the boy, and hold him fast with your hand, for I will make him into a great nation."<sup>19</sup>Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. And she went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink.<sup>20</sup>And God was with the boy, and he grew up.
