He lived in the wilderness and became an expert with the bow.<sup>21</sup>He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.<sup>22</sup>At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do.<sup>23</sup>Now therefore swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me or with my descendants or with my posterity, but as I have dealt kindly with you, so you will deal with me and with the land where you have sojourned."<sup>24</sup>And Abraham said, "I will swear."<sup>25</sup>When Abraham reproved Abimelech about a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized,<sup>26</sup>Abimelech said, "I do not know who has done this thing; you did not tell me, and I have not heard of it until today."<sup>27</sup>So Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant.<sup>28</sup>Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart.<sup>29</sup>And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What is the meaning of these seven ewe lambs that you have set apart?"<sup>30</sup>He said, "These seven ewe lambs you will take from my hand, that this may be a witness for me that I dug this well."<sup>31</sup>Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there both of them swore an oath.<sup>32</sup>So they made a covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army rose up and returned to the land of the Philistines.<sup>33</sup>Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and called there on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God.<sup>34</sup>And Abraham sojourned many days in the land of the Philistines.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is one of the most joyful chapters in Genesis: “The LORD visited Sarah as he had said” (v.1). The promise of decades, the waiting of chapters, the laughing and doubting and wandering — all of it comes to its appointed end in the simplest possible way: God did what he said he would do. Isaac is born. Sarah laughs — not the incredulous laugh of 18:12 but the laughter of fulfilled promise: “God has made laughter for me” (v.6). The name Isaac (he laughs) is now the permanent memorial to the joy of impossible-promise-kept.

The chapter does not remain in this joy for long. The conflict between Ishmael and Isaac erupts at the weaning feast, and Hagar and Ishmael are sent away — a painful episode that troubles modern readers and troubled Abraham greatly (v.11: “the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son”). But God provides for Hagar and Ishmael in the wilderness, meeting them again as he had in chapter 16, and promising that Ishmael too will become a great nation (v.18). The God who keeps his promises to Isaac is also the God who hears the voice of Ishmael (v.17: “God heard the voice of the boy” — Ishmael means “God hears”).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Birth of Isaac and the Expulsion of Hagar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 21 opens with the long-awaited birth of Isaac — the covenant child, born at the appointed time to a 90-year-old mother and a 100-year-old father. The laughter that greeted the promise (17:17; 18:12) becomes the laughter of fulfilled joy: 'God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me.' The impossible has happened. But the joy of Isaac's birth immediately creates a crisis: Ishmael, now a teenager of sixteen or so, is seen 'laughing' (mocking) at the weaning feast, and Sarah demands his expulsion. Abraham is torn; God instructs him to comply; and Hagar and Ishmael are sent into the wilderness, where God provides for them a second time.
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD visits Sarah as he said, and Isaac is born to Abraham at a hundred. Sarah laughs for joy. At the weaning feast Ishmael is seen laughing, and Sarah demands that Hagar and her son be cast out; God tells a grieving Abraham to do it, then hears the boy in the wilderness and opens Hagar's eyes to a well.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul reads the two sons as two covenants and calls the Galatians children of promise, like Isaac (Gal. 4:28). Now: God hears a child "where he is" — not where he ought to be.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD visited Sarah as he had said, and the LORD did to Sarah as he had promised. And Sarah conceived and bore Abraham a son in his old age at the time of which God had spoken to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD visits Sarah as he said, and she conceives and bears Abraham a son in his old age at the appointed time.

As he had said. Three times: God keeps his word exactly.

At the time. God’s timing (18:14).

For worship. Thank God that he does as he has promised.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham called the name of his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac. And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him. Abraham was a hundred years old when his son Isaac was born to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham names him Isaac and circumcises him on the eighth day; he is a hundred years old.

Isaac. “He laughs”.

The eighth day. Obedience to the covenant (17:12).

A hundred. Twenty-five years after the first promise.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sarah said, "God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh over me." And she said, "Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sarah says, “God has made laughter for me; everyone who hears will laugh with me. Who would have said that Sarah would nurse children?”

Laughter transformed. From disbelief (18:12) to joy.

On a Tuesday. God can turn your bitter laughter into joy.

verseByVerse.quote: And the child grew and was weaned. And Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned. But Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, laughing. So she said to Abraham, "Cast out this slave woman with her son, for the son of this slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac." And the thing was very displeasing to Abraham on account of his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Isaac’s weaning feast, Sarah sees Ishmael laughing and tells Abraham to cast out the slave woman and her son, which greatly displeases Abraham.

Laughing. Perhaps mocking (Galatians 4:29, “persecuted”).

Cast out. Harsh words.

Displeased. Abraham loved Ishmael.
verseByVerse.note: “Laughing” may mean laughing in mockery (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to Abraham, "Be not displeased because of the boy and because of your slave woman. Whatever Sarah says to you, do as she tells you, for through Isaac shall your offspring be named. And I will make a nation of the son of the slave woman also, because he is your offspring."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Abraham not to be displeased but to listen to Sarah, for through Isaac his offspring will be named, and he will make Ishmael a nation too.

Through Isaac. The line of promise (Romans 9:7).

Ishmael too. God cares for him.

Galatians 4:21–31. Paul uses Hagar and Sarah as a picture of law and grace: slavery and freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham rose early in the morning and took bread and a skin of water and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder, along with the child, and sent her away. And she departed and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. When the water in the skin was gone, she put the child under one of the bushes. Then she went and sat down opposite him a good way off, about the distance of a bowshot, for she said, "Let me not look on the death of the child." And as she sat opposite him, she lifted up her voice and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham sends Hagar away with bread and water; in the wilderness of Beersheba the water runs out, and she puts the boy under a bush and sits away, so as not to see him die, and weeps.

Early in the morning. Abraham obeys, though it hurts.

She wept. A mother’s despair.

verseByVerse.quote: And God heard the voice of the boy, and the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and said to her, "What troubles you, Hagar? Fear not, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is. Up! Lift up the boy, and hold him fast with your hand, for I will make him into a great nation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hears the boy’s voice, and the angel of God tells Hagar not to fear, for God has heard, and he will make the boy a great nation.

God heard. “Ishmael” means “God hears”.

Fear not. God’s word to the outcast.

For worship. Thank God who hears the cry of the abandoned.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. And she went and filled the skin with water and gave the boy a drink. And God was with the boy, and he grew up. He lived in the wilderness and became an expert with the bow. He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens Hagar’s eyes to see a well; she gives the boy water, and God is with him as he grows into an archer in the wilderness of Paran, where Hagar finds him an Egyptian wife.

Opened her eyes. The provision was there.

God was with the boy. Blessing outside the covenant line.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to open your eyes to his provision.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–34 — The Covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Genesis 21 records Abraham's covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba — a political treaty that establishes Abraham's standing among the peoples of Canaan. Abimelech approaches Abraham not as a king condescending to a foreigner but as an equal seeking a binding agreement: 'God is with you in all that you do' (v.22). The recognition by the Philistine king that Abraham's prosperity is divinely given is a form of covenant blessing (12:3): the nations are acknowledging the covenant God through his servant.
verseByVerse.theology: Abimelech, seeing that God is with Abraham, asks him to swear not to deal falsely. Abraham raises the matter of a seized well, gives seven ewe lambs as witness that he dug it, and the place is named Beersheba. He plants a tamarisk and calls on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Philistine king recognises the blessing of 12:2–3 at work in Abraham. Now: a grievance should be raised with the one who caused it, who may not even know (Matt. 18:15).

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army said to Abraham, "God is with you in all that you do. Now therefore swear to me here by God that you will not deal falsely with me or with my descendants or with my posterity, but as I have dealt kindly with you, so you will deal with me and with the land where you have sojourned." And Abraham said, "I will swear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech and his commander tell Abraham that God is with him in everything, and ask him to swear not to deal falsely with them.

God is with you. Even outsiders notice.

Swear. They want a lasting peace.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abraham reproved Abimelech about a well of water that Abimelech's servants had seized, Abimelech said, "I do not know who has done this thing; you did not tell me, and I have not heard of it until today."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham complains about a well Abimelech’s servants seized, and Abimelech says he did not know.

Water rights. Vital in the dry Negeb.

Honest dealing. Abraham raises the problem openly.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two men made a covenant. Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock apart. And Abimelech said to Abraham, "What is the meaning of these seven ewe lambs that you have set apart?" He said, "These seven ewe lambs you will take from my hand, that this may be a witness for me that I dug this well." Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there both of them swore an oath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham gives Abimelech sheep and oxen and seven ewe lambs as a witness that he dug the well, and the place is called Beersheba.

Beersheba. “Well of seven” or “well of the oath”.

A covenant. Peace with neighbours.
verseByVerse.note: “Beersheba” means “well of seven” or “well of the oath” (ESV note). It marked the southern edge of the land.

verseByVerse.quote: So they made a covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army rose up and returned to the land of the Philistines. Abraham planted a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and called there on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God. And Abraham sojourned many days in the land of the Philistines.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the covenant, Abraham plants a tamarisk tree in Beersheba and calls on the name of the LORD, the Everlasting God, and lives long in the Philistines’ land.

A tamarisk. A long-lived tree: a sign of permanence.

The Everlasting God. El Olam.

For worship. Call on the Everlasting God, who keeps his promises across the generations.

21.theology:
The Children of Promise. Isaac’s birth is the pivot on which Paul’s theology of election turns in Romans 9: “it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Rom. 9:8). Isaac’s birth establishes the principle that membership in God’s family is determined not by bloodline or merit but by the sovereign promise of God. Every believer is an Isaac — a child of the impossible, born of promise, belonging to a family constituted by grace from outside themselves.

The God Who Hears the Voiceless. The Hagar episode in chapter 21, like that of chapter 16, demonstrates that the God who chose Abraham is also the God who hears Ishmael (“God hears”) and sees Hagar (El Roi, “the God who sees”). The particular election of the covenant line does not exhaust God’s care for those outside it. The widow, the orphan, the foreign slave-woman abandoned in the wilderness — all are the special concern of the God whose covenant people are meant to embody that same concern for the overlooked.
21.examples:
Then: The birth of Isaac after decades of waiting would have resonated deeply with Israel’s own experience of long waiting for covenant fulfillment — the four hundred years in Egypt, the forty years in the wilderness, the centuries of waiting for the Davidic king. God’s faithfulness to Sarah was the paradigm and the promise of his faithfulness to Israel. What seemed impossible — a son for a ninety-year-old woman — was the same kind of impossible as redemption from Egypt or return from Babylon.

Now: The laughter of Sarah (v.6) is the appropriate response to every fulfilled promise of God — the joy that should characterize the Christian life, which is a life of accumulated “as he had said” and “as he had promised.” The church gathers weekly to celebrate the fulfilled promise: the seed of Abraham, the Son of promise, has come, has died, has risen. The weaning feast of Isaac is the distant shadow of the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9) — the celebration of the fulfilled promise that will make every previous joy look small.

22.title: The LORD Will Provide
22.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>2</sup>He said, "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you."<sup>3</sup>So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him.<sup>4</sup>On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar.<sup>5</sup>Then Abraham said to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you."<sup>6</sup>And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together.<sup>7</sup>And Isaac said to his father Abraham, "My father!" And he said, "Here I am, my son." He said, "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?"<sup>8</sup>Abraham said, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." So they went both of them together.<sup>9</sup>When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.<sup>10</sup>Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.<sup>11</sup>But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>12</sup>He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me."<sup>13</sup>And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son.<sup>14</sup>So Abraham called the name of that place, "The LORD will provide"; as it is said to this day, "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided."<sup>15</sup>And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven<sup>16</sup>and said, "By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son,<sup>17</sup>I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore. And your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies,<sup>18</sup>and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice."<sup>19</sup>So Abraham returned to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.<sup>20</sup>Now after these things it was told to Abraham, "Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor:<sup>21</sup>Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram,<sup>22</sup>Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel."<sup>23</sup>(Bethuel fathered Rebekah.) These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother.<sup>24</sup>Moreover, his concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
22.overview:
Genesis 22 — the Akedah, the binding of Isaac — is universally recognized as one of the most profound texts in all of human literature. God commands Abraham to take his only beloved son to Moriah and offer him as a burnt offering. Isaac is not merely Abraham’s son; he is the son of promise, the child through whom God had declared all his covenant purposes would be fulfilled. To sacrifice Isaac is to sacrifice the future, the covenant, and the promise itself. The command appears to contradict everything God has done and said for decades.

Abraham obeys. Hebrews 11:17–19 gives us the theological interpretation: “By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac... He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead.” Abraham’s obedience is grounded not in resignation but in resurrection faith: God had said the covenant would continue through Isaac; God had commanded the sacrifice of Isaac; therefore God would raise Isaac from the dead. He did not know how, but he knew who.

The theological weight of this chapter is immense. It is the most luminous prefiguration of Calvary in the Old Testament: a father, a son, a mountain (Moriah — the site of Solomon’s temple and, in Christian tradition, adjacent to Golgotha), a three-day journey, wood laid on the son’s back, the question “where is the lamb?”, and the divine provision of a substitute. The ram caught in the thicket dies in Isaac’s place; the lamb of God dies in ours. But unlike the story of Moriah, there is no angel’s hand to hold back the Father’s. The true Moriah is accomplished.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 22 is the theological summit of the Abraham narrative and one of the most profound passages in all of Scripture. God commands Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering on Mount Moriah. Abraham obeys immediately and completely, proceeding to the point of raising the knife, at which moment the angel of the LORD intervenes and provides a ram as a substitute. The passage is both history and type: it is a real event in the life of a real man, and it is the most detailed Old Testament foreshadowing of the cross, in which God himself provides the sacrifice his own justice requires.
verseByVerse.theology: God tests Abraham: take your only son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him on a mountain in Moriah. Abraham goes at once, lays the wood on Isaac, tells him God will provide the lamb, binds him and takes the knife. The angel stops him; a ram is offered instead of his son; and God swears by himself to bless him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews says Abraham reckoned God could raise the dead (Heb. 11:19). Now: "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all" (Rom. 8:32) — Abraham was stopped, and God was not.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tests Abraham, telling him to take his only son Isaac, whom he loves, to the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt offering.

God tested. Not to tempt him to sin (James 1:13), but to prove and strengthen his faith.

Your son, your only son, whom you love. Each phrase tightens the pain.

Moriah. Later the site of the temple (2 Chronicles 3:1).

Where Christians differ: how could God command this? Some, like Kierkegaard, see faith suspending ethics. Verdict: God, the giver of life, had the right to require it, and never intended it to happen (v. 12). God later forbids child sacrifice absolutely (Deuteronomy 12:31). The test showed that Abraham trusted God above his dearest gift.
verseByVerse.note: Moriah is later named as the hill where Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him. On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar. Then Abraham said to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham rises early, splits the wood, and sets out with Isaac and two servants; on the third day he sees the place, and tells the servants that he and the boy will worship and come back.

Early. Prompt obedience.

We will come back. Faith in resurrection (Hebrews 11:19).

The third day. A hint of another third day.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together. And Isaac said to his father Abraham, "My father!" And he said, "Here I am, my son." He said, "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham said, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." So they went both of them together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac carries the wood, Abraham the fire and knife; Isaac asks where the lamb is, and Abraham answers, “God will provide for himself the lamb.”

The son carries the wood. As Christ carried his cross (John 19:17).

Where is the lamb? The question of the Old Testament, answered in John 1:29.

God will provide. Faith’s answer.

They went both together. Isaac, probably a young man, submits.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood. Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the place, Abraham builds an altar, arranges the wood, binds Isaac, lays him on the altar, and takes the knife.

The binding. In Jewish tradition, the Akedah.

Isaac’s submission. A young man could have resisted an old man.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel of the LORD calls, “Abraham, Abraham!”, and tells him not to harm the boy, for now he knows that Abraham fears God, having not withheld his only son.

Now I know. Not that God learned something, but that Abraham’s faith was shown.

Not withheld. Echoed in Romans 8:32: God did not spare his own Son.

Where Christians differ: justified by works? James 2:21 says Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac; Paul says by faith (Romans 4:2–3). Verdict: Abraham was counted righteous by faith (15:6) years before; here his faith was shown to be real by obedience. James speaks of faith demonstrated; Paul of faith as the means of being right with God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son. So Abraham called the name of that place, "The LORD will provide"; as it is said to this day, "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket and offers it in his son’s place, and names the place “The LORD will provide.”

Instead of his son. Substitution.

The LORD will provide. Yahweh Yireh: “On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided.”

On this mountain. Near where God would provide his own Son.

For worship. Thank God who provided the Lamb in your place.
verseByVerse.note: “The LORD will provide” can also be rendered “the LORD will see” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven and said, "By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son, I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore. And your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies, and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice." So Abraham returned to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel calls again: because Abraham did not withhold his son, God swears by himself to bless him, multiply his offspring, give them their enemies’ gates, and bless all nations in his offspring.

By myself I have sworn. The strongest oath (Hebrews 6:13–18).

Your offspring. Singular: Christ (Galatians 3:16).

All nations. The promise to Abraham confirmed.

On a Tuesday. Is there anything you are withholding from God?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter concludes with a brief genealogical notice about Abraham's brother Nahor and his family. The list is not incidental; it serves the narrative purpose of introducing Rebekah (v.23, 'Bethuel fathered Rebekah') — the woman who will become Isaac's wife in chapter 24. The genealogy bridges the Akedah and the search for Isaac's wife: from the mountain of divine provision to the family that God has been preparing as the provision for Isaac's covenant continuity.
verseByVerse.theology: News comes that Nahor's wife Milcah has borne him eight sons, and in a bracket: "Bethuel fathered Rebekah."
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the wife for Isaac is born and named before the question is asked. Now: God's provision is generally in place long before we look up.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these things it was told to Abraham, "Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor: Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel." (Bethuel fathered Rebekah.) These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother. Moreover, his concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham hears of his brother Nahor’s children, including Bethuel, the father of Rebekah.

Rebekah. Introduced ahead: Isaac’s future wife (chapter 24).

God’s provision continues. Even the bride is being prepared.

For worship. Thank God who plans ahead for his people.
verseByVerse.note: Rebekah’s name appears here, preparing for chapter 24.

22.theology:
Substitutionary Atonement. Genesis 22 is the Old Testament’s clearest picture of substitutionary atonement: the ram dies in the place of Isaac, who deserved death as a member of fallen humanity. The pattern is the scaffolding on which the entire sacrificial system is built and which is finally dismantled at the cross, where the scaffold is replaced by the reality it always pointed toward. The Lamb of God does not merely provide a substitute; he is the substitute, offered by the Father, provided by himself (“God will provide for himself the lamb”).

Resurrection Faith. Hebrews 11:19 identifies the theological ground of Abraham’s obedience as resurrection faith: he “considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.” Abraham did not understand what would happen on Moriah; he trusted the character of the God who had made the impossible promise and who could be trusted to keep it even through death. This is the faith that justifies: not certainty about outcomes but trust in the character of God, who is the God of resurrection.
22.examples:
Then: Moriah is identified in 2 Chronicles 3:1 as the site where Solomon built the temple — the same mountain where Abraham offered Isaac became the place of the permanent altar of Israel’s worship. The geography is theological: the place of the ultimate act of faith became the place of the ongoing memorial of that faith, and in Christian tradition the same hill of Moriah overlooks Golgotha, where the ultimate sacrifice was offered. The mountain carries the whole weight of redemptive history on its slopes.

Now: The Akedah asks every generation the same question: is there anything you love so much that you would not give it back to God? This is the test of the “Isaac” in every life — the person, career, dream, or relationship that has quietly moved from gift to god. The willingness to hold even the most precious things with open hands, trusting the God who gives and takes away, is the maturity that the Akedah both requires and produces. And for the preacher, Genesis 22 is the Old Testament text that most nakedly anticipates the cross — the Father’s love that withholds nothing, the Son who carries the wood, the Lamb who is provided.

23.title: A Burial Place for Sarah
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah.<sup>2</sup>And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.<sup>3</sup>And Abraham rose up from before his dead and said to the Hittites,<sup>4</sup>"I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight."<sup>5</sup>The Hittites answered Abraham,<sup>6</sup>"Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will withhold from you his tomb to hinder you from burying your dead."<sup>7</sup>Abraham rose and bowed to the Hittites, the people of the land.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, "If you are willing that I should bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar,<sup>9</sup>that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he owns; it is at the end of his field. For the full price let him give it to me in your presence as property for a burying place."<sup>10</sup>Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, of all who went in at the gate of his city,<sup>11</sup>"No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the sight of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead."<sup>12</sup>Then Abraham bowed down before the people of the land.<sup>13</sup>And he said to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, "But if you will, hear me: I give the price of the field. Accept it from me, that I may bury my dead there."<sup>14</sup>Ephron answered Abraham,<sup>15</sup>"My lord, listen to me: a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead."<sup>16</sup>Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants.<sup>17</sup>So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over<sup>18</sup>to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of his city.<sup>19</sup>After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah east of Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan.<sup>20</sup>The field and the cave that is in it were made over to Abraham as property for a burying place by the Hittites.
23.overview:
Genesis 23 is the first death in the patriarchal narrative and the first property transaction in the promised land. It is given extraordinary detail — the negotiation, the cultural conventions, the precise legal transfer — because it is theologically significant, not merely biographical. Abraham buys a cave and a field at Machpelah to bury Sarah: the first piece of the promised land becomes a burial ground. The covenant people enter their inheritance through death before they enter through life.

The chapter is a study in grief and faith held together. Abraham mourns and weeps for Sarah (v.2) — genuine, public, unashamed grief. He does not spiritualize or suppress his sorrow; he enters it fully. Then he rises and negotiates for a burial place — grief that acts, that makes provision, that refuses to be paralyzed. Biblical mourning is honest emotion followed by purposeful response. The Psalms of lament follow this same pattern.

The purchase of the cave of Machpelah becomes the family tomb: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah will all be buried there (49:29–32). It is a small plot, purchased at considerable expense, in a land still occupied by others. But it is the first concrete installment on the promise — the first piece of Canaan held in Abraham’s name. Every burial in the cave of Machpelah is an act of faith: the patriarchs choose to be buried in the promised land rather than returning to Mesopotamia, because they believe the promise of the land will be fulfilled even for their bones.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Death of Sarah and the Purchase of Machpelah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 23 records the death of Sarah at 127 years and Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah as a burial site — the first piece of the Promised Land that Abraham actually owns. The transaction is conducted with elaborate courtesy and formal legal precision, and its lengthy narration signals its importance: the purchase of Machpelah is both an act of mourning and an act of faith. Abraham insists on paying full price rather than accepting the land as a gift, creating an irrefutable legal record of his ownership of at least this piece of the land God has promised.
verseByVerse.theology: Sarah dies at 127, and Abraham mourns and weeps. A sojourner with no land, he asks the Hittites for a burial place, refuses Ephron's gift, and pays four hundred shekels in public for the cave of Machpelah — the only part of the promised land he ever owns.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob will all be laid there (49:29–32). Now: believers grieve, but not as those without hope (1 Thess. 4:13), and they stake their bones on the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah. And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sarah dies at 127 in Hebron, and Abraham mourns and weeps for her.

The only woman whose age at death is given. A mark of her importance.

He wept. Faith grieves (1 Thessalonians 4:13): not without hope, but truly.

On a Tuesday. It is right to weep for those you love.
verseByVerse.note: Sarah is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is recorded.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham rose up from before his dead and said to the Hittites, "I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight." The Hittites answered Abraham, "Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will withhold from you his tomb to hinder you from burying your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham tells the Hittites he is a sojourner and foreigner among them, and asks for property for a burial place; they call him a prince of God and offer him their best tomb.

A sojourner. After sixty years in the land, he owns none of it (Hebrews 11:13).

A prince of God. Respected by his neighbours.
verseByVerse.note: The Hittites here are “sons of Heth” (ESV note), a people living in Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham rose and bowed to the Hittites, the people of the land. And he said to them, "If you are willing that I should bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar, that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he owns; it is at the end of his field. For the full price let him give it to me in your presence as property for a burying place." Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, of all who went in at the gate of his city, "No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the sight of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham bows and asks them to persuade Ephron to sell him the cave of Machpelah for its full price, and Ephron offers to give it to him.

For the full price. Abraham wants a clear legal title, not a gift that could be reclaimed.

I give it to you. Polite bargaining.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham bowed down before the people of the land. And he said to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, "But if you will, hear me: I give the price of the field. Accept it from me, that I may bury my dead there." Ephron answered Abraham, "My lord, listen to me: a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead." Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham insists on paying, and Ephron names a price of four hundred shekels of silver, which Abraham weighs out publicly.

Four hundred shekels. A high price.

Before witnesses. An honest, public transaction.

On a Tuesday. Deal honestly and openly in business.
verseByVerse.note: Four hundred shekels was about 10 pounds of silver (a shekel was about 2/5 ounce, ESV note) — a high price.

verseByVerse.quote: So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of his city. After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah east of Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan. The field and the cave that is in it were made over to Abraham as property for a burying place by the Hittites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The field and cave of Machpelah become Abraham’s property, and he buries Sarah there.

A first piece of the promised land. A grave: a down payment of faith.

The family tomb. Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah are buried here (49:29–32).

Burial. The patriarchs’ care for burial reflects hope in the resurrection of the body.

For worship. Thank God for the hope of resurrection for those who die in faith.
verseByVerse.note: The cave of Machpelah at Hebron became the family tomb: Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob were buried there too.

23.theology:
Grief and Faith. Genesis 23 refuses to separate genuine grief and genuine faith. Abraham mourns and weeps; he also rises and acts. The Psalms of lament demonstrate the same integration: honest expression of pain before God, followed by the refrain of trust. The New Testament does not eliminate grief but frames it differently: “that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4:13). The hope of resurrection does not suppress the tears of loss; it gives them a horizon. Weeping now is real; the resurrection morning will be realer.

The Pilgrim Posture. Abraham’s self-description as “sojourner and foreigner” (v.4) becomes the defining identity of the people of God throughout Scripture. 1 Peter 2:11: “I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh.” The pilgrim posture produces a particular kind of freedom: those who know they are passing through are not paralyzed by the conditions of their temporary residence. They can be generous because they are not accumulating; they can be bold because they are not protecting a permanent stake; they can love their neighbors without needing them to be their home.
23.examples:
Then: The elaborate negotiation protocol of Genesis 23 shows a public negotiation at the city gate before witnesses, which some scholars compare to Hittite land law and a formal oral and physical transfer of property. The legal precision was necessary to establish permanent ownership rather than leasehold rights. Abraham’s insistence on purchasing rather than accepting the land as a gift (vv.11–13) was strategic: a gift could be reclaimed, but a legal purchase could not. He was securing the first installment of the promise in the most durable form available.

Now: The chapter speaks to a culture that struggles with death. The modern West has largely removed death from public view, medicalized it, and deprived it of both the honest grief and the faith-framework that Genesis 23 models. Abraham mourns openly and specifically (he weeps for Sarah, not for death-in-general), then acts with faith-grounded purpose (buying a burial place in the promised land). The church that recovers the practice of honest, faith-framed grief for particular people will serve its culture better than one that either suppresses grief with spiritual clichés or drowns in it without hope.

24.title: A Wife for Isaac
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years. And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things.<sup>2</sup>And Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, who had charge of all that he had, "Put your hand under my thigh,<sup>3</sup>that I may make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell,<sup>4</sup>but will go to my country and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac."<sup>5</sup>The servant said to him, "Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me to this land. Must I then take your son back to the land from which you came?"<sup>6</sup>Abraham said to him, "See to it that you do not take my son back there.<sup>7</sup>The LORD, the God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my kindred, and who spoke to me and swore to me, 'To your offspring I will give this land,' he will send his angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there.<sup>8</sup>But if the woman is not willing to follow you, then you will be free from this oath of mine; only you must not take my son back there."<sup>9</sup>So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter.<sup>10</sup>Then the servant took ten of his master's camels and departed, taking all sorts of choice gifts from his master; and he arose and went to Mesopotamia to the city of Nahor.<sup>11</sup>And he made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time when women go out to draw water.<sup>12</sup>And he said, "O LORD, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today and show steadfast love to my master Abraham.<sup>13</sup>Behold, I am standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.<sup>14</sup>Let the young woman to whom I shall say, 'Please let down your jar that I may drink,' and who shall say, 'Drink, and I will water your camels'—let her be the one whom you have appointed for your servant Isaac. By this I shall know that you have shown steadfast love to my master."<sup>15</sup>Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, came out with her water jar on her shoulder.<sup>16</sup>The young woman was very attractive in appearance, a maiden whom no man had known. She went down to the spring and filled her jar and came up.<sup>17</sup>Then the servant ran to meet her and said, "Please give me a little water to drink from your jar."<sup>18</sup>She said, "Drink, my lord." And she quickly let down her jar upon her hand and gave him a drink.<sup>19</sup>When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, "I will draw water for your camels also, until they have finished drinking."<sup>20</sup>So she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran again to the well to draw water, and she drew for all his camels.<sup>21</sup>The man gazed at her in silence to learn whether the LORD had prospered his journey or not.<sup>22</sup>When the camels had finished drinking, the man took a gold ring weighing a half shekel, and two bracelets for her arms weighing ten gold shekels,<sup>23</sup>and said, "Please tell me whose daughter you are. Is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?"<sup>24</sup>She said to him, "I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor."<sup>25</sup>She added, "We have plenty of both straw and fodder, and room to spend the night."<sup>26</sup>The man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD<sup>27</sup>and said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master. As for me, the LORD has led me in the way to the house of my master's kinsmen."<sup>28</sup>Then the young woman ran and told her mother's household about these things.<sup>29</sup>Rebekah had a brother whose name was Laban. Laban ran out toward the man, to the spring.<sup>30</sup>As soon as he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's arms, and heard the words of Rebekah his sister, "Thus the man spoke to me," he went to the man. And behold, he was standing by the camels at the spring.<sup>31</sup>He said, "Come in, O blessed of the LORD. Why do you stand outside? For I have prepared the house and a place for the camels."<sup>32</sup>So the man came to the house and unharnessed the camels, and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and there was water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him.<sup>33</sup>Then food was set before him to eat. But he said, "I will not eat until I have said what I have to say." He said, "Speak on."<sup>34</sup>So he said, "I am Abraham's servant.<sup>35</sup>The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become great. He has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, male servants and female servants, camels and donkeys.<sup>36</sup>And Sarah my master's wife bore a son to my master when she was old, and to him he has given all that he has.<sup>37</sup>My master made me swear, saying, 'You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell,<sup>38</sup>but you shall go to my father's house and to my clan and take a wife for my son.'<sup>39</sup>I said to my master, 'Perhaps the woman will not follow me.'<sup>40</sup>But he said to me, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send his angel with you and prosper your way. You shall take a wife for my son from my clan and from my father's house.<sup>41</sup>Then you will be free from my oath, when you come to my clan. And if they will not give her to you, you will be free from my oath.'<sup>42</sup>"I came today to the spring and said, 'O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, if now you are prospering the way that I go,<sup>43</sup>behold, I am standing by the spring of water. Let the virgin who comes out to draw water, to whom I shall say, "Please give me a little water from your jar to drink,"<sup>44</sup>and who will say to me, "Drink, and I will draw for your camels also," let her be the woman whom the LORD has appointed for my master's son.'<sup>45</sup>"Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out with her water jar on her shoulder, and she went down to the spring and drew water. I said to her, 'Please let me drink.'<sup>46</sup>She quickly let down her jar from her shoulder and said, 'Drink, and I will give your camels drink also.' So I drank, and she gave the camels drink also.<sup>47</sup>Then I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' She said, 'The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bore to him.' So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her arms.<sup>48</sup>Then I bowed my head and worshiped the LORD and blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who had led me by the right way to take the daughter of my master's kinsman for his son.<sup>49</sup>Now then, if you are going to show steadfast love and faithfulness to my master, tell me; and if not, tell me, that I may turn to the right hand or to the left."<sup>50</sup>Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, "The thing has come from the LORD; we cannot speak to you bad or good.<sup>51</sup>Behold, Rebekah is before you; take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master's son, as the LORD has spoken."<sup>52</sup>When Abraham's servant heard their words, he bowed himself to the earth before the LORD.<sup>53</sup>And the servant brought out jewelry of silver and of gold, and garments, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave to her brother and to her mother costly ornaments.<sup>54</sup>And he and the men who were with him ate and drank, and they spent the night there. When they arose in the morning, he said, "Send me away to my master."<sup>55</sup>Her brother and her mother said, "Let the young woman remain with us a while, at least ten days; after that she may go."<sup>56</sup>But he said to them, "Do not delay me, since the LORD has prospered my way. Send me away that I may go to my master."<sup>57</sup>They said, "Let us call the young woman and ask her."<sup>58</sup>And they called Rebekah and said to her, "Will you go with this man?" She said, "I will go."<sup>59</sup>So they sent away Rebekah their sister and her nurse, and Abraham's servant and his men.<sup>60</sup>And they blessed Rebekah and said to her, "Our sister, may you become thousands of ten thousands, and may your offspring possess the gate of those who hate him!"<sup>61</sup>Then Rebekah and her young women arose and rode on the camels and followed the man. Thus the servant took Rebekah and went his way.<sup>62</sup>Now Isaac had returned from Beer-lahai-roi and was dwelling in the Negeb.<sup>63</sup>And Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening. And he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, there were camels coming.<sup>64</sup>And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel<sup>65</sup>and said to the servant, "Who is that man, walking in the field to meet us?" The servant said, "It is my master." So she took her veil and covered herself.<sup>66</sup>And the servant told Isaac all the things that he had done.<sup>67</sup>Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
24.overview:
Genesis 24 is the longest single narrative in Genesis — sixty-seven verses devoted to the search for Isaac’s wife. The length signals the importance: the covenant must continue through the right marriage, and the right marriage requires divine guidance, faithful obedience, and patient waiting. The servant’s mission is a model of what it looks like to seek God’s leading in a specific, practical, consequential decision.

The chapter is saturated with the language of divine providence. The servant prays for a specific sign (vv.12–14), receives the sign immediately (vv.15–20), interprets it as divine guidance (v.26), gives thanks (v.27), and reports it all to Rebekah’s family as God’s own doing (vv.48–49). The word “steadfast love” (hesed) appears in verse 27 — God’s covenant faithfulness, his loyal love, his unfailing commitment — as the theological explanation for what has just happened: the right woman at the right well at the right time is not coincidence but hesed.

The chapter also contains one of the Bible’s most tender ending lines: “Isaac... took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death” (v.67). Love and comfort in a single sentence, grief resolved in grace. This is how God works: covenant purposes fulfilled, human hearts healed, the future secured through a love that is itself a gift of hesed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Abraham's Commission to His Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 24 is the longest chapter in Genesis and one of the most carefully crafted narratives in the entire Old Testament. Its subject is the finding of a wife for Isaac — the third link in the covenant chain (after Abraham and Isaac) — and its method is the providence of God operating through the faithful prayer and discernment of an unnamed servant. The chapter is both a wonderful story of answered prayer and a theological meditation on how God guides his people through ordinary human means: conversation, hospitality, gifts, and the quiet recognitions of a seeking heart.
verseByVerse.theology: Old Abraham makes his servant swear by the LORD not to take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites but from his kindred, and never to take Isaac back there. The LORD will send his angel ahead; if the woman will not come, the servant is released.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the household of promise was not to be absorbed into the religion of the land (Deut. 7:3–4). Now: believers are to marry "only in the Lord" (1 Cor. 7:39).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years. And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things. And Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, who had charge of all that he had, "Put your hand under my thigh, that I may make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell, but will go to my country and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Old and blessed, Abraham makes his chief servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites, but from his own kindred.

Not from the Canaanites. To keep the covenant family from idolatry.

Marrying in the faith. The principle continues: believers should marry believers (1 Corinthians 7:39; 2 Corinthians 6:14).

Under my thigh. A solemn oath linked to offspring.
verseByVerse.note: Putting a hand “under the thigh” was a solemn form of oath.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant said to him, "Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me to this land. Must I then take your son back to the land from which you came?" Abraham said to him, "See to it that you do not take my son back there. The LORD, the God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my kindred, and who spoke to me and swore to me, 'To your offspring I will give this land,' he will send his angel before you, and you shall take a wife for my son from there. But if the woman is not willing to follow you, then you will be free from this oath of mine; only you must not take my son back there." So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant asks what to do if the woman will not come, and Abraham says never to take Isaac back there; God will send his angel ahead, and if she refuses, the servant is free.

Not back to Mesopotamia. Isaac must stay in the land of promise.

His angel before you. Abraham’s confidence in God’s guidance.

On a Tuesday. Trust God to go ahead of you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–27 — The Servant's Journey and Prayer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The servant travels to Mesopotamia, arrives at the city of Nahor in the evening, and pauses at the well outside the city to pray. His prayer is specific and bold: he asks God to show him the woman intended for Isaac by the sign of her offering water to his camels without being asked. He has barely finished praying when Rebekah appears and does exactly what he prayed for — not only giving him water but volunteering to water his camels as well. The servant watches in silence, wondering whether the LORD has prospered his journey.
verseByVerse.theology: At the well of Nahor's city the servant prays for a woman who will offer water to him and to his camels. Before he has finished, Rebekah comes and does exactly that; she is Bethuel's daughter, and the servant bows and blesses the LORD for his steadfast love and faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the sign he asked for revealed character, and it was asked inside a promise already given. Now: guidance is usually recognised afterwards — "the LORD has led me" (v. 27).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the servant took ten of his master's camels and departed, taking all sorts of choice gifts from his master; and he arose and went to Mesopotamia to the city of Nahor. And he made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time when women go out to draw water. And he said, "O LORD, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today and show steadfast love to my master Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant travels with ten camels and gifts to Nahor’s city, makes the camels kneel by the well at evening, and prays for success.

He prayed. Before acting.

Steadfast love. Chesed: covenant faithfulness. A key word of the chapter.
verseByVerse.note: Mesopotamia is “Aram-naharaim” (ESV note), “Aram of the two rivers,” in the north. A string of ten camels marked great wealth.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water. Let the young woman to whom I shall say, 'Please let down your jar that I may drink,' and who shall say, 'Drink, and I will water your camels'—let her be the one whom you have appointed for your servant Isaac. By this I shall know that you have shown steadfast love to my master."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks that the young woman who offers water to him and his camels be the one God has chosen for Isaac.

A sign. A test of character: watering ten camels is hard work.

Where Christians differ: asking for signs today. Some “put out a fleece” for guidance. Verdict: God guides chiefly through his word, wisdom and godly counsel. He may arrange circumstances, but believers should not demand signs to decide what Scripture has already made plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, came out with her water jar on her shoulder. The young woman was very attractive in appearance, a maiden whom no man had known. She went down to the spring and filled her jar and came up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he finishes praying, Rebekah comes out with her jar: very beautiful and a virgin.

Before he had finished. God answered before he asked (Isaiah 65:24).

From Abraham’s family. The granddaughter of Nahor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the servant ran to meet her and said, "Please give me a little water to drink from your jar." She said, "Drink, my lord." And she quickly let down her jar upon her hand and gave him a drink. When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, "I will draw water for your camels also, until they have finished drinking." So she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran again to the well to draw water, and she drew for all his camels. The man gazed at her in silence to learn whether the LORD had prospered his journey or not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant asks for water, Rebekah gives it gladly and offers to water all the camels, and he watches in silence to see whether the LORD has prospered his journey.

She hurried. Four times: a willing servant.

All the camels. Perhaps over a hundred gallons.

Watching in silence. Waiting on God.

verseByVerse.quote: When the camels had finished drinking, the man took a gold ring weighing a half shekel, and two bracelets for her arms weighing ten gold shekels, and said, "Please tell me whose daughter you are. Is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?" She said to him, "I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor." She added, "We have plenty of both straw and fodder, and room to spend the night." The man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD and said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master. As for me, the LORD has led me in the way to the house of my master's kinsmen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gives her gold jewellery, learns her family, and bows to worship the LORD, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and has led him to his master’s kinsmen.

He worshipped. His first response is praise.

The LORD led me. Guidance recognised looking back.

For worship. Thank God for leading you in the way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–67 — The Servant's Report, Rebekah's Consent, and the Marriage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Genesis 24 narrates the servant's reception at Laban's house, his formal recounting of his mission and God's guidance, Laban and Bethuel's agreement to send Rebekah, Rebekah's own consent to the journey, and finally the meeting of Rebekah and Isaac at evening in the Negeb. The chapter ends with the marriage and Isaac's consolation after his mother's death. The narrative is rich with detail, theology, and human dignity — Rebekah is asked for her own consent (unusual in the ancient world), Isaac meets her in the field as he is meditating (or praying), and the marriage is described as a source of comfort to Isaac after his grief.
verseByVerse.theology: Laban welcomes the servant, who will not eat until he has told the whole story. Laban and Bethuel agree that the thing is from the LORD; Rebekah is asked and says, "I will go." Isaac meets her in the field at evening, takes her into Sarah's tent, and loves her, and is comforted after his mother's death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Rebekah's consent echoes Abraham's own call to leave country and kindred. Now: the servant who is never named shows faithfulness that needs no supervising (cf. Matt. 6:3–4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the young woman ran and told her mother's household about these things. Rebekah had a brother whose name was Laban. Laban ran out toward the man, to the spring. As soon as he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's arms, and heard the words of Rebekah his sister, "Thus the man spoke to me," he went to the man. And behold, he was standing by the camels at the spring. He said, "Come in, O blessed of the LORD. Why do you stand outside? For I have prepared the house and a place for the camels." So the man came to the house and unharnessed the camels, and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and there was water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him. Then food was set before him to eat. But he said, "I will not eat until I have said what I have to say." He said, "Speak on."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah runs to tell her household; her brother Laban sees the jewellery, hurries out, and welcomes the servant.

Laban. Impressed by the gold. We will meet him again (chapter 29).

I will not eat until I have told. The servant puts his errand first.

verseByVerse.quote: So he said, "I am Abraham's servant. The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become great. He has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, male servants and female servants, camels and donkeys. And Sarah my master's wife bore a son to my master when she was old, and to him he has given all that he has.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servant explains that he is Abraham’s servant, and how the LORD has blessed Abraham and given him a son in old age, his heir.

God’s blessing. He tells what God has done.

A faithful steward. He speaks of his master, not himself.

verseByVerse.quote: My master made me swear, saying, 'You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell, but you shall go to my father's house and to my clan and take a wife for my son.' I said to my master, 'Perhaps the woman will not follow me.' But he said to me, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send his angel with you and prosper your way. You shall take a wife for my son from my clan and from my father's house. Then you will be free from my oath, when you come to my clan. And if they will not give her to you, you will be free from my oath.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells of his oath to find a wife from Abraham’s family, and Abraham’s confidence that God would send his angel.

Retelling. Repetition emphasises God’s guidance.

verseByVerse.quote: "I came today to the spring and said, 'O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, if now you are prospering the way that I go, behold, I am standing by the spring of water. Let the virgin who comes out to draw water, to whom I shall say, "Please give me a little water from your jar to drink," and who will say to me, "Drink, and I will draw for your camels also," let her be the woman whom the LORD has appointed for my master's son.' "Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out with her water jar on her shoulder, and she went down to the spring and drew water. I said to her, 'Please let me drink.' She quickly let down her jar from her shoulder and said, 'Drink, and I will give your camels drink also.' So I drank, and she gave the camels drink also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He describes his prayer at the spring and how Rebekah came and did exactly as he had asked.

In my heart. His prayer was silent, yet answered.

On a Tuesday. God hears silent prayers.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' She said, 'The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bore to him.' So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her arms. Then I bowed my head and worshiped the LORD and blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who had led me by the right way to take the daughter of my master's kinsman for his son. Now then, if you are going to show steadfast love and faithfulness to my master, tell me; and if not, tell me, that I may turn to the right hand or to the left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells how he learned whose daughter she was, gave her the jewellery, worshipped, and now asks whether they will show steadfast love to his master.

The right way. God led him by a “true way”.

Tell me. He asks for a clear answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said, "The thing has come from the LORD; we cannot speak to you bad or good. Behold, Rebekah is before you; take her and go, and let her be the wife of your master's son, as the LORD has spoken." When Abraham's servant heard their words, he bowed himself to the earth before the LORD. And the servant brought out jewelry of silver and of gold, and garments, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave to her brother and to her mother costly ornaments. And he and the men who were with him ate and drank, and they spent the night there. When they arose in the morning, he said, "Send me away to my master."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban and Bethuel say the thing comes from the LORD; Rebekah may go; and the servant worships and gives gifts.

From the LORD. Even Laban recognises it.

He bowed. Again, worship first.

Gifts. The bride-price.

verseByVerse.quote: Her brother and her mother said, "Let the young woman remain with us a while, at least ten days; after that she may go." But he said to them, "Do not delay me, since the LORD has prospered my way. Send me away that I may go to my master." They said, "Let us call the young woman and ask her." And they called Rebekah and said to her, "Will you go with this man?" She said, "I will go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her family wants her to stay ten days, but the servant asks to leave; they ask Rebekah, and she says, “I will go.”

Do not delay me. Urgency.

I will go. Like Abraham, she leaves her family for the land of promise in faith.

On a Tuesday. When God’s call is clear, do not delay.

verseByVerse.quote: So they sent away Rebekah their sister and her nurse, and Abraham's servant and his men. And they blessed Rebekah and said to her, "Our sister, may you become thousands of ten thousands, and may your offspring possess the gate of those who hate him!" Then Rebekah and her young women arose and rode on the camels and followed the man. Thus the servant took Rebekah and went his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They send Rebekah away with her nurse, blessing her that she may become thousands of ten thousands and her offspring possess their enemies’ gate.

The blessing. Echoes God’s promise to Abraham (22:17).

Her nurse. Deborah (35:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Isaac had returned from Beer-lahai-roi and was dwelling in the Negeb. And Isaac went out to meditate in the field toward evening. And he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, there were camels coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac, living in the Negeb, goes out at evening to meditate in the field and sees camels coming.

To meditate. Or “to walk”, perhaps to pray.

Beer-lahai-roi. Hagar’s well of the God who sees (16:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And Rebekah lifted up her eyes, and when she saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel and said to the servant, "Who is that man, walking in the field to meet us?" The servant said, "It is my master." So she took her veil and covered herself. And the servant told Isaac all the things that he had done. Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah sees Isaac, veils herself, the servant tells him everything, and Isaac takes her into his mother’s tent, marries her, loves her, and is comforted after his mother’s death.

A veil. The bride’s custom.

He loved her. Love after marriage.

Comforted. God provides comfort through a new relationship.

A picture. Some see the servant as the Spirit bringing a bride for the Son. A fitting application, not the direct meaning.

For worship. Thank God for his providence in marriage and family.

24.theology:
Divine Providence in the Particular. Genesis 24 is the Bible’s most detailed account of divine providence operating in the specific details of an ordinary (if important) decision. The servant prays, watches, interprets, gives thanks — treating each moment of the journey as potentially significant, attentive to divine guidance in the sequence of events. This is not superstition but covenantal sensitivity: the God who made and sustains the universe is also present and active in the particular. The doctrine of providence is not about the big sweep of history alone but about “before he had finished speaking” (v.15).

Steadfast Love (Hesed). The servant’s prayer and thanksgiving turn on hesed — the covenant loyalty, the faithful love, the unfailing commitment of God to his promises. This word appears more than two hundred times in the Old Testament and is the primary Old Testament characterization of God’s disposition toward his covenant people. It is the foundation of the Psalms’ confidence (Ps. 136: “his steadfast love endures forever,” 26 times) and the ground of Lamentations’ hope (“the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases,” Lam. 3:22). In the New Testament the same loyal love is seen most fully in the gift of the Son.
24.examples:
Then: Marriage arrangement through a family intermediary was the standard practice in the ancient Near East. The length of the chapter (67 verses) and its detailed reporting of the servant’s prayer and the family’s response were not unusual for a narrative whose stakes were this high — the continuation of the covenant line. That Rebekah was consulted and gave her own consent (v.58) was notable in an ancient context; her personal willingness to go was significant, not merely her family’s agreement.

Now: The chapter speaks to every Christian navigating a significant decision who wants to know God’s leading. The servant’s approach is neither passive fatalism (waiting for God to act without seeking) nor presumptuous control (making the decision without prayer). It is active, prayerful, attentive discernment — doing the work of the mission while watching for the hand of God in its unfolding. And the hesed theology of the chapter is the daily food of every believer: not luck or coincidence, but the steadfast love of a God whose faithfulness is the most reliable constant in the universe.

25.title: Two Nations in Your Womb
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.<sup>2</sup>She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.<sup>3</sup>Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah.<sup>5</sup>Abraham gave all he had to Isaac.<sup>6</sup>But to the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and while he was still living he sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward to the east country.<sup>7</sup>These are the days of the years of Abraham's life, 175 years.<sup>8</sup>Abraham breathed his last and died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people.<sup>9</sup>Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, east of Mamre,<sup>10</sup>the field that Abraham purchased from the Hittites. There Abraham was buried, with Sarah his wife.<sup>11</sup>After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac settled at Beer-lahai-roi.<sup>12</sup>These are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's servant, bore to Abraham.<sup>13</sup>These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, named in the order of their birth: Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael; and Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam,<sup>14</sup>Mishma, Dumah, Massa,<sup>15</sup>Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.<sup>16</sup>These are the sons of Ishmael and these are their names, by their villages and by their encampments, twelve princes according to their tribes.<sup>17</sup>(These are the years of the life of Ishmael: 137 years. He breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.)<sup>18</sup>They settled from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt in the direction of Assyria. He settled over against all his kinsmen.<sup>19</sup>These are the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son: Abraham fathered Isaac,<sup>20</sup>and Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, the sister of Laban the Aramean, to be his wife.<sup>21</sup>And Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she was barren. And the LORD granted his prayer, and Rebekah his wife conceived.<sup>22</sup>The children struggled together within her, and she said, "If it is thus, why is this happening to me?" So she went to inquire of the LORD.<sup>23</sup>And the LORD said to her, "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger."<sup>24</sup>When her days to give birth were completed, behold, there were twins in her womb.<sup>25</sup>The first came out red, all his body like a hairy cloak, so they called his name Esau.<sup>26</sup>Afterward his brother came out with his hand holding Esau's heel, so his name was called Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.<sup>27</sup>When the boys grew up, Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents.<sup>28</sup>Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game, but Rebekah loved Jacob.<sup>29</sup>Once when Jacob was cooking stew, Esau came in from the field, and he was exhausted.<sup>30</sup>And Esau said to Jacob, "Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am exhausted!" (Therefore his name was called Edom.)<sup>31</sup>Jacob said, "Sell me your birthright now."<sup>32</sup>Esau said, "I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?"<sup>33</sup>Jacob said, "Swear to me now." So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob.<sup>34</sup>Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew, and he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
25.overview:
Genesis 25 closes the Abraham narrative and opens the Jacob-Esau story — two enormous transitions in a single chapter. Abraham’s death is described with simplicity and beauty: “gathered to his people” (v.8), a phrase suggesting the continuation of personal existence beyond death, the rejoining of a community that has gone before. The covenant patriarch who was called from Ur of the Chaldeans, who walked with God for a hundred years of journey and failure and faith, dies “full of years.”

The Rebekah narrative introduces the third generation of the covenant line through another barrenness-and-birth story — Isaac prays, God grants, twins are born. But the birth is complicated by conflict: the children struggle in the womb, and the divine word to Rebekah is troubling — “the older shall serve the younger.” This reversal of the natural birth order (Esau first, Jacob second) introduces the great theme of the Jacob narrative: God’s sovereign election, which operates by its own logic rather than the human logic of seniority and merit.
