Paul makes the theological point explicit in Romans 9:10–13: “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad — in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls — she was told, ‘The older will serve the younger.’” The election of Jacob over Esau is the Old Testament’s most concentrated illustration of sovereign grace. God chooses not the obvious, not the firstborn, not the strong — but the younger, the one who lacks natural priority, and works his purposes through him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Abraham's Final Years and Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 25 opens with Abraham's second marriage (to Keturah), his fathering of six more sons, his arrangement of the inheritance (Isaac receives everything; the sons of the concubines receive gifts and are sent east), and his death at 175 years — a 'good old age, full of years.' The section closes with a brief account of Ishmael's twelve sons and his death at 137 years. Abraham's final years and death are narrated with the same economy and dignity as the great tests: he lived, he fathered, he gave, he died. The covenant patriarch's ending is peaceful, his inheritance secure, his legacy fixed.
verseByVerse.theology: Abraham has six more sons by Keturah, gives all he has to Isaac, and sends the others east with gifts. He dies at 175, full of years, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him at Machpelah. Ishmael's twelve princes are listed, and he dies at 137.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God kept his word to Hagar and to Abraham about Ishmael (17:20; 21:18). Now: Abraham "died in faith, not having received the things promised" (Heb. 11:13), and the rest of the Bible is God keeping them.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah. She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah. Abraham gave all he had to Isaac. But to the sons of his concubines Abraham gave gifts, and while he was still living he sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward to the east country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham takes another wife, Keturah, who bears him six sons, including Midian; he gives everything to Isaac and sends the other sons east with gifts.

Father of many nations. Midianites and others descend from Abraham.

All to Isaac. The heir of promise.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the days of the years of Abraham's life, 175 years. Abraham breathed his last and died in a good old age, an old man and full of years, and was gathered to his people. Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field of Ephron the son of Zohar the Hittite, east of Mamre, the field that Abraham purchased from the Hittites. There Abraham was buried, with Sarah his wife. After the death of Abraham, God blessed Isaac his son. And Isaac settled at Beer-lahai-roi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham dies at 175, full of years, and is gathered to his people; Isaac and Ishmael bury him with Sarah.

Full of years. Satisfied.

Gathered to his people. More than burial: joining those who died before. A hint of life beyond death (Matthew 22:32).

Isaac and Ishmael together. Reconciled at their father’s grave.

For worship. Thank God for those who have died full of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Ishmael, Abraham's son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah's servant, bore to Abraham. These are the names of the sons of Ishmael, named in the order of their birth: Nebaioth, the firstborn of Ishmael; and Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael and these are their names, by their villages and by their encampments, twelve princes according to their tribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ishmael’s twelve sons become twelve princes of tribes.

Promise kept. God said so (17:20).

Twelve. As Jacob will have twelve sons.
verseByVerse.note: Ishmael’s twelve princes fulfil the promise of 17:20.

verseByVerse.quote: (These are the years of the life of Ishmael: 137 years. He breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.) They settled from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt in the direction of Assyria. He settled over against all his kinsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ishmael dies at 137, and his descendants settle from Havilah to Shur, over against their kinsmen.

Over against. As foretold (16:12): a life of conflict.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–34 — The Birth of Jacob and Esau; the Birthright
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The final section of Genesis 25 introduces the third generation of the covenant — Jacob and Esau — and establishes from before their birth the pattern that will define their lives: the older will serve the younger, the covenant line will run through the one who was not expected, the promise will be carried forward not by natural priority but by divine election. The oracle before their birth (v.23) is the theological framework for everything that follows in the Jacob narrative.
verseByVerse.theology: After twenty years of prayer Rebekah conceives twins, and the LORD tells her the older shall serve the younger. Esau is born red and hairy, Jacob gripping his heel. The parents take sides, and Esau sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul uses the oracle to show that election is "not because of works but because of him who calls" (Rom. 9:11–12). Now: Esau is the warning of Hebrews 12:16 — the eternal traded for the immediate on an ordinary afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Isaac, Abraham's son: Abraham fathered Isaac, and Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram, the sister of Laban the Aramean, to be his wife. And Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, because she was barren. And the LORD granted his prayer, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac marries Rebekah at forty; she is barren, Isaac prays for her, and the LORD grants his prayer.

Barren again. As Sarah was. The promise depends on God.

Isaac prayed. Twenty years (v. 26).

On a Tuesday. Keep praying for the long-delayed answer.
verseByVerse.note: Paddan-aram is the region of Haran in northern Mesopotamia.

verseByVerse.quote: The children struggled together within her, and she said, "If it is thus, why is this happening to me?" So she went to inquire of the LORD. And the LORD said to her, "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples from within you shall be divided; the one shall be stronger than the other, the older shall serve the younger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The children struggle in her womb, and the LORD tells her two nations are within her, and the older will serve the younger.

She inquired of the LORD. Taking her trouble to God.

The older will serve the younger. Reversing custom.

Where Christians differ: election. Paul quotes this (Romans 9:10–13) to show God’s choice before birth, “not because of works”. Some say it concerns nations, not individuals. Verdict: Paul applies it to individuals and their place in God’s saving purpose, as well as to the nations they founded. Election is by grace, not merit.

verseByVerse.quote: When her days to give birth were completed, behold, there were twins in her womb. The first came out red, all his body like a hairy cloak, so they called his name Esau. Afterward his brother came out with his hand holding Esau's heel, so his name was called Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twins are born: the first red and hairy, named Esau; the second holding Esau’s heel, named Jacob; Isaac is sixty.

Esau. Hairy. Also called Edom, “red”.

Jacob. “Heel-grabber”, one who supplants.
verseByVerse.note: “Jacob” means “he takes by the heel” or “he cheats” (ESV note). “Hairy” (se‘ar) sounds like Seir, the hill country of Edom where Esau’s descendants lived.

verseByVerse.quote: When the boys grew up, Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quiet man, dwelling in tents. Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his game, but Rebekah loved Jacob.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau becomes a skilful hunter, Jacob a quiet man living in tents; Isaac loves Esau for his game, but Rebekah loves Jacob.

Favouritism. Parents divided, a family heading for trouble.

On a Tuesday. Watch for favouritism in your family.

verseByVerse.quote: Once when Jacob was cooking stew, Esau came in from the field, and he was exhausted. And Esau said to Jacob, "Let me eat some of that red stew, for I am exhausted!" (Therefore his name was called Edom.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau comes in exhausted and asks Jacob for some of his red stew.

Exhausted. Physical need.

Red stuff. Hence “Edom”.
verseByVerse.note: “Edom” sounds like the Hebrew for red (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob said, "Sell me your birthright now." Esau said, "I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?" Jacob said, "Swear to me now." So he swore to him and sold his birthright to Jacob. Then Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew, and he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob demands Esau’s birthright for the stew, Esau swears it away, eats, and goes, despising his birthright.

Jacob the schemer. Taking advantage.

Despised. Esau valued his stomach over God’s promise (Hebrews 12:16–17).

What it does not mean. God’s choice of Jacob does not excuse Jacob’s methods.

On a Tuesday. What spiritual blessing are you trading for immediate satisfaction?

For worship. Thank God that his choice rests on grace, not our worth.
verseByVerse.note: The birthright gave the firstborn a double share of the inheritance and headship of the family.

25.theology:
Sovereign Election. Romans 9:10–13 uses the Jacob-Esau election as its primary illustration of the doctrine of election: God’s choice of Jacob over Esau was made “though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls.” Election is not grounded in foreseen faith or foreseen merit but in the sovereign, free, gracious purpose of God. This is not arbitrary — God’s purposes are wise and good — but it is free, dependent on no human qualification.

Despising the Birthright. The Esau-birthright exchange is the Bible’s paradigmatic picture of trading the eternal for the immediate. Hebrews develops it as a warning for the new covenant community: do not exchange your covenant inheritance for the bowl of stew that the present world offers. The disciplines of fasting, prayer, and spiritual formation are, in part, the practice of learning to value the unseen promise over the visible satisfaction — the training of desire toward its true object.
25.examples:
Then: The birthright (bekorah) in the ancient world was a specific legal right: the firstborn son received a double portion of the inheritance and carried the family’s covenantal and social leadership. To sell it for a meal was to trade a legal and spiritual inheritance for a momentary physical satisfaction — a transaction any ancient reader would have found scandalous. That Esau did not reconsider but simply “rose and went his way” (v.34) underscores his indifference to what he had traded.

Now: “Is not this what you are doing?” the chapter asks every generation. The bowl of stew takes a thousand forms in contemporary life: the relationship that offers immediate intimacy at the cost of covenant integrity; the career that offers immediate success at the cost of family and faith; the entertainment that offers immediate pleasure at the cost of spiritual attentiveness. The pattern of Esau is always the same: the present felt need seems more real and more urgent than the promised future. The antidote is always the same: to practice the presence of the one who is more real than any bowl of stew.

26.title: The LORD Is with You
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a famine in the land, besides the former famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Gerar to Abimelech king of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land of which I shall tell you.<sup>3</sup>Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you, for to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father.<sup>4</sup>I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and will give to your offspring all these lands. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed,<sup>5</sup>because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws."<sup>6</sup>So Isaac settled in Gerar.<sup>7</sup>When the men of the place asked him about his wife, he said, "She is my sister," for he feared to say, "My wife," thinking, "lest the men of the place should kill me because of Rebekah," because she was attractive in appearance.<sup>8</sup>When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out of a window and saw Isaac laughing with Rebekah his wife.<sup>9</sup>So Abimelech called Isaac and said, "Behold, she is your wife. How then could you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac said to him, "Because I thought, 'Lest I die because of her.'"<sup>10</sup>Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us."<sup>11</sup>So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death."<sup>12</sup>And Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. The LORD blessed him,<sup>13</sup>and the man became rich, and gained more and more until he became very wealthy.<sup>14</sup>He had possessions of flocks and herds and many servants, so that the Philistines envied him.<sup>15</sup>(Now the Philistines had stopped and filled with earth all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father.)<sup>16</sup>And Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us, for you are much mightier than we."<sup>17</sup>So Isaac departed from there and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there.<sup>18</sup>And Isaac dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped after the death of Abraham. And he gave them the names that his father had given them.<sup>19</sup>But when Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found there a well of spring water,<sup>20</sup>the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, "The water is ours." So he called the name of the well Esek, because they contended with him.<sup>21</sup>Then they dug another well, and they quarreled over that also, so he called its name Sitnah.<sup>22</sup>And he moved from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. So he called its name Rehoboth, saying, "For now the LORD has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."<sup>23</sup>From there he went up to Beersheba.<sup>24</sup>And the LORD appeared to him the same night and said, "I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your offspring for my servant Abraham's sake."<sup>25</sup>So he built an altar there and called upon the name of the LORD and pitched his tent there. And there Isaac's servants dug a well.<sup>26</sup>When Abimelech went to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army,<sup>27</sup>Isaac said to them, "Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have sent me away from you?"<sup>28</sup>They said, "We see plainly that the LORD has been with you. So we said, let there be a sworn pact between us, between you and us, and let us make a covenant with you,<sup>29</sup>that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you and have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace. You are now the blessed of the LORD."<sup>30</sup>So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank.<sup>31</sup>In the morning they rose early and exchanged oaths. And Isaac sent them on their way, and they departed from him in peace.<sup>32</sup>That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well that they had dug and said to him, "We have found water."<sup>33</sup>He called it Shibah; therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.<sup>34</sup>When Esau was forty years old, he took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite,<sup>35</sup>and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
26.overview:
Genesis 26 is the only chapter in Genesis focused solely on Isaac, and it reads as a concentrated echo of his father Abraham’s story. The same covenant is confirmed, the same famine tests, the same wife-sister deception recurs, the same wells are contested. The repetitions are not literary laziness but theological design: the blessing of Abraham passes to Isaac not through Isaac’s moral superiority but through divine faithfulness alone.

Isaac’s failures mirror Abraham’s almost exactly. He lies about his wife, just as Abraham did twice. Yet God protects Rebekah through Abimelech’s own decree and continues the covenant without condition. Grace runs not through the perfection of the patriarchs but through the faithfulness of God. God’s persistent commitment to these flawed men is the ground of all hope for equally flawed readers.

The re-digging of Abraham’s wells is rich with symbolic weight. Isaac does not pioneer new territory; he recovers what his father had opened. The wells are named Esek (contention), Sitnah (enmity), and finally Rehoboth (room): “For now the LORD has made room for us.” The Christian life is often this—recovering grace already available, moving through conflict and opposition toward the spaciousness that God promises. The covenant confirmed to Isaac at Beersheba (“I am with you”) is the foundation of all blessing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Isaac and Abimelech: The Covenant Repeated
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole chapter belongs to Isaac, the middle patriarch, sandwiched between the towering figures of Abraham and Jacob. The chapter is structurally parallel to several key moments in Abraham's life: famine drives Isaac toward Egypt, God redirects him to Gerar, Isaac deceives Abimelech about Rebekah (as Abraham deceived him about Sarah), Isaac prospers greatly, and a dispute over wells leads to a covenant at Beersheba. The parallels are deliberate: Isaac is presented as the faithful carrier of the covenant promises, living out his father's story in his own generation.
verseByVerse.theology: In a famine God forbids Isaac to go to Egypt and renews to him the promise made to Abraham. In Gerar Isaac says Rebekah is his sister, and is found out; Abimelech protects them. Isaac reaps a hundredfold, and the envious Philistines send him away; his father’s wells, stopped up after Abraham’s death, wait to be dug again.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the son repeats a sin he had only heard about, and God blesses him while he lives with the consequences. Now: family patterns travel by story as well as by example.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a famine in the land, besides the former famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went to Gerar to Abimelech king of the Philistines. And the LORD appeared to him and said, "Do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land of which I shall tell you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In another famine Isaac goes to Abimelech king of the Philistines in Gerar, and the LORD tells him not to go to Egypt.

Like father. Famine, and a temptation to go to Egypt.

Do not go down. Stay in the land.

verseByVerse.quote: Sojourn in this land, and I will be with you and will bless you, for to you and to your offspring I will give all these lands, and I will establish the oath that I swore to Abraham your father. I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and will give to your offspring all these lands. And in your offspring all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to be with Isaac, bless him and give him the land, multiply his offspring, and bless all nations in them, because Abraham obeyed his voice and kept his charge.

The promise renewed. Abraham’s promises passed to Isaac.

Because Abraham obeyed. Where Christians differ. Did Abraham earn the promise? Verdict: the promise was given freely before Abraham’s obedience (12:1–3). His obedience was the fruit of faith, which God honours (Hebrews 11:8).

For worship. Thank God for the faith of those who came before you.

verseByVerse.quote: So Isaac settled in Gerar. When the men of the place asked him about his wife, he said, "She is my sister," for he feared to say, "My wife," thinking, "lest the men of the place should kill me because of Rebekah," because she was attractive in appearance. When he had been there a long time, Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out of a window and saw Isaac laughing with Rebekah his wife. So Abimelech called Isaac and said, "Behold, she is your wife. How then could you say, 'She is my sister'?" Isaac said to him, "Because I thought, 'Lest I die because of her.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac settles in Gerar and, afraid, says Rebekah is his sister; Abimelech sees him caressing her and realises she is his wife.

Like father, like son. The same sin (12:13; 20:2).

Caressing. A pun on Isaac’s name, “laughing”.

On a Tuesday. Sins pass down in families. Break the pattern.
verseByVerse.note: Isaac repeats his father’s lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Abimelech said, "What is this you have done to us? One of the people might easily have lain with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us." So Abimelech warned all the people, saying, "Whoever touches this man or his wife shall surely be put to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech rebukes Isaac for putting his people at risk, and warns everyone not to touch Isaac or his wife.

Rebuked again. A pagan king protects the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. The LORD blessed him, and the man became rich, and gained more and more until he became very wealthy. He had possessions of flocks and herds and many servants, so that the Philistines envied him. (Now the Philistines had stopped and filled with earth all the wells that his father's servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father.) And Abimelech said to Isaac, "Go away from us, for you are much mightier than we."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac sows and reaps a hundredfold that year, for the LORD blesses him; he becomes very wealthy, the Philistines envy him and fill his father’s wells, and Abimelech sends him away.

A hundredfold. In a famine year.

Envy. Blessing provokes jealousy.

Stopped wells. An act of hostility.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–35 — Wells, Beersheba, and the Covenant with Abimelech
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaac leaves Gerar and camps in the Valley of Gerar, where he reopens Abraham's wells and digs new ones. The Philistines dispute the first two wells — Esek (contention) and Sitnah (enmity) — but leave the third alone: Isaac names it Rehoboth, 'broad places,' declaring that God has made room for him. At Beersheba, God appears again and renews the covenant; Isaac builds an altar. Abimelech then comes to seek a treaty with Isaac, recognizing that the LORD is with him. The chapter ends with the report of Esau's Hittite wives, which causes grief to Isaac and Rebekah.
verseByVerse.theology: Isaac re-digs his father's wells and yields two disputed wells, Esek and Sitnah, until at Rehoboth the LORD makes room. At Beersheba God appears to him, and he builds an altar. Abimelech comes to make peace, saying the LORD is with him. Esau marries two Hittite women, who make life bitter for his parents.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Philistines could account for Isaac only by saying, "the LORD has been with you." Now: "so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all" (Rom. 12:18).

verseByVerse.quote: So Isaac departed from there and encamped in the Valley of Gerar and settled there. And Isaac dug again the wells of water that had been dug in the days of Abraham his father, which the Philistines had stopped after the death of Abraham. And he gave them the names that his father had given them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac moves to the valley of Gerar and reopens the wells of Abraham, giving them their old names.

Reopening. Recovering what was lost.

On a Tuesday. Return to the old wells of faith: Scripture and prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Isaac's servants dug in the valley and found there a well of spring water, the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, "The water is ours." So he called the name of the well Esek, because they contended with him. Then they dug another well, and they quarreled over that also, so he called its name Sitnah. And he moved from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. So he called its name Rehoboth, saying, "For now the LORD has made room for us, and we shall be fruitful in the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac’s servants dig new wells, the herdsmen of Gerar quarrel over two, and Isaac moves on until he digs one without a quarrel, naming it Rehoboth, for the LORD has made room.

Esek and Sitnah. “Contention” and “Enmity”.

Isaac gives way. A peacemaker (Romans 12:18).

Rehoboth. “Broad places”.
verseByVerse.note: Esek means “contention,” Sitnah “enmity,” and Rehoboth “broad places” or “room” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: From there he went up to Beersheba. And the LORD appeared to him the same night and said, "I am the God of Abraham your father. Fear not, for I am with you and will bless you and multiply your offspring for my servant Abraham's sake." So he built an altar there and called upon the name of the LORD and pitched his tent there. And there Isaac's servants dug a well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Beersheba the LORD appears to Isaac by night, tells him not to fear, and promises to bless him for Abraham’s sake; Isaac builds an altar and calls on the LORD.

Fear not. After conflict, reassurance.

The God of Abraham your father. Covenant faithfulness across generations.

For worship. Build an altar of praise.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abimelech went to him from Gerar with Ahuzzath his adviser and Phicol the commander of his army, Isaac said to them, "Why have you come to me, seeing that you hate me and have sent me away from you?" They said, "We see plainly that the LORD has been with you. So we said, let there be a sworn pact between us, between you and us, and let us make a covenant with you, that you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you and have done to you nothing but good and have sent you away in peace. You are now the blessed of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech comes to Isaac with his officials, saying they see the LORD is with him, and asks for a covenant of peace.

The LORD is with you. Outsiders see God’s blessing.

Peace. Those who drove him away now seek him.

verseByVerse.quote: So he made them a feast, and they ate and drank. In the morning they rose early and exchanged oaths. And Isaac sent them on their way, and they departed from him in peace. That same day Isaac's servants came and told him about the well that they had dug and said to him, "We have found water." He called it Shibah; therefore the name of the city is Beersheba to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac makes a feast, they swear an oath and part in peace, and that day Isaac’s servants find water at the well called Shibah, at Beersheba.

A feast. Reconciliation.

Water. Blessing follows peace.
verseByVerse.note: “Shibah” sounds like the Hebrew for “oath” (ESV note), which is how Beersheba got its name.

verseByVerse.quote: When Esau was forty years old, he took Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite to be his wife, and Basemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and they made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At forty, Esau marries two Hittite women, who make life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.

Outside the covenant. Esau ignores the family’s faith (24:3).

Bitterness. Marriage decisions affect a whole family.

On a Tuesday. Pray for wise choices in your children’s marriages.

For worship. Thank God for his faithfulness to families through generations.
verseByVerse.note: Esau’s Hittite marriages showed the same disregard for the promise as the sold birthright, and grieved his parents.

26.theology:
Genesis 26 is a chapter about the transmission of grace. The Abrahamic covenant does not pass to Isaac because of Isaac’s righteousness; it passes because God is faithful to his word. The patriarchal narratives consistently resist the idea that God’s blessing tracks human virtue. Isaac repeats his father’s sin; God’s promise is repeated unchanged. This is the logic of sovereign grace—the covenant rests on the Giver, not the recipient.

Blessing is the theological key. And the blessing flows despite sin, through sojourning, across contested wells, into Philistine recognition of divine favor. The nations around Isaac already see what Isaac himself is learning: the LORD is with this man. This anticipates Paul’s argument in Romans 4—Abraham’s descendants inherit not through law-keeping but through faith in the God who gives life to the dead (Rom 4:17).
26.examples:
The re-digging of wells speaks to spiritual renewal in every generation. Every generation of the church must re-excavate the wells of grace—the gospel, the Scriptures, the practices of prayer and worship—that previous generations opened but that can become stopped up by worldly pressure, compromise, or neglect. Reformation is not invention; it is recovery.

Isaac’s persistence through Esek and Sitnah to Rehoboth models the patience of faith. The promise of “room” is not immediate; it comes through sustained trust in the God who promised it. This is the shape of the Christian life: not a straight line upward, but a journey through opposition toward the spaciousness that only God provides.

27.title: Jacob Receives the Blessing
27.text: <sup>1</sup>When Isaac was old and his eyes were dim so that he could not see, he called Esau his older son and said to him, "My son"; and he answered, "Here I am."<sup>2</sup>He said, "Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death.<sup>3</sup>Now then, take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt game for me,<sup>4</sup>and prepare for me delicious food, such as I love, and bring it to me so that I may eat, that my soul may bless you before I die."<sup>5</sup>Now Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to his son Esau. So when Esau went to the field to hunt for game and bring it,<sup>6</sup>Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "I heard your father speak to your brother Esau,<sup>7</sup>'Bring me game and prepare for me delicious food, that I may eat it and bless you before the LORD before I die.'<sup>8</sup>Now therefore, my son, obey my voice as I command you.<sup>9</sup>Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats, so that I may prepare from them delicious food for your father, such as he loves.<sup>10</sup>And you shall bring it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."<sup>11</sup>But Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Behold, my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.<sup>12</sup>Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall seem to be mocking him and bring a curse upon myself and not a blessing."<sup>13</sup>His mother said to him, "Let your curse be on me, my son; only obey my voice, and go, bring them to me."<sup>14</sup>So he went and took them and brought them to his mother, and his mother prepared delicious food, such as his father loved.<sup>15</sup>Then Rebekah took the best garments of Esau her older son, which were with her in the house, and put them on Jacob her younger son.<sup>16</sup>And the skins of the young goats she put on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.<sup>17</sup>And she put the delicious food and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob.<sup>18</sup>So he went in to his father and said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?"<sup>19</sup>Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you told me; now sit up and eat of my game, that your soul may bless me."<sup>20</sup>But Isaac said to his son, "How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?" He answered, "Because the LORD your God granted me success."<sup>21</sup>Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come near, that I may feel you, my son, to know whether you are really my son Esau or not."<sup>22</sup>So Jacob went near to Isaac his father, who felt him and said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."<sup>23</sup>And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau's hands. So he blessed him.<sup>24</sup>He said, "Are you really my son Esau?" He answered, "I am."<sup>25</sup>Then he said, "Bring it near to me, that I may eat of my son's game and bless you." So he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.<sup>26</sup>Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come near and kiss me, my son."<sup>27</sup>So he came near and kissed him. And Isaac smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him and said, "See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed!<sup>28</sup>May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth and plenty of grain and wine.<sup>29</sup>Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you!"<sup>30</sup>As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, when Jacob had scarcely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting.<sup>31</sup>He also prepared delicious food and brought it to his father. And he said to his father, "Let my father arise and eat of his son's game, that you may bless me."<sup>32</sup>His father Isaac said to him, "Who are you?" He answered, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau."<sup>33</sup>Then Isaac trembled very violently and said, "Who was it then that hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate it all before you came, and I have blessed him? Yes, and he shall be blessed."<sup>34</sup>As soon as Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and said to his father, "Bless me, even me also, O my father!"<sup>35</sup>But he said, "Your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing."<sup>36</sup>Esau said, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times. He took away my birthright, and behold, now he has taken away my blessing." Then he said, "Have you not reserved a blessing for me?"<sup>37</sup>Isaac answered and said to Esau, "Behold, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants, and with grain and wine I have sustained him. What then can I do for you, my son?"<sup>38</sup>Esau said to his father, "Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, O my father." And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.<sup>39</sup>Then Isaac his father answered and said to him: "Behold, away from the fatness of the earth shall your dwelling be, and away from the dew of heaven on high.<sup>40</sup>By your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but when you grow restless you shall break his yoke from your neck."<sup>41</sup>Now Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him, and Esau said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are approaching; then I will kill my brother Jacob."<sup>42</sup>But the words of Esau her older son were told to Rebekah. So she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, "Behold, your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you.<sup>43</sup>Now therefore, my son, obey my voice. Arise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran<sup>44</sup>and stay with him a while, until your brother's fury turns away—<sup>45</sup>until your brother's anger turns away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and bring you from there. Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?"<sup>46</sup>Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I loathe my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women like these, one of the women of the land, what good will my life be to me?"
27.overview:
Genesis 27 is the most morally complex chapter in the patriarchal narrative. Every major character fails: Isaac resolves to bless Esau against the divine oracle (25:23); Rebekah schemes; Jacob deceives his dying father with deliberate cruelty; Esau’s grief is real but comes too late. Yet through this tangle of human sin and family dysfunction, the divine purpose announced before the boys were born is accomplished. The blessing passes to Jacob.

The chapter is a study in how God works not by circumventing human sinfulness but through it and despite it. This does not excuse the participants. Both Jacob and Rebekah suffer severely for this moment: Jacob flees and never sees his mother again; Rebekah never holds her favorite son again. Sin has consequences even when God overrules it for his purposes.

Theologically, the irrevocability of the spoken blessing carries enormous weight. Isaac says, “I have blessed him—yes, and he shall be blessed” (v.33). Words of covenant blessing, once given, cannot be recalled. This points forward to the irreversibility of God’s own word and promise. The New Testament will read Esau’s tears as the pattern of those who despise what is holy and later find “no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears” (Heb 12:17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 27 is one of the most psychologically complex and theologically demanding chapters in Genesis. Isaac, old and nearly blind, intends to give the covenant blessing to Esau. Rebekah, having received the oracle that the elder would serve the younger (25:23), conspires with Jacob to deceive Isaac and secure the blessing for Jacob. Jacob receives the blessing through deception, Esau arrives too late and receives a subordinate word, and the chapter ends with Esau's murderous rage and Rebekah's plan to send Jacob away. No one in this chapter behaves well: Isaac ignores the divine oracle; Rebekah manipulates; Jacob lies repeatedly; Esau despises covenant values but grieves their loss.
verseByVerse.theology: Blind Isaac sets out to bless Esau in private. Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau's clothes and goatskins, and Jacob lies four times and invokes God to cover it. Isaac blesses him with dew, grain and lordship; then Esau comes in, Isaac trembles and confirms, "he shall be blessed," and Esau weeps for a lesser word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews commends Isaac's faith in this moment (Heb. 11:20) and warns that Esau found no chance to repent (Heb. 12:17). Now: God's word never needed a lie to protect it, and grief over consequences is not repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: When Isaac was old and his eyes were dim so that he could not see, he called Esau his older son and said to him, "My son"; and he answered, "Here I am." He said, "Behold, I am old; I do not know the day of my death. Now then, take your weapons, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt game for me, and prepare for me delicious food, such as I love, and bring it to me so that I may eat, that my soul may bless you before I die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Old and nearly blind, Isaac tells Esau to hunt game and prepare a meal, so that he may bless him before he dies.

Isaac’s plan. To bless Esau, despite God’s word that the older would serve the younger (25:23).

His appetite. As before (25:28), his taste for game shapes his choices.

The blessing. A father’s spoken blessing was believed to carry real power, binding and irrevocable.
verseByVerse.note: A father’s deathbed blessing was believed to be binding and irreversible.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to his son Esau. So when Esau went to the field to hunt for game and bring it, Rebekah said to her son Jacob, "I heard your father speak to your brother Esau, 'Bring me game and prepare for me delicious food, that I may eat it and bless you before the LORD before I die.' Now therefore, my son, obey my voice as I command you. Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats, so that I may prepare from them delicious food for your father, such as he loves. And you shall bring it to your father to eat, so that he may bless you before he dies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah overhears and tells Jacob to bring two goats so she can make the meal, and Jacob can take the blessing in Esau’s place.

Rebekah’s plan. She knows God’s word, but uses deception to bring it about.

The whole family fails. Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Esau are all at fault.

On a Tuesday. God’s ends do not need our crooked means.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Behold, my brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. Perhaps my father will feel me, and I shall seem to be mocking him and bring a curse upon myself and not a blessing." His mother said to him, "Let your curse be on me, my son; only obey my voice, and go, bring them to me." So he went and took them and brought them to his mother, and his mother prepared delicious food, such as his father loved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob worries that Esau is hairy and his father might feel him and curse him; Rebekah says, “Let your curse be on me.”

Fear of being caught. Not of doing wrong.

The curse on me. She will never see Jacob again (v. 44 says “a few days”; it was twenty years).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rebekah took the best garments of Esau her older son, which were with her in the house, and put them on Jacob her younger son. And the skins of the young goats she put on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck. And she put the delicious food and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau’s best clothes, covers his hands and neck with goatskins, and gives him the food.

Disguise. Jacob takes Esau’s place.

Goatskins. Later Jacob is deceived with a goat (37:31). What he sowed, he reaped.

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in to his father and said, "My father." And he said, "Here I am. Who are you, my son?" Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau your firstborn. I have done as you told me; now sit up and eat of my game, that your soul may bless me." But Isaac said to his son, "How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?" He answered, "Because the LORD your God granted me success."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob goes in, says he is Esau, and claims the LORD gave him success in hunting so quickly.

I am Esau. A direct lie.

The LORD your God. Using God’s name to support the lie.

On a Tuesday. Never bring God’s name into a lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come near, that I may feel you, my son, to know whether you are really my son Esau or not." So Jacob went near to Isaac his father, who felt him and said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau." And he did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau's hands. So he blessed him. He said, "Are you really my son Esau?" He answered, "I am." Then he said, "Bring it near to me, that I may eat of my son's game and bless you." So he brought it near to him, and he ate; and he brought him wine, and he drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac feels him, says the voice is Jacob’s but the hands are Esau’s, asks again whether he is Esau, and Jacob says yes; Isaac eats.

Doubts overcome. Isaac trusts his senses rather than his suspicions.

Are you really? A second lie.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his father Isaac said to him, "Come near and kiss me, my son." So he came near and kissed him. And Isaac smelled the smell of his garments and blessed him and said, "See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed! May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth and plenty of grain and wine. Let peoples serve you, and nations bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and blessed be everyone who blesses you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac kisses him, smells his clothes, and blesses him with abundance, rule over nations and his brothers, and curses on those who curse him.

The blessing. Fertility, rule, and Abraham’s promise (12:3).

Lord over your brothers. As God foretold (25:23).

Hebrews 11:20. Isaac blessed by faith, though blind.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, when Jacob had scarcely gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting. He also prepared delicious food and brought it to his father. And he said to his father, "Let my father arise and eat of his son's game, that you may bless me." His father Isaac said to him, "Who are you?" He answered, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau." Then Isaac trembled very violently and said, "Who was it then that hunted game and brought it to me, and I ate it all before you came, and I have blessed him? Yes, and he shall be blessed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jacob leaves, Esau arrives with his meal, and Isaac trembles violently, realising he has blessed another, and says, “Yes, and he shall be blessed.”

Trembled. Isaac realises God’s will has overruled his own.

He shall be blessed. Isaac accepts it.

For worship. Thank God whose purposes stand despite human schemes.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry and said to his father, "Bless me, even me also, O my father!" But he said, "Your brother came deceitfully, and he has taken away your blessing." Esau said, "Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times. He took away my birthright, and behold, now he has taken away my blessing." Then he said, "Have you not reserved a blessing for me?" Isaac answered and said to Esau, "Behold, I have made him lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants, and with grain and wine I have sustained him. What then can I do for you, my son?" Esau said to his father, "Have you but one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, O my father." And Esau lifted up his voice and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau cries out bitterly, begs for a blessing too, and says Jacob is rightly named, having cheated him twice.

Bitter cry. Grief, but not repentance (Hebrews 12:17).

Supplanted me twice. Though Esau sold the birthright himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac his father answered and said to him: "Behold, away from the fatness of the earth shall your dwelling be, and away from the dew of heaven on high. By your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but when you grow restless you shall break his yoke from your neck."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac tells Esau he will live away from fertile land, by the sword, serving his brother, until he breaks the yoke.

Edom. In the dry lands south-east of the Dead Sea.

Break the yoke. Edom later rebelled against Judah (2 Kings 8:20–22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–46 — Esau's Rage and Jacob's Flight
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with Esau's murderous intention (he will kill Jacob after Isaac's death), Rebekah's intervention (she sends Jacob to Laban before Esau can act), and Rebekah's cover story for Isaac (she sends Jacob to find a wife among her family). The flight that began with the oracle of 25:23 now becomes necessary; the deception that secured the blessing now produces the exile that will shape Jacob's character. Every element of the deception has a corresponding consequence: Rebekah loses her son permanently; Jacob loses his home; Esau loses his brother. The stolen blessing produces stolen years.
verseByVerse.theology: Esau plans to kill Jacob once Isaac is dead. Rebekah sends Jacob to Laban "a while," and gives Isaac the Hittite wives as the reason.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "a while" became twenty years, and Rebekah never saw her son again. Now: nobody in the tent got away with anything, and the blessing would have come without one word of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him, and Esau said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father are approaching; then I will kill my brother Jacob." But the words of Esau her older son were told to Rebekah. So she sent and called Jacob her younger son and said to him, "Behold, your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you. Now therefore, my son, obey my voice. Arise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran and stay with him a while, until your brother's fury turns away— until your brother's anger turns away from you, and he forgets what you have done to him. Then I will send and bring you from there. Why should I be bereft of you both in one day?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau plans to kill Jacob after Isaac’s death, so Rebekah tells Jacob to flee to Laban in Haran for a while.

Hatred. Like Cain.

A few days. Twenty years.

Why should I lose you both? Rebekah’s scheme costs her her son.

On a Tuesday. Deception damages families for years.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Rebekah said to Isaac, "I loathe my life because of the Hittite women. If Jacob marries one of the Hittite women like these, one of the women of the land, what good will my life be to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rebekah tells Isaac she is weary of the Hittite women and could not bear it if Jacob married one.

A pretext. True, but also a way to send Jacob away.

For worship. Praise God who works his good purposes through a broken family.

27.theology:
Genesis 27 forces readers to reckon with a disturbing doctrine: God accomplishes his purposes through human sin without thereby endorsing the sin. Jacob’s deception is never praised; its consequences are severe. Yet the blessing passes to Jacob, not Esau, exactly as God said. This is not divine determinism that removes moral responsibility; it is divine sovereignty that operates through human choice without annulling it.

Paul draws on Esau and Jacob in Romans 9 to argue that election does not depend on works or merit but on God who calls (Rom 9:11–12). The point is not that God is indifferent to morality but that God’s purpose is not hostage to human goodness. The heir of promise is not the more deserving son; he is the chosen one. This is the radical grace that the patriarchal narratives exist to demonstrate.

The irrevocability of the spoken blessing (v.33) anticipates the eternal security of the new covenant. God’s word, once given, stands. “The gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom 11:29). What God has blessed cannot be cursed by any human reversal.
27.examples:
Every reader of Genesis 27 recognizes the family dynamics: parents playing favorites, siblings competing for approval, schemes hatched in whispered conversation, irreversible words spoken in the heat of the moment. The patriarchal family is not an idealized portrait but a mirror. Its dysfunction is our dysfunction. Its grace—that God works through these broken families to accomplish redemption—is our grace.

The chapter speaks to those who feel their past is too compromised for God to use. Jacob is not chosen because he is good; he is made good (eventually, after much suffering) because he is chosen. The same grace that overruled Jacob’s deception is available to every deceiver who comes to the God of Jacob in faith.

28.title: Surely the LORD Is in This Place
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Isaac called Jacob and blessed him and directed him, "You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women.<sup>2</sup>Arise, go to Paddan-aram to the house of Bethuel your mother's father, and take as your wife from there one of the daughters of Laban your mother's brother.<sup>3</sup>God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, that you may become a company of peoples.<sup>4</sup>May he give the blessing of Abraham to you and to your offspring with you, that you may take possession of the land of your sojournings that God gave to Abraham!"<sup>5</sup>Thus Isaac sent Jacob away. And he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, Jacob's and Esau's mother.<sup>6</sup>Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he directed him, "You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women,"<sup>7</sup>and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram.<sup>8</sup>So when Esau saw that the Canaanite women did not please Isaac his father,<sup>9</sup>Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife, besides the wives he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham's son, the sister of Nebaioth.<sup>10</sup>Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran.<sup>11</sup>And he came to a certain place and stayed there that night, because the sun had set. Taking one of the stones of the place, he put it under his head and lay down in that place to sleep.<sup>12</sup>And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it!<sup>13</sup>And behold, the LORD stood above it and said, "I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring.<sup>14</sup>Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.<sup>15</sup>Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you."<sup>16</sup>Then Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it."<sup>17</sup>And he was afraid and said, "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."<sup>18</sup>So early in the morning Jacob took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up for a pillar and poured oil on the top of it.<sup>19</sup>He called the name of that place Bethel, but the name of the city was Luz at the first.<sup>20</sup>Then Jacob made a vow, saying, "If God will be with me and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear,<sup>21</sup>so that I come again to my father's house in peace, then the LORD shall be my God,<sup>22</sup>and this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, shall be God's house. And of all that you give me I will give a full tenth to you."
28.overview:
Genesis 28 is the pivot of the Jacob narrative. A fugitive from his own family, fleeing into the wilderness with a stone for a pillow, Jacob meets God. He has done nothing to deserve the vision; he has done much to deserve exile. But the God of Abraham and Isaac appears and renews the covenant with the deceiver. Grace finds Jacob in the wilderness.

The vision of the stairway (or ramp, sullam) with angels ascending and descending is one of the most iconic images in Genesis. Its theological meaning is clear: heaven and earth are connected; God’s realm interpenetrates the human. The LORD stands “above it” (or “beside him,” depending on the Hebrew syntax) and speaks the covenant words that have been spoken to Abraham and Isaac. The blessing is confirmed to a man who did not earn it.

Jesus himself applies this vision to his own person in John 1:51: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.” Jacob’s ladder is not a permanent structure; it is a preview of the incarnation—the place where heaven and earth permanently meet, the one in whom God dwells bodily, the gate of heaven for all who come to the Father through him (John 14:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Isaac's Blessing and Jacob's Dream at Bethel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 28 is a pivotal chapter in the Jacob narrative. Isaac sends Jacob to Paddan-aram with an explicit blessing — not the stolen blessing of chapter 27 but a deliberate, informed covenant blessing: the blessing of Abraham, the promise of land and offspring. Esau, overhearing that the Canaanite wives displeased his father, takes a wife from Ishmael's line — a belated and inadequate attempt to please his parents. Then Jacob encounters God at Bethel, in the most remarkable theophany since God’s appearances to Abraham: a stairway to heaven, angels ascending and descending, and God himself speaking the covenant promise to Jacob directly for the first time.
verseByVerse.theology: Isaac knowingly blesses Jacob with the blessing of Abraham and sends him to Paddan-aram. Esau adds a daughter of Ishmael to his wives. At a nameless place Jacob sleeps on a stone and sees a stairway to heaven with angels on it; the LORD promises land, offspring and his presence. Jacob names the place Bethel and vows a tenth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God swore himself to a fugitive without a single condition. Now: Jesus claims to be the stairway — "the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man" (John 1:51).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaac called Jacob and blessed him and directed him, "You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women. Arise, go to Paddan-aram to the house of Bethuel your mother's father, and take as your wife from there one of the daughters of Laban your mother's brother. God Almighty bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, that you may become a company of peoples. May he give the blessing of Abraham to you and to your offspring with you, that you may take possession of the land of your sojournings that God gave to Abraham!" Thus Isaac sent Jacob away. And he went to Paddan-aram, to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, Jacob's and Esau's mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac blesses Jacob, tells him not to marry a Canaanite but to go to Paddan-aram for a wife, and prays that God Almighty will give him the blessing of Abraham.

Openly now. Isaac blesses Jacob knowingly.

The blessing of Abraham. The covenant promises passed on.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” translates El Shaddai (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him away to Paddan-aram to take a wife from there, and that as he blessed him he directed him, "You must not take a wife from the Canaanite women," and that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and gone to Paddan-aram. So when Esau saw that the Canaanite women did not please Isaac his father, Esau went to Ishmael and took as his wife, besides the wives he had, Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham's son, the sister of Nebaioth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Esau sees that Canaanite women displease his father, and marries a daughter of Ishmael as well.

Trying to please. But adding a third wife, from the rejected line.

Missing the point. Outward change without heart change.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob left Beersheba and went toward Haran. And he came to a certain place and stayed there that night, because the sun had set. Taking one of the stones of the place, he put it under his head and lay down in that place to sleep. And he dreamed, and behold, there was a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven. And behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob, travelling towards Haran, sleeps at a certain place with a stone for a pillow, and dreams of a stairway reaching to heaven, with angels going up and down.

Alone. A fugitive.

A stairway. Perhaps like the ramp of a ziggurat. What Babel tried to build, God provides.

Jesus’ application. He is the stairway: angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man (John 1:51).
verseByVerse.note: The “ladder” may be a stairway (ESV: “a flight of steps”), like the stepped temple-towers of the region.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, the LORD stood above it and said, "I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you lie I will give to you and to your offspring. Your offspring shall be like the dust of the earth, and you shall spread abroad to the west and to the east and to the north and to the south, and in you and your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD stands above it, gives Jacob the land, promises countless offspring and blessing to all families through him, and promises to be with him, keep him and bring him back.

The promise to a cheat. Pure grace.

I am with you. The heart of the promise.

I will not leave you. God’s faithfulness (Hebrews 13:5).

For worship. Thank God that he is with you wherever you go.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it." And he was afraid and said, "How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob wakes and says, “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it,” and in fear calls it the house of God and the gate of heaven.

I did not know it. God was present where Jacob least expected.

Awesome. Reverent fear.

On a Tuesday. God may be present in the place you think most ordinary.

verseByVerse.quote: So early in the morning Jacob took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up for a pillar and poured oil on the top of it. He called the name of that place Bethel, but the name of the city was Luz at the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sets up his stone as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel.

A pillar. A memorial.

Bethel. “House of God”. Formerly Luz.
verseByVerse.note: “Bethel” means “the house of God” (ESV note). It lay about 12 miles north of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob made a vow, saying, "If God will be with me and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat and clothing to wear, so that I come again to my father's house in peace, then the LORD shall be my God, and this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, shall be God's house. And of all that you give me I will give a full tenth to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob vows that if God is with him and brings him back safely, the LORD will be his God, the stone God’s house, and he will give God a tenth of everything.

If. A young faith still bargaining. God had already promised all this.

A tenth. Like Abraham (14:20).

On a Tuesday. Do you treat God’s promises as conditional deals?

For worship. Thank God who is faithful even when our faith is immature.

28.theology:
The ladder of Bethel (Genesis 28) is fulfilled in the incarnation of Christ (John 1:51). Jesus tells Nathanael—an Israelite in whom there is no deceit, unlike Jacob—that he will see greater things: “heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.” Jesus is Jacob’s ladder. He is the meeting place of heaven and earth, the gate of heaven, the house of God (John 2:19–21).

Where Jacob said “how awesome is this place” about a patch of desert, the Christian says this about the person of Christ—in him all the fullness of God dwells bodily (Col 2:9). The place theology of the Old Testament (Bethel, Sinai, Zion, the Temple) moves toward Person theology in the New Testament. Jesus is the true Bethel: the place where God and humanity meet, permanently and finally.

The covenant renewal at Bethel also establishes the pattern of prevenient grace—God’s initiative before human response. Jacob has not repented, has not reformed, has not made any spiritual preparation. God appears anyway. The promise precedes the transformation; the grace precedes the faith it calls forth. This is the order of the gospel.
28.examples:
The image of Jacob asleep on a stone in the wilderness with heaven opened above him is the enduring image of grace finding us where we are. Not in the temple, not in the moment of consecration, not after years of spiritual formation—but in the wilderness, at night, in flight from our own sins. Augustine’s restless heart, Luther’s storm in the field, Wesley’s heart “strangely warmed”—all of these are Bethel moments. The God of Jacob meets people in their wilderness.

The central spiritual experience of the Christian is not achievement but discovery: “Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it.” Many people live without conscious awareness of the divine presence that surrounds them. The gospel is not information that helps us reach God; it is the revelation that God has already come down—in the ladder, in the incarnation, in the Spirit who dwells within—and that we are already held by the God we did not know was there.

29.title: Jacob, Leah, and Rachel
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jacob went on his journey and came to the land of the people of the east.<sup>2</sup>As he looked, he saw a well in the field, and behold, three flocks of sheep lying beside it, for out of that well the flocks were watered. The stone on the well's mouth was large,<sup>3</sup>and when all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.<sup>4</sup>Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where do you come from?" They said, "We are from Haran."<sup>5</sup>He said to them, "Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?" They said, "We know him."<sup>6</sup>He said to them, "Is it well with him?" They said, "It is well; and see, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep!"<sup>7</sup>He said, "Behold, it is still high day; it is not time for the livestock to be gathered together. Water the sheep and go, pasture them."<sup>8</sup>But they said, "We cannot until all the flocks are gathered together and the stone is rolled from the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep."<sup>9</sup>While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess.<sup>10</sup>Now as soon as Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother's brother, Jacob came near and rolled the stone from the well's mouth and watered the flock of Laban his mother's brother.<sup>11</sup>Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.<sup>12</sup>And Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's kinsman, and that he was Rebekah's son, and she ran and told her father.<sup>13</sup>As soon as Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things,<sup>14</sup>and Laban said to him, "Surely you are my bone and my flesh!" And he stayed with him a month.<sup>15</sup>Then Laban said to Jacob, "Because you are my kinsman, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what shall your wages be?"<sup>16</sup>Now Laban had two daughters. The name of the older was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.<sup>17</sup>Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.<sup>18</sup>Jacob loved Rachel. And he said, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel."<sup>19</sup>Laban said, "It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to any other man; stay with me."<sup>20</sup>So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.<sup>21</sup>Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife that I may go in to her, for my time is completed."<sup>22</sup>So Laban gathered together all the people of the place and made a feast.<sup>23</sup>But in the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and he went in to her.<sup>24</sup>(Laban gave his female servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah to be her servant.)<sup>25</sup>And in the morning, behold, it was Leah! And Jacob said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?"<sup>26</sup>Laban said, "It is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn.<sup>27</sup>Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also in return for serving me another seven years."<sup>28</sup>Jacob did so, and completed her week. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.<sup>29</sup>(Laban gave his female servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel to be her servant.)<sup>30</sup>So Jacob went in to Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served Laban for another seven years.<sup>31</sup>When the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.<sup>32</sup>And Leah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Reuben, for she said, "Because the LORD has looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me."<sup>33</sup>She conceived again and bore a son, and said, "Because the LORD has heard that I am hated, he has given me this son also." And she called his name Simeon.<sup>34</sup>Again she conceived and bore a son, and said, "Now this time my husband will be attached to me, because I have borne him three sons." Therefore his name was called Levi.<sup>35</sup>And she conceived again and bore a son, and said, "This time I will praise the LORD." Therefore she called his name Judah. Then she ceased bearing.
29.overview:
Genesis 29 is the great reversal chapter of the Jacob narrative. The deceiver is deceived; the man who wore a disguise to fool his blind father wakes beside a woman who is not who he thought she was. Laban’s substitution of Leah for Rachel is a near-perfect mirror of Jacob’s substitution for Esau. Jacob recognizes the irony even if he does not name it. God is writing a curriculum for Jacob’s transformation through the same kind of suffering he inflicted on others.

The chapter also introduces one of the most poignant subplots in Genesis: the rivalry between Leah and Rachel, and God’s special compassion for the unloved wife. Leah is not beautiful, not chosen, not loved—but the LORD sees her and opens her womb. Her son-naming speeches are a sustained cry of longing for her husband’s love, punctuated by growing recognition that her ultimate security is in God alone.

Theologically, God’s preference for Leah echoes the consistent biblical pattern: the younger over the older, the barren over the fertile, the unloved over the beloved, the weak over the strong. The sovereign God of Israel routinely chooses what the world overlooks. Leah is the mother of Judah, the tribe of David, the line of Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Jacob in Haran: Laban's Daughters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 29 records Jacob's arrival in Haran, his meeting of Rachel at the well, his month with Laban's household, and the extraordinary deception by which Laban substitutes Leah for Rachel on the wedding night. The chapter is rich in covenant parallels and ironies: Jacob arrives at a well (as the servant did in ch.24) and meets the woman he will love; Jacob is deceived by a substitution he did not expect (as Isaac was deceived by a substitution he did not expect); and the deceiver is deceived by the master deceiver, his uncle Laban. What Jacob did to his father, Laban does to him — with the same instrument (darkness, deception, a substitute).
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob comes to a well in Haran, rolls away the stone for Rachel, and weeps. Laban welcomes him, and Jacob serves seven years for Rachel that seem but a few days. On the wedding night Laban substitutes Leah; Jacob serves seven more years for Rachel, and loves her more than Leah.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the deceiver is deceived by a substitution in the dark, his own crime played back to him. Now: "whatever one sows, that will he also reap" (Gal. 6:7), and God uses it to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob went on his journey and came to the land of the people of the east. As he looked, he saw a well in the field, and behold, three flocks of sheep lying beside it, for out of that well the flocks were watered. The stone on the well's mouth was large, and when all the flocks were gathered there, the shepherds would roll the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep, and put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob comes to a well in the east, where shepherds wait for all the flocks to gather before rolling away the large stone.

A well. As with Abraham’s servant (24:11).

Providence. He arrives at the right place.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where do you come from?" They said, "We are from Haran." He said to them, "Do you know Laban the son of Nahor?" They said, "We know him." He said to them, "Is it well with him?" They said, "It is well; and see, Rachel his daughter is coming with the sheep!" He said, "Behold, it is still high day; it is not time for the livestock to be gathered together. Water the sheep and go, pasture them." But they said, "We cannot until all the flocks are gathered together and the stone is rolled from the mouth of the well; then we water the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob learns the shepherds are from Haran and know Laban, and that Laban’s daughter Rachel is coming with his sheep.

Do you know Laban? Guided again.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess. Now as soon as Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban his mother's brother, and the sheep of Laban his mother's brother, Jacob came near and rolled the stone from the well's mouth and watered the flock of Laban his mother's brother. Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud. And Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's kinsman, and that he was Rebekah's son, and she ran and told her father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Rachel comes, Jacob rolls the stone away alone, waters her flock, kisses her, weeps, and tells her he is her relative.

Strength. Jacob moves the stone alone.

He wept. Relief after a long journey.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he ran to meet him and embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things, and Laban said to him, "Surely you are my bone and my flesh!" And he stayed with him a month. Then Laban said to Jacob, "Because you are my kinsman, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what shall your wages be?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, brings him home, and he stays a month.

Laban runs. As when he saw the gold (24:29–30).

My bone and flesh. Family, but Laban will prove as crafty as Jacob.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Laban had two daughters. The name of the older was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel. Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban has two daughters: Leah, with weak eyes, and Rachel, beautiful in form and appearance.

Weak eyes. Perhaps “tender” or lacking sparkle.

The contrast. Sets up the conflict.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob loved Rachel. And he said, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel." Laban said, "It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to any other man; stay with me." So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob loves Rachel and offers seven years’ work for her, and they seem to him only a few days because of his love.

Seven years. In place of a bride-price.

A few days. Love makes the wait light.

On a Tuesday. Love makes service glad.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife that I may go in to her, for my time is completed." So Laban gathered together all the people of the place and made a feast. But in the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and he went in to her. (Laban gave his female servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah to be her servant.) And in the morning, behold, it was Leah! And Jacob said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban holds a wedding feast but brings Leah to Jacob in the dark, and in the morning Jacob sees it is Leah and asks why Laban deceived him.

The deceiver deceived. In the dark, as Jacob deceived his blind father.

Why have you deceived me? Jacob tastes his own medicine.
verseByVerse.note: The deceiver is deceived: Jacob, the younger, took the elder’s place; Laban gives the elder in place of the younger.

verseByVerse.quote: Laban said, "It is not so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn. Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also in return for serving me another seven years." Jacob did so, and completed her week. Then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban says it is not their custom to give the younger before the firstborn, and offers Rachel for another seven years; Jacob agrees.

The firstborn. Jacob, who took the firstborn’s place, is rebuked by custom about the firstborn.

Another seven years. Fourteen in all.

verseByVerse.quote: (Laban gave his female servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel to be her servant.) So Jacob went in to Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served Laban for another seven years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Laban gives Rachel a servant, Bilhah; Jacob marries Rachel too, loves her more than Leah, and serves seven more years.

Polygamy. Scripture records it, and shows its pain. It was never God’s design (2:24).

Loved Rachel more. Favouritism again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–35 — Leah's Children: The LORD Sees the Unloved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with four births from Leah — Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah — each named with a theological comment on Leah's situation: the LORD saw she was hated, the LORD heard her affliction, her husband will be attached to her, this time she will praise the LORD. The naming of Leah's sons is a running commentary on God's care for the unloved. In the covenant pattern of inversion, it is the unloved wife who receives the covenant fruitfulness: the one Jacob did not choose is the one through whom the covenant line's most significant tribes will come (Levi, the priestly tribe; Judah, the royal tribe and the line of Jesus Christ).
