But his sons were with his livestock in the field, so Jacob held his peace until they came.<sup>6</sup>And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him.<sup>7</sup>The sons of Jacob had come in from the field as soon as they heard of it, and the men were indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter, for such a thing must not be done.<sup>8</sup>But Hamor spoke with them, saying, "The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him to be his wife.<sup>9</sup>Make marriages with us. Give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves.<sup>10</sup>You shall dwell with us, and the land shall be open to you. Dwell and trade in it, and get property in it."<sup>11</sup>Shechem also said to her father and to her brothers, "Let me find favor in your eyes, and whatever you say to me I will give.<sup>12</sup>Ask me for as great a bride-price and gift as you will, and I will give whatever you say to me. Only give me the young woman to be my wife."<sup>13</sup>The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, because he had defiled their sister Dinah.<sup>14</sup>They said to them, "We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one who is uncircumcised, for that would be a disgrace to us.<sup>15</sup>Only on this condition will we agree with you—that you will become as we are by every male among you being circumcised.<sup>16</sup>Then we will give our daughters to you, and we will take your daughters to ourselves, and we will dwell with you and become one people.<sup>17</sup>But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, then we will take our daughter, and we will be gone."<sup>18</sup>Their words pleased Hamor and Hamor's son Shechem.<sup>19</sup>And the young man did not delay to do the thing, because he delighted in Jacob's daughter. Now he was the most honored of all his father's house.<sup>20</sup>So Hamor and his son Shechem came to the gate of their city and spoke to the men of their city, saying,<sup>21</sup>"These men are at peace with us; let them dwell in the land and trade in it, for behold, the land is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters as wives, and let us give them our daughters.<sup>22</sup>Only on this condition will the men agree to dwell with us to become one people—when every male among us is circumcised as they are circumcised.<sup>23</sup>Will not their livestock, their property and all their beasts be ours? Only let us agree with them, and they will dwell with us."<sup>24</sup>And all who went out of the gate of his city listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his city.<sup>25</sup>On the third day, when they were sore, two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, took their swords and came against the city while it felt secure and killed all the males.<sup>26</sup>They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword and took Dinah out of Shechem's house and went away.<sup>27</sup>The sons of Jacob came upon the slain and plundered the city, because they had defiled their sister.<sup>28</sup>They took their flocks and their herds, their donkeys, and whatever was in the city and in the field.<sup>29</sup>All their wealth, all their little ones and their wives, all that was in the houses, they captured and plundered.<sup>30</sup>Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble on me by making me stink to the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. My numbers are few, and if they gather themselves against me and attack me, I shall be destroyed, both I and my household."<sup>31</sup>But they said, "Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?"
34.overview:
Genesis 34 is the darkest chapter of the Jacob narrative and one of the most morally complex passages in Genesis. Dinah is violated; Simeon and Levi massacre an entire city in vengeance; Jacob is passive throughout. There are no heroes in this chapter. The text does not editorialize heavily; it simply narrates, and the weight of what has happened is left for the reader to carry.

The chapter stands as a theological warning about what happens when the covenant family settles too comfortably among the Canaanites. Jacob’s purchase of land and building of an altar at Shechem (33:19–20) seemed reasonable; the disaster of chapter 34 follows directly. The intermarriage proposal of Hamor is not predatory in intent (after the violation) but represents the absorption threat that has hung over the covenant family since Abraham: the blessing will be lost if the people of promise are dissolved into the surrounding nations.

Simeon and Levi’s violence is driven by genuine outrage at a genuine atrocity—but the means (massacre, deception, plunder) are lawless and multiply the evil rather than contain it. Jacob’s rebuke focuses on practical danger, not moral principle—his response to the violence is itself morally inadequate. The chapter ends without resolution, only tension. God’s intervention comes in chapter 35, commanding the family to move. Sometimes the only path forward from a moral catastrophe is departure.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — The Defilement of Dinah and the Vengeance of Simeon and Levi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 34 is one of the most troubling chapters in Genesis: Dinah, Jacob's daughter, goes out to visit the women of the land and is seized and raped by Shechem son of Hamor. Shechem then loves her and asks his father to arrange a marriage. Hamor proposes intermarriage and commerce between his people and Jacob's. Jacob's sons, furious at the violation of their sister, propose a condition: all the men of Shechem must be circumcised. On the third day, when the men are in greatest pain, Simeon and Levi kill every male in the city, and the rest of Jacob's sons plunder it. Jacob rebukes them; they answer: 'Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?'
verseByVerse.theology: Shechem the Hivite prince seizes and violates Dinah, then asks his father to get her for him as wife. Jacob holds his peace. Hamor proposes intermarriage and trade; Jacob's sons answer deceitfully, demanding circumcision, and on the third day Simeon and Levi kill every male in the city while the others plunder it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jacob's deathbed curse on their anger (49:5–7) is the book's verdict. Now: a real injustice does not license whatever comes next, and a silent father leaves a vacuum someone else will fill.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to see the women of the land. And when Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the land, saw her, he seized her and lay with her and humiliated her. And his soul was drawn to Dinah the daughter of Jacob. He loved the young woman and spoke tenderly to her. So Shechem spoke to his father Hamor, saying, "Get me this girl for my wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dinah goes out to see the women of the land; Shechem, the prince, seizes her and violates her, then is drawn to her and wants to marry her.

Seized, lay with, humiliated. The language of rape.

What it does not mean. Dinah is not to blame for going out. The sin is Shechem’s.

Love after violence. Desire does not excuse abuse.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jacob heard that he had defiled his daughter Dinah. But his sons were with his livestock in the field, so Jacob held his peace until they came. And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him. The sons of Jacob had come in from the field as soon as they heard of it, and the men were indignant and very angry, because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter, for such a thing must not be done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob hears and keeps silent until his sons return; they are furious, for Shechem has done an outrageous thing in Israel.

Jacob silent. A father’s failure to act.

Outrageous. A violation of God’s people.

On a Tuesday. Do not stay silent when the vulnerable are wronged.

verseByVerse.quote: But Hamor spoke with them, saying, "The soul of my son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him to be his wife. Make marriages with us. Give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves. You shall dwell with us, and the land shall be open to you. Dwell and trade in it, and get property in it." Shechem also said to her father and to her brothers, "Let me find favor in your eyes, and whatever you say to me I will give. Ask me for as great a bride-price and gift as you will, and I will give whatever you say to me. Only give me the young woman to be my wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hamor proposes intermarriage and trade between the peoples, and Shechem offers any bride-price.

No apology. Only a business offer.

Intermarriage. A threat to the covenant family’s identity.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, because he had defiled their sister Dinah. They said to them, "We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one who is uncircumcised, for that would be a disgrace to us. Only on this condition will we agree with you—that you will become as we are by every male among you being circumcised. Then we will give our daughters to you, and we will take your daughters to ourselves, and we will dwell with you and become one people. But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, then we will take our daughter, and we will be gone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob’s sons answer deceitfully that they will agree if every male is circumcised.

Deceitfully. The family trait.

Circumcision misused. The covenant sign used as a weapon.

verseByVerse.quote: Their words pleased Hamor and Hamor's son Shechem. And the young man did not delay to do the thing, because he delighted in Jacob's daughter. Now he was the most honored of all his father's house. So Hamor and his son Shechem came to the gate of their city and spoke to the men of their city, saying, "These men are at peace with us; let them dwell in the land and trade in it, for behold, the land is large enough for them. Let us take their daughters as wives, and let us give them our daughters. Only on this condition will the men agree to dwell with us to become one people—when every male among us is circumcised as they are circumcised. Will not their livestock, their property and all their beasts be ours? Only let us agree with them, and they will dwell with us." And all who went out of the gate of his city listened to Hamor and his son Shechem, and every male was circumcised, all who went out of the gate of his city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hamor and Shechem persuade the city’s men to be circumcised, for the sake of the livestock and wealth they will gain.

Will not all their livestock be ours? Greed on both sides.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day, when they were sore, two of the sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, took their swords and came against the city while it felt secure and killed all the males. They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the sword and took Dinah out of Shechem's house and went away. The sons of Jacob came upon the slain and plundered the city, because they had defiled their sister. They took their flocks and their herds, their donkeys, and whatever was in the city and in the field. All their wealth, all their little ones and their wives, all that was in the houses, they captured and plundered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the third day, while the men are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill every male, take Dinah, and the brothers plunder the city.

Massacre. Revenge far beyond the crime.

Plunder. Greed mixed with fury.

Jacob’s later verdict. He curses their anger (49:5–7).

What it does not mean. Scripture records it but does not approve it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, "You have brought trouble on me by making me stink to the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites and the Perizzites. My numbers are few, and if they gather themselves against me and attack me, I shall be destroyed, both I and my household." But they said, "Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob complains that they have made him odious to the inhabitants and endangered the family; they answer, “Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?”

Jacob’s concern. His reputation and safety, not justice or Dinah.

The brothers’ question. Left unanswered.

No word from God. The chapter is silent about God: a family acting without him.

On a Tuesday. Seek justice God’s way, not by revenge.

For worship. Pray for victims of abuse, and for the justice only God can give.

34.theology:
Genesis 34 functions in the narrative as the consequence of chapter 33’s incomplete obedience. Jacob settled at Shechem when God’s call was toward Canaan and ultimately Bethel. Proximity to the Canaanites without distinctiveness is the structural condition that makes Dinah’s exposure possible. The New Testament warns of the same danger with different language: do not be conformed to the pattern of this world (Rom 12:2); come out from them and be separate (2 Cor 6:17). The covenant people are to be in the world but not absorbed by it.

The chapter also raises the hardest pastoral questions about violence, trauma, and justice. Dinah’s violation is real, her suffering is real, and her brothers’ outrage is proportionate to the offense. Yet vigilante massacre does not restore justice; it multiplies death. The text’s silence on a resolution points toward the need for a justice that is both real and ordered—which the Old Testament will develop in the law and which the New Testament grounds in the cross, where God’s justice and mercy meet.
34.examples:
The pastoral application of Genesis 34 must begin with Dinah: the violated, silent woman whose story is almost entirely narrated through others’ responses. The church’s failure to center victims of sexual violence—to hear their voices, to grieve their suffering, to secure their dignity—is exposed by this text. Dinah is neither defended by her father nor consulted about the proposed marriage. She simply disappears from the narrative. The silence is indicting.

Jacob’s moral passivity in this chapter is a warning to every leader who prioritizes reputation (“you have made me stink”) over justice for those in their care. Good intentions at Shechem’s altar (33:20) are insufficient protection when the family is embedded in a world that does not share its values. The call to Bethel in chapter 35 is a call back to the God who gave the name Israel—not to settle in the comfortable proximity of Shechem.

35.title: Return to Bethel
35.text: <sup>1</sup>God said to Jacob, "Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau."<sup>2</sup>So Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, "Put away the foreign gods that are among you and purify yourselves and change your garments.<sup>3</sup>Then let us arise and go up to Bethel, so that I may make there an altar to the God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone."<sup>4</sup>So they gave to Jacob all the foreign gods that they had, and the rings that were in their ears. Jacob hid them under the terebinth tree that was near Shechem.<sup>5</sup>And as they journeyed, a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob.<sup>6</sup>And Jacob came to Luz (that is, Bethel), which is in the land of Canaan, he and all the people who were with him,<sup>7</sup>and there he built an altar and called the place El-bethel, because there God had revealed himself to him when he fled from his brother.<sup>8</sup>And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried under an oak below Bethel. So he called its name Allon-bacuth.<sup>9</sup>God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him.<sup>10</sup>And God said to him, "Your name is Jacob; no longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name." So he called his name Israel.<sup>11</sup>And God said to him, "I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply. A nation and a company of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come from your own body.<sup>12</sup>The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give the land to your offspring after you."<sup>13</sup>Then God went up from him in the place where he had spoken with him.<sup>14</sup>And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him, a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it.<sup>15</sup>So Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.<sup>16</sup>Then they journeyed from Bethel. When they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labor, and she had hard labor.<sup>17</sup>And when her labor was at its hardest, the midwife said to her, "Do not fear, for you have another son."<sup>18</sup>And as her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin.<sup>19</sup>So Rachel died, and she was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem),<sup>20</sup>and Jacob set up a pillar over her tomb. It is the pillar of Rachel's tomb, which is there to this day.<sup>21</sup>Israel journeyed on and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder.<sup>22</sup>While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine. And Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob's firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.<sup>25</sup>The sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant: Dan and Naphtali.<sup>26</sup>The sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.<sup>27</sup>And Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, or Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned.<sup>28</sup>Now the days of Isaac were 180 years.<sup>29</sup>And Isaac breathed his last, and he died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
35.overview:
Genesis 35 is a chapter of renewals, endings, and sorrows. God commands Jacob back to Bethel, the place of the original vision, and Jacob responds with the first spiritual leadership we have seen from him: he commands the household to put away their foreign gods, purify themselves, and change their garments. The man who tolerated idols in his camp (Rachel’s stolen teraphim, 31:19) now commands their surrender. The Jabbok has begun to produce fruit.

At Bethel, God renews the covenant and the name Israel with formal solemnity. The blessing given to Abraham and Isaac is now transmitted to Jacob in the name of El Shaddai (God Almighty). The pillar Jacob anoints echoes the stone he anointed at Bethel some thirty years before. The circle is complete—but also opened: the promises await fulfillment that Jacob will not see.

The chapter ends with three deaths that bookend the patriarchal era: Deborah (Rebekah’s nurse), Rachel (Jacob’s beloved wife, in childbirth), and Isaac (the second patriarch). Rachel’s death at Bethlehem on the road to Canaan casts a long shadow over the Joseph story that follows—her son Joseph is Jacob’s beloved precisely because she is gone. Bethlehem, where Rachel is buried, will become the birthplace of the King who fulfills what all these deaths anticipate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Return to Bethel; Deaths and Births
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 35 is a chapter of covenant renewal and painful transition. God commands Jacob to return to Bethel and fulfill the vow he made there more than twenty years earlier (28:20–22). Jacob purifies his household of foreign gods, goes to Bethel, and builds an altar. God appears again and confirms the covenant, renewing the name Israel and the promises of land and offspring. Then comes a series of deaths and births that mark the transition to the next generation: Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin; Isaac dies at 180 years; Reuben's violation of Bilhah is noted without elaboration. The twelve sons are listed, completing the roster of the tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: God sends Jacob to Bethel; the household buries its foreign gods, and a terror from God keeps the cities from pursuing. God renews the name Israel and the promises; Jacob sets up a pillar with a drink offering. Rachel dies bearing Benjamin near Bethlehem, Reuben lies with Bilhah, the twelve sons are listed, and Isaac dies at 180.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the twelve names will be on the high priest's breastpiece and on the gates of the city (Exod. 28:21; Rev. 21:12). Now: repentance buries something, and God tells his people more than once who they now are.

verseByVerse.quote: God said to Jacob, "Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau." So Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him, "Put away the foreign gods that are among you and purify yourselves and change your garments. Then let us arise and go up to Bethel, so that I may make there an altar to the God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone." So they gave to Jacob all the foreign gods that they had, and the rings that were in their ears. Jacob hid them under the terebinth tree that was near Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"God said to Jacob, 'Arise, go up to Bethel and dwell there.'" After the massacre at Shechem, with the family in danger and the father paralysed, God speaks — and what he says is: go back to where this started.

Jacob had vowed at Bethel that if God brought him home in peace, "then the LORD shall be my God" and the pillar "shall be God's house" (28:20–22). That was thirty years and one dislocated hip ago, and he has been home for some while and has not gone. God does not scold him. He simply says go, and reminds him whose idea Bethel was: "the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau."

And Jacob's response is the best thing he has done as a father: "Put away the foreign gods that are among you and purify yourselves and change your garments."

He knows they are there. Rachel took her father's household gods out of Haran (31:19); the plunder of Shechem will have brought in more. He has been living with idols in his camp for years, and it takes a summons from God to make him deal with it. Nobody grows out of an idol quietly; it has to be handed over.

"So they gave to Jacob all the foreign gods that they had, and the rings that were in their ears. Jacob hid them under the terebinth tree that was near Shechem." Buried, and left behind, at the scene of the family's worst chapter. The earrings go too — amulets, probably, and worn where everyone could see them. Repentance in Scripture is rarely private and is never merely a change of mind. Something gets buried.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they journeyed, a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob. And Jacob came to Luz (that is, Bethel), which is in the land of Canaan, he and all the people who were with him, and there he built an altar and called the place El-bethel, because there God had revealed himself to him when he fled from his brother. And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried under an oak below Bethel. So he called its name Allon-bacuth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And as they journeyed, a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob."

This is the answer to Jacob's fear in 34:30 — my numbers are few, and if they gather themselves against me I shall be destroyed. They did not gather. God put a dread on the whole district and a family of a few dozen walked through Canaan unmolested with the blood of a city on their hands.

He does not do it because they deserved protection. He does it because they were going to Bethel, and because he had said "I am with you." Mercy of that order is embarrassing to receive and it is the only kind there is.

"And there he built an altar and called the place El-bethel" — the God of Bethel. At 28:19 he named the place after the house; now he names it after the one who lives there. The house was never the point.

"And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried under an oak below Bethel. So he called its name Allon-bacuth" — the oak of weeping. She is mentioned once before, in a single clause, as the nurse who left Mesopotamia with Rebekah a lifetime earlier (24:59). She has no recorded words and no descendants, and the household stops and weeps and names a tree after her. God's book noticed a servant nobody else would have written down.

And note what it implies about Rebekah. She had told Jacob to go away for "a while" (27:44), promising to send for him. Genesis never records that she did, and the death of her nurse is the last we hear of Rebekah’s household.
verseByVerse.note: “El-bethel” means “God of Bethel”; “Allon-bacuth” means “oak of weeping” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him. And God said to him, "Your name is Jacob; no longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name." So he called his name Israel. And God said to him, "I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply. A nation and a company of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come from your own body. The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give the land to your offspring after you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him." And the first thing he does is give him his name a second time: "Your name is Jacob; no longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name."

He was given that name at the Jabbok (32:28), and the narrative has gone on calling him Jacob for two chapters, because he has gone on behaving like Jacob. God says it again — not because the first time failed, but because a man needs telling more than once who he now is.

Anyone who has come to Christ and then watched himself behave exactly as he did before will recognise the mercy in a repeated announcement. Your name is not what you did last week.

"I am God Almighty" — El Shaddai, the name used to Abraham at the moment the promise became impossible (17:1). "Be fruitful and multiply. A nation and a company of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come from your own body. The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you."

Be fruitful and multiply is the creation blessing (1:28), spoken over a family. Kings shall come from your body — the first time royalty is promised to Jacob's line, and it runs through Judah to David and to the King who was born a short way from where the next paragraph happens.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God went up from him in the place where he had spoken with him. And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him, a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it. So Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then God went up from him in the place where he had spoken with him. And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him, a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it."

Thirty years ago he set up a stone here and poured oil on it and made a bargain (28:18–22). He does the same thing again, and this time there is a drink offering with it — wine poured out on the ground, given away entirely, with nothing gained and nothing kept.

The two scenes measure the distance. The first pillar was a deposit on a contract: if you do this, then you will be my God. The second is worship with no terms attached, from a man who has been carried through everything he was afraid of.

Paul reached for the same picture from prison: "even if I am to be poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrificial offering of your faith, I am glad" (Phil. 2:17). It is the offering that cannot be recovered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they journeyed from Bethel. When they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labor, and she had hard labor. And when her labor was at its hardest, the midwife said to her, "Do not fear, for you have another son." And as her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin. So Rachel died, and she was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem), and Jacob set up a pillar over her tomb. It is the pillar of Rachel's tomb, which is there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They leave Bethel, and on the road Rachel goes into labour and it goes badly. "And when her labor was at its hardest, the midwife said to her, 'Do not fear, for you have another son.'"

That is what she had asked for. Years earlier she had cried, "Give me children, or I shall die!" (30:1), and when Joseph was born she named him "May he add" and asked God for another (30:24). She got the second son, and it killed her. God's answer to a prayer is not always safe, and Scripture is honest enough to put the two verses in the same book.

"And as her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin." Ben-oni could mean "son of my sorrow." Her last act is to hang her death round the boy's neck, and one can hardly blame a dying woman for it.

And Jacob will not have it. He renames him Benjamin — "son of the right hand." His mother named him for the worst day of her life; his father named him for a future. A child should not have to carry his parents' grief as an identity, and Jacob, who knew exactly what it was to be called Grabber for most of his life, would not do it to his son.

"So Rachel died, and she was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)." The wife he worked fourteen years for is buried by a roadside a few miles from the town where, centuries later, another son would be born to another family with nowhere to stay.

Jeremiah pictures Rachel weeping at Ramah for her children carried into exile, with God’s promise that they will come back (Jer 31:15–17), and Matthew hears her voice again when Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem (Matt 2:17–18). The mother who died bearing a son is the voice of every grieving mother in Israel, and the comfort comes with the Child who escaped.
verseByVerse.note: Ben-oni could mean “son of my sorrow” or “son of my strength”; Benjamin means “son of the right hand” (ESV notes). Ephrath is Bethlehem.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel journeyed on and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder. While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine. And Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine. And Israel heard of it."

Two sentences, no comment, and then the narrator moves straight on to a list. It is the most casual reporting of a disaster in Genesis.

Bilhah was Rachel's servant and the mother of two of Reuben's brothers. Rachel is not long dead. In that world, taking a father's concubine was a claim on the father's position — Absalom would do it publicly to David for exactly that reason (2 Sam. 16:21–22) — so this is at once a sexual sin against a woman with no power to refuse and a grab at the headship of the family by the eldest son.

"And Israel heard of it." That is all. He does nothing, exactly as he did nothing about Dinah. The silence is not neutral, and it is not forgiveness: on his deathbed he will say to Reuben, "unstable as water, you shall not have preeminence, because you went up to your father's bed" (49:4). He said nothing for forty years and forgot nothing.

"Now the sons of Jacob were twelve." The count is given immediately after the worst behaviour of the eldest, and that placement is the point. This is the family God chose — and the next verses list them all by name anyway.
verseByVerse.note: Reuben’s act cost him the rights of the firstborn.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob's firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin. The sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant: Dan and Naphtali. The sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The twelve are named for the first time as a complete set, grouped by their mothers: Leah's six, Rachel's two, Bilhah's two, Zilpah's two.

Read the list with the last four chapters in mind. Reuben has just disgraced himself. Simeon and Levi wiped out a city. Judah is about to go down to Adullam and behave appallingly with his daughter-in-law. Joseph's brothers will sell him within two chapters. Not one of these men has done anything to earn a place on this list.

And these are the twelve tribes of Israel. Their names will be cut into the stones on the high priest's breastpiece and carried into the presence of God (Exod. 28:21); they will be written on the twelve gates of the city at the end of the Bible (Rev. 21:12). God took a household of liars and murderers and grudge-holders, wrote their names on jewels, and put them over the gates of heaven.

"These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram" — which is not quite exact, since Benjamin was born on the Bethlehem road, and Genesis is summarising rather than misreporting. What it is doing is closing the account of the Haran years. That chapter of the family's life is over.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, or Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned. Now the days of Isaac were 180 years. And Isaac breathed his last, and he died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre." He gets home. Thirty years after a morning in a tent with goatskin on his hands, he stands in front of his father again — and Genesis records not one word between them.

The reunion is given no dialogue at all, and the silence is eloquent. What would they say? Everything that could be said was said in 27:33, when the old man trembled violently and then declared, "yes, and he shall be blessed."

"Now the days of Isaac were 180 years. And Isaac breathed his last, and he died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days." The longest-lived of the three patriarchs, and the least eventful. He re-dug his father's wells, was lied to by his wife and cheated by his son, and blessed the right boy in the end. Scripture treats him with complete respect and gives him a quarter of the space it gives his father.

"And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him." The two brothers stand at the same grave, exactly as Isaac and Ishmael had stood at Abraham's (25:9). The book is deliberate about this: twice now, a family split by God's choosing of one son over another comes back together at a funeral, in peace, and buries its father.

Whatever was between them is over. And the whole account of the wrestling, the limp, the new name, the buried idols and the altar at Bethel has been leading to this — a man who came home, worshipped God, and stood beside his brother at his father's grave.

Isaac in fact lived on into the Joseph story, dying about twelve years after Joseph was sold. Genesis closes his story here, as it closed Terah’s (11:32), so the next chapters can belong to Jacob’s sons.

35.theology:
Genesis 35’s command to “put away the foreign gods” is the Old Testament template for the ongoing work of sanctification. The household of Jacob has carried idols from Haran (Rachel’s teraphim), accumulated jewelry of uncertain provenance, and tolerated religious syncretism. The call to Bethel is the call to decisive renunciation—not gradual diminishment of the old life but burial of it. The Pauline counterpart is the same: “Put off your old self” (Eph 4:22)—the same decisive language of burial and replacement.

Rachel’s death at Bethlehem is a theological anticipation. The place of weeping becomes the place of birth (Benjamin), the city of David, and ultimately the birthplace of the Son of David. The pilgrim’s road through sorrow and death does not bypass Bethlehem; it runs through it. The gospel does not remove suffering from the path but transforms what suffering means: it is the road to glory, not the interruption of it (Rom 8:17–18).
35.examples:
Jacob’s spiritual leadership in verses 1–5 is the first sustained leadership initiative we see from him. He gathers the household, commands the purification, collects and buries the idols, and leads them up to Bethel. The Jabbok has done its work: the man who manipulated his family is beginning to lead them. The transformation is not complete—he will still show favoritism to Joseph—but the direction has changed. Suffering, faithfully received, produces the fruits of leadership that comfort never could.

Benjamin’s renaming from “son of my sorrow” to “son of my right hand” is a small act of grace in the moment of grief. Jacob does not deny Rachel’s sorrow or his own; he refuses to let it be the child’s permanent identity. The pastoral instinct to rename grief without erasing it—to speak of the resurrection without minimizing the death—is modeled here. Sorrow is real; it is not the final word.

36.title: The Generations of Esau

36.overview:
Genesis 36 is the Esau genealogy—forty-three verses of names, clans, chiefs, and kings. Modern readers often skim it; the ancient reader would have understood it as a theological statement of enormous significance. Esau’s line becomes the nation of Edom, with kings and chiefs in abundance, before Israel has a single king. The line that was passed over for covenant blessing nevertheless flourishes in the world. God’s non-election of Esau is not his destruction.

The placement of the Edom genealogy is structurally significant: it closes out the Esau story before the Joseph narrative begins. Genesis consistently disposes of secondary lines (Ishmael in 25, then Esau here) before focusing on the covenant line. The pattern signals narrative priority, not divine indifference—Esau’s descendants are honored with a full genealogy, kings and all.

Theologically, the kings of Edom (vv.31–39)—a list of eight kings, each one dying and being succeeded by a non-son—anticipate Israel’s royal history. Edom has kings before Israel; Israel will eventually have kings too. The note that these kings reigned “before any king reigned over the Israelites” is a quiet forward glance at Saul, David, and all who follow. God’s purpose for Israel runs through a different kind of king than Edom’s.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 36 is entirely devoted to the descendants of Esau — his wives, sons, chiefs, and the kings of Edom who reigned before any king reigned in Israel. The chapter is the most extensive genealogy in the patriarchal narratives, reflecting the importance of Edom as a neighboring nation throughout Israel's history. Like the Ishmael genealogy of chapter 25, the Esau genealogy serves the covenant purpose of completing the account of Abraham's non-covenant descendants before the narrative focuses exclusively on the covenant line through Jacob.
verseByVerse.theology: The descendants of Esau: his wives, sons and chiefs, the Horite clans he displaced in Seir, and eight kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. Esau leaves Canaan to his brother because the land cannot hold them both.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Amalek, Israel's long enemy, comes from this line (v. 12). Now: the world has its kings and cities early, and God's people have a promise and a tent — and God is not mentioned once in Esau's forty-three verses.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom). Esau took his wives from the Canaanites: Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite, and Basemath, Ishmael's daughter, the sister of Nebaioth. And Adah bore to Esau, Eliphaz; Basemath bore Reuel; and Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan. Then Esau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the members of his household, his livestock, all his beasts, and all his property that he had acquired in the land of Canaan. He went into a land away from his brother Jacob. For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together. The land of their sojournings could not support them because of their livestock. So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. (Esau is Edom.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
"These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom)." One of the eleven toledot panels of Genesis, and it follows the book's settled habit: deal fully with the branch that is not the line of promise, then close it and follow the one that is. Ishmael got the same treatment in chapter 25.

His wives are mostly Canaanite — the direction the covenant family had been told not to go — and one is Ishmael’s daughter, taken in a clumsy effort to please his father (28:8–9) — and the chapter states it in the second verse without comment. Genesis has already recorded that these marriages made his parents' life bitter (26:35).

Then a detail worth stopping on: "Their possessions were too great for them to dwell together." That is exactly what happened to Abraham and Lot (13:6), almost word for word — and this time the parting is quiet. No quarrel, no bargaining, no choosing of the well-watered plain. "So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir."

He goes of his own accord, and by doing so leaves Canaan to his brother. The land Jacob schemed and lied to secure ends up in his hands because Esau found it crowded. God does not need anyone's help, and Genesis 27 was never necessary.

The names of Esau’s wives differ from 26:34 and 28:9. People in that world often had more than one name, and a wife could be renamed at marriage; Esau may also have had more wives than either list gives. Basemath here and Mahalath there are both called Ishmael’s daughter, which suggests one woman with two names. Certainty is not possible, but the lists need not contradict.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir. These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, Reuel the son of Basemath the wife of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz. (Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau's son; she bore Amalek to Eliphaz.) These are the sons of Adah, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: she bore to Esau Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau: the chiefs Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz, Korah, Gatam, and Amalek; these are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Adah. These are the sons of Reuel, Esau's son: the chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah; these are the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife: the chiefs Jeush, Jalam, and Korah; these are the chiefs born of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Esau (that is, Edom), and these are their chiefs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons and grandsons of Esau are listed, and the word "chiefs" recurs — clan heads, each with his own territory. This is a nation forming, exactly as God said it would.

One name in the list has a long shadow. "Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau's son; she bore Amalek to Eliphaz" (v.12). The Amalekites will ambush Israel's stragglers coming out of Egypt (Exod. 17:8–16; Deut. 25:17–18), and God will swear that he will have war with Amalek from generation to generation. Saul will lose his kingdom over an Amalekite campaign, and Haman the Agagite, probably of the same stock, will try to exterminate the Jews in the book of Esther.

A concubine's son in a list of Edomite chiefs, and the enmity of Genesis 25:23 running out of him for a thousand years. Genealogies in this book are never merely records; they are fuses.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom. The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister was Timna. These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah; he is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness, as he pastured the donkeys of Zibeon his father. These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah the daughter of Anah. These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran. These are the chiefs of the Horites: the chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, chief by chief in the land of Seir.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These verses list "the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land" — not Esau's descendants at all, but the people who were in Seir before he got there, and whom his family displaced (Deut. 2:12).

It is an unusual thing for Genesis to bother with, and it is characteristic. Scripture keeps records of peoples who are nobody's ancestors and have no part in the covenant. The Horites are named, clan by clan, and their names are in the Bible for ever.

God is the God of the whole earth. He watched the migrations of nations nobody now remembers, and he had them written down. "He made from one man every nation of mankind... having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place" (Acts 17:26).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites. Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, the name of his city being Dinhabah. Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place. Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place. Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place, the name of his city being Avith. Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place. Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place. Shaul died, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place. Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place, the name of his city being Pau; his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites."

Eight kings, each following a predecessor who died. Edom had a monarchy while Jacob's family were still shepherds, and would be a settled kingdom while Israel was making bricks in Egypt.

The comment is not idle. God had promised Jacob that kings would come from him (35:11), and the brother who sold his birthright for soup is producing them first. This is the ordinary experience of God's people watching the world: they have kings, cities and settled succession, and we have a promise and a tent. It looks for a long time as though the wrong brother is winning.

Note also which line lasts. These eight kings do not pass the crown from father to son — each is from a different city, which suggests conquest or appointment rather than a dynasty. Edom got its kings early and could not keep a house. Judah's would come late, and one of them would reign for ever (Luke 1:32–33).

Does this line show the chapter was written after Saul? Moses knew God had promised kings from Jacob (35:11) and gave laws for a future king (Deut 17:14–20), so he could write with that promise in view. Or an inspired later hand updated the list. Neither undermines Moses as the author of the book in substance.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their clans and their dwelling places, by their names: the chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom (that is, Esau, the father of Edom), according to their dwelling places in the land of their possession.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with a second list of chiefs by their dwelling places, and then: "these are the chiefs of Edom (that is, Esau, the father of Edom), according to their dwelling places in the land of their possession."

Land, possession, settled places, named clans. Esau got everything a man would call success, and Genesis records it in full and without a sneer. He was not cheated out of a nation.

What he did not have is the one thing the book is about. There is no altar in this chapter, no appearance of God, no promise, no covenant, no offspring in whom the families of the earth are blessed. Forty-three verses of names and territory, and God is not mentioned once.

That is the whole point of putting it here. The next words in the book are "Jacob lived in the land of his father's sojournings" — sojournings, a tent, no kings, no cities — and the story of redemption goes that way. Esau's descendants are catalogued and closed; Jacob's are followed for fourteen more chapters and then for the rest of the Bible.

Malachi looked back on these two brothers and put it as starkly as it can be put: "Is not Esau Jacob's brother? declares the LORD. Yet I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated" (Mal. 1:2–3), and Paul quotes it in Romans 9. It is hard language and it means what the chapters have shown: God chose one line and not the other, before either had done anything, and the one he chose was not the better man. Esau ends with a kingdom and no God. Jacob ends with a limp and the covenant.

Did God hate Esau? When Malachi says I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated (Mal 1:2–3), the language is of choosing, as when Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah and Leah is called hated (29:30–31). Esau was not chosen to carry the promise, and Edom stood outside the covenant, yet this chapter shows how richly God provided for him.

36.theology:
Genesis 36 teaches that God’s election of one people does not mean his contempt for others. Esau is not chosen for the covenant line; he is also not despised. His descendants fill Seir with chiefs, kings, and clans. God’s common grace extends to all nations, including those outside the covenant. Romans 9’s use of “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (from Malachi 1:2–3) is about God’s free choice, made before the twins were born and resting on his purpose, not their works (Rom 9:11–13). Esau and his line live; they simply live outside the particular stream of redemptive history through which the Messiah will come.

The eight kings of Edom before Israel’s first king remind us that the world’s kingdoms develop according to their own logic while God’s kingdom advances according to a different logic—through barren women, younger sons, suffering servants, and a crucified King. The kingdom that looks most powerful by worldly metrics (Edom with kings) is not the kingdom through which God’s redemptive purposes run. The kingdom that looks weakest (a family of sojourners with no political standing) is the one that produces the Lion of Judah.
36.examples:
Genesis 36 is a pastoral reminder that God’s silence about someone in redemptive history is not God’s indifference to them. Esau gets a full genealogy; his descendants get named and honored. The pastoral implication is that those who feel they are outside the main story of what God is doing—not leaders, not gifted, not prominent in the life of the church—are not outside God’s care. Common grace is real grace. The God who numbers the hairs of his covenant people’s heads is also the God who notes that Anah found hot springs in the wilderness.

The non-dynastic kings of Edom—each dying without a son inheriting—illustrate the instability of human political orders not built on the foundation of God’s covenant. Human kingdoms come and go; the kingdom of God is unshakeable (Heb 12:28). The permanent king has yet to come when Esau’s kings are cycling through Edom. He will come from Judah—Leah’s son, the unloved wife’s son, by the sovereign grace that confounds every human calculation of worth.

37.title: Joseph's Dreams
37.text: <sup>1</sup>Jacob lived in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan.<sup>2</sup>These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father.<sup>3</sup>Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a robe of many colors.<sup>4</sup>But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him.<sup>5</sup>Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more.<sup>6</sup>He said to them, "Hear this dream that I have dreamed:<sup>7</sup>Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and stood upright. And behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf."<sup>8</sup>His brothers said to him, "Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us?" So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words.<sup>9</sup>Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers and said, "Behold, I have dreamed another dream. Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me."<sup>10</sup>But when he told it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebuked him and said to him, "What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves to the ground before you?"<sup>11</sup>And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind.<sup>12</sup>Now his brothers went to pasture their father's flock near Shechem.<sup>13</sup>And Israel said to Joseph, "Are not your brothers pasturing the flock at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them." And he said to him, "Here I am."<sup>14</sup>So he said to him, "Go now, see if it is well with your brothers and with the flock, and bring me word." So he sent him from the Valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.<sup>15</sup>And a man found him wandering in the fields. And the man asked him, "What are you seeking?"<sup>16</sup>"I am seeking my brothers," he said. "Tell me, please, where they are pasturing the flock."<sup>17</sup>And the man said, "They have gone away, for I heard them say, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.<sup>18</sup>They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him.<sup>19</sup>They said to one another, "Here comes this dreamer.<sup>20</sup>Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will become of his dreams."<sup>21</sup>But when Reuben heard it, he rescued him out of their hands, saying, "Let us not take his life."<sup>22</sup>And Reuben said to them, "Shed no blood; throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him"— that he might rescue him out of their hand to restore him to his father.<sup>23</sup>So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors that he wore.<sup>24</sup>And they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.<sup>25</sup>Then they sat down to eat. And looking up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry it down to Egypt.<sup>26</sup>Then Judah said to his brothers, "What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?<sup>27</sup>Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother, our own flesh." And his brothers listened to him.<sup>28</sup>Then Midianite traders passed by. And they drew Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver. They took Joseph to Egypt.<sup>29</sup>When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes<sup>30</sup>and returned to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go?"<sup>31</sup>Then they took Joseph's robe and slaughtered a goat and dipped the robe in the blood.<sup>32</sup>And they sent the robe of many colors and brought it to their father and said, "This we have found; please identify whether it is your son's robe or not."<sup>33</sup>And he identified it and said, "It is my son's robe. A fierce animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces."<sup>34</sup>Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins and mourned for his son many days.<sup>35</sup>All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted and said, "No, I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning." Thus his father wept for him.<sup>36</sup>Meanwhile the Midianites had sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.
37.overview:
Genesis 37 opens the Joseph narrative, which will occupy the final fourteen chapters of Genesis and stands as the longest continuous narrative in the book. Joseph is one of the most sustained types of Christ in the entire Old Testament: the beloved son of his father, hated by his brothers without cause, stripped and sold for silver, descending into a pit, rising to the right hand of the ruler, and ultimately saving the very brothers who rejected him.

The chapter introduces the dynamics that will drive the entire story: Jacob’s favoritism (the robe of many colors), Joseph’s dreaming, the brothers’ murderous hatred, and the providential chain of events—pit, Ishmaelite traders, Egypt—that begins to fulfill what Joseph dreamed without either Joseph or his brothers understanding it.

Throughout the Joseph narrative God speaks only once, to Jacob at Beersheba (46:2–4), and he never appears to Joseph. He works entirely through circumstances, human decisions, and the texture of ordinary life. Yet the theology of divine providence is more concentrated here than anywhere else in Genesis. “You meant it for evil; God meant it for good” (50:20) is the interpretive key that retrospectively illuminates everything in chapters 37–50. Providence works in the dark.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 37 opens the Joseph narrative — the longest continuous narrative in Genesis, spanning chapters 37–50. Joseph, the eleventh son of Jacob and the firstborn of Rachel, is his father's favorite: he receives the famous coat (or robe of distinction), he brings bad reports about his brothers to his father, and he has two dreams in which his brothers and parents bow down to him. The brothers' hatred culminates in a plot to kill him; Reuben diverts the plan to throwing him in a pit; the brothers sell him to Ishmaelite traders; the traders sell him in Egypt; and the brothers present the coat dipped in goat's blood to Jacob, who grieves inconsolably.
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob loves Joseph more than his brothers and makes him a robe; Joseph dreams of sheaves and stars bowing to him. Sent to his brothers, he is stripped and thrown into a dry pit while they eat, then sold for twenty shekels to traders. The brothers show Jacob the robe dipped in goat's blood, and he refuses comfort; Joseph is sold to Potiphar.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the beloved son sent to his brothers "came to his own, and his own people did not receive him" (John 1:11). Now: God is not mentioned once in the chapter, and he is in every line of it (50:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob lived in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan. These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father. Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a robe of many colors. But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"These are the generations of Jacob." The last of the eleven toledot panels, and it runs to the end of the book — and the story it tells is Joseph's. The heading is the father's; the narrative is the son's, because what Genesis is now tracing is what became of the family.

"Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers... And Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father." He is a teenager, working with older half-brothers, and he reports on them. Whether the report was true is not stated and rather beside the point; nobody has ever liked the boy who tells.

"Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons... And he made him a robe of many colors." The Hebrew is uncertain — a long robe with sleeves, or an ornamented one; either way it is not working clothes. It is the garment of somebody who does not have to do anything, and ten men in the fields could see it coming from a distance.

Jacob knew exactly what favouritism does. He grew up in a house where his father loved Esau and his mother loved him, and the family broke in half over it (25:28). He does the same thing to his own sons and puts it on a coat.

"They hated him and could not speak peacefully to him." Not a word of civil greeting for years. The household God chose is a place where brothers cannot say good morning.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the Hebrew for Joseph’s robe is uncertain: perhaps “of many colors” or “with long sleeves” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more. He said to them, "Hear this dream that I have dreamed: Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and stood upright. And behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf." His brothers said to him, "Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us?" So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words. Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers and said, "Behold, I have dreamed another dream. Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me." But when he told it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebuked him and said to him, "What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves to the ground before you?" And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph has two dreams and tells them both, and it is fair to ask whether he had to. Sheaves bowing to his sheaf; then the sun, moon and eleven stars bowing to him — which even his father can decode, and does, with irritation: "Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves to the ground before you?"

The dreams are from God; everything that follows will prove it. But a seventeen-year-old announcing them to the family, twice, in a house that already hates him, is not exercising much wisdom. God gave him the dreams. Nobody told him to describe them at dinner.

That distinction matters. It is possible to have a genuine word from God and handle it in a way that does damage — and the boy who does that is not disqualified, he is simply young. Twenty-two years of Egypt will make him a man who keeps his own counsel and speaks when it helps somebody else.

"And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind." Jacob rebukes him in public and files it away in private. He has been around God's promises long enough to know that they arrive in unwelcome forms, and he is not going to dismiss this one.

Mary would do the same thing about her son: "his mother treasured up all these things in her heart" (Luke 2:51). Parents of children God is doing something with have always had to hold two things at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his brothers went to pasture their father's flock near Shechem. And Israel said to Joseph, "Are not your brothers pasturing the flock at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them." And he said to him, "Here I am." So he said to him, "Go now, see if it is well with your brothers and with the flock, and bring me word." So he sent him from the Valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem. And a man found him wandering in the fields. And the man asked him, "What are you seeking?" "I am seeking my brothers," he said. "Tell me, please, where they are pasturing the flock." And the man said, "They have gone away, for I heard them say, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob sends Joseph to check on his brothers at Shechem — of all places, the town his sons had massacred (34:25) — and the boy's answer is three words that echo through the book: "Here I am." Abraham said it on the way to Moriah; Jacob said it when God spoke to him in a dream (31:11). Joseph says it setting off on a journey his father does not know is one-way.

It is fifty miles from Hebron to Shechem, and they are not there. He wanders in the fields until a stranger finds him — "What are you seeking?" "I am seeking my brothers" — and directs him another fifteen miles north to Dothan.

An unnamed man in a field is the reason the whole story happens. Without him Joseph turns round and goes home, and there is no Egypt, no famine relief, no nation in Goshen and no exodus. Providence is very often a stranger who happened to overhear something and could be bothered to say so.

And keep the boy's answer. He was seeking his brothers, and he found them, and they threw him in a hole. The one sent by the father to his brothers, who came to his own and was not received — the pattern is not accidental, and John says it in so many words (John 1:11).

verseByVerse.quote: They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him. They said to one another, "Here comes this dreamer. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will become of his dreams." But when Reuben heard it, he rescued him out of their hands, saying, "Let us not take his life." And Reuben said to them, "Shed no blood; throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him"— that he might rescue him out of their hand to restore him to his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him." They can see the coat coming across the plain, and they have the plan made before he is within earshot.

"Here comes this dreamer... let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits... and we will see what will become of his dreams." That last line is the key to the chapter. They are not merely murdering a brother; they are trying to kill a word from God, and they say so.

It is the oldest futility there is. Pharaoh tried it with the Hebrew boys, Herod with the children of Bethlehem, and a Sanhedrin with a tomb and a guard. The dreams are the one thing in this chapter that cannot be got rid of, and every single act of the brothers from here on will serve them.

"But when Reuben heard it, he rescued him out of their hands, saying, 'Let us not take his life.'" The eldest intervenes — and only half. He proposes the pit rather than the knife, intending to come back for him later, and he does not tell the others what he is doing. It is a good instinct executed by a weak man, and it saves Joseph's life and nothing else.

Reuben is the man who slept with his father's concubine (35:22) and who will later offer to have his own two sons killed if he fails to bring Benjamin home (42:37). He means well, always, and he never quite carries anything through.
verseByVerse.note: The “pits” were cisterns (ESV note) cut into rock to store rainwater.

verseByVerse.quote: So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors that he wore. And they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it. Then they sat down to eat. And looking up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry it down to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors that he wore." First the coat. The thing they had hated for years comes off before anything else happens to him, and it will come back into the story soaked in goat's blood.

"And they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it." A dry cistern — bottle-shaped, cut into rock, impossible to climb out of. The detail that there was no water in it means he did not drown, and it means he could hear everything.

"Then they sat down to eat."

That is the worst sentence in Genesis. Their brother is in a hole a few yards away and they have lunch. Chapter 42 finally tells us what they could hear: "we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen" (42:21). He was pleading, and they passed the bread.

It is not the violence that is most frightening in this chapter; it is the appetite afterwards. A conscience can be got past, and once it has been got past a man can eat.
verseByVerse.note: Gilead lay east of the Jordan; caravans carried spices to Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judah said to his brothers, "What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother, our own flesh." And his brothers listened to him. Then Midianite traders passed by. And they drew Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver. They took Joseph to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Judah said to his brothers, 'What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites.'"

Judah's proposal is presented as mercy — "let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother, our own flesh" — and it begins with the word profit. He is not saving Joseph; he is monetising him. Slavery instead of murder, and twenty shekels in the bargain.

Twenty shekels of silver is the value the law would later set on a male between five and twenty years old (Lev. 27:5). They got the going rate for their brother. And Zechariah's thirty pieces of silver, and Matthew's, are the same transaction with the price adjusted for inflation (Zech. 11:12–13; Matt. 26:15). The son of Jacob was sold by Judah; the Son of David was sold by a man whose name is the Greek form of the same name — Judas.

"They took Joseph to Egypt." Five words, and the whole of Israel's history is in them.
verseByVerse.note: Twenty shekels was about 8 ounces of silver (ESV note: a shekel was about 2/5 ounce). Ishmaelites and Midianites seem to be overlapping names for the traders.

verseByVerse.quote: When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes and returned to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes and returned to his brothers and said, 'The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go?'"

He had gone off somewhere. His plan required him to be present and he was not, and by the time he came back the caravan was over the hill.

And listen to his lament: the boy is gone, and I, where shall I go? The first half is about Joseph and the second half is about himself. As the firstborn he was accountable to his father, and what he is calculating is what this will cost him.

Good intentions that are not carried through in time are worth almost nothing, and the man who meant to help is left tearing his clothes over a plan he did not finish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they took Joseph's robe and slaughtered a goat and dipped the robe in the blood. And they sent the robe of many colors and brought it to their father and said, "This we have found; please identify whether it is your son's robe or not." And he identified it and said, "It is my son's robe. A fierce animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces." Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins and mourned for his son many days. All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted and said, "No, I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning." Thus his father wept for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then they took Joseph's robe and slaughtered a goat and dipped the robe in the blood."

A goat and a garment. Jacob put goatskin on his hands and wore his brother's clothes to deceive his blind father about which son stood in front of him (27:15–16); now his sons kill a goat and use a coat to deceive him about which son is dead. The instrument of his own great sin is turned round and handed back to him thirty years later.

And the cruelty of the delivery is exquisite. They do not tell him anything. They hand him the coat and say, "please identify whether it is your son's robe or not" — making the old man do the work, so that the conclusion is his and not theirs. They never once say Joseph is dead. They let him say it.

"It is my son's robe. A fierce animal has devoured him." He says the very words they rehearsed in verse 20, and they say nothing.

"All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted." His sons stand round him offering comfort for a grief they manufactured, and keep it up for twenty-two years. It is the longest lie in the Bible.

"No, I shall go down to Sheol to my son, mourning." He expects to grieve until he dies. He has no idea that the boy is alive, that he will see him again, or that God is at that moment beginning the rescue of the whole family. Some of the worst hours of a believer's life are lived on information that is simply not true.
verseByVerse.note: Sheol is the Old Testament name for the place of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Meanwhile the Midianites had sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Meanwhile the Midianites had sold him in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard."

The chapter's last word is meanwhile, and it is doing a great deal of work. While Jacob is refusing to be comforted, the boy is alive and in a house in Egypt. Everything the father believes is false and everything he fears has not happened.

And notice where he lands. Not in a quarry or a field, but in the household of the captain of Pharaoh's guard — the one position in Egypt from which a Hebrew slave could conceivably come to the attention of the throne. Every step of this has been a disaster and every step has been placement.

God is not mentioned once in Genesis 37. Not a word from him, not an appearance, not an altar. He is in every line of it, and the man in the middle of it could not have told you so. Joseph will be able to, many years later: "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (50:20). At seventeen, in the bottom of a dry cistern listening to his brothers eat, he knew nothing of the kind.

37.theology:
Joseph is the most sustained typological portrait of Christ in the Old Testament. The correspondences are detailed and systematic: beloved son of his father (Matt 3:17), sent to his brothers (John 1:11), hated without cause (John 15:25), stripped of his garments (Matt 27:28), sold for pieces of silver (Matt 26:15), delivered into the hands of Gentiles, falsely accused, imprisoned, and ultimately exalted to the right hand of the ruler, where he saves the very brothers who rejected him (Acts 2:23, 36; Rom 11:11–15).

Joseph is not an allegory of Christ—he is a real person whose real story is shaped by the same providential hand that shapes all history toward the Son. The typology is prospective: God so ordered Joseph’s life that it pre-figured the life of the one who was to come. Matthew, John, Acts, and Romans all draw on the Joseph-Christ parallel explicitly or implicitly. The rejected brother who becomes the savior is the deep grammar of redemptive history.

The silence of God in the Joseph narrative is itself a theological statement. Providence works through the ordinary texture of human decision, cruelty, faithfulness, and chance. The Ishmaelite caravan passes at the exact moment needed; a nameless man knows where the brothers went; Reuben’s well-intentioned intervention fails at the crucial moment. God orchestrates through means, not in spite of them.
37.examples:
Joseph’s descent into the pit and into Egypt is the experience of every believer who has been wronged by those closest to them—family, church, colleagues—and who watches the situation become worse, not better, before God acts. The temptation in the pit is to conclude that the dreams were false, that God has abandoned, that prayer has not been heard. The Joseph narrative is written precisely for those in the pit: the dreams are true, God is present, and what looks like the end is the beginning of the providential journey toward the throne.

The Joseph narrative speaks directly to the relationship between suffering and purpose. The suffering is real—Joseph weeps (42:24; 45:2, 14; 46:29); he does not theologize his way above the pain. But the retrospective word of 50:20 illuminates everything: “You meant it for evil; God meant it for good.” This is not a word that can be said at the beginning of the story; it can only be said at the end. In the middle, the only available posture is faithfulness.

38.title: Judah and Tamar
38.text: <sup>1</sup>It happened at that time that Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah.<sup>2</sup>There Judah saw the daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name was Shua. He took her and went in to her,<sup>3</sup>and she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er.<sup>4</sup>She conceived again and bore a son, and she called his name Onan.<sup>5</sup>Yet again she bore a son, and she called his name Shelah.
