Judah was in Chezib when she bore him.<sup>6</sup>And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name was Tamar.<sup>7</sup>But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.<sup>8</sup>Then Judah said to Onan, "Go in to your brother's wife and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her, and raise up offspring for your brother."<sup>9</sup>But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. So whenever he went in to his brother's wife he would waste the semen on the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother.<sup>10</sup>And what he did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death also.<sup>11</sup>Then Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, "Remain a widow in your father's house, till Shelah my son grows up"—for he feared that he would die, like his brothers. So Tamar went and remained in her father's house.<sup>12</sup>In the course of time the wife of Judah, Shua's daughter, died. When Judah was comforted, he went up to Timnah to his sheepshearers, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.<sup>13</sup>And when Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep,"<sup>14</sup>she took off her widow's garments and covered herself with a veil, wrapping herself up, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah was grown up, and she had not been given to him in marriage.<sup>15</sup>When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face.<sup>16</sup>He turned to her at the roadside and said, "Come, let me come in to you," for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, "What will you give me, that you may come in to me?"<sup>17</sup>He answered, "I will send you a young goat from the flock." And she said, "If you give me a pledge, until you send it—"<sup>18</sup>He said, "What pledge shall I give you?" She replied, "Your signet and your cord and your staff that is in your hand." So he gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him.<sup>19</sup>Then she arose and went away, and taking off her veil she put on the garments of her widowhood.<sup>20</sup>When Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to take back the pledge from the woman's hand, he did not find her.<sup>21</sup>And he asked the men of the place, "Where is the cult prostitute who was at Enaim at the roadside?" And they said, "No cult prostitute has been here."<sup>22</sup>So he returned to Judah and said, "I have not found her. Also, the men of the place said, 'No cult prostitute has been here.'"<sup>23</sup>And Judah replied, "Let her keep the things as her own, or we shall be laughed at. You see, I sent this young goat, and you did not find her."<sup>24</sup>About three months later Judah was told, "Tamar your daughter-in-law has been immoral. Moreover, she is pregnant by immorality." And Judah said, "Bring her out, and let her be burned."<sup>25</sup>As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law, "By the man to whom these belong, I am pregnant." And she said, "Please identify whose these are, the signet and the cord and the staff."<sup>26</sup>Then Judah identified them and said, "She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not know her again.<sup>27</sup>When the time of her labor came, there were twins in her womb.<sup>28</sup>And when she was in labor, one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, "This one came out first."<sup>29</sup>But as he drew back his hand, behold, his brother came out. And she said, "What a breach you have made for yourself!" Therefore his name was called Perez.<sup>30</sup>Afterward his brother came out with the scarlet thread on his hand, and his name was called Zerah.
38.overview:
Genesis 38 interrupts the Joseph narrative with the story of Judah and Tamar—an uncomfortable, morally complex tale that seems at first glance to have nothing to do with the main story. Its placement between the sale of Joseph (ch. 37) and Joseph’s rise in Egypt (ch. 39) is not accidental. It shows us what Judah has become while Joseph is descending toward slavery: he has “gone down from his brothers,” married a Canaanite, failed his daughter-in-law, and visited a roadside prostitute who turns out to be his widowed daughter-in-law in disguise.

The chapter’s theological purpose is multiple. It establishes the crisis in Judah’s line—the line through which the Messiah will come (49:10). Tamar’s righteousness (v.26) shames Judah’s failure. The twins born from the union (Perez and Zerah) echo the Jacob/Esau reversal—Perez, who breaks out first despite the thread on Zerah’s wrist, is in the genealogy of David and of Jesus (Matt 1:3). God’s purposes advance through the most irregular means imaginable.

Tamar is one of only four women named in Matthew’s genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:3). She is not there despite her story but because of it: the line of the Messiah runs through scandal, through moral failure, through women who had no other path but the irregular one. Grace runs through the broken places.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 38 interrupts the Joseph narrative with a story about Judah — the brother who proposed the sale of Joseph — and his Canaanite family. Judah marries a Canaanite woman and has three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. He arranges a wife for Er — Tamar — but Er is wicked and the LORD kills him. Onan refuses to give Tamar children, practicing coitus interruptus to avoid raising offspring for his brother, and the LORD kills him too. Judah, fearing his third son will also die, withholds Shelah from Tamar. Tamar disguises herself as a prostitute, has sex with Judah, and becomes pregnant. When Judah discovers the pregnancy and orders her execution, she produces his signet, cord, and staff as proof that he is the father. Judah acknowledges his guilt: 'She is more righteous than I.'
verseByVerse.theology: Judah goes down from his brothers and marries a Canaanite. God puts to death his wicked sons Er and Onan, and Judah sends Tamar home, withholding Shelah. Tamar veils herself by the road to Timnah; Judah takes her for a prostitute and leaves his seal, cord and staff. When he orders her burned, she asks him to identify them, and he says, "She is more righteous than I." She bears Perez and Zerah.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "please identify" is the phrase Judah's brothers used over Joseph's robe (37:32). Now: Matthew names Tamar in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt. 1:3) — the line to the Messiah runs through this chapter, not around it.

verseByVerse.quote: It happened at that time that Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to a certain Adullamite, whose name was Hirah. There Judah saw the daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name was Shua. He took her and went in to her, and she conceived and bore a son, and he called his name Er. She conceived again and bore a son, and she called his name Onan. Yet again she bore a son, and she called his name Shelah. Judah was in Chezib when she bore him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Joseph narrative stops dead and Genesis spends a whole chapter on Judah. Readers often treat it as an interruption. It is not: it is the reason the book has a future, because the line to Christ runs through this chapter and not through Joseph's.

"It happened at that time that Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to a certain Adullamite." Down out of the hill country, and away from the covenant family — a physical move that Genesis uses as a moral one. Joseph has just been taken down to Egypt against his will; Judah walks down out of the family of his own accord.

"There Judah saw the daughter of a certain Canaanite... He took her and went in to her." Saw, took — the verbs of Eden and of the sons of God in chapter 6. And a Canaanite wife, which Abraham had gone to great lengths to prevent (24:3) and which Isaac had commanded Jacob to avoid (28:1). Judah does in one verse what two generations were warned against.

Three sons are born: Er, Onan, Shelah. This is the man who a chapter ago proposed selling his brother for twenty shekels, and he is now the head of a half-Canaanite household outside the camp.

verseByVerse.quote: And Judah took a wife for Er his firstborn, and her name was Tamar. But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death. Then Judah said to Onan, "Go in to your brother's wife and perform the duty of a brother-in-law to her, and raise up offspring for your brother." But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. So whenever he went in to his brother's wife he would waste the semen on the ground, so as not to give offspring to his brother. And what he did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death also. Then Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law, "Remain a widow in your father's house, till Shelah my son grows up"—for he feared that he would die, like his brothers. So Tamar went and remained in her father's house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death." Genesis does not say what he did. It says only that God killed him — one of the very few times in the book where God acts in direct judgment on an individual.

Then the levirate custom, later written into the law (Deut. 25:5–10): a brother marries the childless widow, and the first son counts as the dead man's, so that his name and his inheritance are not lost. It is a provision for the protection of a widow in a world with no other provision for her at all.

"But Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. So whenever he went in to his brother's wife he would waste the semen on the ground." He takes the marital right and refuses the obligation, repeatedly — the Hebrew is a habit, not one occasion. He wants a wife's body, his brother's estate, and no heir to inherit it. God kills him too.

The passage is not primarily about the physical act; it is about a man systematically exploiting a widow while defrauding a dead brother, and Genesis calls it wicked in exactly the same words it used of Er.

"Remain a widow in your father's house, till Shelah my son grows up." And here is Judah's own sin, quietly stated: "for he feared that he would die, like his brothers." He has decided Tamar is the problem. He sends her home in widow's clothes with a promise he has no intention of keeping, and leaves her there — unmarriageable, childless and dependent — for years.

Was Onan’s sin masturbation or contraception? The sin the text names is his refusal to raise up offspring for his dead brother while taking the marriage’s privileges, defrauding both Tamar and Er’s line, and doing it again and again. The passage is not a ruling on birth control or self-gratification as such. Those questions must be settled from Scripture’s wider teaching, not from this verse.
verseByVerse.note: When a man died childless, his brother was to father a child with the widow to carry on the dead man’s name (later written into Israel’s law).

verseByVerse.quote: In the course of time the wife of Judah, Shua's daughter, died. When Judah was comforted, he went up to Timnah to his sheepshearers, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite. And when Tamar was told, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep," she took off her widow's garments and covered herself with a veil, wrapping herself up, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah was grown up, and she had not been given to him in marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah's wife dies. "When Judah was comforted, he went up to Timnah to his sheepshearers" — sheepshearing was a festival, and the man is out of mourning and in the mood for it.

"For she saw that Shelah was grown up, and she had not been given to him in marriage." Tamar has waited. The boy is a man, the promise has not been kept, and nobody is going to do anything about it.

What she does next is indefensible and it is also the act of a woman with no other move on the board. She cannot marry outside the family — she is bound to it. She cannot compel Judah. She has no income, no children, no standing, and no one to appeal to, and she will be a dependent widow in her father's house until she dies.

"She took off her widow's garments and covered herself with a veil, wrapping herself up, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah." She is not seducing a stranger. She is targeting the man who owes her, at a place he must pass, and Genesis will let him pronounce the verdict on the whole business himself in verse 26.

verseByVerse.quote: When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face. He turned to her at the roadside and said, "Come, let me come in to you," for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, "What will you give me, that you may come in to me?" He answered, "I will send you a young goat from the flock." And she said, "If you give me a pledge, until you send it—" He said, "What pledge shall I give you?" She replied, "Your signet and your cord and your staff that is in your hand." So he gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him. Then she arose and went away, and taking off her veil she put on the garments of her widowhood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, for she had covered her face. He turned to her at the roadside and said, 'Come, let me come in to you.'"

No hesitation, no reflection, no question about who she is. The son of Jacob, heir of the covenant of Abraham, propositions a veiled woman by the roadside on his way to a party. Genesis reports it flatly and it is the more damning for it.

Then the haggling, and she plays it perfectly. He offers a young goat — a goat again; this family cannot get away from them — and she asks for a pledge until it comes. "Your signet and your cord and your staff."

Consider what that is. The signet was his seal, worn on a cord round the neck, the instrument by which he signed and authorised anything; the staff was carved and personal. It is the ancient equivalent of handing over a passport, a chequebook and a set of house keys, to a woman whose name he has not asked. A man in that condition will give away anything.

"So he gave them to her and went in to her, and she conceived by him. Then she arose and went away, and taking off her veil she put on the garments of her widowhood." She goes back to being a widow the same afternoon, with his identity in her hand.

verseByVerse.quote: When Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to take back the pledge from the woman's hand, he did not find her. And he asked the men of the place, "Where is the cult prostitute who was at Enaim at the roadside?" And they said, "No cult prostitute has been here." So he returned to Judah and said, "I have not found her. Also, the men of the place said, 'No cult prostitute has been here.'" And Judah replied, "Let her keep the things as her own, or we shall be laughed at. You see, I sent this young goat, and you did not find her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah sends the goat by his friend Hirah — he will not go himself — and the woman cannot be found. The friend asks the locals for the cult prostitute who was at Enaim, and is told there was never one there.

The word he uses is not the ordinary one; it is the word for a shrine prostitute, part of Canaanite fertility religion. Whether he chose it to make the enquiry sound respectable or whether that is genuinely what Judah assumed, it tells you how far into the culture this branch of the family has gone.

"And Judah replied, 'Let her keep the things as her own, or we shall be laughed at.'" There it is. His seal and staff are in the hands of an unknown woman somewhere on the Timnah road, and his one concern is that the story might get out. He is not ashamed; he is worried about looking foolish.

That distinction is worth having, because a great many people mistake the second for the first. Judah has no interest at all in what he has done. He has a very lively interest in what people will say, and he drops the search to protect his reputation — which is exactly what makes the next scene so devastating.
verseByVerse.note: “Cult prostitute” is literally “sacred woman” (ESV note): a woman serving a pagan deity.

verseByVerse.quote: About three months later Judah was told, "Tamar your daughter-in-law has been immoral. Moreover, she is pregnant by immorality." And Judah said, "Bring her out, and let her be burned." As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law, "By the man to whom these belong, I am pregnant." And she said, "Please identify whose these are, the signet and the cord and the staff." Then Judah identified them and said, "She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah." And he did not know her again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"About three months later Judah was told, 'Tamar your daughter-in-law has been immoral. Moreover, she is pregnant by immorality.' And Judah said, 'Bring her out, and let her be burned.'"

Not a trial, not a question, not an hour's delay. Burning was a penalty reserved in Israel for the gravest cases (Lev. 21:9), and he pronounces it on his daughter-in-law instantly — the same man who three months ago paid for a roadside encounter and then worried about being laughed at.

Here is the moral shape of it, and it is entirely familiar. Severity towards other people's sin and complete indulgence towards one's own is not hypocrisy that people notice in themselves; it feels like standards. "Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye?" (Matt. 7:3). Judah is about to have the log handed to him in a bag.

"As she was being brought out, she sent word to her father-in-law, 'By the man to whom these belong, I am pregnant.' And she said, 'Please identify whose these are, the signet and the cord and the staff.'"

Those are the exact words Judah and his brothers used when they handed Jacob the bloodied coat: please identify whether it is your son's robe or not (37:32). She uses his own sentence. The man who made his father do the identifying is now made to do it himself, in public, holding the evidence.

"Then Judah identified them and said, 'She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.'"

He could have burned her and kept the seal. Nobody would ever have known. He says it out loud instead, in front of everybody, and takes the blame in a single sentence with no excuse attached to it. It is the first honest thing anyone in this family has done in two chapters, and it is the turning point of Judah's life. The man who says this is the man who will one day offer himself as a slave in Benjamin's place (44:33).

"And he did not know her again." He does not compound it. Repentance stops.

“She is more righteous than I” does not approve of her method. Tamar sought the heir she was owed by family law, by a deception; Judah had withheld it, and then condemned her for the very sin he had committed with her. Her cause was just and her means were not, and Judah’s guilt was greater.

verseByVerse.quote: When the time of her labor came, there were twins in her womb. And when she was in labor, one put out a hand, and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand, saying, "This one came out first." But as he drew back his hand, behold, his brother came out. And she said, "What a breach you have made for yourself!" Therefore his name was called Perez. Afterward his brother came out with the scarlet thread on his hand, and his name was called Zerah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twins, and a struggle at the birth — as there was with Jacob and Esau (25:24–26), and Genesis means us to hear it. One hand comes out and is tied with a scarlet thread; then the hand withdraws and the other child is born first.

"What a breach you have made for yourself!" — so he is called Perez, breach. The younger comes before the elder again — as Isaac before Ishmael and Jacob before Esau, and as Ephraim will before Manasseh — and now Perez before Zerah. God's choice does not run by seniority, and by now the reader should have stopped expecting it to.

And this is why the chapter is here. Perez is an ancestor of David. The book of Ruth ends by tracing the king's line to him (Ruth 4:18–22), and the first paragraph of the New Testament reads: "and Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar" (Matt. 1:3).

Read that name in that list. Matthew is writing the genealogy of Jesus Christ, and he names Tamar — a widow, probably Canaanite, who dressed as a prostitute to trap her father-in-law — in the third verse. He did not have to. Genealogies routinely named only the fathers, and he goes out of his way to put her in, along with Rahab, Ruth and "the wife of Uriah."

So the line to the Messiah runs through the worst chapter in Genesis. Not around it, not in spite of it — through it. That is not God making the best of a bad situation. It is God saying, in the ancestry of his own Son, exactly what kind of people he came for.
verseByVerse.note: “Perez” means “a breach” (ESV note). Through Perez came David — and Jesus; Tamar is one of the four women named in Matthew’s genealogy.

38.theology:
Genesis 38 teaches that God’s providential purposes run through the morally complex and even scandalous events of human history without being stained by them and without endorsing them. Tamar is “more righteous” than Judah—not in an absolute sense but relative to the specific failure: she was faithful to the levirate obligation; he was not. God does not abandon the Judah line because of Judah’s failures; he works through Tamar’s courage to preserve it.

Judah’s confession (“she is more righteous than I”) is a moment of genuine moral reckoning. It is the same kind of reckoning that will produce the great confession of chapter 44. Judah must be broken before he can become the man who offers himself for Benjamin. The Joseph narrative is not only about Joseph; it is also about the transformation of Judah—and it begins here, on the road to Timnah, when a veiled woman holds up his signet ring.
38.examples:
The placement of the Tamar story between Joseph’s sale and Joseph’s rise invites comparison. While Joseph is being faithful in Egypt despite unjust suffering, Judah is failing morally in Canaan despite freedom and prosperity. The contrast is a pastoral challenge: faithfulness is possible in the pit; unfaithfulness is possible in comfort. Joseph’s circumstances cannot explain his character; Judah’s circumstances cannot excuse his failure. Character is formed in the inner life before it is revealed in external circumstances.

Tamar’s courage in securing what was rightfully hers—at enormous personal risk—and her inclusion in Jesus’s genealogy is an encouragement to those who have been failed by those who should have protected them and who have had to find irregular paths through impossible situations. God sees. God remembers. The irregular path of a desperate woman can be the path through which the Messiah comes into the world.

39.title: The LORD Was with Joseph
39.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, had bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there.<sup>2</sup>The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master.<sup>3</sup>His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD caused all that he did to succeed in his hands.<sup>4</sup>So Joseph found favor in his sight and attended him, and he made him overseer of his house and put him in charge of all that he had.<sup>5</sup>From the time that he made him overseer in his house and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake; the blessing of the LORD was on all that he had, in house and field.<sup>6</sup>So he left all that he had in Joseph's charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.<sup>7</sup>And after a time his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, "Lie with me."<sup>8</sup>But he refused and said to his master's wife, "Behold, because of me my master has no concern about anything in the house, and he has put everything that he has in my charge.<sup>9</sup>He is not greater in this house than I am, nor has he kept back anything from me except you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?"<sup>10</sup>And as she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her.<sup>11</sup>But one day, when he went into the house to do his work and none of the men of the house was there in the house,<sup>12</sup>she caught him by his garment, saying, "Lie with me." But he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house.<sup>13</sup>And as soon as she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled out of the house,<sup>14</sup>she called to the men of her household and said to them, "See, he has brought among us a Hebrew to laugh at us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried out with a loud voice.<sup>15</sup>And as soon as he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled and got out of the house."<sup>16</sup>Then she laid up his garment by her until his master came home,<sup>17</sup>and she told him the same story, saying, "The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought among us, came in to me to laugh at me.<sup>18</sup>But as soon as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment beside me and fled out of the house."<sup>19</sup>As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him, "This is the way your servant treated me," his anger was kindled.<sup>20</sup>And Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison.<sup>21</sup>But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison.<sup>22</sup>And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it.<sup>23</sup>The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph's charge, because the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed.
39.overview:
Genesis 39 is a chapter of double descent and double rise. Joseph descends into slavery; he rises to Potiphar’s steward. He descends into prison; he rises to the prison warden’s trust. The pattern is not coincidental—it is the narrator’s way of showing that Joseph’s descent is always temporary and his rise is always certain, because “the LORD was with Joseph.” That phrase appears four times in this chapter. It is the theological key to everything that follows.

Joseph’s refusal of Potiphar’s wife is one of the great acts of moral courage in Genesis. He is young, far from home, without accountability, in a pagan household. Temptation is persistent (“day after day,” v.10). His argument is not merely legal (“it would be wrong”) but relational and theological: it would betray my master’s trust, and it would be “sin against God.” The sin is against God whether or not anyone else would know. This is the moral formation that positions Joseph to be trusted with a nation.

Potiphar’s wife’s false accusation and Joseph’s imprisonment is the third injustice in Joseph’s descending series: hated, sold, imprisoned. Each step down is also a step toward the throne. The pit, the slave market, and the prison are all stages in a divine itinerary that Joseph cannot see and cannot control. He can only be faithful in each place, and he is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 39 returns to Joseph in Egypt. Sold to Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard, Joseph rises to head of the household through the LORD's manifest blessing on everything he does. Potiphar's wife attempts to seduce Joseph repeatedly; Joseph refuses on grounds of faithfulness to Potiphar and to God; she falsely accuses him; Potiphar has him imprisoned. In prison, the same pattern repeats: the LORD is with Joseph, the warden gives him authority, and Joseph rises to be effectively in charge of the prison. The chapter's theological theme is stated four times: 'the LORD was with Joseph.'
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD is with Joseph in Potiphar's house, and he is put in charge of everything. Potiphar's wife presses him day after day; he refuses — "How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?" — and flees, leaving his garment. She accuses him, and he is imprisoned, where the LORD is with him again and he is put in charge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the same sentence is said over the estate and the dungeon. Now: "Flee from sexual immorality" (1 Cor. 6:18) is a command about your feet, and God's presence is company, not a promise of release.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, had bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there. The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master. His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD caused all that he did to succeed in his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar... had bought him." He is property. Genesis states it without softening: a seventeen-year-old sold across a border, standing in a slave market, purchased.

"The LORD was with Joseph, and he became a successful man." That sentence appears four times in this chapter — twice in Potiphar's house and twice in the prison — and it is the spine of the whole Joseph account. It also has a history: it is what God said to Jacob at Bethel when he was running for his life (28:15), and to Isaac at Gerar (26:3). The promise has come down to the fourth generation and it is being kept in a foreign house.

And notice where it is said. Not while he is prospering at home in the coat, but while he is a slave. The presence of God is not a reward for a good outcome and it is not proof of one. It was true in the pit and it will be true in the dungeon.

"His master saw that the LORD was with him." An Egyptian official, worshipper of Egyptian gods, watching a Hebrew slave work — and what he concludes is that this man's God is in the house. Nobody preached to Potiphar. He drew that conclusion from the way the accounts came out.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph found favor in his sight and attended him, and he made him overseer of his house and put him in charge of all that he had. From the time that he made him overseer in his house and over all that he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake; the blessing of the LORD was on all that he had, in house and field. So he left all that he had in Joseph's charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Joseph found favor in his sight and attended him, and he made him overseer of his house and put him in charge of all that he had."

Think about what those years contained. He is doing the books, running the estate, managing the staff and buying the grain — for a man who owns him, in a country he was trafficked into, with no prospect of ever going home. And he does it so well that Potiphar promotes him twice.

There is no record of Joseph complaining, working slowly, or waiting for a better position before doing his best. Whatever else God did in the twenty-two years, he produced a man who could be trusted with anything, and he produced him by making him serve somebody else's interests for years with no credit. "Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men" (Col. 3:23) was written to slaves, and it describes this chapter exactly.

"The LORD blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake." Potiphar's crops and herds prospered because a believer was on the payroll. God's people are good for the places they are put, and often the places never know it.

"Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance." The narrator drops it in at the end of a paragraph about prosperity, and the next verse explains why he mentioned it. It is the same phrase used of his mother Rachel (29:17). He got her looks, and they are about to cost him everything a second time.

verseByVerse.quote: And after a time his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, "Lie with me." But he refused and said to his master's wife, "Behold, because of me my master has no concern about anything in the house, and he has put everything that he has in my charge. He is not greater in this house than I am, nor has he kept back anything from me except you, because you are his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And after a time his master's wife cast her eyes on Joseph and said, 'Lie with me.'" Two words in Hebrew. No seduction, no pretence of affection — a command from a mistress to a slave, which is what makes it as much an abuse of power as a temptation.

"But he refused." And then he gives his reasons, and they are worth having in order.

First, loyalty: "my master has no concern about anything in the house, and he has put everything that he has in my charge... nor has he kept back anything from me except you, because you are his wife." He will not repay trust with treachery. A man who has been given everything does not steal the one thing withheld — which is precisely the failure of Genesis 3, and Joseph, unlike Adam, sees the fence and honours it.

Then the real reason: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?"

Nobody would have known. His family thinks he is dead, his master is out, the house is empty, and he is a slave with no reputation to protect. Every external restraint has been removed and one remains: there is a God, and this would be against him. That is the whole of Joseph's defence, and it is the only defence that holds when nobody is watching. David said the same thing about a far worse night: "against you, you only, have I sinned" (Ps. 51:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And as she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her. But one day, when he went into the house to do his work and none of the men of the house was there in the house, she caught him by his garment, saying, "Lie with me." But he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And as she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her, to lie beside her or to be with her."

Day after day. This is not one dramatic moment of temptation; it is a grinding, daily campaign in a house he cannot leave, by a woman he cannot refuse without risk. And look at the three-fold refusal the narrator records: he would not listen to her, would not lie beside her, would not be with her. He will not even be in the room.

That is the practical wisdom of the chapter, and take it literally. Joseph does not stand his ground and prove his strength. He avoids her. "Flee from sexual immorality" (1 Cor. 6:18) is a command about your feet, and the man who thinks he is strong enough to keep having the conversation has already started losing it.

"But one day, when he went into the house to do his work and none of the men of the house was there... she caught him by his garment, saying, 'Lie with me.' But he left his garment in her hand and fled and got out of the house."

He runs, and it costs him his coat. That is the second garment torn off this man by somebody who wanted something from him, and the second one used as false evidence against him. Joseph's life keeps being told through clothes he loses: the robe, this cloak, and eventually the prison clothes he changes before standing in front of Pharaoh (41:14).

He would rather be half-dressed in the courtyard than clothed in that room. It is not dignified, and there is no version of purity that always looks dignified.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and had fled out of the house, she called to the men of her household and said to them, "See, he has brought among us a Hebrew to laugh at us. He came in to me to lie with me, and I cried out with a loud voice. And as soon as he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and fled and got out of the house." Then she laid up his garment by her until his master came home, and she told him the same story, saying, "The Hebrew servant, whom you have brought among us, came in to me to laugh at me. But as soon as I lifted up my voice and cried, he left his garment beside me and fled out of the house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She is holding his cloak and she uses it. "See, he has brought among us a Hebrew to laugh at us" — she plays the race card to the household staff first, and there is an edge of contempt for her husband in it too ("he has brought among us"). Then she tells her husband the same story with one word changed: "the Hebrew servant, whom you have brought among us."

The lie is careful. She keeps the garment as evidence, waits for Potiphar to come home, and builds a version in which she cried out — which under the later law was the very thing that proved a woman had not consented (Deut. 22:27).

A woman scorned turns instantly to destruction, and the man has no answer at all. Joseph's word against hers is worth nothing; he is a slave and a foreigner, and he has been in the house alone with her. Genesis records not one sentence of self-defence from him. He never speaks again in this chapter.

False accusation is one of the loneliest things that happens to people, and Scripture is full of it — Naboth, Jeremiah, Stephen, Paul, and one man who "when he was reviled, did not revile in return... but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly" (1 Pet. 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him, "This is the way your servant treated me," his anger was kindled. And Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him... his anger was kindled. And Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison."

Consider what a master could do with a slave who had assaulted his wife. Potiphar was captain of the guard; he could have had Joseph executed on the spot, and nobody would have raised an eyebrow. Instead he puts him in "the place where the king's prisoners were confined" — a political prison in his own jurisdiction, which he administered.

Genesis does not say why, and it is fair to wonder whether Potiphar entirely believed his wife. He has had this man running his whole estate for years; he knows what he is. The anger may well be at the situation rather than at Joseph. But whatever he thought, he did the convenient thing rather than the just thing, and an innocent man went to prison to save a household's face.

Years in a cell for refusing to sin. There is no promise anywhere in Scripture that doing the right thing will work out well in this life, and Joseph is the standing proof. He obeyed God at real cost and the cost was real.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison. And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph's charge, because the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison."

That is the same sentence as verse 2, and the reader is meant to feel the shock of it. Everything has got worse — house to dungeon, overseer to prisoner — and the one thing that has not changed is the thing that matters.

God did not prevent the false accusation, did not clear his name, did not raise up a witness. What he gave was hesed, steadfast love, in a cell. The presence of God is not a substitute for justice and it is not a promise of release. It is company, and Joseph would tell you it was enough, and it took him years to be able to say so.

"And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners." He does it again. Sold into a house, he ends up running the house; thrown into a jail, he ends up running the jail. The man simply cannot help being useful, and he does it in a place where there is no promotion to be had and no one to impress.

"Because the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed." Fourth time. The dungeon and the estate get exactly the same sentence, and Genesis will not let us define success by the address.

39.theology:
“The LORD was with Joseph” is one of the most important theological formulas in Genesis. It appears at every stage of Joseph’s descent: in Potiphar’s house (vv. 2, 3) and in prison (vv. 21, 23). The divine presence is not contingent on Joseph’s circumstances; it is not interrupted by slavery or imprisonment. This is the meaning of Immanuel (God with us)—not that God guarantees comfort, but that God guarantees presence. Jesus’s final promise in Matthew 28:20 (“I am with you always, to the end of the age”) is the fulfillment of the Immanuel promise that Joseph’s story embodies.

The hesed (steadfast love/covenant faithfulness) God shows Joseph in prison (v.21) is the same hesed that runs through all of God’s dealings with his people. It is not conditional on Joseph’s success or freedom. It is unconditional love expressed through providential care. Paul will describe the same reality in Romans 8:38–39: nothing in all creation can separate us from the love of God. The prison cannot separate Joseph from God’s hesed.
39.examples:
Joseph’s moral courage in the face of sustained, private temptation is a model for all believers. The temptation is daily (v.10), private, and comes with power asymmetry (Potiphar’s wife holds enormous social power over an enslaved foreigner). There is no human accountability structure, no witness, no institutional protection. The only protection is the internalized conviction that sin is sin against God whether or not anyone else knows. This is the heart of integrity: the integration of public and private self, sustained by the vision of God who sees all.

Joseph’s experience of doing right and suffering for it (1 Pet 2:20) is the pattern of the Christian life that Peter explicitly invokes using Joseph’s greater antitype: Christ, who “when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Pet 2:23). The prisoner who rose to warden’s trust and then to the throne is the pattern: faithfulness in unjust suffering is not wasted; it is the preparation for exaltation.

40.title: The Cupbearer and the Baker
40.text: <sup>1</sup>Some time after this, the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and his baker committed an offense against their lord the king of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>And Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker,<sup>3</sup>and he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was confined.<sup>4</sup>The captain of the guard appointed Joseph to be with them, and he attended them. They continued for some time in custody.<sup>5</sup>And one night they both dreamed—the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were confined in the prison—each his own dream, and each dream with its own interpretation.<sup>6</sup>When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were troubled.<sup>7</sup>So he asked Pharaoh's officers who were with him in custody in his master's house, "Why are your faces downcast today?"<sup>8</sup>They said to him, "We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them." And Joseph said to them, "Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me."<sup>9</sup>So the chief cupbearer told his dream to Joseph and said to him, "In my dream there was a vine before me,<sup>10</sup>and on the vine there were three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms shot forth, and the clusters ripened into grapes.<sup>11</sup>Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup and placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand."<sup>12</sup>Then Joseph said to him, "This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days.<sup>13</sup>In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office, and you shall place Pharaoh's cup in his hand as formerly, when you were his cupbearer.<sup>14</sup>Only remember me, when it is well with you, and please do me the kindness to mention me to Pharaoh, and so get me out of this house.<sup>15</sup>For I was indeed stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the pit."<sup>16</sup>When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, "I also had a dream: there were three cake baskets on my head,<sup>17</sup>and in the uppermost basket there were all sorts of baked food for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating it out of the basket on my head."<sup>18</sup>And Joseph answered and said, "This is its interpretation: the three baskets are three days.<sup>19</sup>In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head—from you!—and hang you on a tree. And the birds will eat the flesh from you."<sup>20</sup>On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he made a feast for all his servants and lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants.<sup>21</sup>He restored the chief cupbearer to his position, and he placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand.<sup>22</sup>But he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.<sup>23</sup>Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.
40.overview:
Genesis 40 is the chapter of waiting. Joseph is in prison; he will not leave for two more years after this episode. The cupbearer and baker’s dreams are interpreted correctly; Joseph’s plea to be remembered goes unheeded; the cupbearer is restored and forgets. The chapter could be titled “forgotten.” Yet it is structurally essential: it establishes Joseph as an interpreter of dreams (which will bring him before Pharaoh in chapter 41) and demonstrates God’s word as reliable (both interpretations come true exactly as Joseph said).

Joseph’s pastoral attention to the troubled officers is revealing. He is a prisoner himself—unjustly imprisoned, forgotten by his family, carrying years of false accusation—yet he sees that others’ faces are downcast and asks about them. This is the posture of the servant-leader: suffering does not make Joseph inward; it makes him attentive to the suffering of others. It is the posture of Christ himself, who in his own suffering was attentive to the thief beside him (Luke 23:43).

The chapter ends with the most poignant summary verse in the Joseph narrative: “Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.” Two years of forgotten-ness follow. But God does not forget. The cupbearer’s forgetfulness is the necessary dark before the dawn of chapter 41.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Joseph Interprets the Dreams of the Cupbearer and Baker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 40 records the imprisonment of Pharaoh's chief cupbearer and chief baker in the same prison as Joseph. Both men have dreams on the same night; Joseph, seeing their distress, offers to interpret. He interprets the cupbearer's dream as a restoration to his position within three days, and the baker's dream as an execution within three days — and both interpretations come true. Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him before Pharaoh; the cupbearer forgets him. The chapter ends with Joseph still in prison, abandoned by the man he helped.
verseByVerse.theology: Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker are put in the prison where Joseph serves. Seeing their downcast faces, he asks, and they tell him their dreams. "Do not interpretations belong to God?" In three days the cupbearer is restored and the baker hanged, as Joseph said — and the cupbearer forgets him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the forgetting set the alarm two years ahead, for the morning Pharaoh would dream. Now: suffering that God is working in leaves a person still able to see someone else's.

verseByVerse.quote: Some time after this, the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and his baker committed an offense against their lord the king of Egypt. And Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker, and he put them in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, in the prison where Joseph was confined. The captain of the guard appointed Joseph to be with them, and he attended them. They continued for some time in custody.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two of Pharaoh's senior officials — the chief cupbearer and the chief baker — offend the king and land in the same prison as Joseph. The cupbearer tasted the king's wine and had his ear; the baker was responsible for the royal table. These are men of the court, and they are now in a cell in the house of the captain of the guard.

"The captain of the guard appointed Joseph to be with them, and he attended them." The captain of the guard is Potiphar (39:1). The man who put Joseph in here is still assigning him duties, and the duty is to look after two courtiers — which is how a Hebrew slave in a dungeon comes to be within one man's memory of the throne of Egypt.

"They continued for some time in custody." Genesis will not hurry. Between the night of the dreams and the end of the chapter is a matter of days; between the end of the chapter and Pharaoh's dream is two more years.

verseByVerse.quote: And one night they both dreamed—the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were confined in the prison—each his own dream, and each dream with its own interpretation. When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were troubled. So he asked Pharaoh's officers who were with him in custody in his master's house, "Why are your faces downcast today?" They said to him, "We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them." And Joseph said to them, "Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were troubled. So he asked... 'Why are your faces downcast today?'"

Stop on that question, because of who is asking it. Joseph has been sold by his brothers, trafficked, falsely accused and imprisoned, and he is a slave with no prospects — and he notices that two other men look miserable and asks them about it.

Nothing in his circumstances requires it. He could have served the food and said nothing. Long trouble usually makes a person self-absorbed, and the surest sign that God is doing something in a man's suffering is that he can still see somebody else's.

"We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them." In Egypt dream interpretation was a profession with manuals and trained practitioners, and here are two court officials with no access to any of them.

"And Joseph said to them, 'Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me.'" he takes the credit off himself before he has done anything. Dreams got him into this — his own, told at the family table at seventeen — and he does not now present himself as a man with a gift. He points past himself to God and then offers to help.
verseByVerse.note: The cupbearer tasted the king’s wine and was a trusted adviser.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief cupbearer told his dream to Joseph and said to him, "In my dream there was a vine before me, and on the vine there were three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms shot forth, and the clusters ripened into grapes. Pharaoh's cup was in my hand, and I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup and placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand." Then Joseph said to him, "This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days. In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office, and you shall place Pharaoh's cup in his hand as formerly, when you were his cupbearer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cupbearer's dream is a vine with three branches that bud, blossom and ripen, and he presses the grapes into Pharaoh's cup and puts the cup in Pharaoh's hand.

"This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days. In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and restore you to your office." Joseph gives it immediately and with total confidence, and he attaches a date. There is no hedging and nothing that could be read either way. If he is wrong, everyone will know in seventy-two hours.

"Lift up your head" is a courtly idiom for restoring a man to favour — and it is about to be used again in the next dream with a horrible twist.

verseByVerse.quote: Only remember me, when it is well with you, and please do me the kindness to mention me to Pharaoh, and so get me out of this house. For I was indeed stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the pit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Only remember me, when it is well with you, and please do me the kindness to mention me to Pharaoh, and so get me out of this house."

He asks. And there is nothing wrong with asking — trusting God's providence has never meant refusing to use a door when one opens. But note the word: he wants to be remembered, which is the word Genesis uses when God moves (8:1; 19:29; 30:22). Joseph is asking a man to do what only God does reliably.

"For I was indeed stolen out of the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing that they should put me into the pit."

It is the one time in the whole account that Joseph defends himself, and it is brief, accurate and without bitterness. He does not name his brothers. He does not accuse Potiphar's wife. He says: I was stolen, and I did nothing here either. Two sentences, and then he never mentions it again.

He also calls the prison a pit — the same word as the cistern his brothers threw him into. He has been in a hole twice now, and he knows it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, "I also had a dream: there were three cake baskets on my head, and in the uppermost basket there were all sorts of baked food for Pharaoh, but the birds were eating it out of the basket on my head." And Joseph answered and said, "This is its interpretation: the three baskets are three days. In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head—from you!—and hang you on a tree. And the birds will eat the flesh from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said to Joseph, 'I also had a dream.'" he speaks up because he liked the first answer, which is how most people approach the will of God.

Three baskets on his head, with all sorts of baked food for Pharaoh in the top one, and the birds eating it out of the basket. It has the same three-part structure and the same three-day meaning, and it ends in the opposite place.

"In three days Pharaoh will lift up your head — from you! — and hang you on a tree. And the birds will eat the flesh from you."

The idiom is turned into an execution, and Joseph delivers it. He does not soften it, does not find a hopeful reading, does not decline to answer. He tells a frightened man in a cell that he has three days to live.

That is a hard mercy and it is a mercy. A man given seventy-two hours' notice can put things in order and make his peace; a man told a comfortable lie cannot. Anyone who has ever had to say something true to somebody who wanted to hear something else — a doctor, a pastor, a friend — is standing where Joseph stood. The kindest thing available is often the accurate thing, said gently and without flinching.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he made a feast for all his servants and lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants. He restored the chief cupbearer to his position, and he placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand. But he hanged the chief baker, as Joseph had interpreted to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he made a feast for all his servants and lifted up the head of the chief cupbearer and the head of the chief baker among his servants."

The narrator uses the idiom once for both men, and then splits it: one is restored to hand Pharaoh his cup, the other is hanged. Exactly as Joseph said, on the day he said.

Which settles something about the man in the cell. He is not a clever reader of symbols; he has told the future to the day, twice, and both halves came true. "Do not interpretations belong to God?" was not modesty. It was a statement of fact, and the reader now knows that when Joseph speaks about the future, Egypt should listen.

That is the seed of everything in chapter 41. Two years from now Pharaoh will dream, the magicians will fail, and one man in the palace will remember what happened on a birthday.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him."

The chapter ends on that. Not a cliffhanger, not a promise — a flat, deflating sentence, and the two verbs are piled up to make sure it lands: did not remember, and forgot.

The man walked out of prison into the best job in the palace, put the cup back in Pharaoh's hand, and never gave the Hebrew another thought. And the next verse of Genesis begins, "After two whole years..." Two years, because a man in a good mood forgot to mention a name.

Anyone who has been let down like this knows the specific taste of it. It is not persecution; it is being overlooked by somebody who owed you, who is not evil, who is simply getting on with his own life. It is far commoner than persecution and in its own way harder to bear, because there is nobody to blame.

And yet the forgetting is the plan. If the cupbearer had spoken the following week, Joseph would have been released as a favour to a slave and disappeared into Canaan — and there would have been no famine warning, no grain in Egypt, and no family kept alive. The dream Pharaoh needed had not been dreamed yet. God was not failing to act; he was setting the alarm for a morning two years off, when the right man would remember at the exact moment it would put a Hebrew in front of the throne.

Which means the two most useless-looking years of Joseph's life were load-bearing. Hold on to that in a season where nothing is moving and somebody who could have helped did not. Joseph could not see it either, and he was living in the middle of it.

40.theology:
Genesis 40 is a chapter about the gap between promise and fulfillment. Joseph has received a dream from God (chapters 37:5–10) that he will be exalted above his brothers. He has experienced divine presence in Potiphar’s house and in prison. Yet the immediate human story is one of steady accumulation of injustice: sold, falsely accused, imprisoned, and now forgotten. The theological question the chapter poses is: where is God in the forgetting?

The answer Genesis gives is that God’s absence from the narrative surface does not mean God’s absence from the story. The cupbearer’s forgetfulness, the two-year wait, the providential imprisonment in exactly the right facility—all of these will be revealed in retrospect as the scaffolding of God’s plan. Romans 8:28 (“all things work together for good”) is a retrospective claim, not a prospective comfort. In the middle of the story, the faithful posture is Joseph’s: active attention to others, theological confidence in God’s interpretive control, and continued faithfulness in the place assigned.
40.examples:
The cupbearer’s forgetfulness is the experience of every believer who has done the right thing, served faithfully, asked for legitimate help—and been forgotten by those who could have helped. The temptation is to conclude that faithfulness does not pay, that God is not attending, that the dreams were illusions. The Joseph narrative addresses this directly: the forgetting is not the end; it is part of the timing. God uses even the cupbearer’s poor memory to place Joseph before Pharaoh at the exact moment he is needed.

Joseph’s pastoral question—“why are your faces downcast today?”—is the mark of the person whose suffering has produced compassion rather than self-absorption. He is a prisoner attending to other prisoners. This is the pattern of the suffering servant who comes “not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). Those who have been through the pit often have the greatest capacity to see the pit in others’ faces. Suffering, faithfully received, becomes the source of ministry.

41.title: Joseph Interprets Pharaoh's Dreams

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–57 — From Prison to Palace: Joseph Exalted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two years after the cupbearer's forgetting, Pharaoh dreams two disturbing dreams. No Egyptian sage can interpret them. The cupbearer suddenly remembers Joseph. Joseph is summoned from the dungeon, interprets the dreams by God's power, proposes a plan, and Pharaoh elevates him to second in all Egypt. Joseph administers the seven years of abundance, then the seven years of famine begin. The chapter is the hinge of the Joseph narrative: from the pit to the palace, from forgotten prisoner to lord of Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology: After two whole years Pharaoh dreams of cows and ears of grain, and his magicians fail. The cupbearer remembers; Joseph is brought from the pit, says "It is not in me," interprets seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and proposes a plan. Pharaoh sets him over Egypt; he stores grain, names his sons Manasseh and Ephraim, and all the earth comes to him for bread.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do" (v. 55; cf. John 2:5). Now: long obscurity is where God makes people who can be trusted with an answered prayer, and he raises the poor from the dust (Ps. 113:7–8).

verseByVerse.quote: After two whole years, Pharaoh dreamed that he was standing by the Nile, and behold, there came up out of the Nile seven cows, attractive and plump, and they fed in the reed grass. And behold, seven other cows, ugly and thin, came up out of the Nile after them, and stood by the other cows on the bank of the Nile. And the ugly, thin cows ate up the seven attractive, plump cows. And Pharaoh awoke. And he fell asleep and dreamed a second time. And behold, seven ears of grain, plump and good, were growing on one stalk. And behold, after them sprouted seven ears, thin and blighted by the east wind. And the thin ears swallowed up the seven plump, full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and behold, it was a dream.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"After two whole years, Pharaoh dreamed." The chapter opens by counting the silence, and the two years belong to the previous chapter's last verse: a man forgot, and God waited.

Both dreams come out of the Nile, which was Egypt's life — the annual flood made the harvest, and a run of poor floods meant famine. Seven fat cows eaten by seven gaunt ones; seven full ears swallowed by seven blighted ones. God speaks to a pagan king in Egyptian images, about Egyptian agriculture, and does not introduce himself.

And the cows come up out of the river. In Egypt the cow was sacred to Hathor and the Nile itself was worshipped as the giver of life; the images God chooses are the images of Egypt's own religion, and what they show is the sacred river producing famine. God speaks to people in the language they already have, including the language of their idols, and says something their idols cannot.

"And Pharaoh awoke, and behold, it was a dream." Twice he wakes. The second waking has the shock in it — the relief of realising it was only a dream, and the uneasy sense that it was not only a dream.

Does God still speak through dreams? He did here, as he did to Jacob and to Joseph, at a time when he was speaking his word directly. Now he has spoken finally in his Son (Heb 1:1–2), and his word is complete and sufficient (2 Tim 3:16–17). God can use a dream to bring something to mind, but no Christian should seek guidance in dreams or treat one as a message from God. Even Pharaoh’s dream needed a man who said, It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer (v. 16).

verseByVerse.quote: So in the morning his spirit was troubled, and he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but there was none who could interpret them to Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men... but there was none who could interpret them to Pharaoh." Egypt had a professional class for this, with manuals and training. The entire apparatus of the most advanced civilisation on earth is convened, and it produces nothing.

That failure is the point. Daniel's chapter runs the same way in Babylon (Dan. 2:1–11), and both times the wise men of the empire are stood up first so that everyone can see them fail before a believer is brought in. God arranges the silence of the experts.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, "I remember my offenses today. When Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put me and the chief baker in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, we dreamed on the same night, he and I, each having a dream with its own interpretation. A young Hebrew was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. When we told him, he interpreted our dreams to us, giving an interpretation to each man according to his dream. And as he interpreted to us, so it came about. I was restored to my office, and the baker was hanged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, 'I remember my offenses today.'"

He is not confessing that he forgot Joseph. In court language he is apologising for raising an old embarrassment — the time he was in prison — but Genesis lets the sentence stand with its double meaning intact. He remembers his offence today, two years late, because the king is in trouble.

And notice how he describes the man who saved him: "a young Hebrew... a servant of the captain of the guard." No name. He has forgotten it, or never troubled to learn it, and he is about to make the man vizier of Egypt.

"And as he interpreted to us, so it came about." That is the testimony that counts, and it is given by a hostile-to-indifferent witness, unprompted, in front of the whole court. God had put the evidence in a man's memory two years ago and left it there until the morning it was needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they quickly brought him out of the pit. And when he had shaved himself and changed his clothes, he came in before Pharaoh. And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I have had a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it." Joseph answered Pharaoh, "It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they quickly brought him out of the pit." Quickly. Two years of nothing and then everything at once. God's deliverances tend to be slow to arrive and very fast when they do.

"And when he had shaved himself and changed his clothes, he came in before Pharaoh." Hebrews wore beards and Egyptians did not; he is being made presentable for a court that would find him foreign. It is the third change of clothes in his story — the robe stripped off him, the cloak left in a woman's hand, and now prison clothes exchanged for something fit to stand in.

"I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it."

Here is the moment. He is thirty years old, has been a slave for thirteen years, and the most powerful man alive has just credited him with a skill. One sentence of agreement and his position is made.

"Joseph answered Pharaoh, 'It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.'"

He contradicts the king to his face in order to take the credit off himself. Compare the boy of chapter 37, who could not stop talking about his own dreams; thirteen years have produced a man whose first instinct in front of a throne is to point away from himself. That is what the pit and the prison were for.
verseByVerse.note: Egyptians were clean-shaven; Joseph is made presentable for court.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Behold, in my dream I was standing on the banks of the Nile. Seven cows, plump and attractive, came up out of the Nile and fed in the reed grass. Seven other cows came up after them, poor and very ugly and thin, such as I had never seen in all the land of Egypt. And the thin, ugly cows ate up the first seven plump cows, but when they had eaten them no one would have known that they had eaten them, for they were still as ugly as at the beginning. Then I awoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh retells both dreams, and he adds a detail he did not mention the first time: "when they had eaten them no one would have known that they had eaten them, for they were still as ugly as at the beginning."

That is the horror of the thing for a king. It is not merely that the lean years follow the fat; it is that the lean years will consume the fat and be no better for it. Seven years of the greatest harvests Egypt has ever seen, swallowed without a trace.

verseByVerse.quote: I also saw in my dream seven ears growing on one stalk, full and good. Seven ears, withered, thin, and blighted by the east wind, sprouted after them, and the thin ears swallowed up the seven good ears. And I told it to the magicians, but there was no one who could explain it to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He also says something of the wise men that he did not say in verse 8: "there was no one who could explain it to me." He has given them their chance and they have had nothing.

The retelling is longer than the original account, and Genesis gives it in full rather than summarising. Pharaoh is a frightened man going over a bad night in detail, and the length of the speech is the measure of how much it has shaken him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, "The dreams of Pharaoh are one; God has revealed to Pharaoh what he is about to do. The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good ears are seven years; the dreams are one. The seven lean and ugly cows that came up after them are seven years, and the seven empty ears blighted by the east wind are also seven years of famine. It is as I told Pharaoh; God has shown to Pharaoh what he is about to do.
verseByVerse.commentary: "The dreams of Pharaoh are one; God has revealed to Pharaoh what he is about to do." He says it twice, in verses 25 and 28, and it is the sentence the whole chapter turns on. This is not a Hebrew slave decoding symbols. It is God telling a pagan king what is coming, and Joseph names him without hesitation in a court full of other gods.

verseByVerse.quote: There will come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt, but after them there will arise seven years of famine, and all the plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt. The famine will consume the land, and the plenty will be unknown in the land by reason of the famine that will follow, for it will be very severe. And the doubling of Pharaoh's dream means that the thing is fixed by God, and God will shortly bring it about.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The interpretation is simple: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine so severe that the plenty will be forgotten. And then the reason for the doubling: "the doubling of Pharaoh's dream means that the thing is fixed by God, and God will shortly bring it about."

Fixed. Not likely, not probable — settled, and soon. Joseph has been given the future of the greatest empire on earth in a dungeon, and he states it as a certainty.

And notice what that certainty produces. It does not produce fatalism. In the very next verse he proposes doing something about it. A God who has fixed the future is precisely the reason to act, because now you know what you are acting into. Paul told a shipwrecked crew that not one life would be lost, and then told them to stay on board and eat (Acts 27:22–34).

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man, and set him over the land of Egypt. Let Pharaoh proceed to appoint overseers over the land and take one-fifth of the produce of the land of Egypt during the seven plentiful years. And let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming and store up grain under the authority of Pharaoh for food in the cities, and let them keep it. That food shall be a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine that are to occur in the land of Egypt, so that the land may not perish through the famine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nobody asked for this. "Now therefore let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man, and set him over the land of Egypt." He was called in to interpret a dream, and he goes on to propose a national policy: an appointment, a levy of one-fifth during the good years, regional storage in the cities, and a reserve for the famine.

It is competent, specific and immediately workable, and there is not a hint that he is angling for the job. He does not say let Pharaoh appoint me. He describes what is needed and stops.

Two things worth taking from it. First, hearing from God does not excuse a man from thinking. Joseph has a word from heaven and a five-point plan, and Scripture sees no tension whatever between them. Second, this is where thirteen years of running estates and prisons for other people show up. God had been training an administrator in a house and a jail, and the training was invisible until the morning it was needed.

verseByVerse.quote: This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants. And Pharaoh said to his servants, "Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?" Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has shown you all this, there is none so discerning and wise as you are. You shall be over my house, and all my people shall order themselves as you command. Only as regards the throne will I be greater than you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants. And Pharaoh said to his servants, 'Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?'"

An Egyptian king, in an Egyptian court, says that. He may mean less by it than a believer would, but he has watched the whole exchange and drawn the only conclusion available: something is in this man that his own wise men do not have.

"Since God has shown you all this, there is none so discerning and wise as you are. You shall be over my house, and all my people shall order themselves as you command. Only as regards the throne will I be greater than you."

From a cell to the second place in the kingdom, in one conversation. Nothing in Joseph's own conduct that morning was calculated to achieve it; he had declined the credit and given away the plan.

"He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes" (Ps. 113:7–8). Hannah sang it (1 Sam. 2:8), Mary sang it after her, and Genesis 41 is it happening.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt." Then Pharaoh took his signet ring from his hand and put it on Joseph's hand, and clothed him in garments of fine linen and put a gold chain about his neck. And he made him ride in his second chariot. And they called out before him, "Bow the knee!" Thus he set him over all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary: The investiture is described item by item, and every item answers something that was taken from him. The signet ring — the authority to sign in the king's name, and the same kind of object Judah had handed to a woman at a roadside (38:18). Garments of fine linen, after two garments were torn off him. A gold chain round the neck of a man who had worn irons (Ps. 105:18). The second chariot, with heralds calling "Bow the knee!" — which is what the sheaves did in a dream thirteen years ago, and his brothers are one chapter from doing it.
verseByVerse.note: “Bow the knee” renders Abrek, probably an Egyptian word that sounds like the Hebrew for “to kneel” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, and without your consent no one shall lift up hand or foot in all the land of Egypt." And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphenath-paneah. And he gave him in marriage Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On. So Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphenath-paneah. And he gave him in marriage Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On."

He is given an Egyptian name and an Egyptian wife from a priestly family of the sun-cult at On. Genesis makes no comment at all, and the silence is interesting: the sons of this marriage will become two tribes of Israel, and Ephraim will be so prominent that the northern kingdom takes his name. God's covenant family is being built, again, out of an arrangement nobody would have chosen.

Note also that the promotion is real and total, and Joseph does not become an Egyptian in the ways that matter. He names his sons in Hebrew, after what God did. He will make his brothers swear to carry his bones out (50:25). It is possible to serve at the top of a pagan system and belong entirely to God — Daniel did it in Babylon — and it is not comfortable, and Genesis does not pretend it is.

Was it right for Joseph to marry the daughter of a priest of On? It was Pharaoh’s gift to a man he had just raised from prison, and Genesis records it without comment. Joseph gave his sons names that confess God (vv. 51–52), and Jacob adopted them into Israel (48:5). God brought a covenant family out of a marriage made in Egypt; the later law against marrying outside God’s people guards a principle that Joseph’s home kept in its faith.
verseByVerse.note: On was the city of the sun god, later called Heliopolis.

verseByVerse.quote: Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh and went through all the land of Egypt. During the seven plentiful years the earth produced abundantly,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh." He was seventeen in the pit (37:2). Thirteen years: a slave, then a convict, then a forgotten convict.
