Thirty is the age at which a Levite entered full service (Num. 4:3), the age at which David became king (2 Sam. 5:4), and the age at which Jesus began his ministry (Luke 3:23). Genesis gives the number because the reader is meant to see that the waiting had a term on it.

"And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh and went through all the land of Egypt." He starts work immediately, and the work is unglamorous: seven years of surveying, requisitioning, building and accounting, in every district.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph was 17 when sold (37:2) and 30 here: thirteen years as slave and prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: and he gathered up all the food of these seven years, which occurred in the land of Egypt, and put the food in the cities. He put in every city the food from the fields around it. And Joseph stored up grain in great abundance, like the sand of the sea, until he ceased to measure it, for it could not be measured.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Joseph stored up grain in great abundance, like the sand of the sea, until he ceased to measure it." That phrase belongs to the covenant — God had promised Abraham offspring like the sand of the sea (22:17). It is used here of wheat, in a foreign country, in the hands of the son who was sold. The family that will become that innumerable people is at this moment eleven brothers and an old man, starving in Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: Before the year of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera priest of On, bore them to him. Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh. "For," he said, "God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's house." The name of the second he called Ephraim, "For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sons are born in the good years, and Joseph names them both, in Hebrew, after God.

"Manasseh. 'For,' he said, 'God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father's house.'" It cannot mean he lost the memory; he will weep over these people until he is an old man. It means the wound has stopped ruling him. There is a kind of forgetting that is not amnesia but release — the past is still there and it no longer has its hand on your throat.

"Ephraim. 'For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.'" Not fruitful after the affliction, or in spite of it — in it. Egypt is still the land of his affliction; he has not rewritten what happened to him. And in that same country God gave him a family, a name and a harvest.

Read the two names as a sentence, because that is what they are. God took the sting out of what was done to me, and God made something grow in the place where it was done. Anyone praying for either of those things is praying along the lines of Genesis 41:51–52, and both of them took thirteen years.
verseByVerse.note: Manasseh sounds like “making to forget,” Ephraim like “making fruitful” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.quote: The seven years of plenty that occurred in the land of Egypt came to an end, and the seven years of famine began to come, as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread. When all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The seven years of famine began to come, as Joseph had said. There was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread."

Everything happened exactly as the word of God through him had said it would. The dream was fixed by God and it arrived on time, and there was food in Egypt because one man had believed the warning seven years earlier and acted on it.

"Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, 'Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do.'" That is as close as the Old Testament comes to a signpost. There is bread and there is one man who has it, and the king's instruction to a starving nation is to go to him and do what he says. John's Gospel puts almost the same sentence in the mouth of a mother at a wedding: "Do whatever he tells you" (John 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: So when the famine had spread over all the land, Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold to the Egyptians, for the famine was severe in the land of Egypt. Moreover, all the earth came to Egypt to Joseph to buy grain, because the famine was severe over all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Moreover, all the earth came to Egypt to Joseph to buy grain." The nations come to the sold brother for bread. Genesis 12:3 said that in Abraham's offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed, and here it is happening in wheat — and the men who sold him are on the road, and they do not know it yet.

41.overview:
Genesis 41 is the hinge of the Joseph account and one of the great reversals in Scripture. It opens with a Hebrew slave in a dungeon whom nobody has thought about for two years, and closes with him second in the kingdom of Egypt, feeding the world. Between the two lies a single morning.

Pharaoh dreams twice and his professional interpreters fail; the cupbearer finally remembers; Joseph is shaved, dressed and stood in front of the throne, and his first recorded sentence there is “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.” He interprets the dreams, and then — unasked — proposes a national grain policy, and Pharaoh hands him the signet ring.

The chapter is careful to attribute everything to God. God sends the dream, God reveals the meaning, God has fixed the thing and will shortly bring it about, and even Pharaoh says of Joseph, “Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?” Joseph is thirty years old — thirteen years after the pit — and the two sons born to him in the good years are named for what God did with the bad ones: God has made me forget all my hardship, and God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.
41.theology:
Providence in the ordinary machinery of the world. There is no miracle in this chapter. A king sleeps badly, a servant remembers something, an administrator has a good idea, and grain is stored. God governs by dreams and by harvests, by the memory of a courtier and the failure of a guild of magicians, and every link of it lands the right man in the right office in the right year. This is the doctrine Paul states flatly: God “works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Eph. 1:11) — not merely the religious things.

Exaltation after humiliation. The shape of Joseph’s life — the pit, the false accusation, the forgotten years, and then a throne he did not seek — is the shape Scripture keeps returning to, and it reaches its true form in the one who “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death... Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Phil. 2:8–9). Joseph is not Christ; he is a preview, and the resemblance is deliberate rather than accidental.

Common grace and the good of the nations. Joseph’s administration keeps Egypt alive, and then “all the earth came to Egypt to Joseph to buy grain.” The promise that in Abraham’s offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed (12:3) is being paid out in sacks of wheat, to people who had never heard of Abraham.
41.examples:
Then: Egypt’s wealth depended on the Nile flood, and a run of poor inundations meant national famine. The seven-year storage programme Joseph proposes is plausible administration in that world, and the twenty per cent levy is a real tax rate. Pharaoh’s magicians were a professional class with dream manuals; their public failure in front of the court is the point of verse 8. An Egyptian king appointing a Semitic foreigner as vizier, giving him a new Egyptian name and a wife from the priesthood of On, is the kind of thing that happened, and it is exactly how a Hebrew household came to be settled in Goshen.

Now: Two years of silence ended in a single morning, and nothing Joseph did during those two years shortened them. That is the ordinary experience of waiting on God, and the chapter is honest about it: he was not released because he prayed harder or behaved better, but because the moment arrived. The other half is what those years produced. The teenager who announced his dreams at the family table has become a man who says “it is not in me” in front of the most powerful person on earth. Long obscurity is not wasted time; it is where God makes people who can be trusted with an answered prayer.

42.title: Joseph's Brothers Come to Egypt

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–38 — The First Journey: Recognition and Testing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jacob hears there is grain in Egypt and sends ten of his sons—keeping Benjamin—to buy food. Joseph recognizes his brothers immediately but disguises himself and speaks through an interpreter. He accuses them of being spies, tests them, demands they bring Benjamin, and keeps Simeon as surety. On the return journey the brothers discover their money has been returned in their sacks, and fear grips them. Jacob refuses to send Benjamin, and the chapter ends in grief and deadlock.
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob sends ten sons to Egypt for grain but keeps Benjamin. They bow before Joseph, who knows them and speaks roughly, accuses them of spying, holds them three days, and demands Benjamin. They confess to one another their guilt over their brother; Joseph turns away and weeps, binds Simeon, and returns their money. Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the sheaves bow as the dream said (37:7). Now: a wrong never named does not decay; it waits, and "all this has come against me" can be said in the very week God is assembling the rescue.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jacob learned that there was grain for sale in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why do you look at one another?" And he said, "Behold, I have heard that there is grain for sale in Egypt. Go down and buy grain for us there, that we may live and not die." So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt. But Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph's brother, with his brothers, for he feared that harm might happen to him. Thus the sons of Israel came to buy among the others who came, for the famine was in the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Jacob learned that there was grain for sale in Egypt, he said to his sons, 'Why do you look at one another?'" There is a whole household in that question. Ten grown men sitting in a famine, looking at each other, and the old man has to tell them to move.

"Go down and buy grain for us there, that we may live and not die." The stakes are stated plainly. This is not a trading trip; the family of the covenant is starving in the land of promise.

"But Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph's brother, with his brothers, for he feared that harm might happen to him." Twenty-two years on, the favouritism is untouched. Benjamin is the surviving son of Rachel and he is kept at home while ten sons go into danger — and the text says "Joseph's brother," as though the other ten were not.

The wound the coat opened has never healed, and it is about to be operated on.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joseph was governor over the land. He was the one who sold to all the people of the land. And Joseph's brothers came and bowed themselves before him with their faces to the ground. Joseph saw his brothers and recognized them, but he treated them like strangers and spoke roughly to them. "Where do you come from?" he said. They said, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food." And Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Now Joseph was governor over the land... And Joseph's brothers came and bowed themselves before him with their faces to the ground."

There it is. "Behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf" (37:7). Twenty-two years, a pit, a slave market, a false accusation and a prison, and the dream comes true exactly as it was given — with the dreamer himself so changed that his own family cannot pick him out.

"Joseph saw his brothers and recognized them, but he treated them like strangers and spoke roughly to them." He knows them at once. They were grown men when he last saw them and he was a boy; he is now clean-shaven, in Egyptian dress, speaking Egyptian through an interpreter, and thirty-nine years old.

Why the roughness? Not revenge — he had absolute power and could have had them executed in an afternoon. What follows is a designed test, and its object is Benjamin: he needs to know whether the men who sold one of Rachel's sons will do it again to the other. Everything hard in this chapter is aimed at that question.
verseByVerse.note: The brothers bow — Joseph’s dreams come true.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph remembered the dreams that he had dreamed of them. And he said to them, "You are spies; you have come to see the nakedness of the land." They said to him, "No, my lord, your servants have come to buy food. We are all sons of one man. We are honest men. Your servants have never been spies." He said to them, "No, it is the nakedness of the land that you have come to see." And they said, "We, your servants, are twelve brothers, the sons of one man in the land of Canaan, and behold, the youngest is this day with our father, and one is no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And Joseph remembered the dreams that he had dreamed of them." He is standing in the fulfilment. And what he does with the memory is not gloat but act: the dreams told him this family had a future, and he sets about securing it.

"You are spies; you have come to see the nakedness of the land." It is a plausible charge on Egypt's eastern frontier, and it forces them to explain themselves.

Which is exactly what he wants. "We are all sons of one man. We are honest men." They say it twice in this chapter, and the reader knows what they did and what they have been telling their father for twenty-two years.

Then, defending themselves, they volunteer the information he was fishing for: "We, your servants, are twelve brothers... the youngest is this day with our father, and one is no more."

One is no more. It is the sentence they have used at home for two decades, and they say it to his face. He is standing in front of them. Guilty men have a prepared form of words, and they produce it without thinking.

Was Joseph right to deceive his brothers? His purpose was to find out whether they had changed, and the test ends in repentance and reconciliation. Scripture records his methods without approving every detail, and they are no licence to lie (Eph 4:25). The test was the work of a man with the power to punish and the will to forgive.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joseph said to them, "It is as I said to you. You are spies. By this you shall be tested: by the life of Pharaoh, you shall not go from this place unless your youngest brother comes here. Send one of you, and let him bring your brother, while you remain confined, that your words may be tested, whether there is truth in you. Or else, by the life of Pharaoh, surely you are spies." And he put them all together in custody for three days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"By this you shall be tested: by the life of Pharaoh, you shall not go from this place unless your youngest brother comes here."

The oath by Pharaoh's life is an Egyptian formula, and Joseph is playing the part completely. He proposes that one go and nine stay; then, three days later, he reverses it — one stays and nine go. He is not being erratic. He is applying pressure and then relieving it, which is how a wall comes down.

"And he put them all together in custody for three days."

Three days in an Egyptian cell, with nothing to do. Joseph knows exactly what that is worth, because he spent years in one. He is not doing to them what was done to him out of spite; he is giving them the one thing that had made him what he now is — enforced time with nothing to think about but the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day Joseph said to them, "Do this and you will live, for I fear God: if you are honest men, let one of your brothers remain confined where you are in custody, and let the rest go and carry grain for the famine of your households, and bring your youngest brother to me. So your words will be verified, and you shall not die." And they did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"On the third day Joseph said to them, 'Do this and you will live, for I fear God.'"

He says it to reassure them: whatever kind of official I am, I am not arbitrary, because I answer to somebody. Egyptian officials did not usually introduce themselves that way, and it is the first crack of light he gives them.

And he softens the terms considerably. Instead of nine men rotting in prison while one travels, nine go home with grain for starving households and one stays. Their families eat either way.

"So your words will be verified, and you shall not die." The test remains and the cruelty has gone out of the arrangement. Joseph is capable of severity and he never once takes more than the test requires.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said to one another, "In truth we are guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us." And Reuben answered them, "Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy? But you did not listen. So now there comes a reckoning for his blood."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now the chapter's real event, and it happens because of a delay in a cell.

"Then they said to one another, 'In truth we are guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the distress of his soul, when he begged us and we did not listen. That is why this distress has come upon us.'"

Twenty-two years and this is the first time it is said out loud. And notice what surfaces: not the selling, not the money, but the distress of his soul, when he begged us. That is new information for the reader — chapter 37 never told us that Joseph pleaded from the bottom of the cistern while they ate. They have been carrying the sound of it.

Nothing has been mentioned to them about Joseph. Nobody has accused them of anything. A hard week in a foreign country has gone straight to the one thing they have never named, and they connect the two immediately: that is why this distress has come upon us.

"And Reuben answered them, 'Did I not tell you not to sin against the boy?'" The eldest cannot resist it. He is right, and he did say so, and he also went away and let it happen. Being able to say I told you so is not the same as having done anything, and Reuben has spent his life just short of the line.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not know that Joseph understood them, for there was an interpreter between them. Then he turned away from them and wept. And he returned to them and spoke to them. And he took Simeon from them and bound him before their eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They did not know that Joseph understood them, for there was an interpreter between them."

He has been listening to every word. They have confessed their crime in front of the very man they wronged, in a language they assumed he could not follow, because an interpreter stood between them.

"Then he turned away from them and wept."

It is the first of seven times Joseph weeps in this account, and it comes at the moment he hears them own it. He does not weep at the sight of them, nor at the memory of the pit. He weeps when he discovers that they are not what they were.

"And he returned to them and spoke to them. And he took Simeon from them and bound him before their eyes." He dries his face and carries on with the test. Simeon is the second son — Reuben, who tried to save him, is not the one chosen — and Simeon is one of the two who massacred Shechem. The choice is unlikely to be random.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, and to replace every man's money in his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey. This was done for them. Then they loaded their donkeys with their grain and departed. And as one of them opened his sack to give his donkey fodder at the lodging place, he saw his money in the mouth of his sack. He said to his brothers, "My money has been put back; here it is in the mouth of my sack!" At this their hearts failed them, and they turned trembling to one another, saying, "What is this that God has done to us?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, and to replace every man's money in his sack, and to give them provisions for the journey."

He will not take their money. It is a kindness, done in secret, and it is about to terrify them out of their wits.

"He said to his brothers, 'My money has been put back; here it is in the mouth of my sack!' At this their hearts failed them, and they turned trembling to one another, saying, 'What is this that God has done to us?'"

A gift lands as a judgment. They are men who once sold a brother for silver, and now silver keeps appearing where it should not be, and every unexplained thing looks like the hand of God coming for them.

That is what a guilty conscience does. It reads the world as a series of summonses. The same grace looks entirely different depending on what a man is carrying — and, as it happens, they are right that God is in it, and wrong about what he is doing.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to Jacob their father in the land of Canaan, they told him all that had happened to them, saying, "The man, the lord of the land, spoke roughly to us and took us to be spies of the land. But we said to him, 'We are honest men; we have never been spies. We are twelve brothers, sons of our father. One is no more, and the youngest is this day with our father in the land of Canaan.' Then the man, the lord of the land, said to us, 'By this I shall know that you are honest men: leave one of your brothers with me, and take grain for the famine of your households, and go your way. Bring your youngest brother to me. Then I shall know that you are not spies but honest men, and I will deliver your brother to you, and you shall trade in the land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They report to Jacob, and the account they give is largely accurate — and they make two small adjustments. They leave out the three days in custody. And where the man had said "that your words may be tested, whether there is truth in you," they report him as saying, "then I shall know that you are not spies but honest men."

They also add a line he never spoke: "and you shall trade in the land." They are selling the arrangement to their father, and they smooth the edges.

It is a small thing and it is very human. Men who have just confessed to one another in a cell go home and manage the story for the old man. Confession in private is a long way from honesty in the family, and this household still has two chapters to go.

verseByVerse.quote: As they emptied their sacks, behold, every man's bundle of money was in his sack. And when they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid. And Jacob their father said to them, "You have bereaved me of my children: Joseph is no more, and Simeon is no more, and now you would take Benjamin. All this has come against me." Then Reuben said to his father, "Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. Put him in my hands, and I will bring him back to you." But he said, "My son shall not go down with you, for his brother is dead, and he is the only one left. If harm should happen to him on the journey that you are to make, you would bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to Sheol."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As they emptied their sacks, behold, every man's bundle of money was in his sack. And when they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were afraid." Every sack, not just one. Whatever they had told themselves on the road about a clerk's mistake is finished.

"And Jacob their father said to them, 'You have bereaved me of my children: Joseph is no more, and Simeon is no more, and now you would take Benjamin. All this has come against me.'"

He is wrong on every count and he cannot possibly know it. Joseph is alive and governing Egypt. Simeon is safe and will be released within the year. Benjamin will come back. And "all this has come against me" is the exact opposite of the truth — this is God assembling the rescue of the entire family, and it is at this moment that the old man concludes God is against him.

Read that if you are in a season where the evidence is all one way. Jacob's assessment was reasonable, honest, and completely false, and there was no way for him to know it from where he sat. Later he will say it himself: "God Almighty grant you mercy" (43:14), and later still, "God has been my shepherd all my life long" (48:15).

"Then Reuben said to his father, 'Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you.'" It is a grotesque offer — Jacob's own grandsons — and it shows how badly Reuben wants to be the man who fixes something. Jacob does not even answer it. Compare Judah in the next chapter, who offers himself (43:9), and notice which offer the old man accepts.

"My son shall not go down with you, for his brother is dead, and he is the only one left." The only one left. Ten of his sons are standing in front of him as he says it.

42.overview:
Twenty-two years after the pit, ten men bow to the face of the brother they sold, and do not know him. Genesis 42 is the beginning of the longest and most carefully managed reconciliation in Scripture, and Joseph does not rush it.

He recognises them instantly; they do not recognise him. He speaks roughly, accuses them of spying, imprisons them for three days, and then requires that Benjamin be brought — the one thing that will force the household to confront what it did. His conduct looks cruel and is not: he is testing whether these are still the men who could sell a brother and eat their lunch, and the proof comes in verse 21, when they say to one another, “In truth we are guilty concerning our brother.” They have carried it for twenty-two years, and they say it in front of a man they think cannot understand a word.

He turns away and weeps — the first of seven times he weeps in the account — then binds Simeon, fills their sacks, and secretly returns their money. The chapter ends in Canaan with an old man refusing to let Benjamin go and concluding that everything is against him, at the precise moment everything has begun to turn.
42.theology:
The difference between remorse and repentance. The brothers have been miserable about Joseph for two decades, and misery is not repentance. What Joseph is looking for is not regret but change: whether men who once sacrificed a favoured younger son will now do it again when the same choice is put in front of them. Chapter 44 will give the answer. Genesis is showing us that God’s dealings with his people aim at something deeper than feeling bad.

Providence and conscience. “What is this that God has done to us?” The brothers read the returned silver as judgment, and the narrator lets it stand: God does use circumstances to press on a guilty conscience. The money in the sack was Joseph’s kindness and it landed as terror, because guilt turns every unexplained event into a summons.

Severity in the service of love. Joseph is not punishing his brothers; every hard thing he does is calculated to bring them to the point where the family can be whole. Scripture says the same of God’s discipline: it is not pleasant at the time, and it is “for our good, that we may share his holiness” (Heb. 12:10–11). Love that never makes anyone uncomfortable is not the love the Bible describes.
42.examples:
Then: Egypt kept grain reserves and sold to foreigners, and frontier officials genuinely did screen Semitic groups arriving from Canaan — the eastern delta was Egypt’s vulnerable border, and “the nakedness of the land” is the language of a real security concern. Interpreters were standard in official dealings, which is why the brothers spoke freely in Hebrew in front of the vizier. Bowing to the ground before an Egyptian official was ordinary protocol, and the brothers would have thought nothing of it. The reader knows they are fulfilling a dream.

Now: Twenty-two years of a buried secret, and one hard week brings it straight to the surface, in the same words the men had been avoiding since the afternoon they sat down to eat. Nothing is settled by time. A wrong that has never been named does not decay; it waits, and it surfaces the moment pressure is applied. And the chapter ends with Jacob saying “all this has come against me” while God is in fact assembling the rescue of his whole family — which is what almost every believer’s worst week looks like from the inside.

43.title: The Second Journey to Egypt

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–34 — Judah’s Pledge and the Feast with Joseph
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The famine worsens until Jacob has no choice. Judah steps forward with a personal guarantee for Benjamin’s safety—unlike Reuben’s foolish offer, this is genuine surety. Jacob relents, sends gifts and double money, and the brothers return to Egypt with Benjamin. Joseph sees Benjamin and is overwhelmed; he weeps in private. He hosts them at a great feast, assigns Benjamin the largest portion, and the brothers are bewildered. They do not yet know who Joseph is.
verseByVerse.theology: When the grain runs out, Judah pledges himself for Benjamin, and Jacob lets him go: "May God Almighty grant you mercy." In Joseph's house the steward tells the frightened brothers their God put treasure in their sacks, and releases Simeon. Joseph sees Benjamin and weeps in private, then seats them in birth order and gives Benjamin five times as much.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the man who sold a brother offers himself as surety for one. Now: grace often has to be explained before it is recognised as grace, and people do change.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the famine was severe in the land. And when they had eaten the grain that they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, "Go again, buy us a little food." But Judah said to him, "The man solemnly warned us, saying, 'You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.' If you will send our brother with us, we will go down and buy you food. But if you will not send him, we will not go down, for the man said to us, 'You shall not see my face, unless your brother is with you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Now the famine was severe in the land. And when they had eaten the grain that they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them, 'Go again, buy us a little food.'"

Nothing in this family moves until the food runs out. Jacob has spent however many months refusing to send Benjamin, and the refusal holds right up to the last sack. Then: go again, as though the difficulty had never been mentioned.

"A little food" — as if a small purchase might not require the full terms. People negotiate with an unavoidable obedience by trying to do a smaller version of it.

"But Judah said to him, 'The man solemnly warned us... You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you.'" he says it twice in three verses, and he will not be moved: the trip does not happen without Benjamin. Somebody in this household has finally stopped managing the old man.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel said, "Why did you treat me so badly as to tell the man that you had another brother?" They replied, "The man questioned us carefully about ourselves and our kindred, saying, 'Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?' What we told him was in answer to these questions. Could we in any way know that he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?" And Judah said to Israel his father, "Send the boy with me, and we will arise and go, that we may live and not die, both we and you and also our little ones. I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever. If we had not delayed, we would now have returned twice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Israel said, 'Why did you treat me so badly as to tell the man that you had another brother?'" It is an old man's complaint and it is unfair, and the sons answer it patiently: he questioned us carefully, we answered his questions, and how could we have known.

Then Judah steps forward, and this is the sentence the whole Joseph narrative has been waiting for.

"Send the boy with me, and we will arise and go, that we may live and not die, both we and you and also our little ones. I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever."

This is the man who said, "What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood? Come, let us sell him" (37:26–27). He is now offering to stand personally liable for the life of Rachel's other son — the favoured one, the one their father loves best, the same position Joseph occupied when Judah proposed the sale.

He does not offer his children, as Reuben did (42:37). He offers himself. Jacob accepts this and refused that, and the difference is the difference between a man who wants to look responsible and a man who is.

"If we had not delayed, we would now have returned twice." Judah is doing the arithmetic of a wasted season, and it is a fair rebuke. Fear had cost this family months of food.

verseByVerse.quote: Then their father Israel said to them, "If it must be so, then do this: take some of the choice fruits of the land in your bags, and carry a present down to the man, a little balm and a little honey, gum, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds. Take double the money with you. Carry back with you the money that was returned in the mouth of your sacks. Perhaps it was an oversight. Take also your brother, and arise, go again to the man. May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, and may he send back your other brother and Benjamin. And as for me, if I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jacob gives in, and he cannot help managing it: a present of balm, honey, gum, myrrh, pistachios and almonds — the luxuries of Canaan — and double the money, and the returned silver carried back, "perhaps it was an oversight."

The list is worth a second look. Balm and gum and myrrh are exactly what the Ishmaelite caravan was carrying when it took Joseph down to Egypt (37:25). The same goods are going down the same road, this time as a gift to the man they sold.

"May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man." El Shaddai — the name God used when the promise had become physically impossible (17:1). Jacob has run out of arrangements, and the man who has spent his whole life on schemes finally has nothing to do but pray.

"And as for me, if I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved."

It is not a cheerful sentence and it is a real surrender. He is not saying it will be fine; he is saying he has stopped trying to hold what he cannot hold. Esther would say the same thing in the same shape — "if I perish, I perish" (Esth. 4:16). Faith at its lowest ebb is often just this: letting go of what your grip was never going to save anyway.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” is El Shaddai (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So the men took this present, and they took double the money with them, and Benjamin. They arose and went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph. When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, "Bring the men into the house, and slaughter an animal and make ready, for the men are to dine with me at noon." The man did as Joseph told him and brought the men to Joseph's house. And the men were afraid because they were brought to Joseph's house, and they said, "It is because of the money, which was replaced in our sacks the first time, that we are brought in, so that he may assault us and fall upon us to make us servants and seize our donkeys."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They arose and went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph. When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, 'Bring the men into the house... for the men are to dine with me at noon.'"

He sees his brother — his only full brother, whom he last saw as a small child — and he says nothing to him. He gives an order about lunch. The self-control in this chapter is extraordinary and it is costing him.

"And the men were afraid because they were brought to Joseph's house." Being invited into a great man's house should be an honour; they read it as an ambush. "It is because of the money... so that he may assault us and fall upon us to make us servants and seize our donkeys."

They have worked out the worst possible interpretation of an act of hospitality in the time it takes to walk across a courtyard. Guilt does not merely accuse; it predicts. Men who once made another man a slave assume instantly that they are about to be made slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: So they went up to the steward of Joseph's house and spoke with him at the door of the house, and said, "Oh, my lord, we came down the first time to buy food. And when we came to the lodging place we opened our sacks, and there was each man's money in the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight. So we have brought it again with us, and we have brought other money down with us to buy food. We do not know who put our money in our sacks." He replied, "Peace to you, do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your money." Then he brought Simeon out to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They corner the steward at the door before they are even inside, and blurt out the whole story of the money — "our money in full weight. So we have brought it again with us... We do not know who put our money in our sacks."

It is the honest confession of frightened men, and it is the first time these brothers have volunteered an awkward truth to anybody rather than concealing it. The habit of twenty-two years is breaking.

"He replied, 'Peace to you, do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your money.'"

An Egyptian house-steward tells the sons of Jacob that their own God has given them a gift. He is repeating what his master told him to say — but what he says is exactly true, and truer than he knows.

Their money was in their sacks and it terrified them for weeks. It had been put there by the brother they had wronged, out of kindness, and no amount of staring at it would ever have told them so. Somebody had to say it. That is why grace has to be preached: a gift can sit in a man's hands for a month and be taken for a summons until somebody explains it to him.

"Then he brought Simeon out to them." Alive, unharmed, released without condition. The thing they had dreaded all the way from Canaan simply dissolves.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the man had brought the men into Joseph's house and given them water, and they had washed their feet, and when he had given their donkeys fodder, they prepared the present for Joseph's coming at noon, for they heard that they should eat bread there. When Joseph came home, they brought into the house to him the present that they had with them and bowed down to him to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Water for their feet, fodder for their donkeys, and time to prepare the present. They are being treated as honoured guests by a household they expected to be enslaved by.

"When Joseph came home, they brought into the house to him the present that they had with them and bowed down to him to the ground."

The second bowing, and this time all eleven are there. The dream of the sun, moon and eleven stars (37:9) is being filled in piece by piece, and the men completing it have no idea what they are doing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he inquired about their welfare and said, "Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he still alive?" They said, "Your servant our father is well; he is still alive." And they bowed their heads and prostrated themselves. And he lifted up his eyes and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother's son, and said, "Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me? God be gracious to you, my son!" Then Joseph hurried out, for his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep. And he entered his chamber and wept there. Then he washed his face and came out. And controlling himself he said, "Serve the food."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And he inquired about their welfare and said, 'Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he still alive?'"

That is the question he has been waiting twenty-two years to ask, and he has to ask it in the third person, through an interpreter, as a piece of small talk. He calls him "the old man of whom you spoke" because he cannot say my father.

"And he lifted up his eyes and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother's son, and said, 'Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me? God be gracious to you, my son!'"

The narrator supplies the phrase the brothers cannot hear: his mother's son. The only other child of Rachel, who died giving birth to him, in a family where these two were always the outsiders.

"Then Joseph hurried out, for his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep. And he entered his chamber and wept there."

He runs out of his own dining room to cry where nobody can see, and then "washed his face and came out. And controlling himself he said, 'Serve the food.'"

Every instinct in him wants to tell them who he is, and he will not do it yet, because the test is not finished and the family is not ready. Love that can wait, at cost, for the good of the person it loves, is a harder thing than love that speaks — and it is what God has been doing with this household for two decades.

verseByVerse.quote: They served him by himself, and them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because the Egyptians could not eat with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians. And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth. And the men looked at one another in amazement. Portions were taken to them from Joseph's table, but Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs. And they drank and were merry with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three tables: Joseph alone, the Egyptians apart, the Hebrews apart, "for that is an abomination to the Egyptians." The Egyptians would not eat with Asiatics. The most powerful man in Egypt after Pharaoh is eating on his own, unable to sit with his own people or with his adopted one.

"And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth. And the men looked at one another in amazement."

Eleven men seated in exact birth order, by an Egyptian who has never met them. The odds against guessing it are astronomical and they know it. Something is happening in this house that they cannot account for, and Genesis simply records their bewilderment.

"But Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs."

That is the test, and it is beautifully constructed. Here is Rachel's son again, openly favoured at the table in front of the other ten, exactly as a boy in a coloured coat once was. If the old jealousy is still in them, this is where it will show.

"And they drank and were merry with him." Nothing. Not a word, not a look. Twenty-two years ago they could not speak peaceably to a favoured brother (37:4); now they watch one given five times their share and enjoy the afternoon.
verseByVerse.note: Egyptians would not eat with foreigners. Benjamin’s fivefold portion tests whether the brothers will resent a favoured son again.

Do you have another brother?' What we told him was in answer to these questions. Could we in any way know that he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?"<sup>8</sup>And Judah said to Israel his father, "Send the boy with me, and we will arise and go, that we may live and not die, both we and you and also our little ones.<sup>9</sup>I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever.<sup>10</sup>If we had not delayed, we would now have returned twice."<sup>11</sup>Then their father Israel said to them, "If it must be so, then do this: take some of the choice fruits of the land in your bags, and carry a present down to the man, a little balm and a little honey, gum, myrrh, pistachio nuts, and almonds.<sup>12</sup>Take double the money with you. Carry back with you the money that was returned in the mouth of your sacks. Perhaps it was an oversight.<sup>13</sup>Take also your brother, and arise, go again to the man.<sup>14</sup>May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, and may he send back your other brother and Benjamin. And as for me, if I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved."<sup>15</sup>So the men took this present, and they took double the money with them, and Benjamin. They arose and went down to Egypt and stood before Joseph.<sup>16</sup>When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, "Bring the men into the house, and slaughter an animal and make ready, for the men are to dine with me at noon."<sup>17</sup>The man did as Joseph told him and brought the men to Joseph's house.<sup>18</sup>And the men were afraid because they were brought to Joseph's house, and they said, "It is because of the money, which was replaced in our sacks the first time, that we are brought in, so that he may assault us and fall upon us to make us servants and seize our donkeys."<sup>19</sup>So they went up to the steward of Joseph's house and spoke with him at the door of the house,<sup>20</sup>and said, "Oh, my lord, we came down the first time to buy food.<sup>21</sup>And when we came to the lodging place we opened our sacks, and there was each man's money in the mouth of his sack, our money in full weight. So we have brought it again with us,<sup>22</sup>and we have brought other money down with us to buy food. We do not know who put our money in our sacks."<sup>23</sup>He replied, "Peace to you, do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you. I received your money." Then he brought Simeon out to them.<sup>24</sup>And when the man had brought the men into Joseph's house and given them water, and they had washed their feet, and when he had given their donkeys fodder,<sup>25</sup>they prepared the present for Joseph's coming at noon, for they heard that they should eat bread there.<sup>26</sup>When Joseph came home, they brought into the house to him the present that they had with them and bowed down to him to the ground.<sup>27</sup>And he inquired about their welfare and said, "Is your father well, the old man of whom you spoke? Is he still alive?"<sup>28</sup>They said, "Your servant our father is well; he is still alive." And they bowed their heads and prostrated themselves.<sup>29</sup>And he lifted up his eyes and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother's son, and said, "Is this your youngest brother, of whom you spoke to me? God be gracious to you, my son!"<sup>30</sup>Then Joseph hurried out, for his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep. And he entered his chamber and wept there.<sup>31</sup>Then he washed his face and came out. And controlling himself he said, "Serve the food."<sup>32</sup>They served him by himself, and them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because the Egyptians could not eat with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to the Egyptians.<sup>33</sup>And they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his youth. And the men looked at one another in amazement.<sup>34</sup>Portions were taken to them from Joseph's table, but Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs. And they drank and were merry with him.
43.overview:
The grain runs out, and the family has to face the thing it has been avoiding. Genesis 43 is the chapter in which Judah steps forward — the man who proposed selling Joseph for silver offers himself as surety for Benjamin — and Jacob, at the end of his resources, finally lets the boy go with words that are half despair and half faith: “May God Almighty grant you mercy... and as for me, if I am bereaved of my children, I am bereaved.”

In Egypt the brothers are brought into Joseph’s own house and are terrified, certain that the returned silver is about to be used against them. Instead a steward tells them, “Peace to you, do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks for you” — and Simeon is brought out.

Then a meal. Joseph asks after his father, sees Benjamin and has to leave the room to weep, washes his face, comes back and says “Serve the food.” The brothers are seated in exact birth order by a man who cannot possibly know it, and Benjamin is given five times as much as anyone else. The last test is being laid, and they eat and drink and are merry with him.
43.theology:
Substitution. Judah’s “I will be a pledge of his safety... let me bear the blame forever” is the turning point of his life and the theological centre of the Joseph story. The man who sold a brother now offers to be answerable for one, and in chapter 44 he will offer to take his place outright. The tribe of Judah produced David, and out of David came the one who did not merely offer to bear the blame.

Kindness recognised as grace, by a stranger. The steward tells the brothers that their God put treasure in their sacks. An Egyptian servant, briefed by Joseph, hands them a piece of theology they cannot yet receive: the money they are terrified of is a gift. That is exactly what a guilty conscience does with grace, and why it takes revelation to see a gift as a gift.

God Almighty at the end of a man’s resources. Jacob uses the name El Shaddai — the name God took when the promise had become impossible (17:1) — at the moment he has run out of ways to protect his family. His last sentence, “if I am bereaved, I am bereaved,” is the same shape as Esther’s “if I perish, I perish” (Esth. 4:16): not fatalism, but a man letting go of what he cannot hold and putting it in God’s hands.
43.examples:
Then: The gifts Jacob sends — balm, honey, gum, myrrh, pistachios and almonds — are luxuries Egypt did not produce, and three of them (balm, gum and myrrh) are the very goods the caravan was carrying when Joseph was sold (37:25). A hospitality meal in a great man’s house obliged the host to protect his guests, which is why the brothers are relieved rather than reassured to be brought there. And Egyptians did keep strict table separation from Asiatics, so the three-table arrangement in verse 32 is exact reporting rather than awkwardness on Joseph’s part.

Now: Nothing moves in this family until the food runs out. Jacob would have gone on refusing indefinitely if hunger had not made refusing impossible, and God is not above using an empty cupboard to move people who will not be moved by argument. The other half of the chapter is Judah: twenty-two years after the worst thing he ever did, he is the one who steps forward and puts himself on the line for the very son whose favoured status he had once resented in another boy. People do change, and it takes about that long.

44.title: Judah's Plea for Benjamin

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–34 — The Silver Cup and Judah’s Substitution
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joseph engineers a final, decisive test: his silver cup is secretly placed in Benjamin’s sack. The brothers depart joyfully but are quickly overtaken, the cup discovered, and all return to Joseph in despair. Before Joseph, Judah—the one who sold Joseph—now delivers one of the most moving speeches in all Scripture, offering himself as a slave in Benjamin’s place. This is the moment that breaks Joseph.
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph has his silver cup put in Benjamin's sack. The steward overtakes the brothers; the cup is found, and every man tears his clothes and goes back. Judah says God has found out their guilt, and when Joseph offers to keep only Benjamin, Judah tells the whole story from his father's side and asks to remain as a slave instead of the boy.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the brothers face the same choice as twenty-two years before, and refuse it. Now: repentance is proved when the old sin is offered again and not taken, and Judah's substitution is a small true copy of the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev. 5:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he commanded the steward of his house, "Fill the men's sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and put each man's money in the mouth of his sack, and put my cup, the silver cup, in the mouth of the sack of the youngest, with his money for the grain." And he did as Joseph told him. As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away with their donkeys. They had gone only a short distance from the city. Now Joseph said to his steward, "Up, follow after the men, and when you overtake them, say to them, 'Why have you repaid evil for good? Is it not from this that my lord drinks, and by this that he practices divination? You have done evil in doing this.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph sets the trap with great care: every man's money back in his sack again, and "my cup, the silver cup, in the mouth of the sack of the youngest." Then a night's sleep, a dawn departure, and a short distance before the pursuit.

"Why have you repaid evil for good?" — the steward's opening line, which is a question the brothers have never in their lives been able to answer honestly.

"Is it not from this that my lord drinks, and by this that he practices divination?" Joseph has his steward say it, and says it himself in verse 15. Egyptian officials did practise liquid divination, and he is keeping up the character to the last hour. He is not actually reading omens — the man who told Pharaoh "it is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer" (41:16) is not consulting a cup — but the brothers must believe he is, or the test collapses.

The whole thing is theatre, and the object of it is one question: what will these men do when Rachel's last son can be left behind at no cost to themselves?
verseByVerse.note: Diviners read omens in liquid poured into a cup.

verseByVerse.quote: When he overtook them, he spoke to them these words. They said to him, "Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing! Behold, the money that we found in the mouths of our sacks we brought back to you from the land of Canaan. How then could we steal silver or gold from your lord's house? Whichever of your servants is found with it shall die, and we also will be my lord's servants." He said, "Let it be as you say: he who is found with it shall be my servant, and the rest of you shall be innocent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their protest is genuine and it is confident: "Behold, the money that we found in the mouths of our sacks we brought back to you... How then could we steal silver or gold from your lord's house?" They have a good record to point to, which is a new experience for them.

And then they overreach, as innocent men often do: "Whichever of your servants is found with it shall die, and we also will be my lord's servants." It is the rashness of men who are certain — and it is also, uncomfortably, the shape of Jacob's oath about the household gods (31:32), which nearly cost Rachel her life.

The steward quietly reduces it: "he who is found with it shall be my servant, and the rest of you shall be innocent." That is the offer. One man stays, ten go home free and blameless.

verseByVerse.quote: Then each man quickly lowered his sack to the ground, and each man opened his sack. And he searched, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest. And the cup was found in Benjamin's sack. Then they tore their clothes, and every man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And he searched, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest." Slowly, in order, drawing it out — ten sacks of relief and then the eleventh. "And the cup was found in Benjamin's sack."

"Then they tore their clothes, and every man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city."

There is the answer, and it takes one verse. They were free to go. The official had said so, the guilty party was identified, and the road home was open. Not one of them takes it. Twenty-two years ago these men watched Rachel's son taken away and went home with a story; today they turn the donkeys round and go back with him.

verseByVerse.quote: When Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house, he was still there. They fell before him to the ground. Joseph said to them, "What deed is this that you have done? Do you not know that a man like me can indeed practice divination?" And Judah said, "What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak? Or how can we clear ourselves? God has found out the guilt of your servants; behold, we are my lord's servants, both we and he also in whose hand the cup has been found." But he said, "Far be it from me that I should do so! Only the man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my servant. But as for you, go up in peace to your father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house, he was still there. They fell before him to the ground." The third bowing, and the deepest.

"And Judah said, 'What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak? Or how can we clear ourselves? God has found out the guilt of your servants.'"

He does not deny the theft and he does not defend it, because he is not talking about a cup. They are innocent of this and he knows it, and he makes no attempt to argue — he says instead that God has found them out, and every man in that room knows what he means.

"Behold, we are my lord's servants, both we and he also in whose hand the cup has been found." He offers the whole eleven. He will not let Benjamin stand alone.

"But he said, 'Far be it from me that I should do so! Only the man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my servant. But as for you, go up in peace to your father.'"

Joseph closes the door on the group solution and puts the exact choice back in front of them. Go home to your father, in peace, without the boy. It is what they did last time, and he offers it in so many words.

Did Joseph practise divination, which the law forbids (Deut 18:10–12)? He is playing the Egyptian lord. The man who told Pharaoh that interpretation belongs to God (41:16) is saying what such a lord would say, to press his brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judah went up to him and said, "Oh, my lord, please let your servant speak a word in my lord's ears, and let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself. My lord asked his servants, saying, 'Have you a father, or a brother?' And we said to my lord, 'We have a father, an old man, and a young brother, the child of his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother's children, and his father loves him.' Then you said to your servants, 'Bring him down to me, that I may set my eyes on him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Judah went up to him." What follows is one of the longest speeches in Genesis, and there is not a word of theology in it, and it is the finest thing anyone says in the book.

He begins with total deference — "let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself" — and then simply tells the story from the beginning, quoting both sides of every exchange.

verseByVerse.quote: We said to my lord, 'The boy cannot leave his father, for if he should leave his father, his father would die.' Then you said to your servants, 'Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you shall not see my face again.' "When we went back to your servant my father, we told him the words of my lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And listen to what he repeats without flinching: "We have a father, an old man, and a young brother, the child of his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother's children, and his father loves him."

Judah says out loud, to a stranger, that his father loves this one son more than the rest of them. Twenty-two years ago that fact was unbearable and produced a murder plot. He now states it as a plain circumstance, without resentment, as part of the case for saving the boy. The jealousy is gone, and that is the whole distance the family has travelled.

verseByVerse.quote: And when our father said, 'Go again, buy us a little food,' we said, 'We cannot go down. If our youngest brother goes with us, then we will go down. For we cannot see the man's face unless our youngest brother is with us.' Then your servant my father said to us, 'You know that my wife bore me two sons. One left me, and I said, "Surely he has been torn to pieces," and I have never seen him since. If you take this one also from me, and harm happens to him, you will bring down my gray hairs in evil to Sheol.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
He goes on quoting his father, and now he quotes the sentence that must be hardest of all for these ten men to repeat.

"Then your servant my father said to us, 'You know that my wife bore me two sons. One left me, and I said, "Surely he has been torn to pieces," and I have never seen him since. If you take this one also from me, and harm happens to him, you will bring down my gray hairs in evil to Sheol.'"

My wife. Jacob had four women bear him children and he means Rachel, and Judah — a son of Leah — repeats it to an Egyptian official without a flicker. He is not defending his mother's standing or his own. He is trying to save a boy.

And "surely he has been torn to pieces" is the exact conclusion the brothers engineered with a goat and a coat (37:33). Judah quotes his father's grief, which he manufactured, to a man he does not know is the cause of it, in order to prevent a second one.

Whatever else has happened to Judah in twenty-two years, he has learned to see the thing from his father's side. That is generally the last stage of repentance and the hardest: not being sorry about what you did, but understanding what it did to somebody else.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, as soon as I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us, then, as his life is bound up in the boy's life, as soon as he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die, and your servants will bring down the gray hairs of your servant our father with sorrow to Sheol. For your servant became a pledge of safety for the boy to my father, saying, 'If I do not bring him back to you, then I shall bear the blame before my father all my life.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the plea itself, and every line of it is about the old man.

"As his life is bound up in the boy's life, as soon as he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die." Judah has watched his father grieve for twenty-two years and he knows exactly what a second loss would do.

"For your servant became a pledge of safety for the boy to my father." He is holding himself to the promise he made in 43:9, in a foreign court, where nobody could enforce it and nobody would ever know.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers. For how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? I fear to see the evil that would find my father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Now therefore, please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers."

There it is. The man who said "come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites" (37:27) offers to be sold himself so that Rachel's other son can go home. He is innocent of the charge; he offers to take the penalty; he does it so that a father will not be destroyed. It is substitution, offered voluntarily by a guilty man who has stopped being that man.

"For how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? I fear to see the evil that would find my father." He cannot face it. Not the loss of the boy — the sight of the old man's face.

Out of this tribe would come David, and out of David the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev. 5:5), who also stood in front of a judge, innocent, and said nothing in his own defence, and took the place of people who were guilty so that a Father would not lose his children. Judah's speech is a small, true copy of it, made in Egypt by a shepherd, four centuries before there was a nation to hear about it.
verseByVerse.note: Judah, who once sold his brother, now offers himself in his brother’s place.

And he did as Joseph told him.<sup>3</sup>As soon as the morning was light, the men were sent away with their donkeys.<sup>4</sup>They had gone only a short distance from the city.
