You have done evil in doing this.'"<sup>6</sup>When he overtook them, he spoke to them these words.<sup>7</sup>They said to him, "Why does my lord speak such words as these? Far be it from your servants to do such a thing!<sup>8</sup>Behold, the money that we found in the mouths of our sacks we brought back to you from the land of Canaan. How then could we steal silver or gold from your lord's house?<sup>9</sup>Whichever of your servants is found with it shall die, and we also will be my lord's servants."<sup>10</sup>He said, "Let it be as you say: he who is found with it shall be my servant, and the rest of you shall be innocent."<sup>11</sup>Then each man quickly lowered his sack to the ground, and each man opened his sack.<sup>12</sup>And he searched, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest. And the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.<sup>13</sup>Then they tore their clothes, and every man loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city.<sup>14</sup>When Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house, he was still there. They fell before him to the ground.<sup>15</sup>Joseph said to them, "What deed is this that you have done? Do you not know that a man like me can indeed practice divination?"<sup>16</sup>And Judah said, "What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak? Or how can we clear ourselves? God has found out the guilt of your servants; behold, we are my lord's servants, both we and he also in whose hand the cup has been found."<sup>17</sup>But he said, "Far be it from me that I should do so! Only the man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my servant. But as for you, go up in peace to your father."<sup>18</sup>Then Judah went up to him and said, "Oh, my lord, please let your servant speak a word in my lord's ears, and let not your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh himself.<sup>19</sup>My lord asked his servants, saying, 'Have you a father, or a brother?'<sup>20</sup>And we said to my lord, 'We have a father, an old man, and a young brother, the child of his old age. His brother is dead, and he alone is left of his mother's children, and his father loves him.'<sup>21</sup>Then you said to your servants, 'Bring him down to me, that I may set my eyes on him.'<sup>22</sup>We said to my lord, 'The boy cannot leave his father, for if he should leave his father, his father would die.'<sup>23</sup>Then you said to your servants, 'Unless your youngest brother comes down with you, you shall not see my face again.'<sup>24</sup>"When we went back to your servant my father, we told him the words of my lord.<sup>25</sup>And when our father said, 'Go again, buy us a little food,'<sup>26</sup>we said, 'We cannot go down. If our youngest brother goes with us, then we will go down. For we cannot see the man's face unless our youngest brother is with us.'<sup>27</sup>Then your servant my father said to us, 'You know that my wife bore me two sons.<sup>28</sup>One left me, and I said, "Surely he has been torn to pieces," and I have never seen him since.<sup>29</sup>If you take this one also from me, and harm happens to him, you will bring down my gray hairs in evil to Sheol.'<sup>30</sup>"Now therefore, as soon as I come to your servant my father, and the boy is not with us, then, as his life is bound up in the boy's life,<sup>31</sup>as soon as he sees that the boy is not with us, he will die, and your servants will bring down the gray hairs of your servant our father with sorrow to Sheol.<sup>32</sup>For your servant became a pledge of safety for the boy to my father, saying, 'If I do not bring him back to you, then I shall bear the blame before my father all my life.'<sup>33</sup>Now therefore, please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers.<sup>34</sup>For how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? I fear to see the evil that would find my father."
44.overview:
The last test, and it is exact. Joseph has a silver cup planted in Benjamin’s sack, lets the brothers get a short distance from the city, and sends his steward after them. The cup is found in the youngest son’s baggage, and the offer that follows is precisely the choice they faced twenty-two years ago: leave Rachel’s favoured son in Egypt as a slave, and go home free.

They could take it. Nobody would ever know, and they have a ready-made story — they used one before. Instead every man tears his clothes and every man goes back.

Then Judah speaks, and his speech is one of the longest in Genesis and the turning point of his life. He rehearses the whole history from his father’s side, quotes the old man’s words about the wife who bore him two sons, and ends by offering to stay as a slave in Benjamin’s place: “let your servant remain instead of the boy... For how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me?” The man who sold a brother for silver offers his own liberty for one, and the test is over.
44.theology:
Substitution, offered by a man. Judah’s “let your servant remain instead of the boy” is the clearest picture of substitution in Genesis after the ram at Moriah. He is innocent of the charge, he offers to bear the penalty, and he does it so that a father will not be destroyed. Out of this man’s tribe would come David, and out of David’s line the one of whom Judah is here a small and true likeness (cf. Rev. 5:5).

Repentance is proved by the same choice, met again. God does not settle for regret. He arranges for these men to stand in front of the identical decision — a favoured younger son, an easy way to be rid of him, and a father who will never know — and this time they refuse it. That is what a changed man looks like: not one who feels worse about the old sin, but one who is offered it again and will not take it.

“God has found out the guilt of your servants.” Judah is not talking about a cup. They are innocent of the theft and he does not argue the point, because he is speaking about something else entirely and everybody in the family knows what. Sin has a way of being found out long after the file was closed (cf. Num. 32:23).
44.examples:
Then: A silver cup used for divination fits an Egyptian household exactly; liquid divination — reading patterns in oil or wine — was practised, and Joseph is playing his Egyptian part to the end. Stealing from a royal official’s house was a capital matter, and the brothers’ own rash offer — let the guilty man die and the rest be slaves — would have been within the range of a real penalty. The steward reduces it to something survivable before the search even begins, which is the first sign that the whole thing is staged.

Now: Read Judah’s speech aloud. It contains no argument about the law, no protest of innocence, and no attempt to shift the blame. It is simply a description of what this will do to an old man, and an offer to take the consequence himself. If you have ever had to plead for somebody — a child, a friend, a colleague in trouble — this is how it is done: tell the truth about the cost, and put yourself where the cost will fall.

45.title: Joseph Makes Himself Known

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The Great Revelation: ‘I Am Joseph’
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah’s offer breaks Joseph’s composure completely. He clears the room of all Egyptians and weeps so loudly that it is heard throughout Pharaoh’s house. He reveals himself—‘I am Joseph’—and immediately frames the entire history of betrayal as divine providence: ‘God sent me before you to preserve life.’ He embraces Benjamin, weeps over all his brothers, and sends them back with lavish gifts and wagons for Jacob. The chapter ends with Jacob hearing the news and his spirit reviving.
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph clears the room and weeps: "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" He tells his terrified brothers that they sold him, and three times that God sent him to preserve life. He embraces Benjamin and all of them, and after that they talk with him. Pharaoh sends wagons, and Jacob's spirit revives.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "you sold me" and "God sent me" are both true, as Peter preached of the cross (Acts 2:23). Now: forgiveness names the wrong plainly and releases the wrongdoer anyway — and "Do not quarrel on the way."

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph could not control himself before all those who stood by him. He cried, "Make everyone go out from me." So no one stayed with him when Joseph made himself known to his brothers. And he wept aloud, so that the Egyptians heard it, and the household of Pharaoh heard it. And Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" But his brothers could not answer him, for they were dismayed at his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Joseph could not control himself before all those who stood by him." Twice already he has left the room to weep and come back with his face washed (42:24; 43:30–31). This time it goes.

"He cried, 'Make everyone go out from me.'" he clears the room of every Egyptian in it. Whatever is about to happen between him and these men is family business, and he will not have his brothers' crime made public in front of a court he governs. It is an act of protection, and they have no idea yet that they are being protected.

"And he wept aloud, so that the Egyptians heard it, and the household of Pharaoh heard it." He sent them out and they heard him anyway. Twenty-two years of it come out at once.

"And Joseph said to his brothers, 'I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?'"

His first question after the revelation is about his father — and he has already been told twice that the old man is alive. He is not asking for information. It is the cry of a man who has heard the answer and cannot make himself believe it.

"But his brothers could not answer him, for they were dismayed at his presence." The word is strong: terrified, struck dumb. Their worst nightmare and their oldest guilt are standing in front of them wearing the gold chain of Egypt, and every one of them has just heard him say his own name.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph said to his brothers, "Come near to me, please." And they came near. And he said, "I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt. And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life. For the famine has been in the land these two years, and there are yet five years in which there will be neither plowing nor harvest. And God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on earth, and to keep alive for you many survivors. So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Joseph said to his brothers, 'Come near to me, please.' And they came near."

They must have been standing where they had fallen, well back, unable to move. He calls them closer — and he says please. The man who could have had them executed with a word asks them, politely, to come nearer.

"I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt." He names it. There is no pretence that it did not happen or that it was a misunderstanding; he says the worst sentence out loud, and the reader should notice that forgiveness in Scripture never begins by making the offence smaller.

"And now do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life."

And then he says it again in verse 7, and a third time in verse 8, and the third time he puts it as sharply as it can be put: "So it was not you who sent me here, but God."

Hold both halves, because Joseph does. They sold him — he has just said so twice. And God sent him — he says so three times. Neither statement cancels the other, and the Bible never resolves the tension by dropping one. Peter preached the same double truth about the cross: delivered up by the definite plan of God, and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23).

What that means for the brothers is this: their guilt is entirely real, and it is not the last word about what happened. And what it means for anyone reading who has been badly hurt is that God's sovereignty over an evil act is not a reason to call the act less evil. It is a reason to believe he was not absent from it.

Does forgiving mean trusting again? Joseph forgave, but he did not reveal himself until he had seen his brothers change: Judah offering himself in Benjamin’s place (44:33). Forgiveness lets go of revenge; trust is rebuilt as repentance is shown.

verseByVerse.quote: Hurry and go up to my father and say to him, 'Thus says your son Joseph, God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me; do not tarry. You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you shall be near me, you and your children and your children's children, and your flocks, your herds, and all that you have. There I will provide for you, for there are yet five years of famine to come, so that you and your household, and all that you have, do not come to poverty.' And now your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see, that it is my mouth that speaks to you. You must tell my father of all my honor in Egypt, and of all that you have seen. Hurry and bring my father down here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hurry and go up to my father and say to him, 'Thus says your son Joseph, God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me; do not tarry.'"

The urgency is a son's. He has been away twenty-two years and he cannot bear another season of it.

"You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you shall be near me" — the fertile eastern delta, close to the seat of power, and separate enough for a shepherding family that Egyptians would not eat with. He has thought about where they will live and how they will be fed: "There I will provide for you, for there are yet five years of famine to come."

"And now your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin see, that it is my mouth that speaks to you." No interpreter. He speaks to them directly now, with no interpreter, and that is the proof. The interpreter who stood between them in chapter 42 is gone, along with everything else that stood between them.

"You must tell my father of all my honor in Egypt." That is not vanity. Jacob is not going to believe a word of this, and Joseph knows it.
verseByVerse.note: Goshen was fertile land in the eastern Nile delta.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he fell upon his brother Benjamin's neck and wept, and Benjamin wept upon his neck. And he kissed all his brothers and wept upon them. After that his brothers talked with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then he fell upon his brother Benjamin's neck and wept, and Benjamin wept upon his neck. And he kissed all his brothers and wept upon them."

Benjamin first — the only other son of Rachel, who was a small child when Joseph disappeared and is now a grown man with sons of his own. And then all of them: not just the innocent one, but the brothers who threw him in the pit and the one who priced him.

"After that his brothers talked with him."

That short clause is the whole point of the chapter. From 37:4 — "they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him" — to this. Twenty-two years of silence between brothers, ended.

Notice the order, because it is the order of the gospel. He wept on them first, and then they were able to speak. The wronged man moved first, and the embrace came before the conversation, not after it.

verseByVerse.quote: When the report was heard in Pharaoh's house, "Joseph's brothers have come," it pleased Pharaoh and his servants. And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Say to your brothers, 'Do this: load your beasts and go back to the land of Canaan, and take your father and your households, and come to me, and I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat the fat of the land.' And you, Joseph, are commanded to say, 'Do this: take wagons from the land of Egypt for your little ones and for your wives, and bring your father, and come. Have no concern for your goods, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When the report was heard in Pharaoh's house, 'Joseph's brothers have come,' it pleased Pharaoh and his servants." The court is delighted. Whatever the Egyptians thought of Asiatics generally, they are glad for this man.

And Pharaoh goes further than Joseph had: "I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat the fat of the land... take wagons from the land of Egypt for your little ones and for your wives... Have no concern for your goods, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours."

Leave your things behind; everything here is better. It is a royal invitation of the most generous kind, extended to a family of foreign shepherds because of one man's standing with the king.

Sit with that. They come into the best of Egypt entirely on Joseph's account — not because Pharaoh has met them, not because they have anything to offer, but because of who their brother is. It is the shape of every welcome God gives: "accepted in the Beloved," as the older versions put Ephesians 1:6.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Israel did so: and Joseph gave them wagons, according to the command of Pharaoh, and gave them provisions for the journey. To each and all of them he gave a change of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five changes of clothes. To his father he sent as follows: ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and provision for his father on the journey. Then he sent his brothers away, and as they departed, he said to them, "Do not quarrel on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The provisions are itemised, and one detail stands out: "To each and all of them he gave a change of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five changes of clothes."

Five again, as with the portions at the table (43:34). And this time nobody is watching them for a reaction, so it is not a test — it is a brother's affection, and it is also the man who was stripped of a coat handing out clothes to everybody.

"Then he sent his brothers away, and as they departed, he said to them, 'Do not quarrel on the way.'"

It is his last word to them and it is entirely practical. Ten men with a long road ahead, a great deal to explain when they get there, and one obvious subject: whose idea was it, who suggested selling him, who held him down, who should tell the old man. He can see the argument coming and he heads it off.

Forgiveness received from the person you wronged does not automatically produce peace among those who shared the guilt. That is a separate work, and it generally breaks down on the road home. Anyone who has watched a family absorb bad news, or a church absorb a failure, knows exactly what Joseph was preventing.
verseByVerse.note: Three hundred shekels was about 7½ pounds of silver (a shekel was about 2/5 ounce, ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: So they went up out of Egypt and came to the land of Canaan to their father Jacob. And they told him, "Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt." And his heart became numb, for he did not believe them. But when they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived. And Israel said, "It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And they told him, 'Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt.' And his heart became numb, for he did not believe them."

Twenty-two years of grief cannot be undone by a sentence. The Hebrew suggests his heart went cold, or stopped — the physical shock of news too large to take in. And of course he does not believe them; the last time they came home with information about Joseph they were lying.

"But when they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived."

The words, and then the wagons. Egyptian carts, standing in a Canaanite yard, that nobody in that country could have produced. The evidence is physical and it is undeniable, and the old man comes back to life in front of them.

It is a picture of what news of a resurrection does. The disciples "disbelieved for joy" when Jesus stood among them (Luke 24:41), and he gave them something to look at — hands, feet, a piece of broiled fish. God knows what grief does to a person's ability to believe good news, and he does not scold it. He sends wagons.

"And Israel said, 'It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die.'"

Note the name the narrator uses: Israel. He has been Jacob through most of these chapters — the grieving father, the anxious old man. The moment faith comes back he is Israel again, and the last words of the chapter are the words of a man who has something to get up for.

After that his brothers talked with him.<sup>16</sup>When the report was heard in Pharaoh's house, "Joseph's brothers have come," it pleased Pharaoh and his servants.<sup>17</sup>And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Say to your brothers, 'Do this: load your beasts and go back to the land of Canaan,<sup>18</sup>and take your father and your households, and come to me, and I will give you the best of the land of Egypt, and you shall eat the fat of the land.'<sup>19</sup>And you, Joseph, are commanded to say, 'Do this: take wagons from the land of Egypt for your little ones and for your wives, and bring your father, and come.<sup>20</sup>Have no concern for your goods, for the best of all the land of Egypt is yours.'"<sup>21</sup>The sons of Israel did so: and Joseph gave them wagons, according to the command of Pharaoh, and gave them provisions for the journey.<sup>22</sup>To each and all of them he gave a change of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred shekels of silver and five changes of clothes.<sup>23</sup>To his father he sent as follows: ten donkeys loaded with the good things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and provision for his father on the journey.<sup>24</sup>Then he sent his brothers away, and as they departed, he said to them, "Do not quarrel on the way."<sup>25</sup>So they went up out of Egypt and came to the land of Canaan to their father Jacob.<sup>26</sup>And they told him, "Joseph is still alive, and he is ruler over all the land of Egypt." And his heart became numb, for he did not believe them.<sup>27</sup>But when they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had said to them, and when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of their father Jacob revived.<sup>28</sup>And Israel said, "It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive. I will go and see him before I die."
45.overview:
Judah has finished speaking, and Joseph cannot hold it any longer. He clears the room of every Egyptian and weeps so loudly that the palace hears it, and then says the three words the whole book has been moving towards: “I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?”

His brothers cannot answer. So he calls them nearer — “come near to me, please” — and tells them plainly who he is and what they did: “I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.” And in the same breath he takes the weight off them: “do not be distressed or angry with yourselves... for God sent me before you to preserve life.” Three times in four verses he says God sent him, and finishes with “it was not you who sent me here, but God.”

Then arrangements: Goshen, provision, wagons, a message for his father. Pharaoh himself is delighted and adds to the invitation. The chapter closes in Canaan, where an old man hears that his son is alive and does not believe it — until he sees the wagons.
45.theology:
Two hands on the same event. “You sold me” and “God sent me” are both true and neither cancels the other. Joseph does not say that his brothers meant well, or that what they did was small; he says it twice over that they sold him. He also says that God was doing something through it that they knew nothing about. That is the doctrine Peter preached at Pentecost about a far greater crime: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God,” and “you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23) — one sentence, both halves.

Forgiveness that does not require the offence to be minimised. Joseph names what they did in the plainest possible words and then removes the sting from it in the same speech. Real forgiveness is not pretending the thing was less than it was; it is looking straight at it and releasing the person anyway.

A remnant preserved. “God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant on earth.” The word remnant will run through the prophets and into Paul’s argument in Romans 11. The line that carries the promise is repeatedly reduced to almost nothing and repeatedly kept alive, and here it is kept alive by the brother the family tried to be rid of.
45.examples:
Then: Goshen, in the eastern delta, was good pastureland close to the seat of government but outside the Egyptian heartland — ideal for a shepherding clan that Egyptians would not mix with socially. Pharaoh granting land and sending wagons for a vizier’s family is exactly the sort of favour a grateful king extended, and the wagons are the detail that finally convinces Jacob, because Egyptian carts were not a thing anyone in Canaan could have faked.

Now: “Do not quarrel on the way.” It is the last thing Joseph says to them, and it is the most practical sentence in the chapter. Ten men have a long journey ahead in which to work out whose fault it was, and he heads it off. Forgiveness received does not automatically produce peace between the people who shared the guilt; that is a separate work, and it usually breaks down on the road home. And for anyone who has been told good news too large to take in, there is Jacob: his heart went numb, and he did not believe it, and then he saw the wagons.

46.title: Jacob Goes to Egypt

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–34 — The Descent to Egypt: God's Promise and the Family Register
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jacob sets out for Egypt and stops at Beersheba, where God appears in a night vision reaffirming the covenant: 'I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again.' A genealogical register of all who go with Jacob follows—seventy souls in all. The chapter ends with Jacob and Joseph's reunion, and Joseph's practical counsel about settling in Goshen.
verseByVerse.theology: At Beersheba Jacob offers sacrifices, and God tells him not to fear going to Egypt: he will make him a great nation there, go down with him and bring him up again. Seventy persons of the house of Jacob go down. Joseph meets his father in Goshen and weeps on his neck a good while, and briefs his brothers to say they are shepherds.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the exodus is promised four centuries before it happens. Now: God goes down with his people into every Egypt (Isa. 43:2), and his purposes often look far too small to be what he said they were.

verseByVerse.quote: So Israel took his journey with all that he had and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and said, "Jacob, Jacob." And he said, "Here I am." Then he said, "I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again, and Joseph's hand shall close your eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Israel took his journey with all that he had and came to Beersheba, and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac."

Beersheba is the southern edge of the promised land — the last stop before Egypt, and the place where Abraham planted a tamarisk and called on the Everlasting God (21:33), and where Isaac built an altar (26:25). The old man stops at the border of the covenant land and worships.

He has every reason not to. He has Pharaoh's wagons, his son's summons and a famine behind him, and he is a hundred and thirty. He stops anyway, because leaving the land God promised is not a small thing, and he wants to hear from God before he does it. Abraham went down to Egypt without asking and it went badly (12:10–20); Isaac was told not to go at all (26:2). Jacob asks.

"And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night and said, 'Jacob, Jacob.'" The doubled name, as at the burning bush and on the Damascus road. And the reply is the one this family gives: "Here I am."

Then four promises, and they answer everything an old man on that road could fear. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt — the fear is named. There I will make you into a great nation — the promise will grow in Egypt, not in spite of it. I myself will go down with you — the covenant is not attached to a piece of ground. And I will also bring you up again — the exodus, promised in a tent, four centuries early.

And then the tenderest clause in the chapter: "and Joseph's hand shall close your eyes." He will die in Egypt, and his son will be there.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob set out from Beersheba. The sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent to carry him. They also took their livestock and their goods, which they had gained in the land of Canaan, and came into Egypt, Jacob and all his offspring with him, his sons, and his sons' sons with him, his daughters, and his sons' daughters. All his offspring he brought with him into Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The sons of Israel carried Jacob their father, their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons that Pharaoh had sent."

The wagons that convinced him (45:27) now carry him. He is too old to walk to Egypt, and the transport was arranged by a king he has never met, at the request of a son he thought was dead.

"They also took their livestock and their goods, which they had gained in the land of Canaan." They come as a family with property, not as refugees with nothing — which matters, because in four hundred years their descendants will walk out again with a great deal more (Exod. 12:35–36).

"All his offspring he brought with him into Egypt." Everybody. Nobody is left behind in Canaan, and there will be no branch of the family outside what is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the names of the descendants of Israel, who came into Egypt, Jacob and his sons. Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and the sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. The sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah (but Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan); and the sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul. The sons of Issachar: Tola, Puvah, Yob, and Shimron. The sons of Zebulun: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan-aram, together with his daughter Dinah; altogether his sons and his daughters numbered thirty-three. The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli. The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, Beriah, with Serah their sister. And the sons of Beriah: Heber and Malchiel. These are the sons of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to Leah his daughter; and these she bore to Jacob—sixteen persons. The sons of Rachel, Jacob's wife: Joseph and Benjamin. And to Joseph in the land of Egypt were born Manasseh and Ephraim, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera the priest of On, bore to him. And the sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard. These are the sons of Rachel, who were born to Jacob—fourteen persons in all. The son of Dan: Hushim. The sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem. These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to Rachel his daughter, and these she bore to Jacob—seven persons in all. All the persons belonging to Jacob who came into Egypt, who were his own descendants, not including Jacob's sons' wives, were sixty-six persons in all. And the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The register runs by mother: Leah's line first and largest, then Zilpah's, then Rachel's, then Bilhah's. It is a family tree with the fault lines of chapters 29 and 30 still visible in the arrangement.

A few names carry a great deal. Er and Onan are listed and marked as having died in Canaan — the register does not tidy up chapter 38. Perez is here, with his sons Hezron and Hamul, and the line to David and to Christ runs through them (Ruth 4:18–22; Matt. 1:3). Levi's three sons are named — Gershon, Kohath, Merari — and Kohath's line will give Israel Moses and Aaron.

"All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy."

Seventy. That is the whole covenant people at this moment, and it fits on a page. God had promised Abraham offspring like the dust of the earth and the stars of the sky, and in the generations that follow Exodus can say that they multiplied and filled the land (Exod. 1:7). The number here is small on purpose, because Genesis wants the reader to know exactly what God started with.

And seventy is the number of the nations in the table of chapter 10. The family through whom all the families of the earth are to be blessed is itself counted out in seventy names.

How do the numbers work? Leah’s line gives thirty-three, counting Jacob himself and leaving out Er and Onan, who had died; Zilpah’s sixteen, Rachel’s fourteen and Bilhah’s seven make seventy. The sixty-six of verse 26 are those who travelled with Jacob, leaving out Jacob, Joseph and Joseph’s two sons; add those four and the total is seventy. Some named, such as Benjamin’s ten sons, were probably born later, counted in the family line rather than in the wagons.
verseByVerse.note: Seventy persons in all. Stephen gives seventy-five, following the Greek Old Testament, which counts more of Joseph’s descendants.

verseByVerse.quote: He had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to show the way before him in Goshen, and they came into the land of Goshen. Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while. Israel said to Joseph, "Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to show the way before him in Goshen." Not Reuben the firstborn, not Simeon or Levi. Judah is now the son Jacob sends when something matters, and chapter 49 will make the reason public.

"Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while."

The second man of Egypt drives out to a shepherds' district to meet a hundred-and-thirty-year-old herdsman, and stands in a field holding him and crying for a long time. Genesis, which can dispose of the creation of the stars in three words, says "a good while."

"Israel said to Joseph, 'Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive.'"

He is not asking to die. A man has been given back the one thing he had stopped asking for, and finds that it is enough. Simeon said almost the same words holding a baby in the temple: "Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace... for my eyes have seen your salvation" (Luke 2:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household, "I will go up and tell Pharaoh and will say to him, 'My brothers and my father's household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me. And the men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that they have.' When Pharaoh calls you and says, 'What is your occupation?' you shall say, 'Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we and our fathers,' in order that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph briefs them for the audience with Pharaoh, and the briefing is shrewd. Say plainly that you are keepers of livestock, and have been from your youth, and your fathers before you.

"In order that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians."

He is using Egyptian contempt as a tool. Settled Egyptians looked down on herdsmen; if the family declares its trade openly, they will be given pasture in the delta and left alone rather than absorbed into the cities and the court.

Which is the last thing Joseph does for his family before the book turns to Jacob's blessing, and it is the shrewdest. He has seen what Egypt does to a Hebrew who rises in it — a new name, an Egyptian wife, a priest's daughter, a lifetime of eating at a separate table. He arranges for his brothers to be despised and left in peace in Goshen, where they can stay a people.

Four hundred years later that is exactly where they still are, and there are six hundred thousand of them, and the separateness that began as a social insult had kept them a nation. God's protection of his people does not always look like favour. Sometimes it looks like being kept at arm's length by a culture that would otherwise have swallowed them.

And he said, "Here I am."<sup>3</sup>Then he said, "I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation.<sup>4</sup>I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again, and Joseph's hand shall close your eyes."<sup>5</sup>Then Jacob set out from Beersheba. All the persons of the house of Jacob who came into Egypt were seventy.<sup>28</sup>He had sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph to show the way before him in Goshen, and they came into the land of Goshen.<sup>29</sup>Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet Israel his father in Goshen. He presented himself to him and fell on his neck and wept on his neck a good while.<sup>30</sup>Israel said to Joseph, "Now let me die, since I have seen your face and know that you are still alive."<sup>31</sup>Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's household, "I will go up and tell Pharaoh and will say to him, 'My brothers and my father's household, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.<sup>32</sup>And the men are shepherds, for they have been keepers of livestock, and they have brought their flocks and their herds and all that they have.'<sup>33</sup>When Pharaoh calls you and says, 'What is your occupation?'<sup>34</sup>you shall say, 'Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth even until now, both we and our fathers,' in order that you may dwell in the land of Goshen, for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians."
46.overview:
Jacob goes down to Egypt, and Genesis pauses at the border to make sure the reader understands what is happening. At Beersheba — the last stop in the land of promise, and his father’s and grandfather’s place of worship — the old man offers sacrifices, and God speaks to him in the night with four promises: do not be afraid to go down; there I will make you a great nation; I myself will go down with you; and I will also bring you up again.

That is the theological hinge of the whole descent. Israel does not drift into Egypt out of hunger and bad judgment. God sends them, goes with them, and promises the exodus four hundred years before it happens.

Then the register: seventy persons, listed by mother and by tribe — the whole nation of Israel, at this moment, fits on one page. And at the end of it, a reunion: an old man and a son he had buried, and a chariot on a road in Goshen.
46.theology:
God goes down with his people. “I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again.” The covenant is not tied to a plot of ground. Whatever else the years in Egypt would be — and they would end in slavery and brick-making — God’s people were never there without him. Centuries later he told them so again from the exile: “when you pass through the waters, I will be with you” (Isa. 43:2).

The exodus promised in advance. “I will also bring you up again” is spoken to a man in a tent at Beersheba, and it is paid in full at the Red Sea. God had told Abraham the same thing in the dark (15:13–14). Nothing about the four hundred years took him by surprise, and nothing about them was outside the plan.

Seventy persons. The whole covenant people at this point is a list of names that fits on one page — and the promise was offspring like the stars and the sand. God’s purposes routinely look, at any given moment, far too small to be what he said they were.
46.examples:
Then: The delta was Egypt’s traditional entry point for Semitic herdsmen, and Egyptian records show such groups being admitted in famine years. Goshen was pasture rather than arable land, which suited shepherds and kept them out of the Egyptian heartland. Herding was a low-status occupation to settled Egyptians — “every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians” — and Joseph turns that contempt into an advantage, briefing his family to state their trade plainly so that they are settled where they can remain a distinct people.

Now: Jacob stops at the border and offers sacrifices before crossing it. He has permission from Pharaoh, wagons at the door, a son waiting and every practical reason to hurry, and he stops to worship and to ask. That is the difference between the man of chapter 27 and the man of chapter 46: he now checks with God before a move that everything in him already wants to make. And the answer he gets is not advice about the journey. It is a promise about company.

47.title: Jacob Settles in Goshen; Joseph's Administration

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — Goshen Granted; Joseph's Famine Policy; Jacob's Last Request
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joseph presents five brothers and Jacob before Pharaoh. Pharaoh grants Goshen. Jacob blesses Pharaoh twice. Joseph administers the famine throughout Egypt, eventually acquiring all the land for Pharaoh and instituting the one-fifth tax. He settles Israel in Goshen where they are fruitful. Jacob lives seventeen years in Egypt, then as he nears death asks Joseph to swear to bury him in Canaan.
verseByVerse.theology: Pharaoh grants Jacob's family the best of the land, and Jacob blesses Pharaoh twice, calling his 130 years few and evil. Through the famine Joseph takes Egypt's money, livestock and land for Pharaoh, and the people say, "You have saved our lives." Israel is fruitful in Goshen; after seventeen years Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan, and bows in worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the inferior is blessed by the superior (Heb. 7:7), and the old shepherd is the greater man in the room. Now: grief can edit the record of a life God has carried, and faith can be expressed as a funeral arrangement.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph went in and told Pharaoh, "My father and my brothers, with their flocks and herds and all that they possess, have come from the land of Canaan. They are now in the land of Goshen." And from among his brothers he took five men and presented them to Pharaoh. Pharaoh said to his brothers, "What is your occupation?" And they said to Pharaoh, "Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were." They said to Pharaoh, "We have come to sojourn in the land, for there is no pasture for your servants' flocks, for the famine is severe in the land of Canaan. And now, please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen." Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you. The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them settle in the land of Goshen, and if you know any able men among them, put them in charge of my livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph presents five of his brothers to Pharaoh, and they say exactly what he told them to say: "Your servants are shepherds, as our fathers were... please let your servants dwell in the land of Goshen."

They ask for the district that Egyptians would not want, and they get more than they asked for. "The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land." Pharaoh grants Goshen and adds an offer of employment: "if you know any able men among them, put them in charge of my livestock."

Note the word sojourn in verse 4. They do not ask for citizenship or for land of their own; they ask to stay for a while because of the famine. Four hundred years later their descendants are still there and no longer free, and the distance between a temporary arrangement and a permanent one is the whole of Exodus 1.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph brought in Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. And Pharaoh said to Jacob, "How many are the days of the years of your life?" And Jacob said to Pharaoh, "The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their sojourning." And Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from the presence of Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Joseph brought in Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh."

An elderly Semitic herdsman is brought into the throne room of the greatest empire on earth, and he blesses the king. He does it twice, at the start of the audience and at the end.

Hebrews states the principle: "it is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior" (Heb. 7:7). By every visible measure Pharaoh outranks this man beyond comparison. By the measure that actually counts, the old shepherd carrying Abraham's promise is the greater person in the room, and the promise that in Abraham's offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed (12:3) is being paid out over a throne.

"And Pharaoh said to Jacob, 'How many are the days of the years of your life?'"

"The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers."

It is one of the bleakest self-assessments in Scripture. A hundred and thirty years, a lost son restored, a family saved from famine, a king's welcome — and he calls his life short and hard, and compares himself unfavourably with his father and grandfather.

Two things are true of it. Grief that has run for decades does edit the record, and a man can be genuinely unable to see what God has done for him. And he is not wrong about the pain: exile, twenty years under Laban, a raped daughter, a massacre, Rachel dead on the road, Joseph gone, Simeon held hostage. Scripture does not tell him to cheer up. It simply records what he said, and then lets him say something quite different one chapter later — "the God who has been my shepherd all my life long" (48:15).

He also calls it a sojourning, twice. Whatever else he has understood, he knows he has been passing through, and Hebrews builds on precisely that word (Heb. 11:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded. And Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father's household with food, according to the number of their dependents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses."

The city of Rameses was named centuries later (Exod 1:11). As with Dan (14:14), the district is called by the name the reader knew.

The word possession is the word used of the promised land itself, and Genesis uses it here of a district in Egypt. It is a comfortable irony: the family holds property in the wrong country while owning a single field and a cave in the right one.

"And Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father's household with food, according to the number of their dependents." Rationed by household size, carefully, over years. The brothers who sold him for silver eat out of his hand for the rest of the famine, and he keeps the accounts himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was no food in all the land, for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished by reason of the famine. And Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, in exchange for the grain that they bought. And Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh's house. And when the money was all spent in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, "Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our money is gone." And Joseph answered, "Give your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for your livestock, if your money is gone." So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for the horses, the flocks, the herds, and the donkeys. He supplied them with food in exchange for all their livestock that year. And when that year was ended, they came to him the following year and said to him, "We will not hide from my lord that our money is all spent. The herds of livestock are my lord's. There is nothing left in the sight of my lord but our bodies and our land. Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for food, and we with our land will be servants to Pharaoh. And give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not be desolate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the famine policy, told in stages, and Genesis narrates it without a word of praise or blame.

First the money: "Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, in exchange for the grain that they bought." Then, when the money is gone, the livestock: horses, flocks, herds, donkeys, for one year's food. Then, the following year, the last thing left: "There is nothing left in the sight of my lord but our bodies and our land."

"Buy us and our land for food, and we with our land will be servants to Pharaoh. And give us seed that we may live and not die."

The proposal is theirs, not his. They ask to be bought, because the alternative is starving, and the sentence they use — that we may live and not die — is the sentence Jacob used when he sent his sons to Egypt in the first place (42:2).

Be honest about how this reads to a modern eye. A famine has transferred an entire nation's wealth, land and liberty to the crown, administered by a foreigner. Genesis does not defend it and does not attack it. What it does do is record, in verse 25, what the Egyptians themselves said about it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, for all the Egyptians sold their fields, because the famine was severe on them. The land became Pharaoh's. As for the people, he made servants of them from one end of Egypt to the other. Only the land of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had a fixed allowance from Pharaoh and lived on the allowance that Pharaoh gave them; therefore they did not sell their land. Then Joseph said to the people, "Behold, I have this day bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Now here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land. And at the harvests you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four fifths shall be your own, as seed for the field and as food for yourselves and your households, and as food for your little ones." And they said, "You have saved our lives; may it please my lord, we will be servants to Pharaoh." So Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt, and it stands to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth; the land of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh... The land became Pharaoh's. As for the people, he made servants of them from one end of Egypt to the other."

Only the priests are exempt, because they had a state allowance and did not need to sell. Egyptian records confirm both the crown's ownership of most land and the temples' exemption; Joseph is not inventing a system so much as completing one.

Then the terms: seed to sow, and a fifth of the harvest to Pharaoh, four fifths their own. Twenty per cent, with the state carrying the risk in famine years, is not a cruel rate by any standard of the ancient world or most of the modern one.

"And they said, 'You have saved our lives; may it please my lord, we will be servants to Pharaoh.'" That is the verdict of the people who paid, and Genesis gives them the last word on it.

Two things follow, and they sit uncomfortably together, which is why the chapter is honest. Joseph genuinely saved a nation from starvation and was thanked for it. And the machinery he built — a centralised state, a landless population, a crown that owned everything — is the machinery that a later Pharaoh "who did not know Joseph" would use to enslave his descendants (Exod. 1:8–11). Good men build institutions, and institutions outlive the men and are used by whoever inherits them.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly. And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were 147 years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly."

Those are the creation words (1:28) and the covenant words, and they are said of a family of seventy in a foreign country. Exodus will open with the same sentence expanded: "the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly... so that the land was filled with them" (Exod. 1:7).

God's promise to Abraham of a nation is being kept, and it is being kept in Egypt rather than in Canaan. The place of eventual slavery is the place of the growth. God does not need the ideal conditions anyone would have chosen for him.

"And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years." Seventeen — the same number of years he had Joseph at home before the pit (37:2). He lost him at seventeen and he gets seventeen back.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob lived 147 years, 17 of them in Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the time drew near that Israel must die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, "If now I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh and promise to deal kindly and truly with me. Do not bury me in Egypt, but let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burying place." He answered, "I will do as you have said." And he said, "Swear to me"; and he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of his bed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When the time drew near that Israel must die, he called his son Joseph and said to him... 'put your hand under my thigh and promise to deal kindly and truly with me. Do not bury me in Egypt, but let me lie with my fathers.'"

The oath-gesture is the one Abraham required of his servant about a wife for Isaac (24:2) — a solemn swearing on the sign of the covenant. And the request is the same kind of thing: it is about the promise.

He has spent seventeen comfortable years in the best land in the world, fed by his son, honoured by a king. He will not be buried there. Machpelah is a cave in a field his grandfather bought at an inflated price (ch. 23), in a country the family does not own and has been driven out of by famine — and that is where he intends to lie, with Abraham, Isaac, Sarah, Rebekah and Leah.

It is a piece of faith expressed as a funeral arrangement. He is staking his bones on a promise about a land he has left, and Joseph will do the same in the last verses of the book (50:25), and four centuries later Moses will carry those bones out.

"Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of his bed." Too weak to kneel, he worships from where he is lying. Hebrews picks out this exact moment as an act of faith: "By faith Jacob, when dying... bowing in worship over the head of his staff" (Heb. 11:21). The grabber, the schemer, the man with the limp, ends by bowing.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek Old Testament reads “staff” for “bed” (ESV note) — the wording quoted in Hebrews.
