Settle your father and your brothers in the best of the land. Let them settle in the land of Goshen, and if you know any able men among them, put them in charge of my livestock."<sup>7</sup>Then Joseph brought in Jacob his father and stood him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.<sup>8</sup>And Pharaoh said to Jacob, "How many are the days of the years of your life?"<sup>9</sup>And Jacob said to Pharaoh, "The days of the years of my sojourning are 130 years. Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life, and they have not attained to the days of the years of the life of my fathers in the days of their sojourning."<sup>10</sup>And Jacob blessed Pharaoh and went out from the presence of Pharaoh.<sup>11</sup>Then Joseph settled his father and his brothers and gave them a possession in the land of Egypt, in the best of the land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had commanded.<sup>12</sup>And Joseph provided his father, his brothers, and all his father's household with food, according to the number of their dependents.<sup>13</sup>Now there was no food in all the land, for the famine was very severe, so that the land of Egypt and the land of Canaan languished by reason of the famine.<sup>14</sup>And Joseph gathered up all the money that was found in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, in exchange for the grain that they bought. And Joseph brought the money into Pharaoh's house.<sup>15</sup>And when the money was all spent in the land of Egypt and in the land of Canaan, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, "Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our money is gone."<sup>16</sup>And Joseph answered, "Give your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for your livestock, if your money is gone."<sup>17</sup>So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and Joseph gave them food in exchange for the horses, the flocks, the herds, and the donkeys. He supplied them with food in exchange for all their livestock that year.<sup>18</sup>And when that year was ended, they came to him the following year and said to him, "We will not hide from my lord that our money is all spent. The herds of livestock are my lord's. There is nothing left in the sight of my lord but our bodies and our land.<sup>19</sup>Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for food, and we with our land will be servants to Pharaoh. And give us seed that we may live and not die, and that the land may not be desolate."<sup>20</sup>So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, for all the Egyptians sold their fields, because the famine was severe on them. The land became Pharaoh's.<sup>21</sup>As for the people, he made servants of them from one end of Egypt to the other.<sup>22</sup>Only the land of the priests he did not buy, for the priests had a fixed allowance from Pharaoh and lived on the allowance that Pharaoh gave them; therefore they did not sell their land.<sup>23</sup>Then Joseph said to the people, "Behold, I have this day bought you and your land for Pharaoh. Now here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land.<sup>24</sup>And at the harvests you shall give a fifth to Pharaoh, and four fifths shall be your own, as seed for the field and as food for yourselves and your households, and as food for your little ones."<sup>25</sup>And they said, "You have saved our lives; may it please my lord, we will be servants to Pharaoh."<sup>26</sup>So Joseph made it a statute concerning the land of Egypt, and it stands to this day, that Pharaoh should have the fifth; the land of the priests alone did not become Pharaoh's.<sup>27</sup>Thus Israel settled in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen. And they gained possessions in it, and were fruitful and multiplied greatly.<sup>28</sup>And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years. So the days of Jacob, the years of his life, were 147 years.<sup>29</sup>And when the time drew near that Israel must die, he called his son Joseph and said to him, "If now I have found favor in your sight, put your hand under my thigh and promise to deal kindly and truly with me. Do not bury me in Egypt,<sup>30</sup>but let me lie with my fathers. Carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burying place." He answered, "I will do as you have said."<sup>31</sup>And he said, "Swear to me"; and he swore to him. Then Israel bowed himself upon the head of his bed.
47.overview:
Three things happen in Genesis 47, and they belong together. Jacob’s family is formally settled in the best of Egypt; Joseph’s famine administration takes the whole country into Pharaoh’s hands; and an old man makes his son swear that he will not be buried where he is about to die.

The audience with Pharaoh is quietly astonishing: a shepherd of no standing blesses the most powerful man on earth, twice, and is asked how old he is. His answer is one of the saddest self-assessments in Scripture — “few and evil have been the days of the years of my life” — from a man who has just been given back a son he buried.

Then the famine policy, told without comment: money, then livestock, then land and liberty, all exchanged for bread. Egypt survives and Egypt is transformed, and the people themselves say “you have saved our lives.” The chapter closes with Israel fruitful in Goshen and Jacob dying — and refusing, with an oath, to be left in the land that fed him.
47.theology:
Blessing runs from the covenant family outward. Jacob blesses Pharaoh, and Hebrews’ rule applies: “it is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior” (Heb. 7:7). By every visible measure Pharaoh outranks him absolutely. By the measure that matters, an old shepherd carrying the promise of Genesis 12:3 is the greater man in the room, and the nations are being blessed in Abraham’s offspring exactly as God said.

A pilgrim’s account of his own life. Jacob calls his years a sojourning, twice, and Hebrews takes the whole family that way: strangers and exiles on the earth, seeking a homeland (Heb. 11:13–16). His “few and evil” is honest and it is not the last word he speaks about his life; by 48:15 he will call God “the God who has been my shepherd all my life long.”

Faith that makes arrangements about a grave. Jacob will not be buried in Egypt. He makes Joseph swear it, because the land God promised is not where he is living and it is where he intends to be laid. It is the same faith that bought a cave at Machpelah (ch. 23) and the same faith Joseph will show at 50:25 — men staking their bones on a word from God.
47.examples:
Then: The famine policy in verses 13–26 corresponds to what is known of Egyptian land tenure: the crown owned most of the land, the temples held theirs exempt, and a fifth of the harvest was a real rate. Joseph did not invent an oppression — he is credited by the people themselves with saving their lives, and a twenty per cent tax with the state carrying the risk in famine years compares favourably with what most peasants anywhere have paid. Genesis reports the policy without praising or condemning it.

Now: “Few and evil have been the days of the years of my life.” A hundred and thirty years old, reunited with a lost son, settled in the best land in the world by a king, and this is his summary. Grief, when it has gone on long enough, edits the record: it is entirely possible to be a man God has carried and blessed at every turn and to be genuinely unable to see it. Jacob could not see it that day. He could by chapter 48, and what changed was not his circumstances.

48.title: Jacob Blesses Ephraim and Manasseh

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Adoption and Blessing of Joseph's Sons
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Jacob is dying, Joseph brings his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob adopts them as his own sons, equal to Reuben and Simeon. He then blesses them, deliberately crossing his hands to place his right hand on the younger Ephraim rather than the firstborn Manasseh. Joseph tries to correct him, but Jacob insists: 'I know, my son, I know.' He blesses both, but Ephraim will be greater.
verseByVerse.theology: Dying, Jacob adopts Joseph's sons: "Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine." He blesses them with crossed hands, naming "the God who has been my shepherd all my life long" and "the angel who has redeemed me from all evil," and sets Ephraim the younger before Manasseh. He promises that God will bring them back to the land.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: two boys born in Egypt became two tribes of Israel by a father's word. Now: God adopts outsiders as sons (Eph. 1:5), and from the end of a life his shepherding can be seen through years that felt few and evil.

verseByVerse.quote: After this, Joseph was told, "Behold, your father is ill." So he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. And it was told to Jacob, "Your son Joseph has come to you." Then Israel summoned his strength and sat up in bed. And Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me, and said to me, 'Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, your father is ill." Joseph takes his two sons and goes, and the old man "summoned his strength and sat up in bed." He is dying and he means to do this properly.

And he begins where everything in his life begins: "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me." Luz is Bethel, and this is the night with the stairway, seventy years ago, when he was running for his life with a stone under his head.

He quotes the promise: fruitful, multiplied, a company of peoples, "and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession."

He is saying it in Egypt, on his deathbed, having lived most of his life in the promised land and owning a cave in it. Everything he is about to do with these two boys rests on a promise about a country he is not in, made to a frightened young man on a night God did not have to turn up for.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” is El Shaddai (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are. And the children that you fathered after them shall be yours. They shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance. As for me, when I came from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to go to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are."

It is a formal adoption. Two boys born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother, half Egyptian by blood and wholly Egyptian by upbringing, with no natural standing in the covenant family at all, are declared sons of Israel with an inheritance equal to the eldest two.

They did nothing to secure it. They were not consulted. A dying man said "are mine," and from that sentence come two tribes of Israel. Paul had exactly this category in mind when he told Gentile believers that God "predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ" (Eph. 1:5) — outsiders by birth, made heirs by a word from the father.

This is also why the arithmetic of the tribes works. Joseph receives the double portion of the firstborn in the form of two tribes, so Levi can later be set apart for the priesthood with no land and the number still comes to twelve.

"As for me, when I came from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the way." It comes out of nowhere, in the middle of a legal declaration. Forty years on and he is still telling Joseph about it, and he still remembers exactly how far short of Ephrath they were. Some griefs do not shrink; they simply stop being the only thing in the room.
verseByVerse.note: Ephraim and Manasseh are adopted as Jacob’s own sons: Joseph gets the double portion of the firstborn.

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he said, "Who are these?" Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." And he said, "Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them." Now the eyes of Israel were dim with age, so that he could not see. So Joseph brought them near him, and he kissed them and embraced them. And Israel said to Joseph, "I never expected to see your face; and behold, God has let me see your offspring also." Then Joseph removed them from his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he said, 'Who are these?'" his eyes are dim with age — like his father's before him (27:1), and this time nobody is deceiving anybody.

"They are my sons, whom God has given me here." Joseph's answer is the answer of a man who has never stopped crediting God, and the word here is carrying a lot: in this country, in this exile, after all of it.

"And he kissed them and embraced them. And Israel said to Joseph, 'I never expected to see your face; and behold, God has let me see your offspring also.'"

He had buried this son. He had said he would go down to Sheol mourning (37:35), and he had meant it, and he was wrong. God gave him back the son and then gave him grandsons on top of it — more than the thing he had stopped even asking for.

"Then Joseph removed them from his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth." The second man in Egypt goes down on the floor in front of his father's sickbed. He has been doing this all his life without noticing: the dreams said his family would bow to him, and here he is on his face before the old man.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand, and brought them near him. And Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands (for Manasseh was the firstborn). And he blessed Joseph and said, "The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys; and in them let my name be carried on, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph arranges the boys with great care — Manasseh, the elder, at his father's right hand, Ephraim at the left — and Jacob crosses his arms.

Then the blessing, and it is the finest thing Jacob ever says. Three lines, and God is named three ways.

"The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked" — the God of a family and a history, not a private discovery.

"The God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day." That is the first time in Scripture anybody calls God his shepherd, and it is said by a man who spent a lifetime keeping sheep in the open and knew exactly what the word costs. A shepherd walks with the flock, sleeps rough, carries the weak ones and fights off what comes at night.

Set that beside chapter 47, spoken seventeen years earlier: "few and evil have been the days of the years of my life." Nothing about the years has changed. He is simply looking at them from the end, and what he sees is not a bad run but a man who was led the whole way. David picked the word up — "the LORD is my shepherd" (Ps. 23:1) — and one day a man in Jerusalem said, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11).

"The angel who has redeemed me from all evil." Redeemed — goel, the kinsman-redeemer who buys back what his relative has lost. Genesis has not used it before, and Jacob uses it of the one who wrestled him at the Jabbok and would not let him go.

All evil. He means Esau's sword, Laban's cheating, the famine, the loss. He is not saying nothing bad happened; he is saying he was bought out of all of it.

Who is the angel who redeemed Jacob? Jacob sets him in the same blessing as God and gives both one verb: bless the boys, not “bless” twice. He is not a created angel but the angel of the LORD, who is the LORD himself, the one Jacob wrestled at Peniel (32:30). The best reading is that he is the Son before his incarnation, the true Redeemer.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him, and he took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head. And Joseph said to his father, "Not this way, my father; since this one is the firstborn, put your right hand on his head." But his father refused and said, "I know, my son, I know. He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great. Nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations." So he blessed them that day, saying, "By you Israel will pronounce blessings, saying, 'God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh.'" Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him." He assumes a blind old man has made a mistake, and takes his father's hand to move it.

"But his father refused and said, 'I know, my son, I know.'"

Two words, repeated, from a man who cannot see which boy is which. He is not confused. He is doing it on purpose, and everybody in the room can see that his arms are crossed.

Think about who is doing this. Seventy years ago this man took a blessing that belonged to his elder brother, in the dark, from a blind father, by fraud. Now he is the blind father, and he gives the greater blessing to the younger boy openly, in daylight, over the objection of the boy's own father, because God's choosing does not run by birth order and never has.

"He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great. Nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater." Manasseh is not cursed or set aside; he is blessed, and Ephraim is blessed more. Election in Scripture is never the condemnation of everyone not chosen.

And it came true. Ephraim became the dominant northern tribe, so much so that the prophets use the name Ephraim for the whole northern kingdom.

"By you Israel will pronounce blessings, saying, 'God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh.'" Jewish fathers still say those words over their sons on a Friday evening. Two half-Egyptian boys adopted on a deathbed became the standard form of words for blessing a child, and have been for generations.
verseByVerse.note: Again the younger is set over the elder, as with Isaac, Jacob, Judah and Joseph.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Israel said to Joseph, "Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers. Moreover, I have given to you rather than to your brothers one mountain slope that I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and with my bow."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers."

He is dying in Egypt, in comfort, with his family settled in the best of the land and a son running the country. And he tells them plainly that this is not home and they are not staying.

It is the same promise God made to him at Bethel — I am with you, and I will bring you back (28:15) — handed on to the next generation as a certainty. Joseph will repeat it in the last chapter of the book, almost word for word (50:24), and four hundred years later it will happen.

"Moreover, I have given to you rather than to your brothers one mountain slope that I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and with my bow." The Hebrew word for slope is shechem, and this is probably the same district as the ground Jacob bought at Shechem (33:19), though the text speaks of conquest rather than purchase and where Joseph would eventually be buried (Josh. 24:32).

The reference to a sword and a bow is obscure and Genesis does not explain it. What is clear is the shape of the gift: a dying man in Egypt bequeathing a field in Canaan. He owns almost nothing in the world and he is writing a will about the promised land, because he believes the promise more than he believes the address.
verseByVerse.note: “Mountain slope” is shekem in Hebrew, which sounds like the town Shechem (ESV note).

48.text: <sup>1</sup>After this, Joseph was told, "Behold, your father is ill." So he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.<sup>2</sup>And it was told to Jacob, "Your son Joseph has come to you." Then Israel summoned his strength and sat up in bed.<sup>3</sup>And Jacob said to Joseph, "God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me,<sup>4</sup>and said to me, 'Behold, I will make you fruitful and multiply you, and I will make of you a company of peoples and will give this land to your offspring after you for an everlasting possession.'<sup>5</sup>And now your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came to you in Egypt, are mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are.<sup>6</sup>And the children that you fathered after them shall be yours. They shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritance.<sup>7</sup>As for me, when I came from Paddan, to my sorrow Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the way, when there was still some distance to go to Ephrath, and I buried her there on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)."<sup>8</sup>When Israel saw Joseph's sons, he said, "Who are these?"<sup>9</sup>Joseph said to his father, "They are my sons, whom God has given me here." And he said, "Bring them to me, please, that I may bless them."<sup>10</sup>Now the eyes of Israel were dim with age, so that he could not see. So Joseph brought them near him, and he kissed them and embraced them.<sup>11</sup>And Israel said to Joseph, "I never expected to see your face; and behold, God has let me see your offspring also."<sup>12</sup>Then Joseph removed them from his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.<sup>13</sup>And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel's right hand, and brought them near him.<sup>14</sup>And Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, who was the younger, and his left hand on the head of Manasseh, crossing his hands (for Manasseh was the firstborn).<sup>15</sup>And he blessed Joseph and said, "The God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life long to this day,<sup>16</sup>the angel who has redeemed me from all evil, bless the boys; and in them let my name be carried on, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth."<sup>17</sup>When Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand on the head of Ephraim, it displeased him, and he took his father's hand to move it from Ephraim's head to Manasseh's head.<sup>18</sup>And Joseph said to his father, "Not this way, my father; since this one is the firstborn, put your right hand on his head."<sup>19</sup>But his father refused and said, "I know, my son, I know. He also shall become a people, and he also shall be great. Nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations."<sup>20</sup>So he blessed them that day, saying, "By you Israel will pronounce blessings, saying, 'God make you as Ephraim and as Manasseh.'" Thus he put Ephraim before Manasseh.<sup>21</sup>Then Israel said to Joseph, "Behold, I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you again to the land of your fathers.<sup>22</sup>Moreover, I have given to you rather than to your brothers one mountain slope that I took from the hand of the Amorites with my sword and with my bow."
48.overview:
A dying man adopts his grandsons. Jacob takes Ephraim and Manasseh as his own — “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are” — which is why the tribes of Israel are twelve without a tribe of Joseph, and why Levi can be set apart for the priesthood without the number changing.

Then he blesses them, and he crosses his hands. Joseph tries to correct him and is refused: “I know, my son, I know... his younger brother shall be greater than he.” It is not the first time in Genesis that the younger is put before the elder, and this time the old man does it deliberately, with his eyes too dim to see which boy is which.

At the centre of the chapter is the finest thing Jacob ever says — a three-line description of God as the one before whom his fathers walked, the God who has been his shepherd all his life long, and the angel who has redeemed him from all evil. One chapter earlier he called his life few and evil. Nothing has changed except that he is looking at it from the end.
48.theology:
Adoption. Two boys born in Egypt to an Egyptian mother, with no natural claim on the covenant, are declared sons of Israel with a full inheritance alongside Reuben and Simeon. They did nothing; an old man said “are mine.” Paul uses the same category for Gentiles brought into the family of God: “he predestined us for adoption as sons” (Eph. 1:5).

God as shepherd, named for the first time. “The God who has been my shepherd all my life long” is the first time in Scripture that anyone calls God his shepherd, and it is said by a man who spent his life keeping sheep and being driven from place to place. David would take it up (Ps. 23:1), Ezekiel would prophesy it (Ezek. 34), and Jesus would say “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

Election, again, and deliberately. Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Perez over Zerah, and now Ephraim over Manasseh. Jacob had once stolen a blessing meant for the elder; he now gives one to the younger in full daylight, with the boys’ father objecting. God’s choosing does not run by birth order, merit or seniority, and Genesis says so again and again before it ends.
48.examples:
Then: Adoption formulas and deathbed blessings had real legal force in the ancient Near East, and a patriarch’s spoken word about inheritance was binding on the family. Placing the right hand on the head was the gesture of the greater blessing, which is why Joseph tries to move his father’s hand: this is not superstition but law and custom, and Jacob is overruling both on purpose.

Now: “I never expected to see your face; and behold, God has let me see your offspring also.” He had given up. He had said he would go down to Sheol mourning, and he was wrong, and God gave him more than the thing he had stopped asking for. That is not a promise that every grief ends this way; Genesis is honest about the ones that do not. It is a picture of a man discovering at the end that God had been shepherding him through years he could only describe as few and evil while he was living them.

49.title: Jacob's Blessings of His Twelve Sons

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–33 — The Blessing of the Twelve Tribes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jacob calls all twelve sons and delivers prophetic blessings—and in some cases, rebukes—over each. Reuben loses preeminence for his sin with Bilhah. Simeon and Levi are scattered for their violence at Shechem. Judah receives the royal blessing: 'The scepter shall not depart from Judah.' Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, and Naphtali each receive brief oracles. Joseph receives the longest blessing of abundant fruitfulness. Benjamin is described as a ravenous wolf. Jacob then dies.
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob tells his sons what will happen in days to come. Reuben loses the firstborn's place; Simeon and Levi are scattered for their anger; Judah receives the lion and the sceptre "until tribute comes to him." The other tribes are sketched in a line or two, Joseph is blessed at length, and Benjamin is a wolf. Jacob asks to be buried at Machpelah, and dies.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "I wait for your salvation, O LORD" (v. 18) breaks into the poem. Now: the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered (Rev. 5:5), and gifts without character do not hold (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jacob called his sons and said, "Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what shall happen to you in days to come. "Assemble and listen, O sons of Jacob, listen to Israel your father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Jacob called his sons and said, 'Gather yourselves together, that I may tell you what shall happen to you in days to come.'"

The phrase is a prophetic one — the latter days, the far horizon. This is not a father's assessment of his boys' characters; it is a word about tribes and centuries, and it will reach past every king Israel ever crowned.

"Assemble and listen, O sons of Jacob, listen to Israel your father." He uses both his names in one line. The men in front of him are the sons of Jacob the grabber, and they are the sons of Israel, and the whole book is in that double.

verseByVerse.quote: "Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the firstfruits of my strength, preeminent in dignity and preeminent in power. Unstable as water, you shall not have preeminence, because you went up to your father's bed; then you defiled it—he went up to my couch!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Reuben, you are my firstborn, my might, and the firstfruits of my strength, preeminent in dignity and preeminent in power."

Five titles, all genuine. He is the eldest, the first proof of his father's vigour, entitled to a double portion and the headship of the family, and Jacob lists it all before he takes it away.

"Unstable as water, you shall not have preeminence, because you went up to your father's bed."

Water goes wherever the ground slopes. There is nothing wrong with it and there is nothing in it that holds. That is Reuben's whole life: he meant well about Joseph and went away (37:21–29); he offered his own sons as security and was ignored (42:37); and once, briefly, he took Bilhah, and it was the end of him.

Notice that Jacob says nothing at the time — 35:22 reports the sin and then "and Israel heard of it," full stop. Forty years of silence, and then this. Some things are not forgotten because they were never mentioned.

And read the warning in it. Everything Reuben had was real: seniority, strength, position, the natural right. None of it held, because there was nothing steady underneath. Gifts are not character, and a man with the first and not the second will lose both.

verseByVerse.quote: "Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords. Let my soul come not into their council; O my glory, be not joined to their company. For in their anger they killed men, and in their willfulness they hamstrung oxen. Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel! I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords... For in their anger they killed men, and in their willfulness they hamstrung oxen."

This is Shechem (34:25–29), forty years on, and the old man's verdict on it is unqualified: "Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel!"

He is careful about what he curses. Not the men — the anger. Genesis never suggests these two are outside the covenant; they are tribes of Israel and always will be. What is condemned is the thing in them that made a city into a graveyard.

"I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel." Both tribes lose their land. Simeon's territory was absorbed inside Judah's and the tribe faded; Levi received no allotment at all.

And then God did something with Levi's sentence. The tribe scattered through Israel became the priestly tribe, living in forty-eight cities among the others precisely because they had no land — and it was Levi's descendants who stood with Moses at Sinai (Exod. 32:26–29) and who taught Israel the law. The scattering was never revoked. It was transfigured. God is entirely capable of taking the exact terms of a judgment and making them the shape of a calling.
verseByVerse.note: Both tribes were later scattered: Levi had no territory of its own, and Simeon was absorbed into Judah.

verseByVerse.quote: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be on the neck of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down before you. Judah is a lion's cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down; he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him? The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Judah, your brothers shall praise you." His name sounds like "praise," and his mother gave it to him in the one moment of the four when she named a son for God rather than for a marriage (29:35).

"Judah is a lion's cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. He stooped down; he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him?" Strength at rest, which is the most dangerous kind.

Then verse 10, one of the great signposts of the Old Testament:

"The scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples."

Three things in it. Rule belongs to this tribe — and David, centuries later, is from Judah, and every legitimate king of the southern kingdom after him. There is a term on it: until someone comes. And when he comes, the obedience that follows is not Israel's but "the peoples'," the nations.

The Hebrew of "until tribute comes to him" is difficult and is rendered in several ways; the Hebrew as it stands, followed by older English versions, reads a proper name, Shiloh. What is not in doubt is the shape: the sceptre is held in trust for somebody, and the somebody is for all the nations. The Jewish tradition read this messianically long before there were Christians to argue with.

Is this about the Messiah? The best reading is yes. “Until he comes to whom it belongs” (cf. Ezek 21:27) or “until Shiloh comes”: either way, the sceptre waits for one person, and the obedience of the peoples is his. Jewish interpreters long read it of the Messiah, and the New Testament names him: our Lord was descended from Judah (Heb 7:14). Judah’s rule was not lost at the exile; it was held in trust for the Son of David, to whom God would give the throne of his father David forever (Luke 1:32–33).

And John heard it announced in heaven: "Weep no more; behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered" (Rev. 5:5). Then he turned to look at the Lion, and what he saw standing there was a Lamb, looking as though it had been slain.

Consider whose line this is. Judah sold his brother for silver, slept with a woman he took for a prostitute, and condemned her to be burned for the pregnancy he had caused. This is the tribe the sceptre is given to, and Genesis has already told the reader exactly what he was. God did not choose Judah because Judah was the best of them.
verseByVerse.note: The kingship belongs to Judah “until tribute comes to him.” The Hebrew is difficult (ESV note): as it stands it reads “until Shiloh comes,” and a slight emendation gives “until he comes to whom it belongs.” “Your brothers shall praise you” plays on Judah’s name, which sounds like the Hebrew for “praise.”

verseByVerse.quote: Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine and his vesture in the blood of grapes. His eyes are darker than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Binding his foal to the vine and his donkey's colt to the choice vine, he has washed his garments in wine and his vesture in the blood of grapes."

The picture is of a fertility so extravagant that you can tether a donkey to a grapevine and not care what it eats, and wash your clothes in wine because there is more than anyone can drink. It is the abundance of the age the king of verse 10 brings with him.

And two images out of it run a long way. A king riding into Jerusalem on a donkey's colt, with the crowds shouting (Zech. 9:9; Matt. 21:5). And a figure in Isaiah whose garments are stained red, treading the winepress alone (Isa. 63:1–3), which John takes up in Revelation of one whose robe is dipped in blood (Rev. 19:13).

Genesis does not join those up and the reader is not obliged to. But the tribe of the sceptre is described in wine and blood and a donkey's colt, and it is difficult to read it now without seeing where it went.

verseByVerse.quote: "Zebulun shall dwell at the shore of the sea; he shall become a haven for ships, and his border shall be at Sidon. "Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds. He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Zebulun shall dwell at the shore of the sea; he shall become a haven for ships, and his border shall be at Sidon." A one-line geography of a tribe that would sit toward the northern coast and trade.

"Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds. He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor."

This one is a warning and it is very shrewd. Issachar is strong — a powerful working animal — and settles in the fertile Jezreel valley, and finds the land so pleasant that he will do anything rather than leave it. So he takes the yoke, and pays the tribute, and works for somebody else in a beautiful place.

Comfort costs freedom more often than force does. A man who will not be dislodged from a pleasant situation can generally be persuaded to accept any terms that let him stay in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel. Dan shall be a serpent in the way, a viper by the path, that bites the horse's heels so that his rider falls backward. I wait for your salvation, O LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Dan shall judge his people as one of the tribes of Israel." His name sounds like "judge," and Samson — a Danite — would judge Israel for twenty years.

"Dan shall be a serpent in the way, a viper by the path, that bites the horse's heels so that his rider falls backward." A small tribe on the northern invasion route, fighting by ambush rather than by weight. It is not a compliment and it is not quite a rebuke, and the serpent image sits uneasily in a book that opened with one. Dan's tribe would set up its own idols (Judg. 18:30), and Dan is missing from the list of the sealed in Revelation 7.

And then, with no warning and no connection to anything around it, one line:

"I wait for your salvation, O LORD."

A dying man breaks off in the middle of a poem about his sons' futures and prays. He has just seen, tribe by tribe, what is coming — the violence, the forced labour, the ambushes, the idolatry — and he stops and says the only thing there is to say about it.

It is the first time the word salvation appears in the Bible. And it is in the present tense of a man who knows he will not see it: I wait. He is looking down the centuries at a mess and asking God to save. Every believer who has looked at his own family and had nothing to offer but that sentence is in good company.
verseByVerse.note: “Dan shall judge” plays on Dan’s name, which sounds like the Hebrew for “judged.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Raiders shall raid Gad, but he shall raid at their heels. "Asher's food shall be rich, and he shall yield royal delicacies. "Naphtali is a doe let loose that bears beautiful fawns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three tribes in three lines, and each is a small picture.

"Raiders shall raid Gad, but he shall raid at their heels." Gad settled east of the Jordan, on the exposed frontier, and lived under constant raiding — and gave as good as it got. The Hebrew plays on the name three times over. A life of being attacked and getting up again is not a curse in Scripture; it is a description of most of the church's history.

"Asher's food shall be rich, and he shall yield royal delicacies." The fertile north-west, olive oil and wheat, supplying the tables of kings. A quiet, prosperous tribe that never produced anybody famous, and Genesis blesses it without a hint that it should have been more interesting.

"Naphtali is a doe let loose that bears beautiful fawns." Freedom and grace, and nothing else said. It is the gentlest line in the chapter, and it is spent on a tribe most readers could not place on a map. God's word about a person does not have to be dramatic to be a blessing.
verseByVerse.note: “Gad” sounds like the Hebrew for “raiders” and “raid” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Joseph is a fruitful bough, a fruitful bough by a spring; his branches run over the wall. The archers bitterly attacked him, shot at him, and harassed him severely, yet his bow remained unmoved; his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob (from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel), by the God of your father who will help you, by the Almighty who will bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that crouches beneath, blessings of the breasts and of the womb. The blessings of your father are mighty beyond the blessings of my parents, up to the bounties of the everlasting hills. May they be on the head of Joseph, and on the brow of him who was set apart from his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph's blessing is the longest after Judah's, and it begins with fruitfulness: "a fruitful bough by a spring; his branches run over the wall" — a tree so well watered that it grows past its own boundary. His two sons became two tribes.

Then the trouble: "The archers bitterly attacked him, shot at him, and harassed him severely, yet his bow remained unmoved." Brothers, a pit, Potiphar's wife, a prison, a forgotten promise. Jacob knows the outline now, and he describes a man who was shot at for years and did not break.

And then the reason, and it is not Joseph's character: "his arms were made agile by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob (from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel), by the God of your father who will help you, by the Almighty who will bless you."

Five names for God in two verses — the Mighty One of Jacob, the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel, the God of your father, the Almighty. What kept Joseph steady was not Joseph. Jacob has been clear about this since 48:15, and he says it again over the strongest of his sons.

"Blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep that crouches beneath, blessings of the breasts and of the womb" — rain, springs, and children; everything a family needs, from top to bottom of the world.

"On the brow of him who was set apart from his brothers." The word can mean set apart or singled out, and it carries both what was done to him and what God made of it. He was separated from them by their hatred, and he was separated by God for their rescue, and the same word covers both.
verseByVerse.note: “The Mighty One of Jacob,” “the Shepherd,” “the Stone of Israel” and “the Almighty” (Shaddai) are among the earliest titles for God in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: "Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at evening dividing the spoil." All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing suitable to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at evening dividing the spoil."

It is a startling thing to say about the baby of the family, the boy his father could not bear to let out of the house. And the tribe earned it: the Benjamites were formidable fighters, left-handed slingers who could hit a hair (Judg. 20:16), and in a civil war they were themselves nearly wiped out (Judg. 20–21). Israel's first king, Saul, was a Benjamite — and so, centuries later, was a young man holding the coats at a stoning, who ravaged the church until the day he was stopped on a road (Acts 8:3; 9:1; Phil. 3:5).

"All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing suitable to him."

The narrator calls the whole thing a blessing — including the curse on Simeon and Levi and the demotion of Reuben. There is no flattery in it anywhere and it is called a blessing, because a father who tells his sons the truth about themselves has given them something worth more than comfort.

"Each with the blessing suitable to him." Not the same word to all twelve. God does not deal with his people in a single template, and the wolf is not asked to be a doe.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he commanded them and said to them, "I am to be gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite, in the cave that is in the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place. There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah— the field and the cave that is in it were bought from the Hittites." When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poem is over and the old man turns to business, and the business is a grave. "Bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite... which Abraham bought with the field... to possess as a burying place."

He gives the location three times over and names the vendor, like a man reciting a deed from memory, which is exactly what he is doing. It is the only land the family owns, bought at an inflated price a hundred and seventy years earlier (ch. 23).

"There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah."

Leah. The wife he did not choose, did not love, and was tricked into marrying. She is in the family grave with the patriarchs, and Rachel — the one he worked fourteen years for — is under a pillar by a road near Bethlehem. And he says her name here, in his last speech, and intends to be laid beside her.

Genesis says nothing more about it. Whatever Jacob came to understand about Leah in forty years, he is buried with her, and the line to Christ ran through her son.

"When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people."

He does not die mid-sentence. He finishes what he had to say, arranges his own body on the bed, and goes. The grabber who came out of the womb holding a heel lets go of everything, in order, and is gathered to Abraham and Isaac.

May they be on the head of Joseph, and on the brow of him who was set apart from his brothers.<sup>27</sup>"Benjamin is a ravenous wolf, in the morning devouring the prey and at evening dividing the spoil."<sup>28</sup>All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them as he blessed them, blessing each with the blessing suitable to him.<sup>29</sup>Then he commanded them and said to them, "I am to be gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite,<sup>30</sup>in the cave that is in the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, in the land of Canaan, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place.<sup>31</sup>There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife. There they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife, and there I buried Leah—<sup>32</sup>the field and the cave that is in it were bought from the Hittites."<sup>33</sup>When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he drew up his feet into the bed and breathed his last and was gathered to his people.
49.overview:
Jacob gathers his twelve sons and tells them “what shall happen to you in days to come.” It is the longest poem in Genesis and it is not a fond farewell: three sons are given verdicts they will never live down, and the inheritance passes over all three to the fourth.

Reuben forfeits the firstborn’s place for what he did with Bilhah. Simeon and Levi are cursed for the massacre at Shechem, and their tribes will be scattered. And then Judah — the man who proposed a sale and then offered himself in Benjamin’s place — is given the lion, the sceptre, and a promise that runs past every king Israel ever had: “the scepter shall not depart from Judah... until tribute comes to him; and to him shall be the obedience of the peoples.”

The rest are given a line or two each, sometimes affectionate, sometimes blunt. Joseph gets the longest blessing after Judah’s. Then the old man gives instructions about a cave in Canaan, draws up his feet, and dies.
49.theology:
Messianic promise. Verse 10 is one of the great Old Testament signposts. The rule stays in Judah’s line until someone comes to whom it belongs, and when he comes it is not Israel but “the peoples” who obey him. David comes from Judah; so does the one John saw and heard announced as “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David” (Rev. 5:5).

Sin has consequences that grace does not cancel. Reuben, Simeon and Levi are in the covenant and in the tribes, and they lose things they will not get back. Forgiveness is not the same as the removal of every effect, and Genesis is unsentimental about the difference. God did, however, take Levi’s scattering and turn it into the priesthood — the curse worked out, and then transfigured.

“I wait for your salvation, O LORD.” In the middle of the blessings, with no warning, a dying man breaks off and prays one line (v.18). It is the first occurrence of the word salvation in the Bible, and it comes from a man who has just described his sons’ futures and knows he will see none of it.
49.examples:
Then: Tribal poems of this kind, describing the character and territory of clans, are known from the ancient world, and the details here map onto later history: Zebulun toward the coast, Issachar in the fertile Jezreel valley under forced labour, Dan in the north on the invasion route, Gad exposed on the eastern frontier, Asher in the rich soil of the north-west. Simeon’s territory was absorbed into Judah’s, and Levi received no land at all. Jacob is not guessing at temperaments; he is describing tribes.

Now: Read Reuben’s three lines and then his verdict. He is the firstborn, the might, the firstfruits of his father’s strength, preeminent in dignity and power — and then, in one word, unstable as water. Everything he had was real and none of it held, because there was nothing steady underneath. Gifts, position and natural advantage are not character, and the man who has the first three and not the fourth will lose the lot.

50.title: Jacob's Burial; Joseph's Grace and Death

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Mourning, Burial, and Final Forgiveness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joseph mourns his father, has him embalmed, and leads a great procession to bury Jacob at Machpelah in Canaan. After the burial, the brothers fear Joseph will now take revenge. They send a message claiming Jacob had instructed Joseph to forgive them, then fall before him in person. Joseph's response is one of the most magnificent expressions of grace in Scripture: 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.' Joseph lives to see his great-grandchildren and dies at 110, charging his brothers to carry his bones to Canaan when God brings them up.
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph weeps over his father, has him embalmed, and leads a great Egyptian procession to bury him at Machpelah. The brothers, afraid now, beg forgiveness; Joseph weeps and says, "Am I in the place of God? ... you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good." He dies at 110, making them swear to carry his bones out when God visits them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews remembers Joseph for his directions about his bones (Heb. 11:22). Now: forgiveness declines the judge's seat (Rom. 12:19), and God's purpose runs through the very evil men intend (Acts 2:23; Rom. 8:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph fell on his father's face and wept over him and kissed him. And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father. So the physicians embalmed Israel. Forty days were required for it, for that is how many are required for embalming. And the Egyptians wept for him seventy days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Joseph fell on his father's face and wept over him and kissed him."

The second man in Egypt, in front of his servants, lying across a dead man's face. It is the sixth time Joseph weeps in the book, and Genesis has never once treated his tears as weakness.

"And Joseph commanded his servants the physicians to embalm his father." Embalming was Egyptian, expensive and thoroughly bound up with Egyptian religion, and Genesis records it without comment. The practical point is that a body prepared this way can travel hundreds of miles and be buried in a cave.

"Forty days were required for it... And the Egyptians wept for him seventy days." Seventy days is two short of the mourning for a Pharaoh. A whole nation went into official mourning for a foreign shepherd because of the standing of his son.
verseByVerse.note: Embalming took forty days; Egypt mourned seventy days — honour almost fit for a king.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the household of Pharaoh, saying, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying, 'My father made me swear, saying, "I am about to die: in my tomb that I hewed out for myself in the land of Canaan, there shall you bury me." Now therefore, let me please go up and bury my father. Then I will return.'" And Pharaoh answered, "Go up, and bury your father, as he made you swear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph, who governs Egypt, does not go to Pharaoh directly. He asks the household to speak for him: "If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh."

He is probably still in mourning and therefore unshaven and ritually unable to enter the royal presence; he may also be asking a favour large enough that he does not want to press it in person. Either way, the second man in the kingdom approaches the throne with great care about a family matter.

And he reports his father’s oath: "My father made me swear, saying, 'I am about to die: in my tomb that I hewed out for myself in the land of Canaan, there shall you bury me.'" Then the reassurance Pharaoh will want: "Then I will return."

"And Pharaoh answered, 'Go up, and bury your father, as he made you swear.'" The oath settles it. A pagan king respects a promise made to a dying man, and Genesis lets that stand without a word of surprise.

Jacob says he dug his tomb in Canaan, yet the cave was bought by Abraham (49:29–32). He must mean the place he had cut for himself inside the family cave, not a second tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt, as well as all the household of Joseph, his brothers, and his father's household. Only their children, their flocks, and their herds were left in the land of Goshen. And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Joseph went up to bury his father. With him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his household, and all the elders of the land of Egypt... And there went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company."

A state procession: the entire Egyptian court, with a military escort, crossing hundreds of miles of desert to bury a herdsman in a cave.

Read it against how he arrived in this country. He came down that road at seventeen, sold for twenty shekels of silver, one item in an Ishmaelite caravan carrying gum and balm. The same road, in the opposite direction, with chariots.

"Only their children, their flocks, and their herds were left in the land of Goshen." The families stay behind as surety — everyone understands that a large Hebrew party going up to Canaan needs to be seen to be coming back. Israel is not free to leave, and will not be for four hundred years.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, they lamented there with a very great and grievous lamentation, and he made a mourning for his father seven days. When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning on the threshing floor of Atad, they said, "This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians." Therefore the place was named Abel-mizraim; it is beyond the Jordan. Thus his sons did for him as he had commanded them, for his sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah, to the east of Mamre, which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place. After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and all who had gone up with him to bury his father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They stop at the threshing floor of Atad and mourn for seven more days, "with a very great and grievous lamentation," and the Canaanites watching name the place Abel-mizraim — the mourning of Egypt.

"For his sons carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field at Machpelah... which Abraham bought with the field from Ephron the Hittite to possess as a burying place."

Genesis gives the deed one final time. Three generations are now in that cave: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob. Every one of them died believing a promise about a country they had not received, and every one of them insisted on being buried in the one field of it they owned.

"After he had buried his father, Joseph returned to Egypt." He keeps his word to Pharaoh, and the family goes back down. The last chapter of Genesis puts them back in Egypt on purpose. The book does not end at home.
verseByVerse.note: “Abel-mizraim” means “mourning (or meadow) of Egypt” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, "It may be that Joseph will hate us and pay us back for all the evil that we did to him." So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, "Your father gave this command before he died: 'Say to Joseph, "Please forgive the transgression of your brothers and their sin, because they did evil to you."' And now, please forgive the transgression of the servants of the God of your father." Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, 'It may be that Joseph will hate us and pay us back for all the evil that we did to him.'"

Seventeen years. He revealed himself, wept on their necks, settled them in the best land in Egypt, and fed them through five years of famine — and the moment the old man dies they conclude that the whole thing was a performance kept up for their father's sake.

So they send a message rather than going themselves, and the message reports something Jacob is supposed to have said before he died: "Say to Joseph, 'Please forgive the transgression of your brothers and their sin.'" Genesis nowhere records Jacob saying this, and it is quite possible they invented it. Frightened men who do not trust a forgiveness will reach for somebody else's authority to make it stick.

"Joseph wept when they spoke to him."

Not anger. Grief. After seventeen years of a table, a house and provision for their children, they still thought he was waiting for his moment — and the discovery that they had never believed him is what breaks him.

It is a painfully accurate picture of how people treat God. Forgiven, fed, kept, and still privately expecting the reckoning to arrive as soon as the circumstances turn. "There is therefore now no condemnation" (Rom. 8:1) is the plainest sentence in the New Testament, and a great many Christians live exactly like Joseph's brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: His brothers also came and fell down before him and said, "Behold, we are your servants." But Joseph said to them, "Do not fear, for am I in the place of God? As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. So do not fear; I will provide for you and your little ones." Thus he comforted them and spoke kindly to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"His brothers also came and fell down before him and said, 'Behold, we are your servants.'" The dream of the sheaves, one last time (37:7) — and they are offering to make it literal.

"But Joseph said to them, 'Do not fear, for am I in the place of God?'"

He refuses the seat. He has the power to do anything he likes to them, and he declines the office of judge because it is not his. That is the ground Paul gives for never taking revenge: "leave it to the wrath of God" (Rom. 12:19). Forgiveness is not pretending there is no case to answer; it is declining to be the one who tries it.

Then the summit of the book:

"As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today."

Take the sentence apart, because everything is in it.

You meant evil against me. He does not soften it, does not say they were young or that it worked out. Nearly forty years on, with everything restored, it was evil and it was aimed at him.

But God meant it for good. The verb is the same on both sides: they planned it, and God planned it. Not that God tidied up afterwards, or made the best of a mess — the same act was in his purpose, and his purpose in it was good.

To bring it about that many people should be kept alive. And it was not only for Joseph's benefit. Egypt lived, the nations that came for grain lived, and the family through whom the world would be blessed lived.

Two hands on one event, and Scripture never drops either. Peter preached the same double truth about a far greater crime: Jesus was "delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God," and "you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:23). And Paul's "all things work together for good" (Rom. 8:28) is Genesis 50:20 with the promise widened to everyone who loves God.

Be careful how this is used. It is not a sentence to say quickly to somebody in the middle of the wreckage; Joseph said it after nearly forty years, about his own suffering, and nobody said it to him. It is what a person may come to see from the far side, and it repays the wait.

Must the wronged forgive and trust again? Forgiveness is a release of the debt: no revenge, a will to do good, as Joseph promises here. Trust is another matter. It is rebuilt as repentance is shown, and Joseph tested his brothers for months before he revealed himself (chs. 42–44). Scripture calls us to live peaceably so far as it depends on you (Rom 12:18); it does not require a victim to put themselves back in harm’s way, or to give up protection or the justice of the courts (Rom 13:4).

"So do not fear; I will provide for you and your little ones. Thus he comforted them and spoke kindly to them." Literally, he spoke to their hearts. The forgiveness is not a legal release; it is a promise to keep feeding them, and their children.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his father's house. Joseph lived 110 years. And Joseph saw Ephraim's children of the third generation. The children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were counted as Joseph's own.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So Joseph remained in Egypt, he and his father's house. Joseph lived 110 years."

A hundred and ten was the Egyptian ideal lifespan, the number a scribe would write for a man whose life had been complete. Genesis uses the Egyptian figure for a Hebrew, in Egypt, and the reader is meant to feel both.

"And Joseph saw Ephraim's children of the third generation. The children also of Machir the son of Manasseh were counted as Joseph's own."

Great-grandchildren on his knees. The man who spent thirteen years without a family, who named his first son God has made me forget all my hardship, dies surrounded by descendants — and the phrase "counted as Joseph's own" is the same adoption language Jacob used over his own boys (48:5). What was done for him he does for the next generation.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph said to his brothers, "I am about to die, but God will visit you and bring you up out of this land to the land that he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob." Then Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here." So Joseph died, being 110 years old. They embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And Joseph said to his brothers, 'I am about to die, but God will visit you and bring you up out of this land to the land that he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.'"

He is the most powerful man in Egypt, his family is settled and prosperous, and his last word to them is: we are not staying. God will visit you. He names all three patriarchs and the oath, and he speaks of the exodus as a certainty four hundred years before it happens.

"Then Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, 'God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.'"

Not a request to be buried at Machpelah now, as his father was — that could have been arranged in a fortnight with a state escort. He asks to be left unburied in Egypt, in a box, until the day his people leave. His coffin is to sit among them as a standing promise: we are going.

And they did. Moses took his bones out on the night of the exodus (Exod. 13:19), they travelled forty years in the wilderness, and Joshua buried him at Shechem in the field Jacob bought (Josh. 24:32). Four hundred years, and the promise was kept to the letter.

Hebrews, surveying his whole extraordinary life — the dreams, the prison, the throne, the famine — picks out this and only this: "By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones" (Heb. 11:22). Of everything he did, what God noticed was a dying man giving instructions about a coffin because he believed a promise.

"So Joseph died, being 110 years old. They embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt."

That is the last sentence of Genesis, and it is deliberately unfinished. The book opens with God creating heaven and earth and ends with a box in a foreign country. In between: a garden lost, a flood, a tower, a man called out of Ur, a son bound on a mountain, a ladder, a limp, a coat, a pit, and a promise carried down five generations by people who never once saw it kept.

Nothing is resolved. The family is out of the land, the nations are not yet blessed, the serpent's head is unbruised, and the last word in the Hebrew text is Egypt. Genesis ends by pointing forward with both hands, and everything it has promised is still outstanding.

Which is exactly right, because the promise did not depend on any of them. It depended on the God who spoke light out of nothing, walked between the pieces alone while Abraham slept, wrestled a cheat at a river until he asked to be blessed, and meant for good what men meant for evil. A coffin in Egypt is not an ending. It is a man's last act of confidence that the God who began this will finish it.
verseByVerse.note: Moses carried Joseph’s bones out of Egypt, and they were buried at Shechem.

50.overview:
The last chapter of Genesis is a funeral, a confrontation and a coffin.

Joseph weeps over his father, has him embalmed, and takes him home — a state procession of Egyptian officials, chariots and horsemen escorting a shepherd’s body hundreds of miles to a cave his great-grandfather bought. Then the brothers, with their father gone and their protection with him, send a frightened message asking to be forgiven, and fall down in front of him offering to be his slaves.

What Joseph says to them is the summit of the book: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today.” He does not minimise what they did, does not put himself in God’s place as their judge, and promises to provide for them and their children.

And then the last words. Joseph dies at a hundred and ten, in Egypt, having made his brothers swear that when God visits them they will carry his bones out. The book that began “In the beginning God created” ends with a coffin in Egypt and a promise not yet kept.
50.theology:
Genesis 50:20 and the two intentions. The same act, described twice: you meant evil and God meant it for good. The verb is identical in both halves — they planned it, and he planned it. God’s sovereignty over an evil act does not make the act less evil or the agents less guilty, and human wickedness does not put a single event outside his purpose. This is what Paul means by “we know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Rom. 8:28), and it is what Peter preached about the cross (Acts 2:23). Genesis states it before there is a Bible to systematise it.

Forgiveness that refuses the judge’s seat. “Am I in the place of God?” Joseph will not take a role that is not his. That is the ground Paul gives for not avenging yourself: “leave it to the wrath of God” (Rom. 12:19). Forgiveness is not pretending there is no case; it is declining to be the one who tries it.

Faith at the end of a life: a promise, a coffin, and a command. Joseph dies certain of an exodus he will not see. Hebrews picks this out of his whole extraordinary career as the thing to remember him by: “By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones” (Heb. 11:22).
50.examples:
Then: Embalming took forty days and the full mourning period for a great man was seventy — only two days short of the mourning for a Pharaoh. Egyptians did not normally travel to Canaan for a foreign funeral, and the escort of court officials, chariots and horsemen is an extraordinary state honour for the father of a vizier. A coffin in Egypt is exactly right: Egyptian burial used a wooden or stone sarcophagus, and Joseph’s body would have been prepared for permanent keeping — which is precisely what made it possible to carry it out four centuries later (Exod. 13:19).

Now: Watch the brothers’ fear in verse 15. They had been forgiven seventeen years earlier, and they had eaten at his table ever since, and the moment their father died they assumed the whole thing had been a performance. People who have never really believed they are forgiven live like that: waiting for the other person to drop the act. Joseph wept when they spoke to him — not because they had offended him, but because after seventeen years they still did not believe him.
